God works through the ordinary and sometimes brutal machinery of human politics to accomplish his purposes, and neither the emperor's ignorance nor his indifference can obstruct it. Nor does God remove the cost: the couple still walk ninety miles, and Mary still walks them at the end of a pregnancy.

The manger is the detail that has shaped two thousand years of Christian imagination, and rightly. Mary wrapped him in swaddling cloths and laid him in a feeding trough, because there was no place for them in the inn. The word rendered “inn” (katalyma) more often means the guest room of a private house — it is the word used of the upper room at the Last Supper (22:11) — and the likeliest picture is a crowded family home whose guest room was already full.

Either way the scene is the same: the one who is the bread of life is laid in the box the animals eat from; the one who made every star has nowhere to be put. The incarnation is the ultimate act of self-emptying, and Luke communicates it not with theological abstraction but with the concrete detail of the trough.
verseByVerse.theology:
The juxtaposition of Caesar Augustus and the infant Jesus is a statement about the nature of true power. Augustus commanded armies, controlled the Mediterranean, and issued decrees that moved millions across the empire. The child in the manger will command no army for thirty years, will spend his public life in a small region of a minor province, and will die as a criminal.

And yet it is the child, not the emperor, who is worshipped two thousand years later — whose kingdom, as Zechariah sang, has no end. Luke is asking his reader to see, from the first chapter onward, that the power which actually runs the universe does not look like the power that runs an empire.

The swaddling cloths are not merely a practical detail; they are a sign. When the shepherds are told they will find a baby wrapped in swaddling cloths and lying in a manger, the cloths are part of the identifier. They say: he is truly human, wrapped as every newborn was wrapped, indistinguishable at a glance from any other child in Bethlehem.

The manger says the other half: that his humanity is received in the most vulnerable and dependent form imaginable. The eternal Son of God becomes a baby who cannot feed himself, cannot move himself, and cannot survive an hour without his mother.
verseByVerse.examples:
The census that brings Mary and Joseph to Bethlehem is a reminder that God uses inconvenient, uncomfortable, even oppressive circumstances to accomplish his purposes. Joseph and Mary did not choose to travel ninety miles at the end of a pregnancy. The Roman state imposed it. And in the imposition, the plan of God was fulfilled.

The Christian who finds himself in circumstances he did not choose — a redundancy that opens a door, a move that leads to an unexpected church, a disruption that turns out to have been an appointment — is living in the pattern of the incarnation. Being in the centre of God's will has never meant being outside other people's decisions.

The manger has been the comfort of every Christian who has ever felt overlooked, marginalised, or without a place. The Son of God did not insist on suitable accommodation. He took what was available, in the circumstances Providence had arranged, and made it holy.

No circumstance is too humble, and no situation too undignified, to be the place where God chooses to be present. The God who was born in a stable is found in the most improbable places — which is exactly where his people most often need to find him.

verseByVerse.quote: In those days a decree went out from Caesar Augustus that all the world should be registered. This was the first registration when Quirinius was governor of Syria.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Luke sets the birth of Jesus inside the machinery of empire, and he does it with a name that would have made a first-century reader sit up.

Caesar Augustus was the most powerful man alive. He had ended a century of Roman civil war and given the Mediterranean world the Pax Romana, the peace of Rome. His official title was divi filius — son of the deified one, son of god. Inscriptions across the empire called him saviour and lord, and one famous decree in Asia Minor announced that the birthday of the god Augustus was the beginning of good news for the world. Every one of those words is about to be given to somebody else in this chapter, by an angel, over a field of sheep.

That is not accidental. Luke is quietly staging the two claims side by side and letting the reader decide which one held. One of these men issued a decree that moved the world. The other could not yet hold up his own head.

And notice what the decree actually accomplishes. Augustus wants a tax register. God wants a Galilean couple in Bethlehem, because Micah had said seven hundred years earlier that the ruler of Israel would come from there (Mic. 5:2). The most powerful man on earth signs an order, and without the least idea what he is doing, he serves a prophecy he has never read, about a God he does not worship, on behalf of a child he will never hear of. That is how providence works. God governs history by means of people who are convinced they are governing it themselves.

Then Luke does something that has drawn more fire than almost anything else he wrote. He dates it: this was the first registration when Quirinius was governor of Syria. The difficulty is real and is better faced than dodged. Quirinius governed Syria from AD 6 and held a census in that year — the very census whose aftermath Luke himself reports, the revolt of Judas the Galilean (Acts 5:37). But Jesus was born before Herod the Great died, and Herod died in 4 BC. On the face of it Luke is a decade out.

Several answers have been offered. The Greek for first can carry the sense before, so that Luke may be marking this registration off from the famous later one rather than confusing it with it. Quirinius may have held a command in Syria on two separate occasions. A provincial registration may simply have taken years to work through. We cannot settle it from the evidence we have, and honesty serves better here than invented certainty.

But weigh this before concluding that he blundered. Luke plainly knew about the AD 6 census — he reports its consequences himself — so he is hardly the man to have muddled it with another. And wherever this writer can be checked he proves an unusually careful historian, getting a mass of shifting local titles exactly right where a careless man would have stumbled. Such a man has earned the benefit of the doubt at the one point where our own records happen to be thin.

verseByVerse.quote: And all went to be registered, each to his own town. And Joseph also went up from Galilee, from the town of Nazareth, to Judea, to the city of David, which is called Bethlehem, because he was of the house and lineage of David, to be registered with Mary, his betrothed, who was with child.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ninety miles, and Luke gives it a sentence.

From Nazareth to Bethlehem is four or five days on foot for people who are not pregnant. Mary is in the last stage of a first pregnancy. The road runs south through hill country, and every mile of it was ordered by a man in Rome who wanted his revenue figures. Nobody asked whether it was a convenient time.

It is worth staying on that, because the Christmas story is regularly told as though God arranged a gentle providence for the holy family. He did not. He arranged a tax census, a long walk, and an overcrowded town. The plan of salvation ran straight through a bureaucratic imposition that everyone involved would have described as a nuisance, and God did not remove one inch of the road to spare the mother of his Son.

Which is worth remembering by anybody whose life is currently being moved about by decisions taken in rooms they will never enter — a restructure, a policy, a landlord, a letter from an office. Being inside God's will has never meant being outside other people's decisions. Joseph and Mary were in the exact centre of the plan of God and were also, at the same moment, two more names on a Roman list.

Luke gives the reason for the journey twice over, because it is the point: because he was of the house and lineage of David, going up to the city of David. A thousand years earlier a shepherd boy had been anointed in that town (1 Sam. 16:1-13); six centuries earlier the line had been cut off and carried to Babylon; and now the heir of David walks back into his ancestral town to be counted as a taxpayer of a foreign empire. The dynasty had come to this. And it is precisely here that Micah's promise lands.

Then a phrase easily read past: Mary is registered as Joseph's betrothed, not his wife, and she is with child. Matthew tells us they had married by this point (Matt. 1:24-25). Luke's wording is not a contradiction; it is a witness's exactness. This is what their situation looked like to everyone who saw them on that road, and it is very likely how the register recorded it. A woman heavily pregnant, travelling with a man she was not yet fully married to, in a culture where everybody counted the months.

They walked ninety miles under that. There is no record of either of them complaining about it. Whatever else the yes at 1:38 cost, it went on costing all the way to Bethlehem — and the cost was not glorious. It was tiredness, and dust, and the way people looked at them at the wells.

verseByVerse.quote: And while they were there, the time came for her to give birth. And she gave birth to her firstborn son and wrapped him in swaddling cloths and laid him in a manger, because there was no place for them in the inn.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The most important birth in the history of the world is recorded in twenty-nine words, with no adjectives.

The time came for her to give birth. Luke, a physician, records no complication, no cry, no drama. There is a strong argument that Mary herself is the source for these chapters, and the restraint sounds like her.

Three details, and each has been buried under two thousand years of Christmas cards, so it is worth digging them out.

Swaddling cloths. Not a sign of poverty — it is what every mother in that world did with a newborn, binding the limbs straight in strips of cloth. It is the ordinary, competent care of a baby by somebody who knows what she is doing. And it is the first sign of something Luke will not let go of: this is a real infant, with real limbs that need binding.

A manger. A feeding trough for animals. Luke says it three times in thirteen verses, which is his way of underlining. The one who would say I am the bread of life was laid, on the first night, in the box the animals ate out of.

No place for them in the inn. The word is katalyma, and Luke uses a different word for a commercial inn later, in the parable of the good Samaritan. Katalyma is a guest room — it is the word used of the upper room where Jesus eats the Last Supper (22:11). The likeliest picture is not a hard-faced innkeeper with a full register but a crowded family house in Bethlehem, its one guest room already taken by relatives who arrived first, and a couple put in the lower part of the house where the animals were brought in at night. It is a smaller and sadder scene than the pantomime. Nobody turned them away. There simply was no room, and the family made do.

One word here has carried a great deal of church history: firstborn. Luke could have written her son. That he writes her firstborn son is, on the plainest reading, the ordinary way of speaking of a woman's first child, and it naturally implies others came after. Read it alongside Matthew's note that Joseph knew her not until she had given birth (Matt. 1:25), and alongside the four brothers and the sisters named later in the Gospels (Mark 6:3), and the straightforward sense is that Mary and Joseph went on to have a family in the ordinary way.

Rome and the Orthodox East read it differently, holding that Mary remained a virgin all her life and that the brothers were cousins or Joseph's children by an earlier marriage. The word alone does not settle the argument — firstborn was also a legal term for the son who opened the womb and carried the firstborn's rights, which is exactly the status that sends this family to the temple fifteen verses later. But the natural reading is the natural reading, and nothing in Scripture requires straining past it. Nor is anything precious lost by taking it plainly: Mary's honour never rested on what happened after Bethlehem. It rests on the virgin conception, on the child she bore, and on the faith with which she received him.

And there it is. The Word who was in the beginning with God, by whom all things were made and without whom was not anything made that was made, is lying in straw in a back room in an overcrowded village, wrapped in strips of cloth by a teenager, with the smell of animals in the air and nobody in the world aware of it except a few shepherds who have not been told yet. He who upholds the universe by the word of his power is being held up by his mother, because he cannot hold his own head. There is no distance in the universe like the distance he came, and he came all of it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–20 — The Shepherds and the Angels
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The announcement of the birth is made not to the emperor, not to the high priest, not to the Sanhedrin, not to the scholars who could have quoted the prophecy from memory — but to shepherds keeping watch over their flocks in a field at night.

In first-century Jewish society shepherds occupied the lowest rungs of the ladder. Their work made ritual purity nearly impossible to maintain; their testimony was not accepted in a court of law; and the settled respectable classes regarded them with suspicion. It is to these men, in this field, at this hour, that the glory of the Lord appears — the same glory that had filled the tabernacle and had not been seen in Israel since Ezekiel watched it leave the temple.

The angel's announcement is one of the most compressed theological summaries in the New Testament: “For unto you is born this day in the city of David a Saviour, who is Christ the Lord.” Three titles in seven words. Saviour (sōtēr) — the one who rescues; a title Caesar also claimed and could not fulfil. Christ (Christos) — the Anointed One, the fulfilment of Israel's whole prophetic tradition. Lord (kyrios) — the word the Greek Old Testament uses for the divine name. All three at once, all three together, all three true.

The sign given to confirm it is the inverse of every sign of power in human history: a baby, wrapped as every baby was wrapped, lying in a feeding trough. Kings are found in palaces and gods in temples. This one is identified by the humblest container in the village.

Then the sky fills. The word for the multitude is stratia, a military term — the armies of heaven drawn up over a hillside, praising God: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace among those with whom he is pleased.”

That last phrase is sometimes rendered “peace, good will toward men,” following a variant reading behind the older English versions. The better-attested text is the one the ESV follows: the peace comes to the people of God's good pleasure. That is not a colder reading but a warmer one — a goodwill announced to everyone in general is guaranteed to no one in particular, whereas this peace rests on the sovereign choice of God, which does not move.

The section ends where it must. The shepherds go with haste, find exactly what they were told they would find, tell everybody, and go back to work — glorifying and praising God, with the sheep still to be watched and nothing whatever in their circumstances altered.
verseByVerse.theology:
The choice of shepherds is Luke's first major instance of the great reversal that runs through his whole Gospel: the last are first, the humble are exalted, and those the world dismisses are the ones God chooses to honour. Calvin saw in it the pattern of the whole gospel — God shows here, in advance, the design he later carried out when he selected poor and uneducated fishermen for apostles.

The good news comes first to those who have nothing — no status, no ritual purity, no legal standing — because the good news is precisely that God's grace is not distributed on the basis of any of those things.

The sign given to the shepherds requires a different kind of looking than a sign of glory would have required. A God who appears in unexpected humility can be walked past. The shepherds do not go looking for what they would have expected; they go looking for exactly what they were told to expect, and they find it.

And Luke is careful about the response of everyone else. The neighbours wondered — a word he uses often and never confuses with faith. Wonder is a doorway and not a destination. Mary, in the same room, does something different with the same information (v. 19), and the contrast is the point of the paragraph.
verseByVerse.examples:
The shepherds' response — “Let us go over to Bethlehem and see this thing that has happened” — is the model of responsive faith. They do not debate the vision. They do not wait for a second confirmation. They do not propose considering the matter carefully before acting. They go with haste, and they find exactly what they were told they would find.

The gap between hearing the word of God and acting on it is where faith most often quietly dies — not by a decision to disobey, but by a perfectly reasonable delay that becomes permanent. The shepherds closed the gap in about ten seconds.

They then became the first evangelists of the New Testament. Fishermen would follow; a tax collector would follow; a persecutor would follow. But the first to announce the birth of the Saviour were men whose word was not admissible in court and who had nothing to commend them except that they had seen what they had seen.

That is the pattern of Christian witness in every generation: not credentials, not eloquence, not social standing, but the testimony of those who have met God and cannot keep quiet about it. And note what they proclaimed — not their experience of the light and the fear, but “the saying that had been told them.” The message, not the sensation.

verseByVerse.quote: And in the same region there were shepherds out in the field, keeping watch over their flock by night. And an angel of the Lord appeared to them, and the glory of the Lord shone around them, and they were filled with great fear.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Luke leaves the manger and takes the reader out into the dark, and the choice of company is deliberate.

Shepherds were not the gentle figures of the Christmas card. In first-century Jewish society they were near the bottom. The work made ritual purity practically impossible; they were out with animals for days at a time, away from the washings and the synagogue. Later rabbinic lists group them with tax collectors as men whose testimony was not to be trusted in a court, on the assumption that a man grazing flocks on other people's land was probably grazing them where he should not.

These are the men to whom the birth of the Son of God is announced. Not the emperor whose decree opened the chapter. Not the high priest, three hours away in Jerusalem. Not the scholars who could have quoted Micah 5:2 from memory and who, when Herod asked them thirty verses later in Matthew's account, did exactly that and then did nothing about it. The announcement goes to a night shift.

Calvin saw the pattern early: God shows here, in advance, what he would do later when he chose poor and uneducated fishermen for apostles. The news comes first to men with no standing, no purity and no legal credibility — because the news is precisely that God's grace is not distributed on the basis of any of those things.

Keeping watch over their flock by night. Literally, keeping the watches of the night — the shifts. Somebody stayed awake while the others slept, because of wolves and thieves. This is not a spiritual retreat. It is work, at an hour when everybody with a choice is in bed.

A reader will sometimes ask what this does to the date of Christmas, since flocks in the open at night suggest a milder season than late December. It is a fair observation, and the honest answer is that Luke does not tell us when it was; the twenty-fifth of December was fixed by the church centuries later, and no doctrine hangs on it. What Luke does tell us is the hour — night — and he means it, because the whole chapter is about a light arriving in the dark.

And the glory of the Lord shone around them. That phrase is the heaviest in the verse. The kabod, the weight of God's own presence, the thing that filled the tabernacle so Moses could not enter and settled on the temple so the priests could not stand — that glory had not been seen in Israel since Ezekiel watched it leave the temple and go out over the Mount of Olives (Ezek. 10:18-19; 11:23). Five centuries later it comes back, and it comes back in a field, to men who could not have gone into the temple courts without a wash and a change of clothes.

They were filled with great fear — literally, they feared a great fear. Of course they did. This is what happens every time. And the first word out of heaven's mouth is spoken to deal with it.

verseByVerse.quote: And the angel said to them, 'Fear not, for behold, I bring you good news of great joy that will be for all the people. For unto you is born this day in the city of David a Savior, who is Christ the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Fear not. Before any content, the terror is addressed. God's habit of opening with that sentence is worth noticing: he knows exactly what his presence does to people, and he never leaves them standing in it.

Then the announcement, and every word of it is chosen.

I bring you good news — one verb in Greek, euangelizomai, the verb behind gospel. The noun form was Roman public vocabulary: an euangelion was the dispatch announcing a victory, an heir, an emperor's accession. Heaven takes the empire's word for a state announcement and puts it in the mouth of an angel over a sheep field.

Of great joy that will be for all the people. Not for the qualified. Luke will spend twenty-two more chapters showing what all means — a Samaritan, a centurion, a prostitute, a tax collector, a thief on a cross — and Simeon will widen it further before this chapter ends.

Then three titles in a single breath, and each of them was on an inscription of Caesar Augustus somewhere in the empire that year.

A Saviour — sōtēr. Augustus was hailed as saviour of the world for ending the civil wars. He had saved people from each other for a while. He could do nothing at all about what was actually killing them.

Christ — Christos, the Anointed, Messiah: everything Israel had been promised, gathered into one man.

The Lord — kyrios, the word the Greek Old Testament puts wherever the divine name stands. Caesar took that title too. Only one of the two was entitled to it.

And now the pastoral weight of the verse, because it will be read by somebody who cannot feel any of this. Good news of great joy is a hard sentence to be handed in a hard December. There are people for whom Christmas is mainly an empty chair — the first one after a funeral, or the twentieth. There are marriages being held together for the sake of a day. There are people who will sing about joy on Sunday morning and cry in the car park afterwards.

So read what the angel actually says, and notice that it is not an instruction. He does not command anyone to feel joyful. He reports an event: unto you is born this day. The joy in this verse is not a mood the shepherds are told to work up. It is a fact about something that has happened outside them, in a village down the road, whether they feel it tonight or not. That is the only kind of joy that survives a bad year. A joy that depends on the state of your heart will go down with your heart. A joy that rests on a birth that has already occurred, in a place you could walk to, cannot be taken away by grief — it can only be temporarily hidden by it.

And note the two small words in the middle of the sentence: unto you. Not merely a Saviour has been born. A Saviour has been born for you — said to men whose word would not have been accepted in a court of law.

verseByVerse.quote: And this will be a sign for you: you will find a baby wrapped in swaddling cloths and lying in a manger.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
And this will be a sign for you.

The shepherds are given a way of identifying the child, and the identifier is the strangest thing in the chapter. In every other place in Scripture where God gives a sign, the sign is remarkable: a burning bush, a fleece, a shadow going backwards on a sundial, a virgin conceiving. Here the sign is a baby in a feeding trough.

Consider what they were not told. They were not given a street, a house, a family name, or the name of the child. They were told to look for an ordinary newborn in a wholly unsuitable container — and in a village the size of Bethlehem that was enough, because there would be exactly one.

The swaddling cloths and the manger say two different things, and both are load-bearing. The cloths say: he is completely human. Every baby in Bethlehem was wrapped that way; nothing about him looked other than ordinary, and that is the point. There was no halo. The manger says: his humanity has been received in the most dependent form there is. A child in a feeding trough cannot feed himself, cannot move himself, cannot survive an hour without somebody else.

Kings are found in palaces. Warriors are found in fortresses. Gods are found in temples. This King is found in the place the animals eat from, and the shepherds are told so in advance, so that when they see it they will not conclude they have come to the wrong house.

That is worth taking hold of by anyone who has been waiting a long time for God to make himself unmistakable. There is a way of asking for a sign which is really asking for a scene — something loud enough to end the possibility of doubt. God does give signs; he gave one here, and it was a sign that could be walked past by anybody not told what to look for.

The pattern has not changed. What God offers his people is not usually a blaze in the sky but a set of appointed ordinary things: bread, wine, water, a book, a gathering of unimpressive people. The world looks at that and sees a feeding trough. Faith looks at the same feeding trough and sees exactly what it was told it would find.

The shepherds were not asked to work anything out. They were told what to look for, and they went and looked. That is the whole of their part in it, and it turned out to be enough.

verseByVerse.quote: And suddenly there was with the angel a multitude of the heavenly host praising God and saying, 'Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace among those with whom he is pleased!'
verseByVerse.commentary:
One angel had been enough to terrify them. Now the sky opens.

The word Luke uses for the multitude is stratia — a military term. An army. Not a choir in the modern sense but the massed host of heaven, the armies of the LORD of hosts, drawn up over a field outside a village of a few hundred people. And Luke does not say they sang; he says they were praising God and saying. Whatever the sound was, the words were plain enough to be written down.

The song has two lines, and they run from the top of the universe to the bottom.

Glory to God in the highest. Heaven's first response to the incarnation is not relief, or congratulation, or wonder at the mechanism. It is glory given to God — which means the angels understood at once what the human race would take centuries to argue about: that this birth is not chiefly about us. It is about him. Something has just happened that shows God to be more magnificent than the angels had yet seen him, and they say so.

And on earth peace among those with whom he is pleased.

Older Bibles read differently here, and a reader with a King James version will notice: peace, good will toward men. The difference is a single letter in the Greek. One family of manuscripts has eudokia, good will, standing on its own as a third item; the other has eudokias, of good pleasure, attached to the men. The better-attested reading is the second, and it is what the ESV follows: peace among the people of his good pleasure.

The difference in sense is worth having clearly, because it is not trivial. The first reading makes the announcement a general benevolence broadcast over the earth. The second makes it a specific grant to particular people, given because God chose to give it. That is not a colder reading; it is a warmer one. A goodwill announced to everybody in general is a goodwill guaranteed to nobody in particular. What the angels announce is peace that has an owner's name on it — resting not on how the recipients turn out but on the good pleasure of God, which is the one foundation that does not move.

And notice what kind of peace it is. Rome had peace, and had built it out of roads and legions and crucifixion; it lasted as long as the legions did. The peace announced over this field is not the absence of conflict — the child in the trough will say plainly that he did not come to bring that sort (12:51). It is the ending of a war between heaven and earth: having been justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ (Rom. 5:1).

Glory in the highest, and peace at the bottom. Between the two lies the whole distance the Son of God travelled that night, and the angels sing at both ends of it — because the God who is glorified in the highest heaven has just made peace at the lowest point of the world, and there is nothing in creation that has ever cost more or been given more freely.

verseByVerse.quote: When the angels went away from them into heaven, the shepherds said to one another, 'Let us go over to Bethlehem and see this thing that has happened, which the Lord has made known to us.' And they went with haste and found Mary and Joseph, and the baby lying in a manger.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The sky closes. The light goes. And the shepherds, standing in a field that is suddenly very dark and very quiet, say the only sensible thing anyone has said so far in this chapter: Let us go over to Bethlehem.

Look at what is not in that sentence. No debate about whether the vision was genuine. No suggestion of waiting for daylight, or for a second confirmation, or for somebody more qualified. No one says but who will watch the sheep? — and that is not a small point, because those sheep were somebody's property and the shepherds were answerable for them.

They also get the theology exactly right in passing: which the Lord has made known to us. They do not say the angel told them. They say the Lord did. They understood that a messenger is a mouth and not a source.

And they went with haste. The phrase has been used once already in this Gospel, of Mary going up to the hill country (1:39). Luke reserves it for people whose response to a word from God is to start moving.

The gap between hearing something from God and acting on it is where a great deal of faith quietly dies. It is rarely closed by a decision to disobey. It is closed by delay — by the entirely reasonable interval in which a thing is considered, and weighed, and put off until the season is better, and then no longer feels urgent, and then is not mentioned again. What is remarkable about these men is not their piety. It is that the interval was about ten seconds long.

And found Mary and Joseph, and the baby lying in a manger. Exactly as promised, and nothing more than promised. They walked into a crowded house in the middle of the night with a story that must have sounded insane, and there in the animals' quarters was precisely what they had been told they would find.

That is the reward of obedience in this story, and it is worth naming because it is so unglamorous. They were not given a further revelation. They were given confirmation of the one they already had. God's word, acted on, led them to exactly what it said it would — which is the only proof of it anybody ever gets, and the only one anybody needs.

verseByVerse.quote: And when they saw it, they made known the saying that had been told them concerning this child. And all who heard it wondered at what the shepherds told them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They cannot keep it in.

Nobody commissioned these men. There is no instruction anywhere in the angel's message to go and tell people; they were told where to look, and that was all. But having looked, they made known the saying that had been told them concerning this child — and so the first evangelists of the New Testament are a handful of night-shift labourers whose testimony was legally worthless.

That is the pattern Luke will keep to. Fishermen will follow them. A tax collector will follow. A persecutor of the church will follow. Not one of the great preachers of the New Testament had credentials at the point where God took hold of him. What the shepherds had was not eloquence or standing. It was that they had seen what they had seen, and there is no substitute for it and no way of manufacturing it.

Notice also what they told. Not their experience — not the light, or the fear, or how the sky had looked. They made known the saying that had been told them. Their testimony was the message, not the sensation. Which is still the right order: what happened to me is interesting to precisely nobody, and what has happened in Bethlehem is news for everybody.

Then Luke records the response, and he is very exact about it. All who heard it wondered.

Wondering is not believing. It is the emotion of a person for whom something has been genuinely interesting and not yet decisive. Luke uses this word repeatedly, and he is scrupulous about not overstating what it means: crowds marvel at Jesus all through this Gospel, and marvelling saves nobody. The people in that house went to bed amazed, and there is no record that a single one of them followed him thirty years later.

That is a sobering thing to hold beside a Christmas service. It is entirely possible to be moved by this story every December for fifty years — to find it beautiful, to feel something at the carols, to be genuinely glad it is true — and to remain, at the end, exactly where those neighbours were: amazed, and nothing more.

Wonder is a doorway, and it is a good one; Luke never sneers at it. But a doorway is for walking through. Two verses from now Mary will do something different with the same information, and the difference is the whole point of the paragraph.

verseByVerse.quote: But Mary treasured up all these things, pondering them in her heart.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But Mary treasured up all these things, pondering them in her heart.

The but is doing real work. Everybody else in the room wondered; Mary did something else, and Luke marks the contrast deliberately.

Two verbs, and both are concrete. Treasured up — the word means to keep carefully, to preserve, the way a person stores something valuable rather than leaving it out. And pondering is symballousa, literally throwing together: setting things side by side to see how they fit. It is the word a person would use for comparing two accounts, or matching a piece to the pattern.

So this is not vague reverie. Mary is doing something specific and strenuous. She now has in her possession an angel's announcement, a cousin's prophecy, her own song, a birth in a stranger's animal quarters, and a group of shepherds at midnight with a story about an army in the sky. She cannot make one picture of it yet. She lays the pieces alongside each other and keeps turning them.

Luke will say this about her twice more in this chapter (v. 51), and it plainly comes from somewhere. If Mary is the source behind these two chapters — and the intimacy of the detail suggests she is — then this verse is her own account of what she was doing while everybody else was exclaiming, and Luke is telling us how his material came to survive at all.

Now the practical use of it, because this is one of the few places in Scripture that shows a believer's inner method rather than describing it. Something happens that has God's fingerprints on it and no available explanation. The two usual responses are to force a meaning onto it at once, or to let it go as nothing. Mary does neither. She holds it, unexplained, and works at it.

That means keeping a record — mentally or otherwise — of what God has actually done and said, so that it is still there in five years when a piece arrives that makes sense of it. It means resisting the urge to tidy providence into a lesson while it is still happening. And it means being willing to carry an unresolved thing for a long time without either abandoning it or pretending it is resolved.

She was still doing it twelve years later at verse 51, and there is no sign she had it all worked out even then. The mother of the Lord lived most of her life holding things she did not yet understand, and that is not a failure of faith. It is what faith looks like from the inside, over time.

verseByVerse.quote: And the shepherds returned, glorifying and praising God for all they had heard and seen, as it had been told them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And then they went back to the sheep.

That is the sentence, and it deserves to be felt. These men had seen the glory of God break over a hillside, heard the armies of heaven, walked into a house and found the Messiah of Israel lying in a feeding trough, and told everybody in the village. And when the night was over there was nothing for them to do except go back out to the flock, take the next watch, and get on with a job that had not changed in any respect.

Luke does not record that any of them left their trade. There is no suggestion that the shepherds became preachers, or moved to Jerusalem, or were ever heard of again. They returned to exactly the life they had come from — and they returned glorifying and praising God.

That is the note to hold. The night did not deliver them from the ordinary. It went with them into it.

There is something here for everybody who has come down from a mountaintop. The conference ends, the retreat closes, the funeral service that felt like heaven touching the room gives way to Tuesday, and the temptation is to conclude that the real thing was up there and this down here is the interval between. The shepherds' testimony is the opposite. The glory came to them at work, at night, in the middle of a shift, and it sent them back to the same shift with the same sheep — and they went praising.

For all they had heard and seen, as it had been told them. Luke closes the section by underlining that last clause once more. The word came; they acted on it; they found it exactly as promised; and their praise is specifically for the correspondence between the two. That is what the whole chapter has been about since verse 1. A decree was signed in Rome, a prophecy was kept in Bethlehem, an announcement was made in a field, and every part of it fitted.

The shepherds went home in the dark, singing, to a job nobody respected — which is very nearly a definition of the Christian life. And of everyone in Bethlehem that night, they were the only ones who had both heard and obeyed.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 21–40 — Jesus Presented at the Temple
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The presentation is the scene where the old covenant meets the new — where the long story of Israel's worship, sacrifice and waiting encounters the one the whole system had been pointing at.

Joseph and Mary come to Jerusalem for two duties, both required by the law: the purification of the mother forty days after the birth of a son (Lev. 12:1-8), and the presentation of the firstborn to the LORD (Exod. 13:2, 12-15; Num. 18:15-16). They bring the offering of the poor — two birds rather than a lamb and a pigeon — which tells us plainly what the family's circumstances were. The King of heaven and earth was raised in poverty.

Simeon is described in the language of the faithful remnant: righteous, devout, waiting for the consolation of Israel, with the Holy Spirit upon him. That phrase, the consolation of Israel, comes from Isaiah 40 — “Comfort, comfort my people” — the promised end of exile and return of God to his people. Simeon has been waiting inside that chapter his whole life, and the Spirit has promised him he will not die before he sees the Lord's Christ.

Now, as a young couple with the offering of the poor come into the courts, the Spirit moves him. He takes the child into his arms, and everything he has spent his life waiting for is a warm weight in his hands.

His song — the Nunc Dimittis — is among the most moving passages in Luke. The verbs are those of a sentry being stood down after a long watch. He can go now: his eyes have seen God's salvation, and the salvation he is holding is not for Israel only but “a light for revelation to the Gentiles” — the fulfilment of Isaiah's Servant Songs (42:6; 49:6) and the universal scope of the gospel announced before it has begun.

And then the shadow falls. The child is appointed for the falling and rising of many in Israel, a sign to be opposed; and a sword will pierce Mary's own soul. Joy and sorrow are not opposites in Luke's Gospel. They are twins, born of the same truth. The one who is the light of the world will be rejected, and the one whose birth the angels celebrated will die on a cross. Simeon holds the baby and sees all of it.

Anna is the second witness the law required (Deut. 19:15) — a daughter of Asher, one of the tribes long written off as lost, who has given decades of widowhood to fasting and prayer in that building and who arrives at exactly the right hour. And the section closes with the family's return to Nazareth and a single sentence covering the boy's whole childhood: he grew, became strong, was filled with wisdom, and the favour of God was upon him.
verseByVerse.theology:
Simeon's announcement that the child is “a light for revelation to the Gentiles” (v. 32) is the fulfilment of Isaiah's Servant Songs and the theological seed of the entire Gentile mission of Acts. From the moment of the presentation, Luke's Gospel contains within it the global church. The child in Simeon's arms is not merely the king of the Jews; he is the light of the world.

This is why Luke, writing for a Gentile reader, is the Gospel that most fully develops the universal reach of the good news. The trajectory is established here, in the temple courts, by an old man who has waited his whole life to say what he now says and who will be dead within the year.

Simeon's warning to Mary — that a sword will pierce her own soul — has been understood in the tradition as pointing to her presence at the crucifixion (John 19:25-27). The word is rhomphaia, the great broad sword, and Simeon does not soften it. The sword is the sword of grief, of the suffering that participation in the Son's mission inevitably involves.

But the clause “that thoughts from many hearts may be revealed” shows a wider purpose. The coming of Jesus forces a crisis of decision in every heart; he does not leave people neutral. He is “appointed for the fall and rising of many” — the stone of Isaiah 8:14 laid in the middle of the road. His presence divides, and in dividing it discloses what was already there.
verseByVerse.examples:
Simeon's “now you are letting your servant depart in peace” is the model of a death well prepared for — not the resignation of a man who has given up, but the discharge of a sentry who has received what he was waiting for. And notice what his peace does not rest on: not on achievement (we are told nothing of what he accomplished), not on longevity, but on what his eyes have seen.

The Christian who has seen that same salvation — not with physical eyes but with the eyes of faith, and has taken hold of it — has precisely what Simeon had, and may face death on precisely the same terms. Not because death is nothing, but because what lies beyond it is the same Christ known in life.

Anna is Luke's portrait of long faithfulness. She had been waiting most of her adult life — decades of widowhood — for the redemption of Jerusalem. She did not give up, did not grow cynical, and did not stop praying because the answer had not come. When it came, she was exactly where she had always been.

Her years were not the waiting room for her ministry; they were the making of it. Sixty years of fasting and prayer produced a woman who could recognise God in a poor family's arms when everyone around her saw a queue — and who knew, by name, everyone in Jerusalem who was waiting to be told. The reward of patient faithfulness is rarely glamorous. It is being in the right place when God acts.

verseByVerse.quote: And at the end of eight days, when he was circumcised, he was called Jesus, the name given by the angel before he was conceived in the womb.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Eight days old, and the first blood he ever shed was shed in obedience to the law he had written.

Circumcision on the eighth day was the covenant sign given to Abraham (Gen. 17:12) and repeated in the law of Moses (Lev. 12:3). It marked a boy as belonging to the covenant people, under its promises and under its obligations. And it was, for an infant, a real wound.

Stop there for a moment, because Luke gives it half a verse and it is worth more. The Son of God enters his own creation and, before he is nine days old, is cut with a knife in submission to a requirement he himself laid down. He does not stand outside the law and gesture at it from a distance. He steps under it, all the way down: born of woman, born under the law, to redeem those who were under the law (Gal. 4:4-5). There was no way to redeem people who were under something except by getting under it with them.

Then the name. He was called Jesus, the name given by the angel before he was conceived in the womb.

Luke is careful with that clause. The naming was not a family decision made in the weeks after the birth; it was settled by Gabriel before there was anything to name. In Hebrew the name is Yeshua, a shortened form of Joshua, and it means the LORD saves. It was common enough — there are several men of that name in Josephus — and that is part of the point. The name over the cross would be an ordinary name from an unremarkable town.

But hold the two halves of the verse together, because Luke has put them in one sentence for a reason. On the same day the child is cut into the covenant, he is given the name that says how the covenant will finally be kept. The knife and the name arrive together, and they will arrive together again at the end: the blood and the saving, the wound and the rescue, in the same event.

And notice who obeys here. Jesus does nothing in this verse; it is done to him. He is carried, held, named, and cut, entirely passive, at eight days old. Everything in the Christian life will eventually be like that. The first thing the Saviour ever did about our salvation, he did by being handed over to somebody else's hands — and the last thing he did about it, he did the same way.

verseByVerse.quote: And when the time came for their purification according to the Law of Moses, they brought him up to Jerusalem to present him to the Lord (as it is written in the Law of the Lord, 'Every male who first opens the womb shall be called holy to the Lord') and to offer a sacrifice according to what is said in the Law of the Lord, 'a pair of turtledoves, or two young pigeons.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Forty days after the birth the family goes up to Jerusalem, and Luke folds two separate legal duties into one visit.

The first is the purification of the mother. Leviticus 12 laid down that a woman was ceremonially unclean for a period after childbirth — forty days for a son — and then brought an offering. This was never a statement that childbirth was sinful; it belonged to a whole system of laws about blood and life and the boundary between the holy and the ordinary, teaching Israel by repetition that God is not to be approached casually.

The second is the presentation of the firstborn. Every firstborn male in Israel belonged to the LORD, because of the night in Egypt when the firstborn of Israel were spared and the firstborn of Egypt were not (Exod. 13:2, 12-15). A firstborn son had therefore to be bought back — redeemed — for five shekels paid to the priests (Num. 18:15-16).

Now the detail that a reader with Leviticus open will trip over. Luke writes their purification, but the law prescribes purification for the mother alone. The child needs none; Joseph needs none. Luke is almost certainly describing the family's observance as a whole — the household going up together to discharge what the law laid on them — so that the pronoun covers the journey rather than the rite. Some later copies smoothed it to her, which is where the older English reading comes from; but their is the harder and better-attested wording, and a copyist is far likelier to have tidied a difficulty than to have created one.

The oddity is worth sitting with, because the whole scene is saying it. Of every person in the temple courts that day, this forty-day-old child is the one with nothing whatever to be purified from. He is holiness itself, carried in a girl's arms — and he is brought in anyway, counted in with the rest, circumcised on the eighth day and presented on the fortieth like any other son of Israel.

And there is a deeper irony in the redemption money. The law required a firstborn son to be bought back from the LORD. This one would not be. He is the firstborn who was presented and never redeemed — handed over, and left in the Father's hands, so that a much larger price could be paid by him rather than for him.

Then the offering, and it is the quietest sentence in the passage. Leviticus 12 asks for a lamb and a pigeon. It adds that if a woman cannot afford a lamb, two birds will do. Mary brings the birds.

That single detail tells us what the family's finances were, and it should be allowed to land. The King of heaven and earth was raised by people who could not afford the standard offering. He grew up in a house where the cheaper option was chosen because it had to be. Anyone who has ever stood at a counter and taken the smaller thing because the larger one was out of reach has stood where Mary stood that morning — and the child she was carrying grew up in that house on purpose.

She could not afford a lamb. She was carrying one.

verseByVerse.quote: Now there was a man in Jerusalem, whose name was Simeon, and this man was righteous and devout, waiting for the consolation of Israel, and the Holy Spirit was upon him. And it had been revealed to him by the Holy Spirit that he would not see death before he had seen the Lord's Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Luke turns the camera away from the family to an old man crossing the temple courts, and he tells us four things about him in a single verse.

He is righteous and devout — the same covenant vocabulary used of Zechariah and Elizabeth in chapter 1. He is waiting for the consolation of Israel. And the Holy Spirit was upon him.

The consolation of Israel is a phrase with an address. It comes from the great turn in Isaiah: Comfort, comfort my people, says your God (Isa. 40:1) — the announcement that the exile is over, that the warfare is ended, that God is coming back to his people along a road made straight in the desert. Simeon has been living inside that chapter. He is not waiting for a general improvement in the national mood. He is waiting for God to keep a specific promise in a specific book.

Notice how often the Spirit appears in these three verses: upon him, revealing to him, moving him into the temple. Luke is establishing something. Israel had had no prophet for four centuries, and now the Spirit is everywhere in this Gospel's opening — on Elizabeth, on Zechariah, on Mary, on Simeon, on Anna. The silence is not merely being broken. It is being flooded.

It had been revealed to him by the Holy Spirit that he would not see death before he had seen the Lord's Christ.

We are not told when that promise was given, or how long ago. Luke's word is a perfect: it had been revealed, and it stood. Which means Simeon had been carrying a private word from God for years — possibly for decades — with no way of proving it to anybody, no date attached, and a body that was visibly running out of time. Every year that passed made the promise harder to hold and closer to fulfilment, and he had no means of telling which.

That is a position a good many older believers know from the inside: the thing God once made you sure of, which has still not happened, and which you have long since stopped mentioning to people because of the way they look at you. Simeon's promise was kept. It was kept at the last possible end of a long life, in a place he had walked through a thousand times, on a morning that began like every other.

He was not waiting for a sign in the sky. He was waiting for a person. And the reason he did not miss him, when he finally came in through the gate in the arms of a poor couple carrying two pigeons, is that he had spent his whole life learning what to look for.

verseByVerse.quote: And he came in the Spirit into the temple, and when the parents brought in the child Jesus, to do for him according to the custom of the Law, he took him up in his arms and blessed God and said,
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he came in the Spirit into the temple.

Luke does not say Simeon decided to go to the temple that morning; he says he came in the Spirit. Something moved him, and he went — on a day when the courts were full of people, at an hour when one young couple among many were bringing a child in for a routine legal observance.

Consider the arithmetic of that morning. The temple complex covered something like thirty-five acres. Mary and Joseph had come to do a small, ordinary thing that dozens of families did every week. They were not expecting to be met. Simeon did not know who he was looking for; he had a promise, not a description. And out of all that crowd the old man walks straight to the right child.

Neither party is aware of what is about to happen. That is worth sitting with, because most of the appointments God keeps are like that from the inside. There is no sense in the room of a scene being staged. There is an old man following an impulse, a young couple doing their duty, a queue for the offerings, and a providence that has been arranging this meeting for longer than anyone present has been alive.

He took him up in his arms and blessed God.

Stop at that. It is one of the great pictures of Scripture, and it is easy to hurry past because it is so quiet.

Here is the old covenant, in the person of a man near the end of his life, standing in the temple that had been the centre of Israel's worship for a thousand years — and it reaches out and takes the new covenant into its arms, in the form of a six-week-old baby. Everything the temple existed to do, everything the sacrifices had been pointing at, everything the prophets had been promising, is now a warm weight in an old man's hands. The whole system is holding the thing it was built to announce, and the thing it was built to announce is going to make the system unnecessary.

And what does he do with him? Not a speech to the crowd. Not an announcement to the priests. He blessed God. The first response of a man who has just received what he waited a lifetime for is to turn away from the gift and speak to the Giver.

That is what a life of waiting had made of him. Held the Christ, and looked past him to the Father — which is precisely what the Christ himself would spend his ministry teaching people to do.

verseByVerse.quote: 'Lord, now you are letting your servant depart in peace, according to your word; for my eyes have seen your salvation that you have prepared in the presence of all peoples, a light for revelation to the Gentiles, and for glory to your people Israel.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Simeon's song has been sung at evening prayer in the church for something like fifteen hundred years, and it is the shortest of the three songs in Luke's opening. It is also the only one sung by somebody who is about to die.

Lord, now you are letting your servant depart in peace. Two words carry the picture. Lord here is not the usual kyrios but despotēs — the word for the master of a household with absolute authority over his slaves; and servant is doulos, the slave himself. And depart is apolyeis, to release, to discharge, to stand a man down. The image is military or domestic: a sentry who has been posted, who has held the position through the night, and who is now formally relieved. Simeon is not saying he wants to die. He is saying his watch is over and he may go off duty.

For my eyes have seen your salvation. He is holding a forty-day-old baby, and he does not say I have seen the one who will bring salvation. He says he has seen salvation itself. In his arms. A person, not a programme.

That you have prepared in the presence of all peoples, a light for revelation to the Gentiles, and for glory to your people Israel.

This is where the song opens out, and the moment ought to be felt. A devout old Jew, standing in the temple of Israel, holding the Messiah of Israel, announces that this child is a light for the nations. He is quoting Isaiah's Servant Songs, where the LORD says it is too small a thing for the Servant merely to restore Israel: I will make you as a light for the nations, that my salvation may reach to the end of the earth (Isa. 49:6; cf. 42:6). Before Jesus has spoken a word, before a single disciple is called, the global reach of the gospel is announced in the temple courts by a man who will be dead within the year. Every Gentile who has ever come to Christ came in through a door that Simeon saw standing open.

Now the pastoral weight, because this passage is read at more funerals than almost any other in Luke. Simeon is the picture of a death well prepared for — and notice what it does not depend on. Not on achievement: we are told nothing whatever about what he accomplished. Not on longevity, or on being ready in some general sense. He can go because my eyes have seen your salvation. His peace rests entirely on something outside himself which he has laid hold of.

That is available. Nobody now will hold the infant Christ in the temple. But the salvation Simeon saw with his eyes is the same salvation offered to faith, and the man or woman who has taken hold of it has exactly what Simeon had, and may be discharged on exactly the same terms.

He asked for nothing else. He had been given a promise and he had waited on it, and when it was kept he wanted no extension. There is a whole doctrine of contentment in an old man who holds the Christ and says: that will do. Now let your servant go.

verseByVerse.quote: And his father and his mother marveled at what was said about him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And his father and his mother marveled at what was said about him.

One verse, and it does more work than its length suggests.

These two have had more supernatural confirmation than anyone in Scripture since Moses. Mary has had an angel in her room, a prophecy from Elizabeth, and a song of her own. Joseph has had an angel in a dream. There have been shepherds at the manger with an account of an army in the sky. And now, six weeks later, a total stranger in the temple takes their baby out of their arms and says things about him that leave them astonished.

They marvelled. Which means they had not exhausted this. There was more in the child than they had grasped, and they knew it.

That is a curiously encouraging verse for anyone who has been a Christian for a long time and quietly suspects everyone else understands more than they do. If the mother of Jesus, forty days in, with the archangel Gabriel's words still ringing, could be astonished by something a stranger said about her own son, then the ordinary experience of finding that Christ keeps exceeding your account of him is not a sign of immaturity. It is a sign of accuracy.

Luke also lets a small phrase stand without comment: his father and his mother. He has spent a chapter and a half establishing that Joseph is not this child's father. Now he calls him one, and does it again at v. 48 in Mary's own words. There is no contradiction and no carelessness. Joseph is the father of this boy in every way that a life is lived — he named him, redeemed him, taught him a trade, protected him, and raised him — and Luke is content to use the ordinary word for it.

Which is worth noticing by any man raising a child who is not his by blood. The Son of God was brought up by one, and Scripture calls that man his father without a footnote.

verseByVerse.quote: And Simeon blessed them and said to Mary his mother, 'Behold, this child is appointed for the fall and rising of many in Israel, and for a sign that is opposed (and a sword will pierce through your own soul also), so that thoughts from many hearts may be revealed.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Simeon has blessed God. Now he blesses the parents — and then turns to Mary alone and says something that must have taken the warmth out of the morning.

Behold, this child is appointed for the fall and rising of many in Israel.

The word is appointed: set, placed there on purpose. And note the order — fall first, then rising. Simeon is quoting Isaiah, where the LORD of hosts says he will become a stone of offence and a rock of stumbling, and many shall stumble on it; they shall fall and be broken (Isa. 8:14-15). The child is a stone laid in the middle of Israel's road, and it is not possible to walk past him without either tripping over him or standing on him.

And for a sign that is opposed. Literally, a sign spoken against. Simeon does not say the child will meet some opposition; he says that being contradicted is part of what the sign is. Anyone who has hoped that a sufficiently winsome presentation of Christ would stop people objecting to him has hoped for something Simeon ruled out in the temple courts before Jesus could speak.

So that thoughts from many hearts may be revealed. That is the purpose clause, and it explains the rest. He does not merely divide people; he shows what was already there. Everybody who meets him ends up disclosing something about themselves that they might otherwise never have had to face. The reaction to Jesus is a reading of the person reacting.

And in the middle of it, in brackets, the sentence that was for Mary alone: and a sword will pierce through your own soul also.

The word for sword is not the small blade a soldier carried at his belt. It is rhomphaia, the great broad sword, the one used in the Greek Old Testament for Goliath's weapon. Simeon does not soften it.

There is no mistaking what he means, and John records the moment it happened: standing by the cross of Jesus were his mother… (John 19:25). She was there. She watched him die, and there was nothing whatever she could do, and the last thing he did was arrange for somebody else to look after her.

So this is a word spoken to a mother about her son, and it is worth handling as one. There are parents reading this who have watched a child suffer and could do nothing — an illness, an addiction, a court, a coffin. It is a particular kind of pain and it does not answer to the usual comforts, because the wound is not in you, and the helplessness is the whole of it.

Two things stand in this verse for such a reader. The first is that Mary was told in advance, thirty-three years in advance, and it did not make it easier; God does not seem to think forewarning is the same as sparing. The second is heavier and better. The sword went through her because the nails went through him — and he was there by appointment, and what looked from the foot of that cross like the end of everything was the hour the whole world had been waiting for since Eden. The grief was real. It was not the last word about the grief.

verseByVerse.quote: And there was a prophetess, Anna, the daughter of Phanuel, of the tribe of Asher. She was advanced in years, having lived with her husband seven years from when she was a virgin, and then as a widow until she was eighty-four. She did not depart from the temple, worshiping with fasting and prayer night and day. And coming up at that very hour she began to give thanks to God and to speak of him to all who were waiting for the redemption of Jerusalem.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The law required two witnesses for a matter to be established (Deut. 19:15). God provides them: an old man, and now an old woman.

Luke gives Anna a genealogy, which is unusual for a woman in an ancient text and is not decoration. She is the daughter of Phanuel, of the tribe of Asher — one of the ten northern tribes carried off by Assyria seven centuries earlier and popularly written off as lost. Here is a daughter of Asher, in the temple, at the presentation of the Messiah. Whatever else the exile did, it did not lose anybody God intended to keep.

Her age is given in a phrase that translations handle differently, and the difference is worth a sentence. The Greek can mean that she had been a widow until she was eighty-four, or that she had been a widow for eighty-four years — which, with seven years of marriage from girlhood, would put her well over a hundred. Either reading gives the same picture, and it is the picture that matters: a woman married in her teens, widowed after seven years, and never remarried, who then gave the whole remaining length of her life to God in that building.

Do the arithmetic on what that meant. Decades of turning up. Fasting and prayer, night and day, in a temple that had grown corrupt and would be a den of robbers by the time her Messiah cleared it. Nothing to show for any of it. No congregation, no title, no record — and, so far as anyone watching could tell, no answers.

She kept praying anyway. That is the whole of Anna's biography until this morning.

And then: coming up at that very hour. Not that day. That hour. She walks into the right court at the right moment after roughly sixty years of showing up, and immediately begins to give thanks and to speak of the child to all who were waiting for the redemption of Jerusalem — which tells us something else about her. She knew who those people were. She had a list. Sixty years in that temple had shown her exactly which of the crowd were praying for the same thing she was, and when the answer came she knew where to take it.

Something needs saying here for the reader whose life looks more like Anna's sixty years than like Anna's one hour. There are believers who have prayed for a marriage, a child, a church, a country, for decades, and have watched nothing move. It is very easy to conclude that the years were the waste and the answer would have been the point.

Anna's years were not the waiting room for her ministry. They were the making of it. Sixty years of fasting and prayer are what produced a woman who could recognise God in a poor family's arms when the priests around her saw a queue — and who had, ready to hand, the names of everyone in Jerusalem who needed to be told. The single hour was the harvest. The decades were the field.

verseByVerse.quote: And when they had performed everything according to the Law of the Lord, they returned into Galilee, to their own town of Nazareth. And the child grew and became strong, filled with wisdom. And the favor of God was upon him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Luke closes the infancy narrative the way he opened it — with obedience to the law — and then covers a dozen years in a sentence.

And the child grew and became strong, filled with wisdom. And the favor of God was upon him. The growth is genuine. Luke uses very nearly the same words of John at 1:80, and he will use them again of Jesus at v. 52. A real boy, developing in a real body, in an ordinary Galilean village, with the favour of God resting on him — not as a reward earned, but as the settled delight of a Father in his Son.

This verse also raises the sharpest question in the two birth narratives, and it is better faced than stepped over. Read Matthew 2 alongside it and the accounts appear to collide. Matthew has the magi arriving, the flight into Egypt, Herod's killing of the boys of Bethlehem, and only after Herod's death the settling in Nazareth. Luke moves from the temple courts to Nazareth in a single sentence, as though nothing came between.

But look at what Luke's sentence actually claims. He says they had performed everything according to the Law of the Lord — he is closing the temple business, not publishing the next morning's itinerary. And Matthew leaves exactly the room Luke needs. The magi come to a house (Matt. 2:11), not to a stable; and Herod kills the boys two years old and under, reckoning by what the magi had told him (Matt. 2:16), which places their visit months and possibly more than a year after the night of the manger.

So a sequence holds both accounts without strain: the birth, circumcision on the eighth day, presentation on the fortieth, a settled stay in Bethlehem, the magi, Egypt, Herod's death, and the return north. And it is Matthew who supplies the reason for the very move Luke reports here without explaining it — they went to Nazareth rather than back to Bethlehem because Archelaus was now reigning in Judea and Joseph was afraid to go there (Matt. 2:22).

The two Gospels are not competitors. They are two witnesses telling what each was given to tell. Matthew writes from Joseph's side, with Judea's danger in view; Luke writes from Mary's side, with the temple's faithfulness in view. Luke is not concealing Egypt. He told us at the outset that he had sifted his material and arranged it (1:3), and no witness who selects is thereby lying about what he leaves out.

What Luke gives instead of the drama is the thing Matthew does not: eleven silent years in a hill town, and one sentence to cover them. The Son of God spent the overwhelming majority of his earthly life doing nothing that anybody thought worth writing down.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 41–52 — The Boy Jesus in the Temple
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The only story from Jesus's childhood in any of the four Gospels is this one: Jesus at twelve, in the temple, sitting among the teachers, leaving the learned astonished. Luke includes it not as a charming anecdote but as a theological statement. Before the public ministry begins, Jesus is already defined by a relationship with his Father that supersedes every other claim on him — including the entirely legitimate claim of his parents.

It is worth noticing what the story is not. The apocryphal gospels of later centuries are full of tales of the boy Jesus working wonders and settling scores. In the one childhood story Scripture preserves, he performs no miracle at all. He asks questions, and then goes home and does as he is told.

The setting is Passover — the feast of Israel's redemption, commemorating the night the LORD passed over the houses marked with blood. Jesus is twelve, the year before a Jewish boy took on personal responsibility for the commandments, and this is the last Passover of his childhood. The irony Luke intends is deep: the Passover Lamb has come up to keep the Passover.

When Mary and Joseph discover him missing from the caravan and search three days, her question is entirely natural and entirely human: “Son, why have you treated us so? Behold, your father and I have been searching for you in great distress.” Scripture lets her say it, and does not correct her tone.

Jesus's answer contains the first recorded words of his life, and they are a claim of identity: “Did you not know that I must be in my Father's house?” The word must (dei) is one of Luke's great theological words, marking the divine necessity that drives the whole redemptive plan. And the Father he names is not Joseph. He distinguishes — gently, but unmistakably — between the father who has been searching for him and the Father whose house he is in.

He had not run away, and he had broken no commandment; his surprise is genuine that after twelve years they had to be told where he would be. And then, having said it, he goes down with them to Nazareth and is subject to them for another eighteen years.
verseByVerse.theology:
The word dei — “it is necessary,” “I must” — appears some forty times across Luke and Acts and marks the divine necessity driving the story forward: the Son of Man must suffer (9:22); he must rise on the third day (24:7); the Scripture must be fulfilled (22:37). Here, at twelve years old, Jesus uses it for the first time.

This is not a child defying his parents. It is the Son of God expressing the first law of his existence: he must be about his Father's business. The whole of Luke's two-volume work is the outworking of that single must, from the temple courts in Jerusalem to the ends of the earth.

Jesus's submission after the episode — “he went down with them and came to Nazareth and was submissive to them” (v. 51) — is the answer to anyone who reads his words in the temple as a claim to be exempt from ordinary human obligations. He is subject to his parents, and Luke's verb is continuous: not one act of compliance but a settled condition sustained for eighteen years.

And he genuinely grows (v. 52). The one who knows all things grows in knowledge; the one who is all-powerful grows in stature; the one in whom all wisdom is hidden grows in wisdom. This is the mystery of two natures in one person, and it means the incarnation was never a costume. It was real human life, lived fully from the inside.
verseByVerse.examples:
Mary and Joseph “did not understand the saying that he spoke to them” (v. 50) — and Mary “treasured up all these things in her heart” (v. 51). For the second time in the chapter Luke shows her holding what she does not yet understand, refusing to let go of it, waiting for the understanding to arrive.

This is one of the most honest and most encouraging pictures of faith in the Gospel. The mother of the Son of God did not always understand what he was doing. But she did not discard what she could not explain. She kept it, turned it over, and waited — and she was still carrying this one twenty years later when she stood at the foot of a cross and it began to make sense.

The closing verse is the New Testament's summary of the hidden years: Jesus increased in wisdom and in stature and in favour with God and man. Eighteen years of silence before the public ministry begins — of growing, learning, working, and being formed in a village nobody wrote about.

The God who could have compressed everything into three years of public ministry chose instead to spend thirty in ordinariness. That is the pattern of divine formation: the long preparation, the hidden years, the slow work of wisdom and character before the public work begins. Anyone impatient to skip the hidden years has not yet understood how God shapes the people he uses.

verseByVerse.quote: Now his parents went to Jerusalem every year at the Feast of the Passover. And when he was twelve years old, they went up according to custom.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two verses of background, and both matter more than they look.

Now his parents went to Jerusalem every year at the Feast of the Passover. The law required adult males to appear before the LORD three times a year (Deut. 16:16), and by this period most Galileans managed one. Joseph and Mary went annually, and Mary went too, which was not required of her. This is a devout household, and it is a poor one — the journey is eighty miles each way, on foot, and it costs a working man the better part of two weeks every spring.

Nothing in Luke's account of Jesus's upbringing suggests anything unusual about it except the thoroughness of its ordinary godliness. The boy learned the Scriptures in a village synagogue, worked in a builder's shop, and walked to Jerusalem with his family every Passover for twelve years.

And it is Passover, which Luke has not chosen at random. This is the feast of the lamb whose blood on the doorposts meant the destroyer passed over the house; the feast of Israel's redemption out of Egypt; the meal that every year told a nation how it had been bought. The Lamb of God is twelve years old and has come up to keep it.

He will come up to keep it again, and the last time he does, he will take the bread in his hands at that meal and say something no one had ever said about it before.

And when he was twelve years old. A Jewish boy took on personal responsibility for the commandments at thirteen; the formal ceremony came later in history, but the principle was long established, and twelve was the year of preparation for it. So this is the last Passover of his childhood and the threshold of his responsible life — which is exactly the moment Luke chooses to show him, once, before drawing the curtain again for eighteen more years.

It is the only story from Jesus's childhood in any of the four Gospels. The apocryphal writings of the following centuries are full of tales of the boy Jesus — making clay birds fly, striking a playmate dead and raising him again — and the contrast is worth a moment. The real Gospels record one incident, and in it the boy does nothing miraculous at all. He asks questions in a temple and goes home and does as he is told.

verseByVerse.quote: And when the feast was ended, as they were returning, the boy Jesus stayed behind in Jerusalem. His parents did not know it, but supposing him to be in the group they went a day's journey, but then they began to search for him among their relatives and acquaintances, and when they did not find him, they returned to Jerusalem, searching for him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the part every parent reads with a tightening in the chest.

The feast ends. The Galilean pilgrims form up and start north, and the boy stays behind. Luke is careful to say that his parents did not know it — this is not negligence in the modern sense. Pilgrim caravans travelled in extended family groups, often with the women and younger children setting out earlier and the men catching up, and a twelve-year-old on the threshold of adulthood could plausibly have been with either party. Each parent had every reason to assume he was with the other.

They go a day's journey before they begin looking. Then they search among their relatives and acquaintances — the horrible widening circle, the same question asked of one face after another, each of whom says no and looks worried. And then a day's walk back, alone, in the dark of the mind, to a city of tens of thousands full of Passover crowds.

After three days they found him. Count it honestly: a day out, a day back, and a day of searching Jerusalem. Three days in which the two people responsible for the safety of the Son of God did not know where he was.

Luke uses that number deliberately. He is a careful writer and he knows what he is doing; he will use it again, and the next time it is Mary's son who is lost for three days and then found — and the finding will be in the same city, at the same feast, and the grief of those three days will be immeasurably worse.

There is a use for this passage that has comforted believers for centuries, and it is worth stating plainly because it is exactly the shape of an ordinary Christian trouble.
