For I am lost; for I am a man of unclean lips,” Isa. 6:5), of Job before the whirlwind (Job 42:5-6), of John falling as dead at the feet of the risen Christ (Rev. 1:17). It is what happens when a creature with a conscience encounters holiness. Nothing had been said about sin; a boatload of fish had told him who was in the boat.

Jesus's answer to the confession of unworthiness is not agreement and not dismissal but a commission: “Do not be afraid; from now on you will be catching men.” The fear that holiness produces is not the end of the encounter; it is the beginning of the calling — because the calling was never going to rest on Peter's worthiness.

The verb is zōgreō, to take alive — the word the Greek Old Testament uses for sparing captives in battle. Fishing is bad news for fish; this net means the opposite. The trade is the same and the direction is reversed.

“From now on” is one of Luke's phrases for a hinge. They bring the boats to land, leave everything — including the greatest catch of their lives, lying on the shingle — and follow him.

And this is not the first meeting. Jesus was in Simon's house a chapter earlier (4:38-39), and John records an earlier introduction at the Jordan (John 1:35-42). Matthew and Mark give the decisive moment; Luke shows what was behind it. Most people are called the way Simon was — not all at once, but finally.
verseByVerse.theology:
The miraculous catch authenticates the call. Jesus does not simply appear on the shore and invite Peter to follow; he first demonstrates, in the domain where Peter's competence is greatest, that Peter's competence is not the final authority over the natural world.

The one who commands the fish is the one who made them. Peter's professional knowledge is real and valuable, and it is relativised — not demeaned. In the presence of the maker of the sea, every human expertise finds its proper place, which is a genuine place and not the top one.

The commission “you will be catching men” describes a rescue rather than an occupation. The disciples are being called to pull people alive out of the water that was drowning them — which is why the calling that begins with a catch of fish reaches its first great haul at Pentecost, when three thousand are taken alive in a day (Acts 2:41), and has not stopped since.

And the pattern of the encounter is the pattern of every conversion: an approach from Christ's side, a demonstration that leaves the man with nothing to stand on, an honest confession of unworthiness, and a calling that does not depend on the confession being answered with reassurance.
verseByVerse.examples:
“At your word I will let down the nets” — spoken after a night of futile effort, in the daylight hours when fishing is least productive, on the instruction of someone who is not a fisherman — is the model of obedient trust.

It is not blind obedience. Peter states the professional futility of the exercise plainly and is entirely right to state it. But he has heard something that overrides his own competence, and the reason he gives is the only one he has: not that the strategy makes sense, but that the one who commands can be trusted.

“They left everything and followed him” (v. 11) is the most radical vocational change in the New Testament. James and John leave their father in the boat — not just a career but a family business and a family obligation. The “everything” is genuinely everything: livelihood, security, plans, and the future they had imagined.

Not every disciple is told to leave a trade; Luke's own Gospel sends several people home. But everyone who follows has a moment when something must be left on the beach — and it is very often the thing that had only just started going well.

verseByVerse.quote: On one occasion, while the crowd was pressing in on him to hear the word of God, he was standing by the lake of Gennesaret, and he saw two boats by the lake, but the fishermen had gone out of them and were washing their nets. Getting into one of the boats, which was Simon's, he asked him to put out a little from the land. And he sat down and taught the people from the boat.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Luke introduces the first disciples through a sermon, not a miracle. The crowd is pressing in on him to hear the word of God — pushing, physically crowding — and he needs a platform. The lake provides one: water carries a voice across a shore remarkably well, and a boat pushed out a few yards turns a beach into an auditorium.

So he borrows Simon's boat. The relationship that will become the central human relationship of this Gospel begins as a practical arrangement between a preacher who needs a pulpit and a fisherman who has one going spare.

And look at the state Simon is in. The men are washing their nets — the last job of a night shift, done by people who want to go home. Luke has already told us why the mood is what it is: they caught nothing. These are not prosperous boat-owners at leisure. They are labourers at the end of a wasted night, cleaning weed out of nets that earned nothing, and a teacher climbs into the boat and asks for a favour.

Jesus enters their exhaustion and their disappointment before he asks anything of them, and he asks for something small before he asks for everything.

A reader working through the Gospels side by side will pause here. Matthew and Mark tell the call of these same four men in a few brisk lines by the lakeside, with no sermon and no catch of fish — Jesus walks past, says follow me, and they go (Matt. 4:18-22; Mark 1:16-20). Luke gives a whole morning. Is this the same event told differently, or a different one?

Notice that Luke has already put Jesus inside Simon's house one chapter earlier, healing his mother-in-law of a fever (4:38-39), and here Jesus steps into Simon's boat as a man borrowing from someone he knows. Luke plainly does not think this is their first meeting. And John fills in the earlier stage: Andrew and another disciple met Jesus by the Jordan, and Andrew had already brought his brother to him (John 1:35-42).

So the picture that holds all four together is not a single lightning-bolt summons but a deepening — an introduction at the Jordan, an acquaintance in Capernaum, and then this morning on the shore, when the acquaintance becomes a leaving of everything. Matthew and Mark give the decisive moment; Luke shows what was behind it.

Most people are called the way Simon was. Not all at once, but finally.

verseByVerse.quote: And when he had finished speaking, he said to Simon, 'Put out into the deep and let down your nets for a catch.' And Simon answered, 'Master, we toiled all night and took nothing! But at your word I will let down the nets.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Put out into the deep and let down your nets for a catch.

Consider how that sounded. Simon has fished this lake all his working life. Night is when you fish these waters — the nets are visible to the fish in daylight — and he has just worked the whole of it for nothing. It is now morning, the worst time, and the gear has been cleaned and stowed. And a carpenter from an inland village is giving him instructions about where to fish.

Luke lets the objection stand: Master, we toiled all night and took nothing! The exclamation mark is right. This is not a pious man swallowing his doubts. He states the professional reality plainly, and he is entirely correct to state it.

Then: But at your word I will let down the nets.

That is one of the great sentences of the Gospel, and its greatness lies in what it does not claim. Simon does not say he now expects fish. He does not say he has received an inner assurance, or felt a stirring, or reconsidered the science of it. He says the reason, and there is exactly one: at your word.

This is what faith looks like from the inside far more often than the confident version people imagine. Faith is not the disappearance of the objection. It is the objection stated honestly, and then the obedience anyway, because of who is speaking.

Notice also what he calls him: Master — epistatēs, a word Luke alone uses, meaning someone in charge, a superintendent. It is a real title and it is not yet Lord. Three verses from now it will be. He knows enough to obey; he does not yet know who he is obeying. That is where most obedience begins, and there is no other way to start.

And the obedience is costly in a way that is easy to miss. The nets were clean. Letting them down again means several hours of work at the end of a shift, in front of a crowd on the shore, at a time of day when everyone watching knows it will not work. Simon is not risking his life. He is risking looking a fool, which for most people is harder.

verseByVerse.quote: And when they had done this, they enclosed a large number of fish, and their nets were breaking. They signaled to their partners in the other boat to come and help them. And they came and filled both the boats, so that they began to sink.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Luke does not describe the fish arriving. He describes the equipment failing.

Their nets were breaking. They signaled to their partners in the other boat. They came and filled both the boats, so that they began to sink. Torn nets, a shout across the water, two boats down to the waterline and going under. The miracle is reported from the point of view of men trying to cope with it.

That excess is the message. A moderate catch would have been a pleasant surprise and could have been put down to luck; a good fisherman has strange mornings. What happens here cannot be absorbed into anybody's experience. The gear that was designed for this work cannot handle it, and neither can the boats.

And it happens in the one arena where Simon is the expert. That is not accidental. Jesus does not demonstrate his authority to these men in a synagogue, where they would have deferred to him anyway; he does it in their own trade, on their own water, at the exact point where their competence was greatest and had just failed. Simon's professional knowledge is real and it is not overturned so much as put in its place. In front of him is someone the fish obey.

Then a detail worth having: they could not manage it alone. The catch was so large that the men in the second boat had to be called, and even then both crews together barely coped. There is a picture in that of everything that follows in Luke's second volume — a haul too big for one boat, and partners signalled for.

It is worth noticing that this is the same lake, and very possibly the same men, on the morning after the resurrection in John's Gospel, when a voice from the shore says cast the net on the right side and the net comes up full and unbroken (John 21:6, 11). Simon's story begins and ends with a catch he did not earn, from a word he did not expect, in water he had already worked all night for nothing.

verseByVerse.quote: But when Simon Peter saw it, he fell down at Jesus' knees, saying, 'Depart from me, for I am a sinful man, O Lord.' For he and all who were with him were astonished at the catch of fish that they had taken,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Simon's response is not the one anybody would predict.

He does not shout. He does not count the fish. He does not thank Jesus, or ask how it was done, or invite him back tomorrow. He goes down on his knees in a sinking boat full of the largest catch of his life and asks the man responsible to go away.

Depart from me, for I am a sinful man, O Lord.

Nothing has been said about sin. There has been no sermon on repentance, no accusation, no exposure of anything Simon has done. There has only been a boatload of fish. And the fish have told him something about the man in the stern that his conscience cannot survive standing next to.

This is the oldest pattern in Scripture. Isaiah sees the LORD high and lifted up and the first word out of him is Woe is me! For I am lost; for I am a man of unclean lips (Isa. 6:5). Job argues for thirty-eight chapters, meets God, and says I despise myself, and repent in dust and ashes (Job 42:6). John, who had leaned on Jesus's chest at supper, sees him in glory and falls down as though dead (Rev. 1:17). Not one of them is told to feel this way. It is simply what happens when a creature with a conscience gets close to holiness.

And notice the title. Two verses ago he said Master. Now he says Lord — kyrios, the word the Greek Old Testament uses for the divine name. The fish have moved his vocabulary. He is a very long way from understanding, and he has understood the one thing that matters: the gap between himself and this man is not the ordinary gap between two men.

Now the pastoral weight, because depart from me is a sentence a great many people have felt without ever saying aloud. There is a species of shame that does not want to be forgiven so much as to be left alone — that finds the nearness of God unbearable and would genuinely prefer distance to exposure. Simon is not being falsely modest. He means it.

What is worth seeing is that he is right about himself and wrong about what to do with it. He is a sinful man. That is the accurate diagnosis, and it is the reason Jesus got into the boat.

verseByVerse.quote: and so also were James and John, sons of Zebedee, who were partners with Simon. And Jesus said to Simon, 'Do not be afraid; from now on you will be catching men.' And when they had brought their boats to land, they left everything and followed him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not be afraid.

It is the fourth time in this Gospel. Gabriel said it to Zechariah, and to Mary; the angel said it to the shepherds; and now Jesus says it to a fisherman on his knees. The encounter with holiness always produces the fear, and the answer to the fear is always the same word.

And note that he does not argue with the diagnosis. Simon says I am a sinful man, and Jesus does not say nonsense or you are being hard on yourself. He does not correct the self-assessment at all. He simply declines to leave, and gives the man a job.

From now on you will be catching men.

Luke's phrase from now on is one he reserves for hinges. Everything before this morning was one kind of life; everything after it is another.

And the word for catching is stronger than English lets on. Luke does not use the ordinary verb for fishing. He uses zōgreō, which means to take alive — the word the Greek Old Testament uses for sparing captives in battle rather than killing them (Num. 31:18; 2 Sam. 8:2). Fishing, after all, is not good news for the fish; the net means death. This net means the opposite. Simon is not being told he will collect people the way he collected bream. He is being told he will pull them out alive, out of the water that was drowning them.

The trade is the same. The direction is reversed. And nothing of who he is gets discarded — the patience, the nerve, the long nights, the knowledge of when to move: all of it is taken up and turned round. The first great haul comes on a morning in Jerusalem when three thousand are taken alive in a day (Acts 2:41).

And when they had brought their boats to land, they left everything and followed him.

Everything includes the fish. That is worth stopping on. They had just landed the catch of a lifetime — enough money to change a family's year — and they beached the boats and walked away from it. They did not sell it first. The greatest professional success of Simon's life lasted about ten minutes and was abandoned on the shingle.

Not everyone is called to leave a trade; Luke's own Gospel is full of people sent home. But everyone who follows Christ has a moment where something has to be left on the beach, and it is usually the thing that had just started going well.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
A man “full of leprosy” comes to Jesus. The description is Luke's medical precision: this is not an early skin complaint but an advanced case. Leprosy in the ancient world covered a range of chronic conditions, all of which rendered the sufferer ritually unclean (Lev. 13-14).

The consequences were total. He lived outside the settlement, was required to warn others of his approach — “Unclean! Unclean!” (Lev. 13:45-46) — and was excluded from worship. He was the ultimate social and religious exile, and not because of anything he had done. He simply had a condition, and the condition put him outside.

His approach is itself an act of desperation and faith: he is in a city he may not enter, on his face in public, saying “Lord, if you will, you can make me clean.” He does not doubt the power. He is uncertain only about the will — which is exactly the right question to bring, and the answer is the most intimate thing in the chapter.

Jesus reaches out his hand and touches him: “I will; be clean.” The touch is the miracle inside the miracle. Any rabbi could have spoken healing from a safe distance; a word would have done it. Instead the hand lands on the one body in Galilee nobody had been permitted to touch for years.

Under the law, contact ran one way: touching a leper made you unclean. Here the direction is reversed. The holiness of Jesus is not contaminated by the leper; the leper is cleansed by the holiness.

The instruction to show himself to the priest and offer what Moses commanded (Lev. 14) is not legalism but pastoral wisdom. The priest's certificate was the man's ticket back into the community; without it, even a healed leper could not go home. Jesus heals the disease in a second, then walks the man through the process that heals everything else the disease had done to him — and the certificate stands in the temple records as “a proof to them.”

“Tell no one” is the recognition that a reputation as a healer will bury the preaching under a crowd of the desperate. It does, immediately. And Jesus's answer to growing fame is the one Luke keeps recording: he withdraws to desolate places and prays.
verseByVerse.theology:
The touch of the leper is the incarnation in miniature. The Son of God who became flesh did not keep a hygienic distance from the contaminated human condition. He entered it, touched it, took on himself what should have made him unclean, and transferred his own wholeness to the sufferer.

This is what Paul means: “he made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God” (2 Cor. 5:21). The direction of the transaction never varies. He takes what is ours; we receive what is his. The leper's healing is a parable of salvation performed on a real body.

The willingness Jesus expresses — “I will” (thelō) — is the answer to every theology that doubts the desire of God to save. The leper's “if you will” is the question of everyone who has been told, explicitly or by implication, that God may not want them, that their case may be outside the scope of his grace, that they may be too far gone.

The reply is not merely “I can.” The power was never in question. It is “I will” — the desire, the purpose, the determination to cleanse, as absolute as the power.
verseByVerse.examples:
The leper models the prayer of humility. He falls on his face; he presumes nothing about Jesus's willingness; he makes no claim on his own account — and he comes. The combination of complete certainty about the power (“you can make me clean”) with complete submission about the will (“if you will”) is the posture faith takes before sovereign grace.

It is not the prayer of someone with low expectations. He expects everything. It is the prayer of someone who knows exactly what he is asking and knows he cannot command the answer. He can only ask, and trust the character of the one he asks.

Jesus's withdrawal to desolate places in the middle of growing popularity (v. 16) is the model of spiritual formation under pressure — and Luke's grammar makes it a habit, not an episode. The more the ministry succeeded by external measures, the more he went away.

The pattern refuses the assumption that fruitfulness makes prayer less necessary. For Jesus, fruitfulness was the reason to pray more, because fruitfulness creates demands that only communion with the Father can carry. The minister who cuts prayer in order to meet ministry demands has confused the cause with the effect.

verseByVerse.quote: While he was in one of the cities, there came a man full of leprosy. And when he saw Jesus, he fell on his face and begged him, 'Lord, if you will, you can make me clean.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
A man full of leprosy — and Luke, the physician, is the only one who grades it. Not early, not doubtful. Advanced.

The word in the Bible covers more than the disease we now call by that name; it was a category of chronic, disfiguring skin conditions. But the medical detail is not the point of the man's life. The law was: He shall remain unclean as long as he has the disease… He shall live alone. His dwelling shall be outside the camp (Lev. 13:46). And when anyone came near, he was to cover his upper lip and call out Unclean, unclean.

Take in what that meant. No home. No synagogue. No temple. No work. Nobody has touched him in years — not a handshake, not a hand on the shoulder, not an embrace at a funeral. He has been required, by the law of God, to announce his own contamination to anyone who came near. And he was not being punished for anything. He had done nothing. He simply had a condition, and the condition put him outside.

And here he is in one of the cities, which he is not allowed to be in, on his face in front of a crowd, breaking the law to get to Jesus.

Lord, if you will, you can make me clean.

That is one of the most exactly worded prayers in the Gospels, and both halves matter.

You can is not a request; it is a statement. He has no doubt whatever about the power. He is not asking Jesus to try.

If you will is where the uncertainty is, and it is not doubt so much as the absence of any claim. He does not tell Jesus why he deserves this. He does not bargain, or promise, or point to how long he has suffered. He puts the whole thing in the other man's hands and leaves it there.

That is the shape of real petition, and it is worth learning. It is not the prayer of low expectations — he expects everything. It is the prayer of someone who knows exactly what he is asking for and knows he cannot command it. He can only ask, and trust the character of the one he is asking.

And underneath it is a fear a good many people carry and few say out loud. Not is God able? but is God willing — for someone like me?

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus stretched out his hand and touched him, saying, 'I will; be clean.' And immediately the leprosy left him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And Jesus stretched out his hand and touched him.

Read that again slowly, because it is the miracle inside the miracle.

He did not need to. Every healing in this chapter so far has been done by a word; he will heal a centurion's servant from a different part of town without going near him. A word from three feet away would have cleansed this man perfectly. Instead the hand goes out, and lands on the one body in Galilee that nobody had been permitted to touch for years.

Under the law, touching a leper made you unclean. The contamination ran in one direction, and everyone knew which. What happens here reverses it. Jesus is not defiled by the leper; the leper is cleansed by Jesus. The holiness is the stronger thing, and it moves outward.

That is the incarnation in a single gesture, and it is what Paul means: he made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God (2 Cor. 5:21). The direction of the transaction never changes. He takes what is ours; we receive what is his.

Then the two words, and they answer the exact thing the man was unsure of.

He had not questioned the power — you can make me clean was said as settled fact. What he did not know was the will. And Jesus replies to precisely that, and to nothing else: I will.

Not I can. The power was never in question. I will — the desire, the readiness, the glad determination to make this man clean.

It is worth saying plainly why that matters, because the leper's uncertainty is one a great many people carry about God. Not is he able to save me? but is he willing to save someone like me — this far gone, this unclean, this long shut out? A whole life of exclusion had taught this man to expect a no, or at best a reluctant and distant maybe.

What he got was a hand on the skin nobody would touch, and a word with not a hair's breadth of hesitation in it.

Here is what he is like, then, and it has not altered since. He is not standing at a safe distance weighing whether a case qualifies. He is not reluctant, and he does not have to be persuaded, and he has never once recoiled from anybody who came to him. The hand goes out first. The word is I will.

verseByVerse.quote: And he charged him to tell no one, but 'go and show yourself to the priest, and make an offering for your cleansing, as Moses commanded, for a proof to them.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two instructions, and they look as though they cancel each other: tell no one, and go and show yourself to the priest.

They do not. The second is a legal procedure, not a publicity campaign, and it is the thing the man most needs.

Leviticus 14 lays down the ritual by which a healed leper is examined, declared clean, and restored: the priest inspects him, two birds are taken, one killed and one released alive over running water, and after eight days there are offerings and the man is pronounced clean and may go home. Without that certificate, a healed man is still, in every practical sense, a leper. He cannot re-enter the town, or the synagogue, or his own family's house.

So Jesus heals the disease in a second and then sends the man through a week-long process to heal everything else the disease had done to him. That is worth noticing about how he works. He could have declared the man clean on the spot with more authority than any priest in Israel. He sends him to the priest anyway, because the man needs to be received back by his community, and there is an appointed way for that to happen.

Grace does not despise process. There is a kind of spiritual enthusiasm that thinks anything procedural is beneath it. Jesus, who could have skipped every step, walks the man through all of them.

For a proof to them. That phrase carries an edge. The priests will have to examine this man and certify him — which means that somewhere in Jerusalem, a priest opened his records and wrote down that a man full of leprosy had been made clean. The establishment that would shortly decide Jesus was a blasphemer had, in its own files, a legal attestation of what he could do.

And the tell no one? It is a restraint Jesus imposes repeatedly in Galilee, and the next verse shows why it was needed. A reputation as a healer would bury the preaching under a crowd of the desperate — which is exactly what happens anyway. He came to announce a kingdom, and the miracles were the announcement made visible, not a service he had come to provide.

verseByVerse.quote: But now even more the report about him went abroad, and great crowds gathered to hear him and to be healed of their infirmities. But he would withdraw to desolate places and pray.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two sentences, set deliberately side by side, and the but between them is the whole point.

But now even more the report about him went abroad, and great crowds gathered. The instruction to keep quiet has failed, as such instructions generally do. And notice what the crowds come for: to hear him and to be healed of their infirmities. Both, in that order — Luke does not sneer at them. They want the word and they want their bodies mended, which is a perfectly reasonable pair of things to want.

But he would withdraw to desolate places and pray.

Luke's grammar is worth having: the tense is continuous. This was not a single retreat but a habit — he used to withdraw. Again and again, the busier it got, the more he went away.

And the word for the place is erēmos, the same word used for the wilderness where the devil met him in chapter 4. He goes back to the empty country on purpose. There is nothing there. That is what it is for.

Now the thing to see, because it inverts the usual assumption. The natural reading of a growing ministry is that prayer becomes a luxury one can no longer afford — the demands are real, the people are genuinely needy, and the hours have to come from somewhere. Jesus does the opposite. As the crowds increase, so does the withdrawal. He treats fruitfulness as a reason to pray more, not less.

Which suggests he understood something about crowds that is easy to miss. A large and admiring crowd is not a neutral thing to stand in front of. It is one of the most dangerous places a person can be, and the pressure it exerts — to be what they want, to keep producing, to believe their estimate of you — is not resisted by good intentions. He met it by leaving.

There is a plain diagnostic here for anyone in Christian work, and it is uncomfortable. If prayer is the thing that gets cut when the demands rise, the demands are being served and the ministry is being hollowed out — because what the crowds actually needed from Jesus came out of the desolate places, and he never once let them have it on any other terms.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
This is the first confrontation between Jesus and the religious authorities in Luke, and it is carefully staged. Pharisees and teachers of the law have come from every village of Galilee, and from Judea, and from Jerusalem — a gathering with the shape of an inspection. They are seated. And Luke notes, before anything happens, that the power of the Lord was with Jesus to heal.

Meanwhile four men are carrying a paralysed friend, and the crowd has made the door impassable. So they go up on the roof, take it apart, and lower the man on his mat into the middle of the room, through the ceiling, in front of everyone. It is rude, destructive and entirely out of order — and Luke calls it faith.

The faith Jesus sees is not the paralysed man's alone. It is “their” faith: the faith of friends who refused to be stopped. The man himself says nothing in the entire passage. His only contribution is to lie there and be carried, and everything that follows happens because other people would not leave him outside.

What Jesus then says is not what anyone came for: “Man, your sins are forgiven you.” Not “rise and walk.” The physical healing is four verses away; forgiveness comes first.

The scribes and Pharisees recognise the claim at once: “Who is this who speaks blasphemies? Who can forgive sins but God alone?” Their theology is entirely correct — only God can forgive sins against God. Their reasoning is impeccable and their conclusion is upside down. They have the premise right and the observation right, and instead of following the argument where it leads, they reach for blasphemy.

Jesus's challenge is pedagogical. “Which is easier, to say 'Your sins are forgiven you,' or to say 'Rise and walk'?” It is easier to say the first, because nothing visible follows and nobody can check. The second is the dangerous sentence. So he does the checkable one — as the credential for the claim that cannot be checked: “that you may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins.”

The miracles are never the message in this Gospel. They are the authentication of it.

And the man rises, picks up the mat he has spent his life lying on, walks out through the crowd, and goes home glorifying God — leaving a room full of people, dignitaries included, filled with awe and saying, “We have seen extraordinary things today.”
verseByVerse.theology:
Forgiveness before healing establishes the priority of Luke's whole Gospel: the deepest human need is not physical. The paralysis is real, the suffering is real, the exclusion from ordinary life is real — and Jesus removes all of it. But he deals first with something that would still have been wrong after the legs worked.

This is not a denigration of physical suffering, and it is emphatically not a suggestion that the paralysis was caused by the man's sin; Jesus explicitly rejects that reasoning elsewhere (John 9:3). It is a statement about what finally matters — the standing before God that sin destroys.

The scribes' objection is the most important theological sentence in the passage, and Jesus does not answer it by denial. He never says they are wrong about the exclusive divine prerogative. He acts on it, and offers the visible miracle as the proof.

“Son of Man” sounds modest in English and is not. It is Daniel 7:13-14, where one like a son of man comes to the Ancient of Days and receives dominion, glory, and a kingdom that all peoples shall serve. In a room full of men who knew Daniel, that title while forgiving sins was the claim doubled — and “on earth” presses it further still. The authority is here, at ground level, exercised by a man they can see.
verseByVerse.examples:
The four friends are the model of intercessory persistence. They could not bring their friend by the normal route, so they found another. They could not get through the door, so they went through the roof. Their determination is not disrespect for the gathering; it is the overflow of confidence that Jesus can and will do what they believe he can.

This is what intercession looks like when it becomes serious: not eloquence, not technique, but the refusal to accept that the door is the only way, and a willingness to look foolish on somebody else's behalf.

“When he saw their faith” — the faith Jesus responds to is the faith of the group. That is a significant detail for understanding how the church actually works. The person who cannot bring themselves to pray, whose faith is exhausted or paralysed by their suffering, can be carried to Jesus by the faith of those around them.

People do get carried. There are seasons — grief, depression, shame, sheer exhaustion — when a believer will not get themselves into the room, and somebody else has to do the carrying. This passage says the carrying counts.

verseByVerse.quote: On one of those days, as he was teaching, Pharisees and teachers of the law were sitting there, who had come from every village of Galilee and Judea and from Jerusalem. And the power of the Lord was with him to heal. And behold, some men were bringing on a bed a man who was paralyzed, and they were seeking to bring him in and lay him before Jesus,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The religious authorities appear in Luke's narrative for the first time, and they are sitting down.

Luke is careful about who they are and where they have come from: Pharisees and teachers of the law… from every village of Galilee and Judea and from Jerusalem. That is not a few curious locals. Word has reached the capital, and men have travelled to see for themselves. Whatever this gathering formally was, it has the shape of an inspection.

And they are seated while everyone else is pressed in standing. They have been given the places of honour in the room, and they are watching.

Then Luke adds a sentence that has no obvious grammatical business being there: And the power of the Lord was with him to heal. He states it before anything happens, like a stage direction. The room is full of the men who decide what may be believed in Israel — and the power that actually matters is already present, and it is not with them.

And behold, some men were bringing on a bed a man who was paralyzed, and they were seeking to bring him in and lay him before Jesus.

Luke's and behold is the narrator turning the reader's head. Outside, while the inspection proceeds, four men are carrying a fifth on a mat.

Consider what that took before they reached the door. Somebody had to notice him. Somebody had to decide it was worth a day. Four men had to be found, and a route agreed, and a paralysed body carried through streets on a pallet, with all the awkwardness and slowness and public spectacle of it — and at the end of the journey, a house so full that there was no way in.

Luke says they were seeking — the imperfect, meaning they kept trying. They did not arrive, see the crowd, and go home. They worked at it.

The man on the mat has not said a word and will not say one in the whole passage. Everything that is about to happen to him happens because other people would not give up on getting him in front of Jesus.

verseByVerse.quote: but finding no way to bring him in, because of the crowd, they went up on the roof and let him down with his bed through the tiles into the midst before Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But finding no way to bring him in, because of the crowd, they went up on the roof.

Stop and picture the actual logistics, because familiarity has made this scene charming and it was not charming.

An outside stair, four men, and a stretcher with a grown man on it. Then a roof — and a roof over a room that is at that moment packed with people, including every religious dignitary from Galilee to Jerusalem. And they begin taking it apart.

Dust and debris coming down on the heads of the seated Pharisees. An interruption that cannot be politely absorbed. Somebody's property being damaged, and no evidence that anybody asked the owner. It is rude, it is destructive, it is entirely out of order — and Luke, in the next verse, calls it faith.

That is worth sitting with. The four men did not have better theology than the men in the room; they had a friend they refused to leave outside. They could not get to Jesus by the obvious route, so they made a new one. The obstacle sent them upward.

Which is the model of intercession when it becomes serious. Not eloquence. Not technique. The refusal to accept that the door is the only way, and the willingness to look foolish and cause a commotion on somebody else's behalf.

And the man they lowered could do nothing at all. He could not walk to Jesus, could not push through a crowd, could not climb a stair. His entire contribution was to lie there. Whatever faith he had, Luke does not mention it separately — he says Jesus saw their faith, and the man's part in the sentence is as the thing being carried.

There is a whole doctrine of the church in that. People do get carried. There are seasons when a believer cannot pray, cannot come, cannot generate any momentum whatever — grief, depression, exhaustion, shame — and the honest truth is that they will not get themselves into the room. Somebody else has to do the carrying, and the carrying counts.

One small detail draws the charge that Luke did not know Palestine. Mark says the men dug through the roof and broke it up (Mark 2:4), which fits an ordinary Galilean house of beams, branches and packed clay; Luke says through the tiles. But tiled roofs were the normal Greco-Roman construction and had long since appeared in the towns of the region — and in any case Luke is writing for readers across the empire, who would picture a roof the moment he named its material. Two witnesses describing the same hole from different sides of the Mediterranean is not a contradiction.

verseByVerse.quote: And when he saw their faith, he said, 'Man, your sins are forgiven you.' And the scribes and the Pharisees began to question, saying, 'Who is this who speaks blasphemies? Who can forgive sins but God alone?'
verseByVerse.commentary:
And when he saw their faith, he said, Man, your sins are forgiven you.

Nobody in that room expected that sentence, and it is worth registering how strange it is.

Four men have gone to enormous trouble for one thing. The man on the mat wants one thing. The whole audience is waiting for one thing. And Jesus looks at a paralysed man lowered through a hole in somebody's ceiling and deals with his sins.

He will heal the paralysis. It is four verses away. But he does the other thing first, and the order is deliberate, and it has to be handled carefully because it can be heard cruelly. Jesus is not saying the paralysis does not matter — he removes it. He is not suggesting the paralysis was caused by the man's sin; he says nothing of the kind here, and elsewhere he explicitly denies that reasoning (John 9:3). What he is doing is treating the deeper condition first, in a man who had not come about it and may not have known he had it.

That is a hard word and a merciful one. The thing wrong with all of us that will still be wrong after every other thing is put right is not physical. A man who is healed and unforgiven has been given a working body and a few more decades, and the account is still open.

And the scribes and the Pharisees began to question, saying, Who is this who speaks blasphemies? Who can forgive sins but God alone?

Now, this is important: their theology is correct. Entirely correct. Only God can forgive sins committed against God — that is not a Pharisaic invention, it is the plain teaching of the Old Testament, and any faithful Jew in that room would have said the same.

Their reasoning is impeccable and their conclusion is upside down. They have the major premise right — only God forgives sins. They have the observation right — this man has just forgiven sins. And instead of following the argument where it leads, they reach for blasphemy.

Which is worth noticing about the whole of Luke's Gospel. The people who reject Jesus are almost never the people who understand him least. They are usually the people who have grasped exactly what he is claiming.

verseByVerse.quote: When Jesus perceived their thoughts, he answered them, 'Why do you question in your hearts? Which is easier, to say, ‘Your sins are forgiven you,’ or to say, ‘Rise and walk’? But that you may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins'—he said to the man who was paralyzed—'I say to you, rise, pick up your bed and go home.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
When Jesus perceived their thoughts. They had not spoken. Luke says they began to question — inwardly — and Jesus answers the argument going on inside their heads, which is itself a demonstration of something only God does.

Which is easier, to say, Your sins are forgiven you, or to say, Rise and walk?

The question is sharper than it looks, and the answer is not the obvious one.

Which is easier to say? Plainly the first. Anyone can announce that a man's sins are forgiven, because nothing visible follows and nobody can check. Saying rise and walk to a paralytic is the dangerous sentence: in three seconds everyone in the room will know whether it worked.

So Jesus does the checkable one, and he says exactly why: that you may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins. The healing is not the point. The healing is the evidence for the claim that cannot be verified — a visible miracle offered as the credential for an invisible one.

That is the logic of miracle throughout the Gospels, and it is worth getting right. The miracles are never the message. They are the authentication of the message. A Jesus who heals bodies and cannot deal with guilt would be a remarkable physician and no use at all at the end.

The Son of Man. This is Jesus's habitual way of referring to himself, and it sounds modest in English — a son of man is just a human being. It was not modest. He is quoting Daniel 7:13-14, where one like a son of man comes on the clouds to the Ancient of Days and is given dominion and glory and a kingdom, that all peoples, nations, and languages should serve him. In a room full of men who knew Daniel, choosing that title while forgiving sins was not a retreat from the claim. It was the claim, doubled.

And note the two small words in the middle: on earth. Everyone in that room believed sins were forgiven in heaven, by God, at the appointed time and through the appointed sacrifices. Jesus says the authority is here, at ground level, in a crowded house in Capernaum, exercised by a man they can see.

Which means that the thing the whole temple system existed to deal with has walked into a room and dealt with it, in one sentence, for free, for a man who did not ask.

verseByVerse.quote: And immediately he rose up before them and picked up what he had been lying on and went home, glorifying God. And amazement seized them all, and they glorified God and were filled with awe, saying, 'We have seen extraordinary things today.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
And immediately he rose up before them and picked up what he had been lying on and went home, glorifying God.

Luke lingers on the bed. The man picked up what he had been lying on — the phrasing draws attention to it. That mat was the whole visible history of his life: what he was carried on, what he lay on, the thing other people had to lift. He walks out with it under his arm.

And he walks out through the crowd. Through the doorway they could not get him in by, past the seated dignitaries, into a street where everyone knew him. Whatever else that town discussed that week, it discussed this.

Glorifying God. Luke says it of the man, and then immediately of the crowd — they glorified God and were filled with awe. Not with admiration of a technique. With awe.

The word for what they said is worth having: we have seen extraordinary things today is, in Greek, paradoxa — things contrary to expectation, things that overturn the settled order. Our word paradox comes from it. They have no category for what they have watched, and they say so.

Notice too that Luke says amazement seized them all. All of them — which, in that room, includes the delegation from Jerusalem. They are not converted. Luke does not say they believed; he says they were amazed and afraid, and by chapter 6 they will be watching him to accuse him. It is entirely possible to witness the undeniable, glorify God out loud, and go home unchanged.

And the man went home. That is where Jesus sent him — not into the itinerant company, not into public ministry. Go home. There was a house somewhere in Capernaum where a family had been carrying this man for years, and that evening he walked in on his own feet, carrying the mat.

Whatever the four friends had imagined when they started taking the roof apart, they got more than they had come for. They came for a pair of working legs. They went home with a man whose sins had been forgiven by someone with the authority to do it, and a Saviour they had not known they needed.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
From the crowded house Luke moves straight to one of the most understated calls in the Gospel. Jesus sees Levi at his tax booth and says “Follow me.” And Levi left everything and followed him.

The form is identical to the call of Peter, James and John (v. 11) — an encounter, a bare imperative, and complete abandonment. But Levi's “everything” carries a different weight. Tax collectors in the Roman system had purchased the franchise; leaving the booth meant writing off a substantial investment with no prospect of return, and no possibility of going back. The fishermen could have returned to fishing. Levi could not return to a tax booth.

He was also, by the reckoning of every devout person who walked past him, beyond the pale: a collaborator with Rome, a legally protected extortioner, ritually unclean, inadmissible as a witness. Jesus called him without an assessment, a probation, or an interview.

Levi's first act as a disciple is to throw a great banquet and fill it with the only people he knows — a large company of tax collectors and others. He has no theology and no method. He has a house and a contact list, and he puts Jesus in the middle of them.

The Pharisees and their scribes complain, and they complain to the disciples rather than to Jesus: “Why do you eat and drink with tax collectors and sinners?” The objection is not mere snobbery. Table fellowship in that world was a public declaration of acceptance and solidarity — closer to a signed statement than a meal — so this is a serious question about the boundaries of the people of God.

Jesus's answer is the programmatic statement of the whole ministry: “Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick. I have not come to call the righteous but sinners to repentance.”

The word “righteous” is ironic. Everyone in that house is sick; the difference between the two groups is entirely in what they know about themselves. A man who does not believe he is ill will not send for a doctor, however available the doctor makes himself. And the last two words are not decoration — he called sinners to repentance. The table at Levi's house is a doctor's visit, and doctors do not visit in order to agree with the disease.
verseByVerse.theology:
The call of Levi is Luke's announcement that the kingdom of God comes to the most unexpected people. Matthew's Gospel tells us this is Matthew himself (Matt. 9:9). The author of one of the four Gospels is a man whom the respectable religious society of his day considered beyond the reach of God's grace.

And of the four apostle lists in the New Testament, the only one that attaches “the tax collector” to his name is the one he wrote (Matt. 10:3). He never got over it.

“I have not come to call the righteous but sinners to repentance” is not a statement about two classes of people — the righteous who do not need Jesus and the sinners who do. Scripture is unambiguous that there are no righteous: “none is righteous, no, not one” (Rom. 3:10).

It is a statement about two self-perceptions. The “righteous” are the self-righteous, whose assessment of their own spiritual condition is so favourable that they see no need of a physician. The tragedy of the Pharisees is not their theology, most of which was sound. It is their self-knowledge. They could not be called to repentance because they did not believe they needed to repent.
verseByVerse.examples:
Levi's banquet is the instinctive evangelism of someone who has just received grace and immediately wants the people he loves to meet the one who gave it. No training, no method, no strategy — he invites his friends to his house and invites Jesus to the same room.

The criticism this drew is the criticism grace-shaped evangelism has always drawn: it happens in the wrong places, with the wrong people, without sufficient concern for the reputation of those involved. Jesus's presence at that table is the answer to every objection of the kind.

“Why do you eat and drink with tax collectors and sinners?” is the perennial complaint of those who would like the church to be more selective in its welcome. The instinct to keep the table clean — to eat only with the already acceptable — is deeply human, and it rests on a real principle: that holiness is preserved by separation.

What it has not reckoned with is a holiness that works the other way round, which the same chapter has already shown at a leper's skin. Jesus's table is where the sick come for medicine, not where the well gather to congratulate each other on their health.

verseByVerse.quote: After this he went out and saw a tax collector named Levi, sitting at the tax booth. And he said to him, 'Follow me.' And leaving everything, he rose and followed him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
After this he went out and saw a tax collector named Levi, sitting at the tax booth. And he said to him, Follow me.

Two words, and no preliminaries whatever.

What a tax booth was in Capernaum is worth spelling out, because it explains the shock. Capernaum sat on a trade route at a border; the booth taxed goods in transit. The man in it had bought the franchise from the authorities, paid Rome its assessment, and kept whatever else he could extract. That is not an incidental abuse of the job; it is how the job worked.

So Levi is three things at once to everyone walking past: a collaborator with the occupying power, a thief with legal protection, and ritually unclean from constant contact with Gentiles. He could not have given evidence in court. He would not have been received in a synagogue in any meaningful way. And he was, without question, rich.

Jesus walks past his table and calls him — with the same bare imperative he used on the fishermen, no assessment, no probation, no interview.

And leaving everything, he rose and followed him.

Luke uses the same phrase he used at verse 11, and for Levi it costs differently. The fishermen left boats and nets; boats and nets are still there tomorrow, and a man can go back to fishing, which several of them eventually tried. Levi leaves a purchased franchise. There is no going back to a tax booth once you have walked away from one — the post will be filled by the next bidder within the week. He is burning the only asset he has, and he does it standing up.

One more thing about this man, which Luke does not tell you and Matthew does. Luke calls him Levi; so does Mark. But when the First Gospel reaches this same scene it names him Matthew (Matt. 9:9), and when it lists the twelve apostles it calls him Matthew the tax collector (Matt. 10:3) — a description none of the other lists bothers to add.

Two names for one man was entirely ordinary then, as Simon was also Peter and Saul was also Paul. Which means the man rising from that booth is the man who would write the Gospel that opens the New Testament. And of the four lists of apostles in the New Testament, the only one that pins tax collector to that name is the one he wrote himself.

He never got over it.

verseByVerse.quote: And Levi made him a great feast in his house, and there was a large company of tax collectors and others reclining at table with them. And the Pharisees and their scribes grumbled at his disciples, saying, 'Why do you eat and drink with tax collectors and sinners?'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Levi's first recorded act as a disciple is to throw a party.

He has no theology yet, no training, no idea what is coming. What he has is a house — a large one, evidently — and a contact list. So he fills the room with the only people he knows: a large company of tax collectors and others, which is Luke's polite way of describing the social world a man in that trade moved in.

And he puts Jesus in the middle of it.

That is the instinct of somebody who has just been given something and immediately wants the people he cares about to meet the one who gave it. It is not a strategy. It is a man who cannot think of anything better to do with his house.

Then the objection, and it is worth understanding rather than dismissing. Why do you eat and drink with tax collectors and sinners?

Table fellowship in that world was not a casual matter. To recline at a man's table was to declare peace with him, to accept him, to be publicly associated with him. It was closer to a signed statement than to a meal. The Pharisees are not complaining about the menu; they are asking a serious question about the boundaries of the people of God, and by their own logic they are entirely right to ask it.

Their premise is that holiness is preserved by separation — that you keep clean by keeping away. It is not a stupid premise. It is most of the book of Leviticus, and it had kept Israel identifiable through centuries of pressure.

What they have not reckoned with is a holiness that works the other way round. They had watched it three sections earlier and missed it: a hand stretched out to a leper, and the cleanness travelling from the toucher to the touched.

And notice who they complain to. Not to Jesus — they grumbled at his disciples. They go round him. It is the oldest form of religious criticism there is: raise it with the followers, where it will do most damage and cost least.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus answered them, 'Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick. I have not come to call the righteous but sinners to repentance.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick.

The answer is a proverb, and its force is that nobody can disagree with it. A doctor found among the sick is not compromising his profession; he is doing it. His presence in the ward is not evidence that he approves of illness. It is evidence that he is a doctor.

So the question why do you eat with sinners answers itself the moment you know what he came for.

Then the sentence that states the mission: I have not come to call the righteous but sinners to repentance.

Two things need saying, and the second matters more.

First, the word righteous here is ironic, and everyone at that table knew it. Jesus is not conceding that the Pharisees are righteous and therefore outside his remit. Scripture is unambiguous that there are none — none is righteous, no, not one (Rom. 3:10, quoting the Psalms). He is using their own self-description back at them.

Second, and this is the thing to hold: the difference between the two groups at Levi's dinner is not their condition. Everyone in that house is sick. The difference is entirely in what they know about themselves. The tax collectors are aware of it; the men in the doorway are not. And a man who does not believe he is ill will not send for a doctor however available the doctor makes himself.

That is the whole tragedy of the Pharisees, and it is not primarily a moral tragedy. They were not, by most measures, bad men. They were disciplined, serious, orthodox, and self-denying, and they had a diagnosis of themselves that was wrong — and being wrong in that particular direction is the one condition Christ cannot treat, because it is a refusal of treatment.

And note the last two words, because they are easily lost: to repentance. He does not say he came to call sinners and leave them as they were. He came to call them to turn round. The table at Levi's house is not an endorsement of anybody's life. It is a doctor's visit, and doctors do not visit in order to agree with the disease.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The question about fasting is deceptively simple — why do Jesus's disciples not fast like John's disciples and the Pharisees? — and the answer, in two images and an observation, reframes the whole relationship between the old covenant and the new.

The bridegroom image is the most significant, because it is a claim about identity. In the Old Testament there is one bridegroom, and he is God: “Your Maker is your husband” (Isa. 54:5); “I will betroth you to me forever” (Hos. 2:19; cf. Jer. 2:2). Israel is the bride, and every apostasy is described as adultery. To explain his disciples' behaviour by saying the bridegroom is present is to say who has arrived — and John the Baptist had already made the same identification, placing himself in the wedding party rather than at its centre (John 3:29).

The disciples do not fast because this is not the season for it. Fasting at a wedding is not more serious; it is out of time.

Then the shadow: “The days will come when the bridegroom is taken away from them, and then they will fast in those days.” The verb is violent — removed by force. It is the first hint of the cross in Jesus's own teaching in Luke, dropped without warning into an argument about religious observance. Nobody at that table could have understood it.

The garment and the wineskin press the same point. A patch cut from a new coat ruins the new and does not match the old; new wine in a hardened skin bursts the skin and is lost. The kingdom Jesus inaugurates is not a reform of Judaism but its fulfilment — and fulfilment is not the same as continuation.

The new covenant is organically connected to the old; Jesus keeps the law, goes to the synagogue weekly, sends the leper to the priest. But what has arrived could not be contained by what preceded it, not because the old was worthless but because it was never designed to hold this.

And the last line is the sharpest: “no one after drinking old wine desires new, for he says, 'The old is good.'” It is not a compliment to the old wine. It is a description of a palate — and of the men in the doorway, who refused Jesus not because they had examined him and found him wanting but because they were comfortable, and he did not taste of what they were used to.
verseByVerse.theology:
The bridegroom language is one of the most significant implicit claims to deity in the Synoptic Gospels. In the prophets, the husband of Israel is the LORD himself, and the relationship between God and his people is consistently described in bridal terms.

Revelation carries the image to its conclusion — the marriage supper of the Lamb, the new Jerusalem coming down as a bride adorned for her husband (Rev. 19:7-9; 21:2-9). The fasting question in Luke 5 is a thread that runs all the way to the last page of the Bible.

The observation in v. 39 is not a sociological aside about wine preferences. It is a precise description of the spiritual condition of people who have grown comfortable in the old forms: they feel no need of new wine, because what they have is satisfying.

That is the condition of the Pharisees, and it was not a moral failure. The old wine of the law and the tradition was genuinely good — God gave it. This is the most dangerous spiritual position there is, because it requires a good thing to settle into: contentment with something genuinely good, in the presence of something better.
verseByVerse.examples:
The bridegroom's presence is the reason for the disciples' joy, and it remains the reason for Christian joy. The resurrection did not remove the bridegroom; it confirmed that he is alive and with his people until he returns.

So Christian fasting is not the fast of the men who asked the question. Jesus assumes his people will fast — “they will fast in those days,” and those days are these — but it is the fast of people who have known him, live between his going and his return, and want him back. Not a technique for getting God's attention. A body saying what the heart already knows: that the best thing is still ahead.

The new wineskins are a standing challenge to every Christian tradition, and the question has to be asked honestly. Not “is this old?” — age is no argument either way. But: is this form still carrying the life, or has it set hard around a shape the life has outgrown?

This is not a call to theological novelty. The wine is always the same wine, the gospel of the crucified and risen Christ, and it is the oldest thing there is. But a wineskin's only job is to hold wine, and the moment it begins to be valued for itself it has started to fail at the one thing it was for.

verseByVerse.quote: And they said to him, 'The disciples of John fast often and offer prayers, and so do the disciples of the Pharisees, but yours eat and drink.' And Jesus said to them, 'Can you make wedding guests fast while the bridegroom is with them? The days will come when the bridegroom is taken away from them, and then they will fast in those days.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The third complaint of the section, and it is about fasting.

The disciples of John fast often and offer prayers, and so do the disciples of the Pharisees, but yours eat and drink. The observation is accurate. The law required one fast a year, on the Day of Atonement; the devout added two a week. John's followers, in particular, were an austere group, and their teacher was in prison. And here is Jesus at a tax collector's banquet.

He answers with a wedding.

Can you make wedding guests fast while the bridegroom is with them? A Jewish wedding ran for seven days, and the guests were released from certain religious obligations for the duration — including, by some rabbinic reckoning, fasting. The point is not that fasting is wrong. It is that fasting at a wedding is absurd. It is not more serious; it is out of time.

But the image is doing something much larger than settling a dispute about diet, and the men who asked would have felt it. In the Old Testament there is one bridegroom, and he is God. Your Maker is your husband (Isa. 54:5). I will betroth you to me forever (Hos. 2:19). Israel is the bride, and every failure of the nation is described as adultery.

So when Jesus explains his disciples' behaviour by saying that the bridegroom is present, he is not reaching for a pleasant metaphor about joy. He is saying who has arrived. John the Baptist had already made the same identification and put himself in the wedding party rather than at its centre: the friend of the bridegroom… rejoices greatly at the bridegroom's voice (John 3:29).

And then the shadow. The days will come when the bridegroom is taken away from them, and then they will fast in those days.

The verb is violent — taken away, removed by force. This is the first hint of the cross in Luke's record of Jesus's own teaching, and it is dropped into an argument about religious observance without warning or explanation. Nobody at that table could have understood it. He knew already.

So: should Christians fast? Jesus plainly assumes it — they will fast in those days, and those days are these. But it is not the fast of the men asking the question. It is the fast of people who have known the bridegroom, live between his going and his return, and want him back. Not a technique for getting God's attention. A body saying what the heart already knows.

verseByVerse.quote: He also told them a parable: 'No one tears a piece from a new garment and puts it on an old garment. If he does, he will tear the new, and the piece from the new will not match the old.
verseByVerse.commentary:
No one tears a piece from a new garment and puts it on an old garment. If he does, he will tear the new, and the piece from the new will not match the old.

Luke's version of this saying is sharper than the others, and the sharpness is the point. Matthew and Mark speak of unshrunk cloth on an old coat; Luke has a man cutting up a new garment to patch an old one. So the loss is doubled. He ruins the new one by cutting it, and the patch does not match anyway.

The question underneath is the one the whole section has been circling. Has Jesus come to repair Judaism? Is the kingdom of God a renovation of the existing arrangement — the same religion with better preaching, a bit of fresh material sewn over the worn places?

The answer is no, and the reason is not that the old garment was bad. God gave it. The law, the temple, the sacrifices, the priesthood were all his own design, and Jesus keeps every one of them — he sends the leper to the priest, he goes to the synagogue weekly, he will keep the Passover. The old garment is not being criticised. It is being finished with, because what it was for has come.

This has to be held carefully in both directions, because the saying gets abused in both.

It is abused by people who use it to junk everything old. New wine, they say, and away goes the creed, the confession, the fifteen centuries of the church's thinking, on the grounds that God is doing a new thing. But the wine in this parable is not new ideas. It is the gospel of the crucified and risen Christ, which is the oldest thing there is.

And it is abused by people who cannot distinguish between the fabric and the pattern — for whom every inherited practice is a doctrine, and any change is apostasy. That is the Pharisees' error exactly, and Jesus is answering it here.

What is genuinely new is not a programme. It is a person, and a covenant sealed in his blood, and a Spirit poured out on ordinary people. Nothing that existed before could hold it — not because the old was worthless, but because it was never designed to.

verseByVerse.quote: And no one puts new wine into old wineskins. If he does, the new wine will burst the skins and it will be spilled, and the skins will be destroyed. But new wine must be put into fresh wineskins.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The same point, with a better image.

Wineskins were made from whole animal hides, sewn and sealed. A new skin was supple and could stretch; fermenting wine gives off gas, and the skin expanded with it. But a skin that had already been through one fermentation was set hard — it had done its stretching, and it had nothing left. Pour actively fermenting wine into it and the pressure has nowhere to go. The skin splits, and you lose both.

Notice what Jesus says is lost: the new wine will burst the skins and it will be spilled, and the skins will be destroyed. Both. This is not a saying about how the old is expendable. It is a warning that forcing new life into hardened forms wastes the life and wrecks the form.

But new wine must be put into fresh wineskins.

And that is the whole prescription. Not: throw away the wine. Not: pretend the old skin is fine. Get the wine into something that can move with it.

The point is not that novelty is good. It is that living things expand, and whatever contains them has to be able to give. That was true of the first Christian generation in the most literal way — within thirty years of this conversation the gospel had gone to Gentiles who did not keep the food laws, met on a different day, had no temple and no priesthood, and were being told that the whole apparatus had been a shadow of what had now come (Col. 2:17). Not because the shadow was false, but because the substance had arrived.

And it remains an honest question for any Christian tradition to put to itself, provided it is put honestly. Not is this old? — age is no argument either way. But: is this form still carrying the life, or has it set hard around a shape the life has outgrown? A wineskin's only job is to hold wine. The moment it starts being valued for itself, it has begun to fail at the one thing it was for.

What must never move is the wine. Everything else is leather.

verseByVerse.quote: And no one after drinking old wine desires new, for he says, ‘The old is good.’'
verseByVerse.commentary:
And no one after drinking old wine desires new, for he says, The old is good.

Luke alone records this line, and it is the most quietly devastating sentence in the chapter. It is also frequently misread, because it sounds at first as though Jesus is conceding the point.

He is not commending old wine. He is describing a palate.

Anyone who knows wine knows the old is better; new wine is raw and still working. That is exactly why the observation lands where it does. Jesus is not making a claim about the merits of the two covenants. He is stating a fact about human beings: having settled into something, we do not want the alternative, and we will always find a reason. The old is good. And so it is. And that is what makes it so hard to leave.

This is the diagnosis of everyone in the doorway at Levi's house, and it explains them better than anything else in the passage. Their problem was never that they had chosen something bad. Their problem was that they had something genuinely good — a real law, given by God; a real tradition, hard-won; real discipline, real reverence, real Scripture — and they were comfortable in it, and it had made the arrival of something better feel like a disturbance rather than a fulfilment.

That is the most dangerous spiritual position there is, and it is not available to obvious sinners. It requires a good thing to settle into. Levi could be reached in two words at his tax booth; the men outside had spent thirty years acquiring a taste that made the new wine unpalatable.

And it is worth asking honestly where the sentence lands now, because it does not only apply to first-century Pharisees. Every long-standing Christian has an accumulated set of preferences — a way of worship, a style of preaching, a shape of church life, a period of hymnody, a translation — much of which is genuinely good and none of which is the gospel. The test is not whether we like the old. Of course we like the old. The test is what happens when God does something that does not taste of it.

Nobody in this chapter refused Jesus because they had examined him and found him wanting. They refused him because they were comfortable, and he was not what they were used to.

5.text: <sup>1</sup> On one occasion, while the crowd was pressing in on him to hear the word of God, he was standing by the lake of Gennesaret, <sup>2</sup> and he saw two boats by the lake, but the fishermen had gone out of them and were washing their nets. <sup>3</sup> Getting into one of the boats, which was Simon's, he asked him to put out a little from the land. And he sat down and taught the people from the boat. <sup>4</sup> And when he had finished speaking, he said to Simon, “Put out into the deep and let down your nets for a catch.” <sup>5</sup> And Simon answered, “Master, we toiled all night and took nothing! But at your word I will let down the nets.” <sup>6</sup> And when they had done this, they enclosed a large number of fish, and their nets were breaking. <sup>7</sup> They signaled to their partners in the other boat to come and help them. And they came and filled both the boats, so that they began to sink. <sup>8</sup> But when Simon Peter saw it, he fell down at Jesus' knees, saying, “Depart from me, for I am a sinful man, O Lord.” <sup>9</sup> For he and all who were with him were astonished at the catch of fish that they had taken, <sup>10</sup> and so also were James and John, sons of Zebedee, who were partners with Simon. And Jesus said to Simon, “Do not be afraid; from now on you will be catching men.” <sup>11</sup> And when they had brought their boats to land, they left everything and followed him. <sup>12</sup> While he was in one of the cities, there came a man full of leprosy. And when he saw Jesus, he fell on his face and begged him, “Lord, if you will, you can make me clean.” <sup>13</sup> And Jesus stretched out his hand and touched him, saying, “I will; be clean.” And immediately the leprosy left him. <sup>14</sup> And he charged him to tell no one, but “go and show yourself to the priest, and make an offering for your cleansing, as Moses commanded, for a proof to them.” <sup>15</sup> But now even more the report about him went abroad, and great crowds gathered to hear him and to be healed of their infirmities. <sup>16</sup> But he would withdraw to desolate places and pray. <sup>17</sup> On one of those days, as he was teaching, Pharisees and teachers of the law were sitting there, who had come from every village of Galilee and Judea and from Jerusalem. And the power of the Lord was with him to heal. <sup>18</sup> And behold, some men were bringing on a bed a man who was paralyzed, and they were seeking to bring him in and lay him before Jesus, <sup>19</sup> but finding no way to bring him in, because of the crowd, they went up on the roof and let him down with his bed through the tiles into the midst before Jesus. <sup>20</sup> And when he saw their faith, he said, “Man, your sins are forgiven you.” <sup>21</sup> And the scribes and the Pharisees began to question, saying, “Who is this who speaks blasphemies? Who can forgive sins but God alone?” <sup>22</sup> When Jesus perceived their thoughts, he answered them, “Why do you question in your hearts? <sup>23</sup> Which is easier, to say, ‘Your sins are forgiven you,’ or to say, ‘Rise and walk’? <sup>24</sup> But that you may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins”—he said to the man who was paralyzed—“I say to you, rise, pick up your bed and go home.” <sup>25</sup> And immediately he rose up before them and picked up what he had been lying on and went home, glorifying God. <sup>26</sup> And amazement seized them all, and they glorified God and were filled with awe, saying, “We have seen extraordinary things today.” <sup>27</sup> After this he went out and saw a tax collector named Levi, sitting at the tax booth. And he said to him, “Follow me.” <sup>28</sup> And leaving everything, he rose and followed him. <sup>29</sup> And Levi made him a great feast in his house, and there was a large company of tax collectors and others reclining at table with them. <sup>30</sup> And the Pharisees and their scribes grumbled at his disciples, saying, “Why do you eat and drink with tax collectors and sinners?” <sup>31</sup> And Jesus answered them, “Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick. <sup>32</sup> I have not come to call the righteous but sinners to repentance.” <sup>33</sup> And they said to him, “The disciples of John fast often and offer prayers, and so do the disciples of the Pharisees, but yours eat and drink.” <sup>34</sup> And Jesus said to them, “Can you make wedding guests fast while the bridegroom is with them? <sup>35</sup> The days will come when the bridegroom is taken away from them, and then they will fast in those days.” <sup>36</sup> He also told them a parable: “No one tears a piece from a new garment and puts it on an old garment. If he does, he will tear the new, and the piece from the new will not match the old. <sup>37</sup> And no one puts new wine into old wineskins. If he does, the new wine will burst the skins and it will be spilled, and the skins will be destroyed. <sup>38</sup> But new wine must be put into fresh wineskins. <sup>39</sup> And no one after drinking old wine desires new, for he says, ‘The old is good.’”

6.title: The Sermon on the Plain
6.overview:
Chapter 6 is Luke's equivalent of Matthew's Sermon on the Mount — shorter, sharper, and structurally parallel, though not identical. Before the sermon comes the choosing of the twelve and two Sabbath controversies that frame the sermon's radical ethics with a theological question: by what authority does Jesus define what is lawful, and what kind of community does that authority create? The Sermon on the Plain (vv. 20–49) is the charter of the kingdom community — the description of what it looks like to live under the reign of God when that reign runs against every instinct of the natural self.

The beatitudes and woes (vv. 20–26) are the most direct statement in the chapter: the kingdom reverses the world's value system. The poor are blessed; the rich are warned. The hungry are filled; the full are emptied. Those who weep now will laugh; those who laugh now will mourn. This is not a promise that poverty is virtuous or that comfort is sinful; it is a statement about the direction of the kingdom. God's attention, God's blessing, God's purposes consistently run toward those whom the world has left behind — and consistently challenge those who have arranged their lives to need nothing from anyone, including God.

The ethical core of the sermon (vv. 27–45) — love your enemies, do not judge, produce good fruit — is the most demanding teaching in Luke's Gospel, and it rests entirely on the character of God. Love your enemies because your Father is kind to the ungrateful and evil. Do not judge because you will be judged by the measure you use. Bear good fruit because the tree is known by its fruit. The final image — the house on the rock — is the sermon's warning: hearing these words is not enough. The one who hears and does not do is building on sand. The storm will come, and only the house that is built on hearing and doing will stand.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — Jesus Is Lord of the Sabbath
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Two Sabbath controversies open the chapter, and together they establish the claim that makes everything in the sermon possible: Jesus is Lord of the Sabbath.

The first is about disciples plucking grain as they walk through fields. Gleaning was expressly permitted (Deut. 23:25), so the objection is not theft; it is that plucking counts as reaping and rubbing as threshing, both forbidden on the Sabbath by the scribal fence built around the commandment.

That fence did not begin in wickedness. It began in a serious desire not to sin, by people whose nation had gone into exile for ignoring precisely this commandment. And it had become unbearable — a gift turned into an audit, a day given to relieve working people now governed by case law only the leisured could master.
