Jesus's response reaches back to 1 Samuel 21:1-6. David, on the run and hungry, ate the bread of the Presence, which the law reserved for priests, and shared it with his men — and Scripture records it without a word of censure. The point is not that rules do not matter. It is that the law of God has an order of priorities inside it, and the ceremonial provision was never meant to override the life it was given to serve. Jesus is not appealing over the head of Scripture; he is appealing to Scripture against a reading of it.

The choice of precedent is not accidental either. Of all the cases available, he reaches for the one about God's anointed king, rejected and on the run, with his own small band of followers, doing what the authorities called unlawful.

Then the conclusion: “The Son of Man is lord of the Sabbath.” He does not argue that the Sabbath is unimportant. He claims that he is the one who determines its meaning — which, given that the Sabbath is rooted in creation, enshrined in the Ten Commandments, and named as the sign of the covenant between the LORD and Israel, is a claim about who he is.

The Pharisees are not wrong to take the Sabbath seriously. They are wrong to think their authority over it exceeds the authority of the one who instituted it.
verseByVerse.theology:
“The Son of Man is lord of the Sabbath” is a divine claim in Jewish ears. The Sabbath is God's own institution — rooted in creation (Gen. 2:2-3), enshrined in the Ten Commandments (Exod. 20:8-11), and described as a sign of the covenant between the LORD and Israel for ever (Exod. 31:12-17).

To be Lord of the Sabbath is to exercise authority over the covenant sign of God himself. Jesus is not relativising the day; he is claiming to be its author. This is among the most compact and most decisive of the implicit claims to deity scattered through the Synoptic Gospels.

And the title he uses to say it is the one from Daniel 7:13-14 — the figure who comes to the Ancient of Days and receives everlasting dominion. It sounds modest in English and was not.

What is worth adding is what this lordship is for. He is not lord of the Sabbath in order to abolish rest, but to give it back. The day always pointed at a person, and the person has arrived.
verseByVerse.examples:
The complaint about grain-plucking is a case study in confusing the purpose of a law with the law itself. The Sabbath was given as a gift — a day of rest for those who worked, and a sign of trust that God would provide without their constant labour.

The Pharisees' elaborate hedge of regulations (the Mishnah tractate on the Sabbath runs to twenty-four chapters) had turned that gift into a burden. When a law loses contact with the grace and wisdom that gave it, it becomes oppression. Jesus does not abolish the Sabbath; he liberates it from the accretion that had buried what it was for.

The sequence is worth watching for, because it is not confined to the first century and does not require bad motives: a good practice, a rule to protect it, a further rule to protect the rule — and, three generations on, people who can tell you exactly what is forbidden and have entirely lost sight of the point.

The test is simple enough to apply. When a religious rule and a hungry person meet, which one does the rule-keeper find himself defending?

verseByVerse.quote: On a Sabbath, while he was going through the grainfields, his disciples plucked and ate some heads of grain, rubbing them in their hands. But some of the Pharisees said, 'Why are you doing what is not lawful to do on the Sabbath?'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Hungry men walking through a field, pulling heads of grain and rubbing the husks off between their palms as they go. It is the most ordinary thing in the chapter, and it starts a fight that ends at a cross.

First, what is not the objection. The Pharisees are not accusing the disciples of theft. The law expressly permitted it: If you go into your neighbour's standing grain, you may pluck the ears with your hand (Deut. 23:25). Israel's law had a built-in provision for the hungry traveller, and the disciples are within it.

The objection is that it is a Sabbath, and that plucking is reaping and rubbing is threshing. Which sounds absurd until you understand where the reasoning came from — and it is worth being fair to them, because caricature makes the passage useless.

The fourth commandment forbids work on the Sabbath and does not define work. So the rabbis, trying to obey, drew up definitions: thirty-nine categories of labour, of which reaping and threshing are two. And around those definitions they built what they called a fence — additional restrictions, so that a man would stop well short of the actual line and never break the commandment by accident. The Mishnah's tractate on the Sabbath runs to twenty-four chapters.

None of that began in wickedness. It began in a serious desire not to sin, by people who had watched their nation go into exile for ignoring precisely this commandment.

And it had become unbearable. A gift had turned into an audit. The day God gave to relieve working people had acquired a body of case law that only the leisured could master, and the men enforcing it were now standing in a cornfield watching hungry men eat.

That is the sequence worth watching for, because it is not confined to the first century and it does not require bad motives. It requires only this: a good practice, a rule to protect it, a further rule to protect the rule — and, three generations on, people who can tell you exactly what is forbidden and have entirely lost sight of what the thing was for.

The test is simple enough to apply. When a religious rule and a hungry person meet, which one does the rule-keeper find himself defending?

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus answered them, 'Have you not read what David did when he was hungry, he and those who were with him: how he entered the house of God and took and ate the bread of the Presence, which is not lawful for any but the priests to eat, and also gave it to those with him?'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus answers with a story from their own Scriptures, and the way he introduces it has an edge: Have you not read…? To men whose life's work was reading.

The episode is 1 Samuel 21. David is on the run from Saul, with a handful of men and no food. He comes to the sanctuary at Nob and asks the priest for bread, and the only bread in the building is the bread of the Presence — twelve loaves set out weekly before the LORD, which the law says plainly is for Aaron and his sons and no one else (Lev. 24:5-9). The priest gives it to him. David eats it, and shares it with his men.

And Scripture does not condemn him. That is the whole force of the citation. The narrative records it without a word of censure, and the anointed king of Israel walks away fed.

Now what is Jesus arguing? Not that rules do not matter, and not that hunger dissolves the law. Something more precise: that the law of God has an order of priorities inside it, and that the ceremonial provision was never meant to override the life it was given to serve. He is not appealing over the head of Scripture. He is appealing to Scripture, against a reading of it.

There is a further thing in the choice of story, and the men listening would have felt it. Why David? Of all the possible precedents — and there were others — he reaches for the one about God's anointed king, on the run, rejected, with his own small band of followers, doing something the authorities would call unlawful.

The parallel is not accidental and it is not subtle. Here is another anointed king, gathering another company, being told by the officials of the day that what he does is not lawful. If David's men could eat, so can his.

Which means the argument is not chiefly about corn at all. It is about who this is — and the next verse says so out loud.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, 'The Son of Man is lord of the Sabbath.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Son of Man is lord of the Sabbath.

Nine words, and they are among the largest claims Jesus ever made.

Consider what the Sabbath was. Not a custom, not a national tradition, not a piece of religious furniture that could be rearranged. It is written into the account of creation itself — God rested on the seventh day and made it holy (Gen. 2:2-3). It stands in the Ten Commandments, spoken by God from the mountain in fire and thunder (Exod. 20:8-11). And it is named as the sign of the covenant between the LORD and Israel for ever: it is a sign forever between me and the people of Israel (Exod. 31:17).

There is no institution in Judaism more directly and personally God's than this one. And a Galilean carpenter says he is its lord.

Take the sentence apart and there is no soft reading available. He does not say the Sabbath is unimportant. He does not say his disciples were within the rabbinic rules after all. He does not say the Pharisees have misapplied a principle. He says that the authority to determine what this day is and how it works belongs to him — which is to say, that he stands where the Lawgiver stands.

A man may say the Sabbath has been misunderstood. Only its author can say he is its lord.

And the title he uses to say it is the one from Daniel 7 again — the figure who comes to the Ancient of Days and receives everlasting dominion. It sounds humble in English; it was not.

So the confrontation that began over a handful of grain has arrived, in five verses, at the question the whole Gospel is about. Not what may be done on the Sabbath but who is this? Every dispute in Luke ends there eventually, and the Pharisees are quite right to be alarmed. Somebody in that cornfield is either speaking blasphemy or telling the truth, and there is no third possibility on offer.

What is worth adding is what this lordship turns out to be for. He is not lord of the Sabbath in order to abolish rest. He is its lord in order to give it back — and in a few chapters he will say what he means: Come to me, all who labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest (Matt. 11:28). The day always pointed at a person. The person has arrived, and he is not standing in the cornfield to take anything away.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–11 — A Man with a Withered Hand
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The second Sabbath controversy involves a man with a withered right hand — which, in a manual economy, meant an inability to earn a living. Luke the physician notes which hand.

The scribes and Pharisees are watching to see whether Jesus will heal, “so that they might find a reason to accuse him.” The watching is calculated and hostile, and it is worth registering how ugly it is: they are in a house of God, on the day of God, hoping a disabled man will be healed so that they can bring a charge. His hand interests them only as evidence.

Jesus knows exactly what they are doing, and he does not avoid the confrontation — he creates it. He tells the man to stand up in the middle, where everyone can see, and puts a question to the room: “Is it lawful on the Sabbath to do good or to do harm, to save life or to destroy it?”

That question is the interpretive key to his whole Sabbath theology, and it is why they cannot answer. They came prepared to argue that healing is work and that a hand withered for years can wait until sundown — a reasonable position on their own terms. Jesus refuses the terms. He removes the neutral square marked “wait until tomorrow”: to be able to relieve suffering and to decline is not inaction but a choice, and it belongs in the other column.

The Sabbath is not a day of inaction. It is a day defined by the character of its author — and the God who rested on the seventh day is the God who sustains life on every day. Their silence answers the question for them.

Then he heals without touching. The man is simply told to stretch out the hand he cannot stretch out, and the strength arrives inside the obedience. There is nothing to accuse.

And the response is fury — the first time in Luke that anyone discusses killing Jesus. It has taken six chapters, and the cause was a question they could not answer and a mercy they could not permit.
verseByVerse.theology:
The hardness that sets in at this point — “they were filled with fury” — begins the trajectory that ends at the cross. The fury is not primarily moral; it is theological. Jesus has publicly claimed authority over the Sabbath, healed in defiance of their interpretation, and refused to be intimidated by their watching.

Every confrontation confirms what they most fear: this man is either a blasphemer or he is what he claims to be. They have decided he is a blasphemer, and from that decision every subsequent action follows with a terrible logic.

Luke's word for their state means, literally, a filling with unreason — a rage that has stopped thinking. It is what a framework does when it has been exposed in public and its owners are unwilling to revise it. The alternative was to admit that a Galilean had understood the law of God better than the men who guarded it, and that admission would have cost them everything they were.

So these Sabbath controversies are not peripheral disputes about religious practice. They are the opening moves of the confrontation that will define history.
verseByVerse.examples:
The man with the withered hand is told to stand up and come out into the middle — to be visible, exposed, in front of everyone. He obeys, knowing his disability will be on display, and Luke records that he rose and stood there.

There is a kind of help that cannot be received privately. The person who keeps their need hidden, who manages a difficulty from the edge of the community, does not receive what the one standing in the middle receives. Jesus consistently calls his healings into the light.

And the command he gives is the one thing the man cannot do — stretching out that hand is the definition of his condition. The healing does not come first so that obedience becomes possible. He is told to do the impossible thing, and discovers in the doing that it is possible.

That is very often the order in the Christian life. The command comes before the strength to keep it, and the strength arrives inside the obedience — which is why so much of following Christ feels like being told to move a hand that does not work.

verseByVerse.quote: On another Sabbath, he entered the synagogue and was teaching, and a man was there whose right hand was withered. And the scribes and the Pharisees watched him, to see whether he would heal on the Sabbath, so that they might find a reason to accuse him. But he knew their thoughts, and he said to the man with the withered hand, 'Come and stand here.' And he rose and stood there.
verseByVerse.commentary:
On another Sabbath. A different day, a different setting, the same question — and this time the stakes are a man's livelihood.

A withered right hand, and Luke the physician notes which one. In a manual economy that is not an inconvenience; it is the end of a man's ability to earn. He is in the synagogue on the Sabbath, as he presumably is every week, with a hand that has not worked for years and no expectation that today will differ.

And the scribes and Pharisees watched him. Luke's verb suggests watching closely, keeping under observation — and he tells us exactly why: so that they might find a reason to accuse him.

Sit with that for a moment, because it is uglier than it first appears. They are in a house of God, on the day of God, and they are hoping a disabled man will be healed so that they can bring a charge. The man's hand is of no interest to them except as evidence. They are not asking whether healing is right; they have already decided, and they are waiting for their case to walk in.

That is what religion becomes when it has stopped serving God and started defending itself. It can sit in a service, look at a suffering man, and see an opportunity.

But he knew their thoughts. Luke says it flatly, as he did at 5:22. Jesus is not walking into this unaware, and what he does next is therefore entirely deliberate.

Come and stand here. Literally, rise and stand in the middle.

He could have healed the man where he sat, quietly, at the end of the service, and nobody could have proved anything. Instead he puts him in the centre of the room, in front of everyone, and makes the confrontation unavoidable.

And the man goes. And he rose and stood there. He has spent years managing a disability from the edge of the room, and he is now standing in the middle of it with his hand exposed and a row of officials staring. He does not know what is coming. He knows he has been called out.

There is a kind of help that cannot be received privately. Some things have to be brought into the middle, in front of people, before anything can be done about them.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus said to them, 'I ask you, is it lawful on the Sabbath to do good or to do harm, to save life or to destroy it?' And after looking around at them all he said to him, 'Stretch out your hand.' And he did so, and his hand was restored.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I ask you, is it lawful on the Sabbath to do good or to do harm, to save life or to destroy it?

The question is deadly, and it is worth seeing why they cannot answer it.

They came prepared for a different argument. Their case was that healing is work, that this man's condition is not life-threatening, and that a hand withered for years can perfectly well wait until sundown — which, on their own terms, is a reasonable position. Even their own tradition permitted saving a life on the Sabbath. Nobody's life is at risk here.

Jesus refuses the terms. He does not ask whether healing counts as work. He asks whether it is lawful to do good — and by pairing it with its opposite he removes the middle ground they were standing on. There is no neutral square marked wait until tomorrow. To be able to relieve suffering and to decline is not inaction. It is a choice about a man, and it belongs in the other column.

That is the principle behind the whole of his Sabbath teaching, and it is not lax. It is stricter than theirs. Their rule asked what may be avoided. His asks what may be done — and a day designed by a God who never stops sustaining his creation cannot be a day for withholding mercy.

And after looking around at them all. Luke pauses the scene. He waits. The look goes round the room, one face at a time, and nobody says anything — and in that silence they have already answered, and they know it.

Stretch out your hand.

Notice that he does not touch him. There is nothing to accuse. A man is told to move, and moves — and even the strictest reckoning could not call that work by anybody.

And notice what is asked. Stretch out your hand is the one thing this man cannot do; it is the definition of his condition. The healing does not come first, so that he could then obey. He is told to do the impossible thing, and in the doing of it he discovers it is possible.

That is very often the order. The command comes before the strength to keep it, and the strength arrives inside the obedience — which is why so much of the Christian life feels like being told to move a hand that does not work.

verseByVerse.quote: But they were filled with fury and discussed with one another what they might do to Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But they were filled with fury and discussed with one another what they might do to Jesus.

Luke's word for their state is a strong one — literally, they were filled with mindlessness, unreason, a rage that has stopped thinking. And it is the response to a man's hand being made whole.

Nothing has been stolen. No law of Moses has been broken — Jesus was careful about that, and did not so much as touch him. A disabled man in their own congregation can work again. And the reaction of the religious leadership of Israel is not merely disagreement but the beginning of a plot.

This is the first time in Luke's Gospel that anybody discusses killing Jesus, and it should be registered as the turning point it is. From here the shadow does not lift. It has taken six chapters, and the cause was a question they could not answer and a mercy they could not permit.

Why such rage? Not because they were unusually wicked men. Because he had made their position untenable in public, and they were not willing to revise it. Fury is what a framework does when it has been exposed and its owners have decided to keep it. The alternative was to admit that a Galilean had understood the law of God better than the men who guarded it, and that admission would have cost them everything they were.

So the mind goes past the argument to the arguer. If the position cannot be defended, remove the man who exposed it.

And it is worth being honest about how ordinary that mechanism is. It does not require a Sanhedrin. It happens in churches, in families, in any relationship where somebody has said something true that cannot be answered — and the response is not to weigh it but to look for a way of discrediting the person who said it. The fury feels like conviction from the inside. It is nearly always the sound of a defence that has run out.

These men went home from a service in which God had healed a cripple in front of them, and began working out how to get rid of him.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Before choosing the twelve, Jesus spends the whole night in prayer on the mountain. This is characteristic of Luke: the major decisions of the ministry are set in the context of prayer. And the placing is deliberate — Luke has just recorded the first plot against Jesus's life, and the next thing he records is a night on a hillside.

The choice of twelve from a larger body of disciples is not made lightly or impulsively. Luke gives the two stages precisely: he called the disciples, and from them he chose twelve.

The number is not convenient; it is theological. Israel had twelve tribes named for twelve sons, and no Jew could hear the number accidentally. Jesus is not assembling a staff. He is constituting a people — and at the end of the Bible the wall of the city has twelve foundations bearing these men's names (Rev. 21:14).

They are called apostles here for the first time in Luke — apostoloi, sent ones. They remain disciples, learners; but a disciple who has been given an errand is something more.

The list itself is a study in unlikely combinations. Peter, who three chapters ago asked Jesus to leave because he was a sinful man. Matthew, the tax collector from the booth. And Simon the Zealot — a man of the party of armed resistance to Rome, whose programme held that collaborators deserved a knife. In ordinary life Matthew and Simon would not have shared a road. They shared a purse and a mission for three years.

Several of the twelve are otherwise unknown: Bartholomew, Thaddaeus, James the son of Alphaeus. No recorded words, no recorded deeds — nothing but a name in three lists.

And the list ends with Judas Iscariot, “who became a traitor.” Luke will not let his reader meet him without the ending attached, and the wording matters: not who was a traitor but who became one. He was chosen after the night of prayer, with the others, and heard and saw everything they did.
verseByVerse.theology:
The apostles are distinguished from disciples by a specific function: they are sent ones, commissioned witnesses rather than merely learners. Their testimony to the life, death and resurrection of Jesus will be the foundation of the church's proclamation.

Paul will later say the church is “built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Christ Jesus himself being the cornerstone” (Eph. 2:20). The night of prayer before the choice establishes that this foundation is not a human selection but a divinely guided one, even though the divine guidance works through a human process.

Luke's parenthesis on Judas — chosen deliberately, after a night of communion with the Father, and yet becoming a traitor — is a weight the reader is not permitted to set down. Election to office is not the same as salvation, and proximity to Christ is no protection.

He handled the money, was sent out with power like the rest, and heard every word of the sermon that follows. The verb Luke chooses describes a process, not a category — which should sober anyone who has been near the things of God for a long time.
verseByVerse.examples:
The night of prayer before the choice models the principle that consequential decisions belong to God before they belong to us. Not every decision requires a night of prayer — but every decision that will shape the community of God's people belongs first to the Father.

The Jesus who spent a whole night praying before choosing twelve men puts a question to every leader, every elder board, every appointment committee: have we prayed as long and as seriously as this decision actually deserves?

And the composition of the twelve is a standing rebuke to congregations divided along political lines. Whatever holds a church together, it is not agreement about Rome, and the New Testament never once suggests it should be.

If a former agent of the Roman revenue and a man committed to the violent overthrow of Rome could eat from the same bag for three years, the divisions that currently make Christians unable to sit in the same room deserve a harder look than they usually get.

verseByVerse.quote: In these days he went out to the mountain to pray, and all night he continued in prayer to God. And when day came, he called his disciples and chose from them twelve, whom he named apostles:
verseByVerse.commentary:
In these days he went out to the mountain to pray, and all night he continued in prayer to God.

Luke has just recorded the first plot against his life. The next thing he records is a night on a hillside.

And this is not a phrase to skim. All night he continued in prayer — the whole night, from dark to first light, alone. Luke has shown us Jesus praying at the Jordan (3:21) and withdrawing to desolate places (5:16). This is the longest, and it comes before the largest personnel decision of his ministry.

It is worth asking what the Son of God was doing out there for eight or nine hours, because the honest answer is that we are not told and it is better not to invent. What Luke gives us is the fact and the proportion: a whole night, for twelve men.

And when day came, he called his disciples and chose from them twelve.

Two stages, and the wording matters. He called the disciples — a larger group; Luke will mention seventy-two of them later — and from that number he chose twelve. This is selection, and it is his, and it comes out of the night.

Twelve is not a convenient number. Israel had twelve tribes, named for twelve sons; a Jew could not hear it accidentally. Jesus is not assembling a staff. He is constituting a people — and the implication is enormous, because a man does not lay the foundations of Israel unless he is entitled to. At the end of the Bible, the wall of the city has twelve foundations, and on them the names of these men (Rev. 21:14).

They are called apostles here for the first time in Luke: apostoloi, sent ones, from the verb to send. The word marks the difference. A disciple is a learner, and they remain that. An apostle has been given an errand.

And there is something quietly steadying in the sequence. The men who now decide he must be destroyed have made their decision by committee, in fury, after a service. His decision was made alone, on a mountain, after a night of asking his Father — and it is the one that is still standing.

verseByVerse.quote: Simon, whom he named Peter, and Andrew his brother, and James and John, and Philip, and Bartholomew, and Matthew, and Thomas, and James the son of Alphaeus, and Simon who was called the Zealot, and Judas the son of James, and Judas Iscariot, who became a traitor.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Twelve names, and Luke sets them down without comment. But look at who is in the list.

Simon, whom he named Peter — a fisherman who three chapters ago asked Jesus to go away because he was a sinful man, given a new name meaning rock, which he will spectacularly fail to live up to before he grows into it.

Matthew — the tax collector from the booth in chapter 5. A man who took money from his own people on behalf of Rome.

Simon who was called the Zealot. And here the list becomes remarkable. The Zealots were the party of armed resistance to Rome — men whose programme was that collaborators should be killed, and who occasionally killed them. Whatever precise stage the movement had reached by this date, the label meant a man of that conviction.

So in one company of twelve, Jesus put a former agent of the Roman revenue and a man who believed such agents deserved a knife. In ordinary life these two would not have shared a road, let alone a purse and a mission. They walked the same country together for three years.

That is worth pausing on, because it is not resolved in the text and Luke does not tell us it was easy. He simply records that both names are there. Whatever holds a church together, it is not political agreement, and the New Testament never once suggests it should be. If Matthew and Simon could eat from the same bag, the divisions that currently make Christians unable to sit in the same room deserve a harder look than they usually get.

Several of the twelve are otherwise unknown — Bartholomew, Thaddaeus, James the son of Alphaeus. No recorded words, no recorded deeds, nothing but a name in three lists. They gave their lives to this and history kept only that they were chosen.

And then the last name, with Luke's terrible parenthesis: Judas Iscariot, who became a traitor.

He is in the list. He was chosen, after the night of prayer, with the others. He heard everything they heard, saw everything they saw, was sent out with power like the rest, and handled the money.

Luke will not let his reader meet him without the ending attached. He does not say who was a traitor. He says who became one — which is a sentence about a process, and it should frighten anyone who has been near the things of God for a long time.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The Sermon on the Plain begins with a declaration that sounds like a mistake on first reading: “Blessed are you who are poor, for yours is the kingdom of God.”

Luke's beatitudes are addressed directly to the disciples — “blessed are you” — unlike Matthew's more generalised forms. And they are paired with woes Matthew does not include. The poor are blessed and the rich are warned; the hungry are promised satisfaction and the full are warned of hunger; those who weep now will laugh, and those who laugh now will mourn.

The poverty is not romanticised. Luke does not say “poor in spirit” but simply “poor” — ptōchoi, the destitute, those with nothing of their own who depend entirely on what others give. This is not a spiritualisation of poverty; it is the announcement that the kingdom belongs to those whose condition leaves no room for self-sufficiency. Not because poverty is virtuous, but because the poor have no resources to trust except God.

Set beside Matthew's “poor in spirit,” the two hold opposite ends of one truth, and neither is safe alone. Luke without Matthew makes an empty purse a ticket. Matthew without Luke lets “poor in spirit” be quietly spiritualised until it costs nothing. Matthew names the poverty God blesses; Luke names the room such people are usually standing in.

The woes are the other edge of the same blade. “Woe” (ouai) is the prophets' word, carrying grief as much as warning (Isa. 5:8-23; Amos 6:1-7). It is not a wish for harm but a declaration that those who have “received their consolation” — a commercial term meaning paid in full — have nothing further outstanding.

The last woe is the most searching: “Woe to you, when all people speak well of you, for so their fathers did to the false prophets.” Israel's true prophets were consistently unwelcome; the popular ones were the ones who told the king what he wanted to hear.

And the final beatitude (vv. 22-23) is the only one about something the disciples bring on themselves. Four escalating forms of social death — hated, excluded, reviled, name thrown out as evil — and the command attached is not endurance but leaping.
verseByVerse.theology:
The beatitudes and woes together express the eschatological reversal — the biblical pattern in which the last days invert the present order. Mary sang it in the Magnificat: the mighty brought down, the humble exalted, the hungry filled, the rich sent away empty.

This is not a programme of economic analysis; it is a prophetic announcement about the direction of God's kingdom. Those whose present condition drives them to dependence on God are in the right position to receive what the kingdom gives; those who can be self-sufficient are in the wrong one.

Read through the whole gospel, these blessings and woes are far more than social reversal — they are anchored in Christ himself, who entered the very conditions he calls blessed. He became poor though he was rich (2 Cor. 8:9), hungered in the wilderness (4:2), wept real tears, and was hated, excluded and reviled for us.

The great reversal is therefore no abstract law of history but a sure thing purchased in him. We are not blessed for managing to be poor or hungry, but by being joined to the One who was made poor that we might be made rich, and who fills the empty out of his own fullness. And the woes are not cruelty but mercy raising its voice — a warning to the comfortable to loosen their grip on thin, passing riches before the day the tables turn.
verseByVerse.examples:
The beatitudes are often preached as comfort to those who suffer, and they are that. But they are also diagnosis and invitation. The question they put to every hearer is: in which column do you find yourself? The sermon does not allow a neutral answer; it creates a crisis of self-knowledge.

And the woes have to be applied honestly, because almost everyone reading them is, by any measure the world has ever used, among the rich. The question is not whether you enjoy good things but where your consolation actually comes from — what steadies you when the day has gone badly. A God who cannot be lost, or an arrangement that can?

“Rejoice in that day, and leap for joy” (v. 23) is the response Jesus commands to persecution — not stoic endurance, not grim determination, but leaping joy. The verb is the one used of the unborn John moving in Elizabeth's womb (1:41).

This is eschatological joy: the joy that knows how the story ends and can afford to leap because the future is secure. It is what Paul means in Romans 8:18 — the sufferings of this present time are not worth comparing with the glory that is to be revealed. The leap is only possible if the landing is sure.

verseByVerse.quote: And he came down with them and stood on a level place, with a great crowd of his disciples and a great multitude of people from all Judea and Jerusalem and the seacoast of Tyre and Sidon, who came to hear him and to be healed of their diseases. And those who were troubled with unclean spirits were cured. And all the crowd sought to touch him, for power came out from him and healed them all.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus comes down from the mountain with the newly chosen twelve and stands on a level place, and Luke builds the scene before a word is preached.

The crowd is enormous and it is deliberately described: all Judea and Jerusalem and the seacoast of Tyre and Sidon. Judea and Jerusalem are the religious heartland. Tyre and Sidon are Gentile — pagan cities on the Phoenician coast, the country Elijah was sent to at 4:26. Luke's map is already the map of Acts.

They come to hear him and to be healed, and both happen. Power came out from him and healed them all — dynamis, and the phrase is striking: something goes out of him. Healing is not a technique he applies. It costs him something.

So the sermon that follows is not addressed to a neutral audience. Every person in earshot has just seen the demonised freed and the sick made well, and many have felt it in their own bodies. When he says blessed are you who are poor, he is saying it to people who have already had evidence.

The setting also raises the question this chapter is famous for. Luke says Jesus came down and stood on a level place; Matthew says he went up on the mountain and sat down (Matt. 5:1). What follows in each has obvious overlap — beatitudes, love of enemies, judge not, the tree and its fruit, the two builders at the end — and equally obvious differences. Matthew runs to three chapters where Luke runs to thirty verses; Luke adds four woes Matthew does not have; Matthew includes long stretches on the law, prayer and fasting that Luke places elsewhere. So: one sermon or two?

Both answers have been held by careful readers and neither damages anything. Some take them as the same occasion from different angles — the phrase Luke uses need not mean flat ground at the foot of a hill; it can as easily mean a plateau or a shelf on the hillside, and Matthew's crowds are equally present. Others take them as two occasions, which is simply what travelling preachers do. Jesus spent perhaps three years saying these things village by village, and no teacher says a thing once. On that reading Matthew records one delivery and Luke another — shorter, sharper, to a different crowd, with the woes added.

Either way the words are his, and the differences are not contradictions but the ordinary shape of a real ministry. The same voice is speaking in both, and it is asking for the same life.

verseByVerse.quote: And he lifted up his eyes on his disciples, and said: 'Blessed are you who are poor, for yours is the kingdom of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he lifted up his eyes on his disciples, and said: Blessed are you who are poor, for yours is the kingdom of God.

Luke's beatitudes are in the second person. Not blessed are the poor but blessed are you — spoken while looking at them, to actual people whose actual circumstances everyone standing there could see.

And Luke's word is ptōchoi, which is not the word for someone of modest means. It means destitute — a beggar, a person with nothing of their own who depends entirely on what others give. Luke uses it consistently that way throughout his Gospel, and his concern for the materially poor is not a modern imposition on the text; it is one of the most obvious features of this book.

So take the sentence at face value first. Jesus looks at a crowd containing day-labourers and widows and people who own nothing anyone would want, and tells them the kingdom of God is theirs. Present tense — yours is. Not a promise for later. Heaven keeps a different ledger from the one the world keeps.

But a reader who knows Matthew will stop here, because Matthew reads blessed are the poor in spirit (Matt. 5:3), and Luke's flat blessed are you who are poor sounds like a different sentence. Did one of them adjust the Lord's words?

Better to see that they hold two ends of one truth, and that neither end is safe alone.

Take Luke without Matthew and you get the error that poverty itself saves — as though an empty purse were a ticket. That would make the gospel a matter of income, and would leave a poor man who trusts in nothing but his own grievance exactly where he was.

Take Matthew without Luke and you get the opposite and far more respectable error: poor in spirit quietly spiritualised until it costs nothing, a humble feeling entertained by comfortable people whose actual lives stay precisely as they were.

Put them together and it stands clear. Matthew names the poverty God blesses — the poverty of a man who knows he has nothing to bring. Luke names where such people are usually found, and it is not where the world looks. It is far easier to know you have nothing when you actually have nothing. Not because God prefers the poor as people, but because money is extraordinarily good at hiding from us the emptiness we all have before him.

Both evangelists are describing the same person: the one with empty hands held out. Matthew names the hands. Luke names the room they are usually standing in.

verseByVerse.quote: 'Blessed are you who are hungry now, for you shall be satisfied. 'Blessed are you who weep now, for you shall laugh.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two more blessings, and both are stated in the plainest possible terms with a now attached.

Blessed are you who are hungry now, for you shall be satisfied. Luke means it as flatly as it sounds — people who did not eat enough yesterday. And the promise is the great reversal Mary had already sung over an unborn child: he has filled the hungry with good things, and the rich he has sent away empty (1:53).

The kingdom does not romanticise an empty stomach. Hunger is not a virtue and Jesus never says it is. What he says is that the condition which the world reads as God's absence is, in his accounting, the condition of people who are about to be filled — and the filling is not a metaphor. There is a table at the end of this book, and the guest list was drawn up from the streets and lanes (14:21).

Blessed are you who weep now, for you shall laugh.

Notice that he does not tell them to stop. There is no instruction here to cheer up, no suggestion that the tears are a failure of faith, no advice about perspective. He lets the weeping stand and puts a date on it.

And the promised end of it is not relief, or peace, or resignation. It is laughter — which is a startling word to use of the far side of grief, and he chose it. The psalmist had reached for the same thing: Those who sow in tears shall reap with shouts of joy (Ps. 126:5). Not a quiet settling. Shouting.

Both blessings turn on that little word now, and it is the hinge of the whole sermon. The hunger is now. The weeping is now. Neither is denied, minimised, or explained. What is denied is that now is the last word about them.

This is not a technique for feeling better, and it will not work as one. It is a claim about how the story ends, made by the only person entitled to make it — and it is worth noticing who is speaking. The one who promises to fill the hungry had gone forty days without food in a desert (4:2). The one who promises laughter to the weeping wept himself at a friend's grave. He is not calling out advice from the dry ground. He has been in the water.

verseByVerse.quote: 'Blessed are you when people hate you and when they exclude you and revile you and spurn your name as evil, on account of the Son of Man! Rejoice in that day, and leap for joy, for behold, your reward is great in heaven; for so their fathers did to the prophets.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The fourth beatitude is the longest, the most specific, and the only one about something the disciples will bring on themselves.

Four verbs, and they escalate. Hate — the inward turn. Exclude — the word for being put out of the synagogue, cut off from the community that was your whole social world. Revile — insult to the face. Spurn your name as evil — literally to throw your name out as a wicked thing, the destruction of a reputation.

That is a complete social death, staged in four moves, and Jesus describes it to men who have followed him for perhaps a few weeks.

And the qualifier is essential: on account of the Son of Man. This is not a blessing on being disliked. There is no promise here for the Christian who is excluded for being rude, or reviled for being a fool, or hated for opinions that have nothing to do with Christ. The clause is narrow on purpose. Persecution counts when it is about him.

Then the command, and it is not what anyone would expect: Rejoice in that day, and leap for joy.

Not endure. Not bear it patiently. Luke's second verb means to skip or jump — it is the word used of the unborn John moving in Elizabeth's womb (1:41). Jesus tells people who are about to lose their standing, their livelihood and their families to jump for joy on the day it happens.

Two reasons are given, and they are the only two available.

The first: your reward is great in heaven. The joy is not about the circumstance; it is about the accounting. Something is being stored where none of this can reach it.

The second is stranger and more comforting: for so their fathers did to the prophets. Exclusion is company. If you are being treated like this, look at who else was — and every one of them turned out to have been right, and every one of them is now honoured by the descendants of the men who threw them out.

The leap is only possible if the landing is certain. Nobody jumps in the dark. What makes this command sane rather than cruel is that the man giving it knows exactly how the story ends, and is himself, within three years, going to be hated, excluded, reviled, and have his name thrown out as evil.

verseByVerse.quote: 'But woe to you who are rich, for you have received your consolation. 'Woe to you who are full now, for you shall be hungry. 'Woe to you who laugh now, for you shall mourn and weep.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the other edge, and Luke is the only evangelist who records it.

The word is ouai — woe. It is not a curse and not a wish for harm. It is the cry of the Old Testament prophets, and it carries grief in it as much as warning: Isaiah's woe to those who join house to house (Isa. 5:8), Amos's woe to those who are at ease in Zion (Amos 6:1). It is the sound a man makes looking at people walking towards a cliff.

Woe to you who are rich, for you have received your consolation.

The phrase you have received is a commercial term — it is the word used on a receipt, meaning paid in full. That is the whole argument in one verb. It is not that the rich are excluded. It is that they have already collected. The account has been settled, the comfort has been drawn, and there is nothing further outstanding.

Woe to you who are full now, for you shall be hungry. Woe to you who laugh now, for you shall mourn and weep. Each woe is the exact mirror of a blessing, and each turns on the same now.

And this has to be applied honestly, because almost everyone reading it is, by any measure the world has ever used, among the rich. It will not do to hurry past into a general observation about the dangers of materialism.

So let it be put as a question rather than an accusation, since that is how Jesus put it. Where is your consolation actually coming from? Not what you would say in church — what actually steadies you when the day has gone badly. A God who cannot be lost, or an arrangement that can?

Because the danger these verses describe is not enjoying good things. It is being consoled by them — reaching a level of comfort at which the kingdom stops sounding like news and starts sounding like an optional extra for people whose lives are not working.

Which is why the rich, in Luke's Gospel, are so consistently in trouble. Not because God dislikes them. Because a man who has been paid already does not come to collect.

verseByVerse.quote: 'Woe to you, when all people speak well of you, for so their fathers did to the false prophets.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Woe to you, when all people speak well of you, for so their fathers did to the false prophets.

This is the most searching sentence in the sermon, and it is aimed squarely at anyone who speaks for God.

The logic is exact. Israel had true prophets and false ones, and there was a reliable way to tell them apart from the outside — not their doctrine, which took discernment, but their popularity. The true prophets were nearly always unwelcome. Jeremiah was thrown into a cistern. Micaiah was kept in prison on bread and water because he never prophesied good concerning the king (1 Kgs. 22:8). Amos was told to go and prophesy somewhere else. Elijah was the most wanted man in the kingdom.

The false prophets, meanwhile, were doing very well. They had access, standing, and a hearing at court, and the reason is not mysterious: they told people what people wanted to be told. Peace, peace, when there was no peace (Jer. 6:14).

So Jesus offers his hearers a diagnostic that cannot be faked, and it is uncomfortable in exactly the direction nobody wants. If everyone is speaking well of you, something has gone wrong. Either you have said nothing worth opposing, or you have said what people wanted to hear.

Two guards are needed, because this verse is easy to misuse.

It is not a licence for being obnoxious. Some people are disliked for reasons that have nothing to do with Christ, and a man who has made himself unpleasant may console himself that he is being persecuted when he is only being avoided. The beatitude four verses earlier was carefully limited — on account of the Son of Man — and this woe carries the same limit.

Nor is it a rule that a Christian must always be in conflict. Scripture elsewhere expects believers to have a good reputation with outsiders (1 Tim. 3:7), and Luke will shortly commend a centurion whom the whole town liked.

What it forbids is the pursuit of universal approval by a man who is meant to be carrying a message. There is a particular temptation, in preaching and in ordinary Christian conversation, to shave the corners off — to find the version of the truth that will not cost anything with this person, in this room. It works. Everyone speaks well of you.

And that is precisely what the false prophets did, and every one of them was well liked, and every one of them was wrong.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
“But I say to you who hear: Love your enemies, do good to those who hate you, bless those who curse you, pray for those who abuse you.” This is probably the most demanding ethical command in the New Testament, and it is not an aspiration but an imperative, repeated in four parallel forms.

All four are verbs of action, and none is a verb of feeling — which matters enormously for anyone who has read this and concluded they cannot do it. He does not command warm feelings; he commands treatment. And the four escalate in cost: do good can be done at a distance; bless requires words; pray for is hardest, because it cannot be done insincerely for long.

The natural instinct is reciprocity — love those who love you, do good to those who do good to you. Jesus points out that reciprocal love proves nothing: “even sinners love those who love them.” It requires no faith and no change of heart; self-interest produces it unaided. The question the passage forces is whether anything in a Christian's life could not have been produced by ordinary human decency.

The ground of the command is not the worthiness of the enemy. There is no suggestion that the enemy deserves love. The ground is the character of God, “for he is kind to the ungrateful and the evil.” The disciple who loves enemies is not performing an act of heroic willpower; he is showing a family resemblance.

The concrete instructions in vv. 29-30 — the cheek, the cloak, the beggar, the goods taken — have been read both as absolute commands and as radical illustrations of a disposition. What is certain is their subject: a backhanded blow was an insult to honour, and the cloak is a lawsuit. These are about personal affront and personal loss, and what is forbidden is the reflex of retaliation and the worship of one's own dignity.

They are not, and have never been, a command to remain within reach of violence. Jesus walked away from a crowd that meant to kill him (4:29-30); Paul invoked his citizenship against an unlawful flogging (Acts 16:37).

“Be merciful, even as your Father is merciful” (v. 36) is the summary — and mercy presupposes a real debt and then declines to collect it.
verseByVerse.theology:
The command to love enemies is the most radical expression of grace in the New Testament — and it is exactly what God has done towards his own. “God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us… while we were enemies we were reconciled to God by the death of his Son” (Rom. 5:8, 10).

The cross is the supreme act of love towards enemies. The disciple who loves an enemy is not doing something beyond what God has done; he is doing what has already been done to him, and doing it because he received it. The ethics of the sermon flow from its gospel: we love because he first loved us (1 John 4:19).

Luke's “be merciful, even as your Father is merciful” is a different formulation from Matthew's “be perfect, as your heavenly Father is perfect” (Matt. 5:48), and the difference is instructive. Matthew names the standard; Luke names the specific attribute this whole section reflects. In a passage about enemies, what perfection looks like is mercy.

And the order can never be reversed. Nobody loves their enemies into becoming a child of God. It is because he loved his enemies that there is anybody in the family at all — which is also why the sentence begins “your Father,” addressed to people who already hold the position they are being asked to display.
verseByVerse.examples:
The command to love enemies has been the most transformative teaching in Christian history — the basis of martyrdom (Stephen dying while forgiving, Acts 7:60), of peacemaking, of every real reconciliation in the church's story.

It has also been the teaching most frequently domesticated into something manageable: being pleasant to people who are slightly difficult, or to former enemies who are now friends. The test is not whether we are kind to the kind. It is what we do with the person who is actively hostile, who has genuinely wronged us, and who continues to wish us harm.

The Golden Rule (v. 31) has parallels in nearly every ethical tradition — and almost all of them state it negatively: do not do to others what you would not want done to you. A man can keep that rule perfectly by doing nothing at all.

Jesus states it positively, which cannot be kept by inaction. It requires initiative, imagination, and going towards somebody at your own cost without being asked. And there is a mercy in how he frames it: he does not ask for an abstract theory of the good but for the one piece of moral knowledge nobody lacks — how you would want to be treated — applied in the other direction.

verseByVerse.quote: 'But I say to you who hear, Love your enemies, do good to those who hate you, bless those who curse you, pray for those who abuse you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But I say to you who hear. The qualifier is not decoration. Jesus is about to say the hardest thing in the sermon, and he marks off in advance the people who are actually listening.

Then four commands, in four parallel lines, all aimed at the same target.

Love your enemies. Do good to those who hate you. Bless those who curse you. Pray for those who abuse you.

The first thing to notice is that all four are verbs of action, and none is a verb of feeling. That matters enormously for anyone who has read this and concluded they cannot do it. He does not command warm feelings towards a person who has wronged you; he commands treatment. You do not have to like your enemy to do good to him, and the command does not wait for the emotion to arrive.

The second thing is that the enemy is real. Luke gives four words for what this person is doing — hating, cursing, abusing — and none of them describes a mild difficulty. Jesus is not talking about a colleague who irritates you. He is talking about somebody who wishes you harm and is acting on it.

And the four commands escalate in cost. Do good is an action, which can be done at a distance and without much of yourself. Bless requires words, and words about a person come out of somewhere. Pray for is the hardest, because it cannot be done insincerely for long. It is very difficult to keep asking God to be good to somebody and go on hating them; one or the other will give way, which is presumably the point.

There is a practical order in that worth using. Nobody arrives at loving an enemy by working on their feelings. It generally goes the other way round — an act, then a word, then a prayer, and somewhere in the third the heart begins to move.

And two guards. This is not a command to pretend nothing happened; forgiveness in Scripture never requires the pretence that the wrong was not a wrong. Nor is it a command to remain within reach of harm; the next entry deals with that directly. What is forbidden is the natural, satisfying, entirely human project of returning what was given.

verseByVerse.quote: To one who strikes you on the cheek, offer the other also, and from one who takes away your cloak do not withhold your tunic either. Give to everyone who begs from you, and from one who takes away your goods do not demand them back.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Four illustrations, and they are meant to shock. A blow to the face, a coat taken, a beggar's hand, goods carried off — and in each case the response is the opposite of the reflex.

The first needs its background. A strike on the cheek, in that culture, was normally a backhanded blow, and it was not primarily an assault. It was an insult — the way a superior humiliated an inferior, the way an argument was ended by putting a man in his place. It appears in rabbinic law under fines for damaged honour rather than damaged bodies.

So to offer the other cheek is not to invite a beating. It is to refuse the humiliation on its own terms — to decline to be drawn into the exchange the insult was designed to start.

Now something must be said plainly here, because few verses in the Bible have been so cruelly misused. Turn the other cheek has been quoted to battered wives, to abused children, to the bullied and the trafficked, to tell them Christ requires them to stay and keep absorbing the blows. He requires no such thing, and it is a wickedness to say he does.

Look again at what he is describing: an insult to a man's honour, and a lawsuit over a coat. This is about personal affront and personal loss — the wound to pride and pocket that makes us itch to hit back and stand on our rights. What is forbidden is the reflex of retaliation and the worship of our own dignity. He is not handing a violent man a licence, and he is not telling his victim to hold still.

Jesus himself walked away from a crowd that meant to kill him (4:29-30). Paul, no coward, invoked his Roman citizenship against an unlawful flogging (Acts 16:37; 22:25) and let the believers lower him over a wall in a basket rather than be murdered (Acts 9:25). And the same love that will not retaliate for itself is fiercely bound to protect the weak — sometimes from the very person harming them.

So if you are being harmed, hear this clearly. Getting to safety is not a failure of this verse. Removing yourself or a child from a violent home, calling for help, insisting that the law do its work — none of that is retaliation, and none of it is forbidden here.

What dies in these verses is the right to hit back for your own honour. Not the duty to keep the defenceless, including yourself, out of the reach of evil.

verseByVerse.quote: And as you wish that others would do to you, do so to them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And as you wish that others would do to you, do so to them.

It is the most famous sentence Jesus ever spoke about ethics, and it sits here for a reason: it is the engine of everything around it. The commands on either side are extraordinary and difficult; this is the principle that makes them intelligible rather than arbitrary.

Versions of the rule existed before him and outside him. Hillel, a generation earlier, summarised the law as what is hateful to you, do not do to your neighbour. Confucius said something similar; so did the Stoics; so does most of the ethical thinking of the human race. It is one of the few moral instincts that turns up everywhere.

And almost every version of it is negative. Do not do. Refrain. Abstain.

Jesus states it positively, and the difference is not cosmetic. The negative form can be satisfied by a man who does nothing at all. Sit still, harm nobody, and you have kept it perfectly — which is why it is such a comfortable rule and why it has been so widely admired.

The positive form cannot be kept by inaction. It requires initiative. It requires imagining what you would want if you were in that person's position, and then going and doing it, at your own cost, without being asked.

Consider what that means for the man on the other side of these verses — the enemy, the one who struck you, the one who took your coat. The negative rule permits you to leave him alone, which is very nearly what you wanted to do anyway. The positive rule asks what you would want if you were him, and sends you towards him.

There is also a hidden mercy in the way it is framed. Jesus does not ask you to work out an abstract theory of the good. He tells you to use the one piece of moral knowledge nobody lacks — the vivid, detailed, entirely reliable understanding of how you would like to be treated. Every person alive is an expert in that. He simply says: apply it in the other direction.

And there is a test in it that is uncomfortably easy to run. Take the person you are currently having difficulty with, and ask what you would want from them if the positions were exactly reversed. The answer arrives immediately. It always does. That is the whole trouble with this verse.

verseByVerse.quote: 'If you love those who love you, what benefit is that to you? For even sinners love those who love them. And if you do good to those who do good to you, what benefit is that to you? For even sinners do the same. And if you lend to those from whom you expect to receive, what credit is that to you? Even sinners lend to sinners, to get back the same amount.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Three questions, all the same shape, and each one dismantles a way of feeling good about yourself.

If you love those who love you, what benefit is that to you? For even sinners love those who love them.

The word translated benefit is charis — the word for grace. What Jesus is asking, quite literally, is: what grace is there in that? And the answer is none, because grace by definition is unearned, and love returned for love is a transaction that has been earned.

Then the same move twice more, covering the three main forms of human exchange: affection, kindness, money. Do good to those who do good to you — a favour repaid. Lend to those from whom you expect to receive — credit extended against security. Each is perfectly respectable, and each is done by everyone.

That is the sting. Jesus's comparison is not with wicked people but with ordinary people. Even sinners — a word that in this Gospel means the openly disreputable, the ones the Pharisees would not eat with. Even they manage reciprocal love. It requires no faith, no Spirit, no change of heart whatever. Self-interest produces it unaided.

So the question the passage forces is not am I a decent person? Most people are, in this sense, and it proves nothing. The question is whether there is anything in your life that self-interest could not have produced.

And that is a harder audit than it sounds, because reciprocity is very good at looking like generosity. The friendships that are mutually enjoyable. The kindnesses to people who will be pleased and will say so. The giving that goes where thanks will come back. None of it is wrong. All of it would happen anyway.

Jesus is not condemning any of these things. He is saying they establish nothing about who you belong to — and that if the whole of a Christian's love could be accounted for by ordinary human decency, then something is missing that the gospel was supposed to have put there.

The test is not the warmth of your affections. It is whether anything you do costs you something that will never be returned.

verseByVerse.quote: But love your enemies, and do good, and lend, expecting nothing in return, and your reward will be great, and you will be sons of the Most High, for he is kind to the ungrateful and the evil.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But love your enemies, and do good, and lend, expecting nothing in return.

The three questions are answered by repeating the three commands with the reciprocity stripped out. And that last phrase is the one that bites: expecting nothing in return. Not lending at generous rates. Not lending patiently. Lending with the expectation of repayment removed from the transaction — which, in plain terms, is giving with paperwork.

Then two things are promised, and the second is far larger than the first.

Your reward will be great. Notice that Jesus has no embarrassment about reward. He does not say the disciple should want nothing; he says the disciple should stop expecting it from the debtor and start expecting it from God. The money is not written off. It is transferred to a different account.

And you will be sons of the Most High.

This is the real payment, and it needs unpacking. In Hebrew idiom, to be called the son of something is to bear its character — sons of thunder, son of encouragement, sons of disobedience. To be a son of the Most High is to be recognisably like him.

And then the reason, which is the whole theology of the sermon in nine words: for he is kind to the ungrateful and the evil.

Not kind to the deserving. Not kind to those who respond well. Kind to the ungrateful — people who take what he gives and never once acknowledge where it came from. Kind to the evil — people actively opposed to him. The sun comes up over both. The rain falls on both. Every meal an atheist eats came out of the ground God keeps making fruitful.

So the command to love enemies is not an arbitrary height set for spiritual athletes. It is a description of the family resemblance. God has been doing this since the world began, and he did the ultimate version of it at a cost nobody had guessed: while we were enemies we were reconciled to God by the death of his Son (Rom. 5:10).

That is the order, and it cannot be reversed. Nobody loves their enemies into becoming a child of God. It is because he loved his enemies that there is anybody in the family at all.

verseByVerse.quote: Be merciful, even as your Father is merciful.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Be merciful, even as your Father is merciful.

One sentence, and it is the summary of everything from verse 27 onwards.

Matthew's version of this line reads be perfect, as your heavenly Father is perfect (Matt. 5:48). Luke's word is merciful, and the difference is worth having, because the two are saying the same thing from different sides. Matthew names the standard; Luke names the specific divine attribute the whole passage has been describing. In a section about enemies, what perfection looks like is mercy.

And mercy needs defining, because it is a word people use warmly without knowing what it means. Mercy is not being nice. It is not tolerance, and it is not the belief that the offence was minor. Mercy is what happens when someone deserves one thing and is given another — it presupposes a real debt, and then declines to collect it.

Which means mercy can only exist where there is a genuine wrong. You cannot be merciful to someone who has not injured you; you can only be pleasant to them. The command therefore requires that the injury be taken seriously — named, understood as an injury — and then not paid back. Any account of forgiveness that begins by minimising what happened has skipped the only step that makes mercy possible.

Then the standard: as your Father is merciful. Not as much as you can manage. Not proportionate to the offence. The measure given is God's own conduct, which is the reason this command can never be marked complete.

And it is the reason it is not crushing. The sentence begins with your Father. It is addressed to people who are already in the family, who have already received exactly the treatment they are being told to give, and who are not being asked to earn a position they already hold.

That is the whole logic of the sermon in miniature. The mercy comes first, from him, at the cross, unearned and unasked. The command comes second, and it is not be merciful in order to become his. It is: you have seen how your Father behaves. Do it like that.

Nothing in this section is possible for someone who has not been on the receiving end of it. Everything in it becomes possible, slowly, for someone who has.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 37–45 — Judging Others and the Tree and Its Fruit
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The teaching on judging (vv. 37-42) and on fruit (vv. 43-45) form one unit held together by the theme of discernment: how we assess others and ourselves.

“Judge not” is one of the most misquoted sentences in the Bible, taken to mean that no moral assessment of anyone is ever permitted. It cannot mean that. Four verses later Jesus tells his hearers to remove the log from their own eye so that they will see clearly to remove a brother's speck — an instruction to make a judgement, having first qualified oneself to make it. Two verses after that he explains how to tell a good tree from a bad one.

What is forbidden is not discernment about conduct but condemnation — pronouncing a verdict on a person, assigning their final worth and destiny. That work belongs to a court, and there is only one. The difference is felt easily enough: “that was a lie” assesses an act; “he is a liar” delivers a summary of a life, and requires access to motives and history that no human being has.

The image of the measure in v. 38 is from a grain market: filled, pressed down to compact it, shaken so the grains settle, then heaped until it spills over into the fold of a man's garment. It is not a level measure. It is a merchant who has decided to be ridiculous.

The blind guide and the log-and-speck follow, and the comedy is deliberate. A man with a plank in his eye leaning in to extract a splinter is an optical impossibility, and the audience can see it. Note that Jesus does not say “leave the speck alone.” The brother is still to be helped; what is corrected is the order. “First take the log out of your own eye, and then you will see clearly.”

The tree-and-fruit teaching is the positive counterpart: character produces conduct. This is not moralism — it does not say “try harder to produce good fruit.” It is a statement about the direction of causation. The fruit reveals the tree; what a person does consistently reveals what they are.

And the source is the treasury of the heart: “out of the abundance of the heart his mouth speaks.” Literally, out of the overflow. Speech is not what a person decides to say; it is what spills when the container is full and nobody is watching.
verseByVerse.theology:
The measure-for-measure principle of v. 38 recurs across both testaments (Matt. 7:2; Rom. 2:1; Jas. 2:13). It is not mechanical karma but a reflection of God's character — the God who shows himself merciful to the merciful and severe to the severe (Ps. 18:25-26).

The warning is not that God will be unkind to those who judge. It is that a person who approaches God without mercy will meet his justice applied with the rigour they themselves used. Someone who has received grace and then withholds mercy has fundamentally misunderstood what grace is.

The word “hypocrite” at v. 42 needs care. In ordinary English it means a conscious fraud. But the man Jesus describes genuinely does not see the log — it is stated twice. The hypocrisy is not deliberate pretence but a failure of self-knowledge so complete that the man is entirely sincere.

Which is more frightening, not less. A conscious fraud could stop. This man is doing his best — and the blind guide of v. 39 is in the same condition, sincerely certain he knows the way, which is exactly why the pit is certain.
verseByVerse.examples:
The log-and-speck has a sharp application for every relationship involving authority: parents with children, leaders with congregations, employers with employees, elders with members. The right to speak into another person's life is not conferred by position; it is earned or forfeited by the quality of one's own self-examination.

The mentor who has faced his own worst and found mercy at the bottom of it can be trusted with somebody else's failure, because he is no longer using it to feel better about himself. There is a practical test before speaking: ask what this conversation will cost you, and whether you are looking forward to it.

“Everyone when he is fully trained will be like his teacher” (v. 40) is one of the most useful sentences in the New Testament for anyone choosing whom to learn from. Formation works. The ceiling of what you become is set by the person you follow, whether or not you intend it.

And “out of the abundance of the heart his mouth speaks” (v. 45) is the most usable diagnostic Jesus gave. Not what a person says when trying to impress, but what comes out when they are tired, unobserved, or talking about people who are not in the room. That is the overflow, and it is a straight readout of the treasury. Nor can it be fixed by monitoring speech — that produces a careful hypocrite. What must change is the treasury, and only one person restocks it.

verseByVerse.quote: 'Judge not, and you will not be judged; condemn not, and you will not be condemned; forgive, and you will be forgiven; give, and it will be given to you. Good measure, pressed down, shaken together, running over, will be put into your lap. For with the measure you use it will be measured back to you.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Four commands in a row, two negative and two positive, each with a consequence attached.

Judge not, and you will not be judged. These are probably the three most quoted words of Jesus in the modern world, and they are quoted almost entirely wrongly — usually to mean that no one may ever assess anyone's conduct, which would make the sentence unusable and its speaker inconsistent.

Jesus cannot mean that, and the proof is in the surrounding paragraph. Four verses later he tells his hearers to take the log out of their own eye so that they will see clearly to take out the speck from a brother's — which is an instruction to make a judgement, having first qualified yourself to make it. Two verses after that he explains how to tell a good tree from a bad one by its fruit. And he has just called some men hypocrites.

The word here is about condemning — pronouncing a verdict on a person, assigning them their final worth and destiny. That is a work that belongs to a court, and there is only one. What is forbidden is not discernment about conduct but the taking of the judge's seat over a life.

The distinction is practical and it is not hard to feel. There is a difference between that was a lie and he is a liar; between assessing what a person did and delivering a summary of what they are. The first is often required of us. The second requires access to information — motives, history, what a person was given to work with, what they have resisted — that no human being has.

Then the positives: forgive, and you will be forgiven; give, and it will be given to you.

And the image Luke uses for the giving is from a grain market, and it is worth seeing. A measure is filled, then pressed down to compact it, then shaken together so the grains settle, then heaped until it spills — and poured into the fold of a man's outer garment, which he held out as a bag. This is not a level measure. It is a merchant who has decided to be ridiculous.

For with the measure you use it will be measured back to you.

That is not a transaction and it is not karma. It is a description of how the same person meets God at both ends: the one who has understood mercy well enough to give it is the one who will know what to do with it when it comes.

verseByVerse.quote: He also told them a parable: 'Can a blind man lead a blind man? Will they not both fall into a pit? A disciple is not above his teacher, but everyone when he is fully trained will be like his teacher.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two short sayings, and Luke has placed them exactly where they explain the one before.

Can a blind man lead a blind man? Will they not both fall into a pit?

It is a joke with a knife in it. The picture is obviously absurd, and the audience would have laughed, and then stopped laughing — because they knew who it was aimed at. The men who had been watching him in the synagogue, hoping to build a charge out of a crippled hand, were the recognised guides of Israel. Jesus has just described the man who cannot see his own log while extracting a speck. Here is what happens when such a man takes on followers.

Note that the blind guide is sincere. Nobody in the parable is lying. He genuinely believes he knows the way, which is exactly why the pit is certain. A guide who knew he was blind would stop.

A disciple is not above his teacher, but everyone when he is fully trained will be like his teacher.

This is the sober half, and it is one of the most useful sentences in the New Testament for anyone choosing whom to learn from.

The claim is simply that formation works. A trained disciple ends up resembling the man who trained him — not partly, not in some respects, but characteristically. Which means the ceiling of what you will become is set by the person you are following, and it is set whether or not you intend it.

Two things follow, and both are practical.

The first is a question about intake. Whose voice is actually forming you? Not whose books are on the shelf, but whose sentences come out of your mouth when you are tired — the preacher you always listen to, the writer whose tone you have absorbed, the friend whose judgement you find yourself repeating. You are going to end up like them. That is not a warning against having teachers; it is an argument for choosing them deliberately.

The second is a warning to anyone who teaches. You are not merely transmitting content. You are reproducing yourself, including the parts you would rather not pass on — and the reproduction will be more thorough than the instruction.

Which is why the sermon's own answer to the whole problem is a person rather than a syllabus. There is one teacher whose disciples, fully trained, will be like him, and that is not a disaster.

verseByVerse.quote: Why do you see the speck that is in your brother's eye, but do not notice the log that is in your own eye? How can you say to your brother, ‘Brother, let me take out the speck that is in your eye,’ when you yourself do not see the log that is in your own eye? You hypocrite, first take the log out of your own eye, and then you will see clearly to take out the speck that is in your brother's eye.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The picture is comic, and the comedy is doing the work. A man with a plank of wood protruding from his eye socket, leaning in with great concern to remove a splinter from somebody else's. Jesus is not describing a moral failing so much as an optical impossibility, and everyone listening can see it.

What he is describing is the most reliable feature of human moral vision: our resolution is astonishing at range and useless up close. We can detect a small fault in another person — an evasion in their tone, a self-serving detail in their account, an inconsistency between what they said last week and this — with real precision. And we walk about with structural failures of our own that everybody else can see from across a room.

The word he uses for such a man is hypocrite, and it is worth being exact about it. In ordinary English that means a conscious fraud, a man who knows he is play-acting. But the picture Jesus draws is of somebody who genuinely does not see the log — that is stated twice. The hypocrisy here is not deliberate pretence.
