She found out where he was. And she went — into the house of a Pharisee, which is the last building in that town where a woman like her would be welcome, carrying something expensive.

She had already worked out what she was going to do before she got there. The flask was bought, or fetched, or dug out from wherever such things were kept.

verseByVerse.quote: and standing behind him at his feet, weeping, she began to wet his feet with her tears and wiped them with the hair of her head and kissed his feet and anointed them with the ointment.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Luke slows down and gives five actions in a single sentence, and every one of them is a scandal.

Standing behind him at his feet. She takes the only position available to her, which is also the lowest place in the room.

Weeping. Luke does not say why. She has not been rebuked, and nothing has yet happened. Whatever this is, it started before she arrived.

She began to wet his feet with her tears. The verb is the one used of rain falling. This is not a discreet tear or two; there are enough of them to wash the dust off a man's feet, and they keep coming.

And wiped them with the hair of her head. Here the room would have gone very quiet. A respectable woman did not unbind her hair in public; it was done at her wedding, and after that in private, and to loosen it in front of men was so improper that it appears in rabbinic discussion as grounds for divorce. She takes down her hair in a Pharisee's dining room, in front of his guests, and uses it as a towel.

And kissed his feet. Luke's verb is continuous — she kept kissing them, over and over. The feet: the dirtiest part of a man in a sandalled country, the part a slave washed.

And anointed them with the ointment. The flask was alabaster, which was how the costly ointments were kept. And she pours it on his feet — not his head, which is where you anoint a guest of honour. She does not consider herself entitled to his head.

Now the thing to see. Every one of these acts is either socially ruinous or physically degrading, and she does not appear to notice.

She is not performing; there is no sign she is aware of the audience at all. She is not negotiating; she asks for nothing and says nothing — she is the only major figure in this chapter who never speaks. She is not trying to earn something, and the parable Jesus is about to tell will make that explicit: the debt was cancelled first, and this is what came after.

She has already forfeited her reputation years ago, and now she spends what is left of her dignity in about ninety seconds, in public, on a man's feet — because she has been forgiven, and there is nothing else she can think of to do with it.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when the Pharisee who had invited him saw this, he said to himself, 'If this man were a prophet, he would have known who and what sort of woman this is who is touching him, for she is a sinner.' And Jesus answering said to him, 'Simon, I have something to say to you.' And he answered, 'Say it, Teacher.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now when the Pharisee who had invited him saw this, he said to himself.

Simon says nothing out loud. He is far too well brought up for a scene at his own table. The whole objection happens behind his face.

If this man were a prophet, he would have known who and what sort of woman this is who is touching him, for she is a sinner.

The logic is tidy and it is worth laying out, because Simon is not a fool. A prophet has supernatural knowledge; a prophet who knew what she was would not let her touch him; this man is letting her touch him; therefore either he does not know, or he does not care — and either way, he is not a prophet.

What Simon cannot conceive is a third possibility: that Jesus knows exactly what she is, better than Simon does, and is letting her touch him anyway.

Notice also the two words he uses of her — who and what sort. He wants Jesus to know not merely her name but her category. She is, in his mind, a type before she is a person, and the type is the whole of what needs to be said.

And Jesus answering said to him, Simon, I have something to say to you.

Luke's word is answering. Simon has not spoken. Jesus answers him anyway — which is the third time in this Gospel that he replies to an unspoken thought (5:22; 6:8), and it disposes of Simon's question before the conversation has properly started. Simon wanted to know whether this man had prophetic knowledge. He has just had a demonstration and has not noticed.

And observe how it is done. Not I know what you are thinking, and it is disgraceful. He uses the man's name and asks for permission to speak. There is no ambush and no humiliation in front of the guests — a courtesy, incidentally, that Simon had not extended to him.

Say it, Teacher.

Simon is polite, and he is condescending. Teacher is a perfectly respectful word, and it is a good deal less than Lord, which is what the centurion called him in verse 6 without ever having met him.

verseByVerse.quote: 'A certain moneylender had two debtors. One owed five hundred denarii, and the other fifty. When they could not pay, he cancelled the debt of both. Now which of them will love him more?' Simon answered, 'The one, I suppose, for whom he cancelled the larger debt.' And he said to him, 'You have judged rightly.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The parable is four sentences long and it dismantles the room.

A certain moneylender had two debtors. One owed five hundred denarii, and the other fifty.

A denarius was a day's wage for a labourer. So the debts are roughly twenty months' wages and roughly two months' wages — a serious difference, and both figures are real money. Neither man is being teased with a trifle.

When they could not pay, he cancelled the debt of both.

Two things are established in one clause, and both matter. First, neither man could pay — the difference in the size of the debts made no difference whatever to the outcome, because fifty denarii a man does not have is as unpayable as five hundred. Second, the cancelling is entirely the lender's act. Nobody negotiated. Nobody offered instalments.

The Greek for cancelled is echarisato — from charis, grace. He graced them both.

Now which of them will love him more?

And Simon walks into it, with a small hedge that gives him away: The one, I suppose, for whom he cancelled the larger debt.

That I suppose is beautifully observed. He can see the answer coming and he can also see that it is going somewhere he will not enjoy, so he answers correctly and holds it at arm's length. It is the tone of a man who has just realised he is in a conversation he did not start.

You have judged rightly.

Now hold on to what the parable does and does not say, because this is the theological hinge of the whole scene and it is regularly got backwards.

The love does not produce the cancellation. In the story, the cancelling comes first, and the loving comes after, and it comes in proportion to how much was cancelled. Love is the effect. Grace is the cause.

Which means the question the parable leaves hanging over Simon's dining table is not who is the better person? It is: how big do you think your debt was? Simon is not being told that he is unforgiven. He is being told that his estimate of what he owed is the reason his welcome was so cool.

verseByVerse.quote: Then turning toward the woman he said to Simon, 'Do you see this woman? I entered your house; you gave me no water for my feet, but she has wet my feet with her tears and wiped them with her hair. You gave me no kiss, but from the time I came in she has not ceased to kiss my feet. You did not anoint my head with oil, but she has anointed my feet with ointment.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then turning toward the woman he said to Simon, Do you see this woman?

Two things happen in that sentence, and Luke has arranged them carefully. Jesus turns to face her — for the first time in the scene, since she has been behind him throughout — and he speaks to Simon.

So he is looking at her while he talks about her. She hears every word of what follows with his eyes on her.

Do you see this woman? Simon has seen nothing but a category. He looked at her and read a file. Jesus asks him to look again, and then tells him what is actually there.

What follows is three comparisons, and each has the same structure: you did not… but she has…

I entered your house; you gave me no water for my feet. Water for a guest's feet after a dusty road was not an extravagance. It was the minimum — a jug and a basin, usually handled by a servant. Simon did not provide it.

You gave me no kiss. The kiss of greeting was the ordinary courtesy between host and guest, the equivalent of a handshake at the door.

You did not anoint my head with oil. A little olive oil on the head of an honoured guest — cheap, customary, pleasant.

None of the three was legally required. All three were what any host in Galilee did without thinking. And Simon, who had invited this man to his own house in front of his own friends, omitted every one of them.

That is not an oversight. Three courtesies are not forgotten by accident. Simon wanted Jesus at his table and was not prepared to honour him at it — he invited him as a curiosity, and treated him accordingly, and everyone in the room would have registered it as the small public slight it was.

And against each omission, Jesus sets what she did — and every one of hers is enormously larger than the courtesy Simon skipped. No water: she used tears and her own hair. No kiss: she has not stopped kissing his feet since she came in. No oil on the head: ointment from an alabaster flask on his feet.

Simon withheld the cheap minimum. She gave the costly maximum, at the lowest place in the room, to the dirtiest part of a man.

The one who thought he had nothing much to be forgiven gave nothing much.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore I tell you, her sins, which are many, are forgiven—for she loved much. But he who is forgiven little, loves little.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore I tell you, her sins, which are many, are forgiven — for she loved much. But he who is forgiven little, loves little.

This is one of the most misread verses in the New Testament, and it is worth taking slowly, because a great deal hangs on it.

Read quickly, her sins are forgiven, for she loved much sounds as though her love bought the forgiveness — that she earned it by the extravagance of what she did on the floor. That reading has a long history, and it is the natural sense of the English as it stands.

It cannot be right, for three reasons drawn from the passage itself.

First, it reverses the parable Jesus has just told and Simon has just agreed with. In the story, the debt is cancelled and then the loving follows in proportion. If love produced forgiveness here, the parable would have to run backwards, and Jesus has spent five verses establishing which way round it goes.

Second, the tense. The Greek for are forgiven is a perfect — an action completed in the past whose result stands in the present. Her sins have been forgiven, and remain so. That happened before she entered the house. It is why she came in.

Third, three verses later he tells her plainly what saved her, and it is not her love: your faith has saved you.

So what does the for mean? It is the for of evidence, not of cause. We use it constantly: it rained last night, for the ground is wet. Nobody thinks the wet ground made it rain. The wet ground is how you know.

That is exactly the logic here, and the second half of the verse proves it: he who is forgiven little, loves little. Notice which way the causation runs in that clause. Not he who loves little is forgiven little. The forgiveness is the input; the love is the output. And Jesus has just used the same test to read the room — Simon's cold hospitality was evidence of Simon's small sense of debt, exactly as her tears were evidence of her large one.

This matters pastorally as much as theologically. If love earns forgiveness, then every anxious believer must ask whether they have loved enough, and the honest answer is always no. If love is the evidence of forgiveness, the question changes entirely — and the way to love more is not to squeeze harder but to look longer at what you have actually been forgiven.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to her, 'Your sins are forgiven.' Then those who were at table with him began to say among themselves, 'Who is this, who even forgives sins?' And he said to the woman, 'Your faith has saved you; go in peace.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he said to her, Your sins are forgiven.

He has been speaking about her to Simon. Now he turns and speaks to her, and it is the first time anyone in the scene has addressed her at all.

She already knew. The perfect tense in the previous verse means the thing was settled before she came through the door, and her tears were the evidence of it. So why say it out loud?

Because she needed to hear it said, in that room, in front of those people. A woman who has spent years as the town's byword had just crawled to the feet of a rabbi at a Pharisee's dinner party, and the whole room was watching to see what he would do with her. He tells her, where everyone can hear, that her sins are gone.

There is a great deal of pastoral practice in that. Assurance is not merely a private transaction with God. People need to be told, in words, by somebody with the authority to say it — which is a good part of what preaching and the Lord's Table are for.

Then those who were at table with him began to say among themselves, Who is this, who even forgives sins?

The same question as at the paralytic's healing (5:21), and it is the right question. Only God forgives sins committed against God; everyone at that table knew it. They have understood the claim perfectly and, once again, drawn no conclusion from it.

And notice what Jesus does with the murmur: nothing. He does not turn to defend himself or argue the point. He has one more thing to say and it is not to them.

And he said to the woman, Your faith has saved you; go in peace.

Not your love has saved you. The love was the fruit; the faith was the root — the trust that got her through a door she had no business entering, to the feet of a man she believed would not throw her out.

And she was right about him. That is all her faith consisted of, and it was enough.

Here, then, is what he is like. A woman with no name in the record, no standing, no argument and no words walks into a room full of men who despise her, and puts everything she has left on the feet of Christ — and he does not flinch, does not distance himself, does not manage the situation. He receives it, defends her to the man whose house it is, tells her out loud that she is forgiven, and sends her out through the same door in peace. There has never been a sinner too far gone for that welcome, and there is not one now.

7.text: <sup>1</sup> After he had finished all his sayings in the hearing of the people, he entered Capernaum. <sup>2</sup> Now a centurion had a servant who was sick and at the point of death, who was highly valued by him. <sup>3</sup> When the centurion heard about Jesus, he sent to him elders of the Jews, asking him to come and heal his servant. <sup>4</sup> And when they came to Jesus, they pleaded with him earnestly, saying, “He is worthy to have you do this for him, <sup>5</sup> for he loves our nation, and he is the one who built us our synagogue.” <sup>6</sup> And Jesus went with them. When he was not far from the house, the centurion sent friends, saying to him, “Lord, do not trouble yourself, for I am not worthy to have you come under my roof. <sup>7</sup> Therefore I did not presume to come to you. But say the word, and let my servant be healed. <sup>8</sup> For I too am a man set under authority, with soldiers under me: and I say to one, ‘Go,’ and he goes; and to another, ‘Come,’ and he comes; and to my servant, ‘Do this,’ and he does it.” <sup>9</sup> When Jesus heard these things, he marveled at him, and turning to the crowd that followed him, said, “I tell you, not even in Israel have I found such faith.” <sup>10</sup> And when those who had been sent returned to the house, they found the servant well. <sup>11</sup> Soon afterward he went to a town called Nain, and his disciples and a great crowd went with him. <sup>12</sup> As he drew near to the gate of the town, behold, a man who had died was being carried out, the only son of his mother, and she was a widow, and a considerable crowd from the town was with her. <sup>13</sup> And when the Lord saw her, he had compassion on her and said to her, “Do not weep.” <sup>14</sup> Then he came up and touched the bier, and the bearers stood still. And he said, “Young man, I say to you, arise.” <sup>15</sup> And the dead man sat up and began to speak, and Jesus gave him to his mother. <sup>16</sup> Fear seized them all, and they glorified God, saying, “A great prophet has arisen among us!” and “God has visited his people!” <sup>17</sup> And this report about him spread through the whole of Judea and all the surrounding country. <sup>18</sup> The disciples of John reported all these things to him. And John, <sup>19</sup> calling two of his disciples to him, sent them to the Lord, saying, “Are you the one who is to come, or shall we look for another?” <sup>20</sup> And when the men had come to him, they said, “John the Baptist has sent us to you, saying, ‘Are you the one who is to come, or shall we look for another?’” <sup>21</sup> In that hour he healed many people of diseases and plagues and evil spirits, and on many who were blind he bestowed sight. <sup>22</sup> And he answered them, “Go and tell John what you have seen and heard: the blind receive their sight, the lame walk, lepers are cleansed, and the deaf hear, the dead are raised up, the poor have good news preached to them. <sup>23</sup> And blessed is the one who is not offended by me.” <sup>24</sup> When John's messengers had gone, Jesus began to speak to the crowds concerning John: “What did you go out into the wilderness to see? A reed shaken by the wind? <sup>25</sup> What then did you go out to see? A man dressed in soft clothing? Behold, those who are dressed in splendid clothing and live in luxury are in kings' courts. <sup>26</sup> What then did you go out to see? A prophet? Yes, I tell you, and more than a prophet. <sup>27</sup> This is he of whom it is written, ‘Behold, I send my messenger before your face, who will prepare your way before you.’ <sup>28</sup> I tell you, among those born of women none is greater than John. Yet the one who is least in the kingdom of God is greater than he.” <sup>29</sup> (When all the people heard this, and the tax collectors too, they declared God just, having been baptized with the baptism of John, <sup>30</sup> but the Pharisees and the lawyers rejected the purpose of God for themselves, not having been baptized by him.) <sup>31</sup> “To what then shall I compare the people of this generation, and what are they like? <sup>32</sup> They are like children sitting in the marketplace and calling to one another, ‘We played the flute for you, and you did not dance; we sang a dirge, and you did not weep.’ <sup>33</sup> For John the Baptist has come eating no bread and drinking no wine, and you say, ‘He has a demon.’ <sup>34</sup> The Son of Man has come eating and drinking, and you say, ‘Look at him! A glutton and a drunkard, a friend of tax collectors and sinners!’ <sup>35</sup> Yet wisdom is justified by all her children.” <sup>36</sup> One of the Pharisees asked him to eat with him, and he went into the Pharisee's house and reclined at table. <sup>37</sup> And behold, a woman of the city, who was a sinner, when she learned that he was reclining at table in the Pharisee's house, brought an alabaster flask of ointment, <sup>38</sup> and standing behind him at his feet, weeping, she began to wet his feet with her tears and wiped them with the hair of her head and kissed his feet and anointed them with the ointment. <sup>39</sup> Now when the Pharisee who had invited him saw this, he said to himself, “If this man were a prophet, he would have known who and what sort of woman this is who is touching him, for she is a sinner.” <sup>40</sup> And Jesus answering said to him, “Simon, I have something to say to you.” And he answered, “Say it, Teacher.” <sup>41</sup> “A certain moneylender had two debtors. One owed five hundred denarii, and the other fifty. <sup>42</sup> When they could not pay, he cancelled the debt of both. Now which of them will love him more?” <sup>43</sup> Simon answered, “The one, I suppose, for whom he cancelled the larger debt.” And he said to him, “You have judged rightly.” <sup>44</sup> Then turning toward the woman he said to Simon, “Do you see this woman? I entered your house; you gave me no water for my feet, but she has wet my feet with her tears and wiped them with her hair. <sup>45</sup> You gave me no kiss, but from the time I came in she has not ceased to kiss my feet. <sup>46</sup> You did not anoint my head with oil, but she has anointed my feet with ointment. <sup>47</sup> Therefore I tell you, her sins, which are many, are forgiven—for she loved much. But he who is forgiven little, loves little.” <sup>48</sup> And he said to her, “Your sins are forgiven.” <sup>49</sup> Then those who were at table with him began to say among themselves, “Who is this, who even forgives sins?” <sup>50</sup> And he said to the woman, “Your faith has saved you; go in peace.”

8.title: The Word, the Storm, and the Power of the Kingdom
8.overview:
Chapter 8 is organised around the question of hearing and responding to the word — the parable of the sower, the lamp under a jar, and Jesus's redefinition of family as those who hear the word and do it all converge on the same theme before the chapter moves into four great demonstrations of kingdom power. After the teaching section, the chapter becomes a series of astonishing encounters: Jesus calms a storm on the Sea of Galilee, casts a legion of demons into a herd of pigs, heals a woman who has been bleeding for twelve years, and raises Jairus's daughter from the dead. The four miracle stories are not loosely connected anecdotes; they form a theological argument. Jesus has authority over the forces of nature, over the powers of darkness, over the long suffering of a diseased body, and over death itself. Nothing is outside the reach of his word.

The opening note about the women who accompanied Jesus and provided for the ministry out of their means (vv. 1–3) is characteristic Luke — he notices and names women at a point in history when their testimony was not counted and their presence was not recorded. Mary Magdalene, Joanna the wife of Chuza, Susanna, and many others: they are not background figures but named participants in the mission, financing the ministry that will change the world. Luke's Gospel is consistently attentive to those whom history overlooks.

The parable of the sower (vv. 4–15) is the parable about parables — the key to how the whole teaching ministry of Jesus works. The word is the seed; the hearts of the hearers are the soil; the response to the word determines everything. But the parable also functions as a warning and a comfort simultaneously: a warning that most hearers will not bear fruit, for a variety of reasons; a comfort that some will — “an hundredfold.” The harvest is certain; it comes to those who, hearing the word, hold it fast in an honest and good heart and bear fruit with patience.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Luke records that Jesus travelled through cities and villages proclaiming the kingdom of God, accompanied not only by the twelve but by a group of women who had been healed of evil spirits and infirmities. The list is striking in its specificity: Mary called Magdalene, from whom seven demons had gone out; Joanna, the wife of Herod's household manager Chuza; Susanna; and many others. These women “provided for them out of their means” — they financed the Galilean ministry. The Greek word is diekōnoun, the same root as diakonos (deacon/servant) — they served the mission with their resources.

The significance of this brief passage is easily underestimated. In a culture where women were generally excluded from the public teaching and travel of a rabbi, Jesus's entourage included women as named, active participants. Mary Magdalene will be the first witness of the resurrection (24:10); Joanna is named again at the empty tomb. The women who provided for the ministry in Galilee are the same women who will be present at the cross (23:49) and the empty tomb (24:1–11). They are not peripheral; they are among the most faithful witnesses in the whole narrative. Luke sees them and names them when the other accounts would have left them anonymous.
verseByVerse.theology: The inclusion of women in the travelling band around Jesus is a quiet revolution in the social world of first-century Judaism. Rabbis did not travel with female disciples; the association would have been scandalous. Jesus's practice reflects his consistent pattern of including those whom the religious establishment excluded — and it anticipates the full inclusion of women in the life of the new covenant community (Acts 2:17–18; Galatians 3:28). The kingdom of God does not replicate the social hierarchies of the world it enters; it consistently subverts them in the direction of the image of God that every human person bears.
verseByVerse.examples: The women who supported Jesus's ministry “out of their means” are the model of financial stewardship in service of the gospel. They did not merely believe; they gave. The resources they had — probably income from estates or from their own trades — they placed in service of the ministry. The theology of giving that runs through Paul's letters (2 Corinthians 8–9; Philippians 4:14–19) has its roots in this practice: those who share in the blessings of the gospel are those who share their resources with those who carry it forward. The women of Luke 8:1–3 are the first and clearest expression of this pattern in the New Testament.

verseByVerse.quote: Soon afterward he went on through cities and villages, proclaiming and bringing the good news of the kingdom of God. And the twelve were with him, and also some women who had been healed of evil spirits and infirmities: Mary, called Magdalene, from whom seven demons had gone out, and Joanna, the wife of Chuza, Herod's household manager, and Susanna, and many others, who provided for them out of their means.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This passage is easily passed over, but Luke's inclusion of it is characteristic and important. Jesus travels with the Twelve and with a named group of women — Mary Magdalene, Joanna, Susanna, and many others. These women are not spectators; they are supporters and companions of the mission, travelling with the group and funding it out of their own resources. In a first-century Jewish context, this is remarkable: a rabbi travelling with female disciples was without precedent. The women are not on the margins; they are in the company.

Each is identified by what Jesus has done for her: healed of evil spirits and infirmities. Their service flows from their redemption. Mary Magdalene had seven demons cast out — a detail that indicates the depth of what was reversed, and explains the extravagance of her devotion throughout the Gospel. Joanna is notable: the wife of Herod's household manager, moving between the court of Herod and the company of Jesus. The kingdom of God draws from every stratum of society.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 4–15 — The Parable of the Sower and Its Explanation
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The parable of the sower is Jesus's own explanation of why his ministry produces such varied responses — and why the disciples should not be surprised or discouraged by it. He tells the story publicly (vv. 4–8) and then explains it privately to the disciples (vv. 9–15), with an intervening comment about the purpose of parables. The story is simple: a sower scatters seed, and the seed falls on four different kinds of ground. On the path, the birds take it. On the rock, it sprouts but withers. Among thorns, it grows but is choked. In good soil, it grows and produces a hundredfold. “He who has ears to hear, let him hear.”

The disciples ask what the parable means, and Jesus's answer is one of the most important passages in all the Gospels on the purpose of parabolic teaching: “To you it has been given to know the secrets of the kingdom of God, but for others they are in parables, so that 'seeing they may not see, and hearing they may not understand.'” This is an echo of Isaiah 6:9–10, the commission given to Isaiah after his vision of the seraphim — the hardening that results from persistent rejection of revelation. The parables are not simple stories designed to make things clear to everyone; they are an act of divine judgment on those who have already refused the light. Those who are open receive understanding; those who are closed find the parable becomes further opacity.

The explanation identifies the seed as the word of God and the four soils as four kinds of hearers. The path is the person who hears and the devil immediately takes the word away, lest they believe and be saved. The rock is the person who receives the word with joy but has no root — they believe for a while and fall away in a time of testing. The thorns are those who hear but are choked by cares and riches and pleasures of life. The good soil is those who hear the word, hold it fast in an honest and good heart, and bear fruit with patience. The fourfold typology is not a rigid psychological classification; it is a searching mirror that each hearer is invited to hold up to themselves. Which soil am I?
verseByVerse.theology:
The parable of the sower is the foundational parable — Mark 4:13 records Jesus saying “Do you not understand this parable? How then will you understand all the parables?” It establishes the principle that governs all the rest of Jesus's teaching: the response to the word determines everything. The word itself does not change; the seed is the same in all four soils. What varies is the condition of the heart that receives it. This is the basis of the New Testament's consistent call to prepare the heart — through humility, through the removal of competing loves, through the patient reception of the word — before the word can do its work.

The description of the good soil — “an honest and good heart” (kardia kalē kai agathē) — is the Greek ideal of the kalos kagathos, the beautiful and good person, applied to the inner life. But the content is entirely biblical: the honest and good heart is not the morally superior heart but the heart that is open, receptive, and fruitful — the heart that has been prepared by grace to receive grace. The “patience” (hypomonē) with which the good soil bears fruit is the patient endurance that the New Testament consistently associates with mature faith: not the impatient demand for immediate harvest but the willingness to tend the word and wait for God's timing.
verseByVerse.examples:
The parable of the sower is a diagnostic tool for self-examination. The question it asks every hearer is not “have you heard the gospel?” but “what has happened to the word in you?” Has it been snatched away before it could take root — by distraction, by the noise of competing messages, by the immediate interruption of the enemy? Has it produced initial enthusiasm that has not survived the first significant test? Has it been growing alongside competing loves — the love of money, the anxiety of life, the pleasures that crowd out the word? Or is it growing, quietly and with patience, toward a harvest?

The thorns — “cares and riches and pleasures of life” — are the most insidious of the four soils because they do not produce an obvious rejection of the word. The person choked by thorns is not an unbeliever in any obvious sense; they are someone in whom the word is growing alongside competing loves, and the competition is gradually winning. Jesus says the word is “choked” — strangled, cut off from light and nutrients. The diagnosis is not apostasy; it is suffocation. The remedy is not more effort but the deliberate removal of what is strangling the word — the act of dying to the competing loves so that the word has room to grow.

verseByVerse.quote: And when a great crowd was gathering and people from town after town came to him, he said in a parable: 'A sower went out to sow his seed. And as he sowed, some fell along the path and was trampled underfoot, and the birds of the air devoured it. And some fell on the rock, and as it grew up, it withered away, because it had no moisture. And some fell among thorns, and the thorns grew up with it and choked it. And some fell into good soil and grew and yielded a hundredfold.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The parable is addressed to a large and enthusiastic crowd — which is itself part of its meaning. Jesus is not discouraging large crowds; he is clarifying what happens inside them. The same seed falls on four different types of soil; only one produces fruit. The crowd in front of him is itself a mixture of all four. Some will hear and the word will be snatched away before it takes root; some will respond with immediate enthusiasm and then fall away; some will be choked by the competing claims of life; some will receive the word and bear fruit a hundredfold. The parable does not tell Jesus's hearers which soil they are. It invites them to ask.

He who has ears to hear, let him hear — the call to hearing is more than a request for attention. It is a call for the kind of hearing that penetrates below the surface to understanding and response. The parable is itself a test of hearing: those who receive it as a teaching about soil types have not heard it; those who receive it as a question about themselves have.

verseByVerse.quote: And when his disciples asked him what this parable meant, he said, 'To you it has been given to know the secrets of the kingdom of God, but for others they are in parables, so that seeing they may not see, and hearing they may not understand.'
verseByVerse.commentary: The disciples ask for the explanation — they do not assume they already understand. That asking is itself the fulfilment of the parable: they are the ones pressing in further rather than receiving the surface and moving on. The secrets of the kingdom (the word mysteria means things previously hidden but now being revealed) are given to those who stay, who ask, who press past the parable to its meaning. The citation of Isaiah 6:9–10 is not a statement that Jesus intends to prevent understanding; it is a recognition that the same word that opens some hearts hardens others, depending on the condition of the soil in which it falls.

verseByVerse.quote: 'Now the parable is this: The seed is the word of God. The ones along the path are those who have heard; then the devil comes and takes away the word from their hearts, so that they may not believe and be saved.'
verseByVerse.commentary: The seed is identified as the word of God — not a technique, not a personality, not an atmosphere, but the word. The first soil type is the hardened path: the word lands but never penetrates. The agent of removal is the devil, who takes it away before it can begin the work of faith. Notice what the enemy's primary strategy is: not to corrupt the word but to prevent it from being received at all. The word does not need to be destroyed; it only needs to be taken away before the ground opens to it. Distraction, noise, the busy surface of a life that never slows down enough to let the word in — these are the devil's tools here.

verseByVerse.quote: 'And the ones on the rock are those who, when they hear the word, receive it with joy. But these have no root; they believe for a while, and in time of testing fall away.'
verseByVerse.commentary: The second soil type is particularly important because it involves genuine initial response — joy, belief. This is not the casual hearer of the path soil; this is the enthusiastic new convert. But there is no root: the joy is real, the belief is real, but the depth is not. In time of testing — the Greek peirasmos can mean temptation or trial — they fall away. The test reveals the depth. This is not an argument against joy or enthusiasm; it is an argument for the necessity of the word going deep, for depth that can only come through the extended, costly work of genuine reception. Rootless faith cannot survive the seasons it will inevitably face.

verseByVerse.quote: 'And as for what fell among the thorns, they are those who hear, but as they go on their way they are choked by the cares and riches and pleasures of life, and their fruit does not mature.'
verseByVerse.commentary: The third soil type is perhaps the most common in comfortable Western Christianity. The thorns are named: cares, riches, pleasures of life. They do not prevent germination; they prevent fruitfulness. The word takes root, the plant grows — but the thorns grow with it, competing for the same nutrients and light, eventually choking what could have been fruitful. The word does not fail here; it is crowded out. The diagnostic question for any life is: what is competing with the word for my primary attention? The cares and pleasures of life are not evil in themselves; they become thorns when they are allowed to take the place the word must occupy.

verseByVerse.quote: 'As for that in the good soil, they are those who, hearing the word, hold it fast in an honest and good heart, and bear fruit with patience.'
verseByVerse.commentary: The good soil is defined not by natural quality but by posture: an honest and good heart that holds the word fast and bears fruit with patience. Hold it fast — the word implies an active, sustained grip, not passive reception. Patience — the fruit does not arrive overnight. The parable ends on this note: the good soil is characterised by a combination of honest reception, active retention, and patient endurance. These are not dramatic qualities; they are the quiet, daily disciplines of a life that has decided the word is worth holding on to, whatever the season brings.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–21 — A Lamp Under a Jar and True Family
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Two brief teachings follow the parable's explanation. The first is the lamp saying: “No one after lighting a lamp covers it with a jar or puts it under a bed, but puts it on a stand, so that those who enter may see the light.” The saying applies the parable's logic to the disciples: the word they have received is not private property to be kept; it is a lamp to be put on a stand so that others can see. The hiddenness that the parable warned about (the word snatched away, the word choked) is the enemy; the visibility and fruitfulness of the lamp on the stand is the goal. “For nothing is hidden that will not be made manifest, nor is anything secret that will not be known and come to light.” The word that is received will eventually be revealed by its fruit.

The second saying comes when Jesus's mother and brothers arrive wanting to see him, and he redefines family: “My mother and my brothers are those who hear the word of God and do it.” This is not a rejection of Mary or his brothers — Luke has already shown us the depth of the relationship between Mary and her son. It is a declaration that the primary identity of the community gathered around Jesus is not biological but covenantal: those who hear the word and do it. The hearing-and-doing of 6:46–49 (the two builders) now defines the family of God. This is the new covenant community — not a family by blood but a family by the word, held together not by DNA but by their shared response to the same Father's voice.
verseByVerse.theology: The lamp saying (v. 16) and the hearing-and-doing of the family redefinition (v. 21) are the application of the parable to the disciples' own vocation. They have been given the secrets of the kingdom (v. 10) — not for private illumination but for public proclamation. The word they have received is the lamp; the stand is the world they are being sent into. The parable of the sower describes what happens when the word meets different soils; the lamp saying describes what the disciples are to do with the word they have received — put it where others can see it.
verseByVerse.examples: The redefinition of family as those who “hear the word of God and do it” is the basis of the extraordinary community the church creates across every natural human division. People who share nothing by blood, culture, language, or class are family because they share the same word and the same response to it. This is the sociological miracle of the first-century church, which drew together Jews and Gentiles, slaves and free, men and women, into a community that the ancient world had no category for. It is the ongoing miracle of every church that takes the hearing-and-doing of the word as its defining identity rather than any natural affinity.

verseByVerse.quote: 'No one after lighting a lamp covers it with a jar or puts it under a bed, but puts it on a stand, so that those who enter may see the light. For nothing is hidden that will not be made manifest, nor is anything secret that will not be known and come to light. Take care then how you hear, for to the one who has, more will be given, and from the one who has not, even what he thinks that he has will be taken away.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The lamp saying follows the parable of the sower and applies it to the question of hearing. A lamp is not lit to be hidden; the word is not given to be kept private. What has been revealed to the disciples — the secrets of the kingdom — is given in order to be proclaimed, not hoarded. The warning about hiddenness becoming manifest is a double-edged word: nothing good that is hidden will stay hidden, and nothing bad that is concealed will remain so.

Take care how you hear — the quality of hearing determines what you receive. The person who hears with genuine reception will receive more; the one who hears carelessly will lose even the appearance of what they have. This is not a threat against the insecure; it is a diagnosis of the dynamics of spiritual growth. Genuine receptivity produces more capacity for reception; pseudo-hearing atrophies.

verseByVerse.quote: Then his mother and his brothers came to him, but they could not reach him because of the crowd. And he was told, 'Your mother and your brothers are standing outside, desiring to see you.' But he answered them, 'My mother and my brothers are those who hear the word of God and do it.'
verseByVerse.commentary: The episode about Jesus's family follows the lamp saying and the seed parable, and it provides the defining example of what true hearing looks like in terms of relationship. Jesus does not deny or dishonour his biological family; he redefines family around the hearing and doing of the word of God. This is not a rejection of Mary; it is an elevation of the category of belonging. The family of Jesus is constituted by those who hear the word and act on it — which is precisely what the parable of the sower was describing as good soil. Mary is, of course, the supreme example of one who heard the word of God and did it (1:38). The redefinition includes her; it expands the category she represents.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Jesus and the disciples set out across the lake. Jesus falls asleep. A windstorm comes down on the lake — and these are fishermen, men who know this lake intimately, who have worked it in all weathers. When they wake Jesus with “Master, Master, we are perishing!” the fear in their voice is real: this is not an anxious overreaction; they are experienced mariners who know when a storm is going to kill them. Jesus “rebuked the wind and the raging waves” — the same language used for the exorcism of the demon in 4:35 — “and they ceased, and there was a calm.” And then he turns to the disciples: “Where is your faith?”

The disciples' question to each other — “Who then is this, that he commands even winds and water, and they obey him?” — is the question the chapter has been building toward. The four miracle stories of chapter 8 each answer it from a different angle. He commands the wind and the water and they obey: this is the language of God's sovereignty over chaos in the Old Testament. In Psalm 107:28–29, the sailors in distress “cried to the LORD in their trouble, and he delivered them from their distress. He made the storm be still, and the waves of the sea were hushed.” The disciples are living through the scene that Psalm 107 described — except that the one who stills the storm is asleep in the back of their boat. The Lord of the storm is asleep in the stern.

Jesus's sleeping in the storm is itself a theological image. He is not asleep because he is unconcerned; he sleeps because he is at peace. The one who says “do not be anxious” (12:22) practises what he preaches: there is no storm in the created order that can threaten the one who made it. His sleep is the sleep of perfect trust in the Father — the same trust he calls his disciples to embody. They wake him because they are perishing; he wakes because his disciples need him, not because the storm has threatened him. “Where is your faith?” — the question is not a rebuke for feeling fear, but an invitation to bring the fear to the one who is already in the boat with them.
verseByVerse.theology: The stilling of the storm is the New Testament's most direct claim that Jesus exercises the prerogatives of the Creator God over the natural world. In the Old Testament, only YHWH commands the winds and the sea: “He stilled the storm to a whisper; the waves of the sea were hushed” (Psalm 107:29); “You rule over the surging sea; when its waves mount up, you still them” (Psalm 89:9). The disciples' question “who then is this?” has only one answer: the one who rules the sea is present in their boat. The storm narrative is one of the most compact Christological proofs in the Synoptic tradition.
verseByVerse.examples: The disciples have Jesus in the boat and they are terrified. They have heard the sermon on the plain, they have seen the miracles, they have received the explanation of the parables — and when the storm comes, they are “afraid and marvelled” (v. 25). This is the honest portrait of early discipleship: knowing who Jesus is, in the abstract, is not the same as trusting him in the specific, embodied crisis of the storm. The passage is not primarily about the disciples' failure; it is about the Jesus who is in the boat with them. He does not abandon them in the storm; he stills it. And then he invites them to examine where their faith was during the storm — not to condemn but to grow.

verseByVerse.quote: One day he got into a boat with his disciples, and he said to them, 'Let us go across to the other side of the lake.' So they set out, and as they sailed he fell asleep. And a windstorm came down on the lake, and they were filling with water and were in danger. And they went and woke him, saying, 'Master, Master, we are perishing!' And he awoke and rebuked the wind and the raging waves, and they ceased, and there was a calm.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus falls asleep — a detail of genuine humanity. He is tired from the ministry. The storm that blows up on the Sea of Galilee would have been a serious matter even to experienced fishermen: the lake is set in a basin that funnels wind from the surrounding hills with sudden violence. The disciples, several of whom are professional fishermen, judge the situation as life-threatening. They wake Jesus with the cry of people who have given up: we are perishing.

Jesus wakes and rebukes the wind and the waves. The word rebuked is the same word used for casting out demons — the forces of nature are addressed with the same authority as the forces of evil. They obey. The sudden calm is as dramatic as the sudden storm: one moment, chaos; the next, flat water. The disciples have asked for rescue; they have received a demonstration of who is in the boat with them.

verseByVerse.quote: He said to them, 'Where is your faith?' And they were afraid, and they marvelled, saying to one another, 'Who then is this, that he commands even winds and water, and they obey him?'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The question — where is your faith? — is not a rebuke for having woken him. It is a question about what they believe about him. They have been with him through healings, exorcisms, and the raising of the dead. The storm should not have found them without the resource of knowing who was in the boat. Their fear of the storm was reasonable; their forgetting of Jesus was not.

The question who then is this? is the central question of Luke's entire Gospel, and it surfaces here in its full weight. To command the wind and the waves was, in the Old Testament, the prerogative of God alone (Ps. 107:25–30; Job 38:8–11). The disciples are asking, without fully realising it, the only question whose answer makes sense of everything they have seen.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 26–39 — Jesus Heals a Man with a Demon
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
On the other side of the lake — the Gerasene (Gentile) territory, east of the Jordan in the Decapolis — a man possessed by a legion of demons meets Jesus and falls at his feet. The description is harrowing: he wore no clothes, lived not in a house but among the tombs, had repeatedly broken the chains placed on him, was driven by the demons into desert places. He is a man who has been comprehensively dehumanised — stripped of clothing (the mark of dignity), of home (the mark of community), and of the capacity for self-determination (the mark of personhood). He is not a person; he is a site of demonic occupation.

The demons recognise Jesus immediately — “What have you to do with me, Jesus, Son of the Most High God? I beg you, do not torment me.” The plural “legion” suggests an enormous number — a Roman legion numbered roughly six thousand soldiers. Whether the number is precise or hyperbolic, the point is the same: this man is under a massive, overwhelming demonic oppression. The demons beg Jesus not to cast them into the abyss (the place of their ultimate confinement) but to allow them to enter the herd of pigs on the hillside. Jesus permits this; the pigs rush down into the lake and drown; the herdsmen flee to report to the city. The local people come out and find the man “clothed and in his right mind” — sitting at Jesus's feet. And they are afraid.

The townspeople's response — they ask Jesus to leave — is one of the most telling details in the chapter. They have seen a man who was a terror to the community restored to sanity and dignity. They have lost a herd of pigs. And they want Jesus gone. The economic cost of the miracle, or perhaps the uncanny power that produced it, is more frightening to them than the man who was living among the tombs. The restored man himself wants to follow Jesus, but Jesus sends him home: “Return to your home, and declare how much God has done for you.” He becomes the first missionary to the Gentile Decapolis — the witness sent not across the world but to the people who already know his story.
verseByVerse.theology:
The healing of the Gerasene demoniac is the most comprehensive exorcism narrative in the Gospels — and it is performed in Gentile territory, on a Gentile man, before an audience of Gentile pig-herders. The geography is the theology: the kingdom of God does not stop at the borders of Israel. The power over demonic oppression is not limited to the covenant people; it extends to every person who is under the dominion of the enemy, whatever their ethnicity or religious background. The Gerasene man is the Gentile counterpart to the Nazareth synagogue's demonised man (4:33) — both are liberated by the same word, with the same authority.

The man restored to his “right mind” (sōphrōn — the same word used for the sober-mindedness the New Testament calls for in leaders and in the Christian life generally) is sitting at Jesus's feet — the posture of the disciple (cf. Mary in 10:39; Paul at Gamaliel's feet, Acts 22:3). The demonic occupation has been replaced by the discipleship posture. This is the pattern of every genuine deliverance: the life that was dominated by the enemy is not merely emptied but reordered around Jesus. The sitting at the feet is not incidental; it is the theological point of the healing.
verseByVerse.examples:
The townspeople who ask Jesus to leave after seeing the man restored are the cautionary portrait of a community that values its economic security more than its neighbour's liberation. The pigs are gone; the man is well. The calculus should be straightforward. But the fear is real: something happened here that we do not control, and the loss of the pigs is tangible and immediate. The community that prioritises what it can calculate and control over what it cannot understand or manage will always find a reason to ask Jesus to leave. Every generation of the church has had to decide whether to welcome the disruptive grace of God or to manage it into something more comfortable.

The man's desire to follow Jesus — and Jesus's refusal, with the instruction to “declare how much God has done for you” — is the missionary call in its most particular form: go to the people who already know you. His witness among the ten cities of the Decapolis (Mark 5:20) plants seeds that will bear fruit when the early church moves into the Gentile world. The most powerful testimony is often not the stranger's proclamation but the neighbour's transformation. “Return to your home” is not a lesser commission; it is the first and most necessary mission.

verseByVerse.quote: Then they sailed to the country of the Gerasenes, which is opposite Galilee. When Jesus had stepped out on land, there met him a man from the city who had demons. For a long time he had worn no clothes, and he had not lived in a house but among the tombs. When he saw Jesus, he cried out and fell down before him and said with a loud voice, 'What have you to do with me, Jesus, Son of the Most High God? I beg you, do not torment me.' For he had commanded the unclean spirit to come out of the man.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Gerasene region is Gentile territory — across the lake from Galilee. Jesus has crossed a geographic and cultural boundary, and he arrives to find the most extreme human wreckage in the Gospel: a man with many demons, naked, living in tombs, cut off from all human community. The tombs make him ceremonially unclean; the nakedness marks his dehumanisation; the length of his suffering — a long time — establishes that this is not a passing crisis. He is beyond the reach of anyone who could help him.

Two things about this crossing will stop a reader with a map or a harmony. The first is the place. Luke calls it the country of the Gerasenes, but Gerasa lay some thirty miles inland — no herd could run from there down a steep bank into the lake. Matthew names the Gadarenes, and Gadara is about six miles off, still not on the shore; some manuscripts of all three Gospels read Gergesenes. The likeliest answer is that Gergesa, modern Kursi, was the actual spot — a small place on the eastern shore where the hills drop sharply to the water, exactly as the story requires — while Gerasa and Gadara were the two well-known cities whose districts reached down to that coast. Each writer named the region by the city his own readers would recognise, much as one might place a village in greater London. The steep bank is still there.

The second is the arithmetic. Luke describes one man, and so does Mark; Matthew says there were two (Matt. 8:28). Neither is denying the other — Matthew adds a second man, he does not subtract one. Where a pair is involved and only one does the talking and only one is left with a story to tell, a writer will naturally follow him and let the other pass. Mark and Luke keep their camera on the man who spoke, who was named Legion, who begged to come along and was sent home instead. Matthew, who tends to record the fuller count, tells you there was another. The same thing happens at Jericho, where Matthew has two blind men and Mark names only Bartimaeus.

The demon's question — What have you to do with me? — is a stock formula of confrontation, used also in 4:34. The recognition of Jesus as Son of the Most High God is accurate; the terror behind it is real. The demon pleads not to be tormented before its time — which implies an awareness of a coming judgment from which no demon can escape. Jesus's authority over the demonic world is total; the only question is the timing of its exercise.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus then asked him, 'What is your name?' And he said, 'Legion,' for many demons had entered him. And they begged him not to command them to depart into the abyss. Now a large herd of pigs was feeding there on the hillside, and they begged him to let them enter these. So he gave them permission. Then the demons came out of the man and entered the pigs, and the herd rushed down the steep bank into the lake and drowned.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The name Legion — a Roman military unit of up to 6,000 soldiers — communicates both the number and the organised nature of the occupation. A legion does not wander; it occupies. This man's condition is not casual spiritual interference; it is systematic possession by a multitude.

The demons beg not to be sent to the abyss — their ultimate destination — but to enter the pigs instead. Jesus permits it. The pigs rush into the lake and drown. Two questions press on any thoughtful reader here. Why did Jesus permit the request? And what is the drowning of the pigs meant to say? The pigs may function as a visible demonstration of what the demons had been doing to the man all along — destroying what they inhabited. The lake that swallowed them is the same lake over which Jesus had just demonstrated his authority. The two episodes are connected: the Lord of the storm is also the Lord over the powers that destroy human beings.

But the first question — why did Jesus permit it at all? — deserves a straight answer, because sceptics have long pointed to the drowned herd as proof that Jesus was careless of property and cruel to animals. Three things dissolve the charge. First, notice who does the drowning. Jesus does not command the pigs into the lake; he grants the demons' request, and it is the demons who stampede the herd to its death — doing to two thousand animals in a moment what they had been doing to the man for years. The destruction is theirs, and it unmasks them: this is what these powers always do to whatever they occupy, and the lake full of drowned swine is the plainest possible evidence of what the man had been living under. Second, weigh the exchange honestly. One human being — made in the image of God, a neighbour, a son — was pulled out of a living death; a herd of pigs was lost. Jesus refuses the arithmetic that counts the livestock and forgets the man. “Of how much more value is a man than a sheep!” he says elsewhere (Matt. 12:12), and the same scale applies here; a man is worth more than any number of animals, and a Saviour who would leave a man in the tombs to protect a herd would be no Saviour at all. Third, the ruined herd forced the district to a decision it could no longer avoid — and the next verses show which way it went. Scripture does not linger over the owners' loss, not because the loss did not happen but because the point of the story is standing there clothed and in his right mind. The pigs are the price tag the town could see; the man is the treasure it could not.

verseByVerse.quote: When the herdsmen saw what had happened, they fled and told it in the city and in the country. Then people went out to see what had happened, and they came to Jesus and found the man from whom the demons had gone, sitting at the feet of Jesus, clothed and in his right mind, and they were afraid. And those who had seen it told them how the demon-possessed man had been healed. Then all the people of the surrounding country of the Gerasenes asked him to depart from them, for they were seized with great fear. So he got into the boat and returned.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The townspeople come out and find the man sitting at Jesus's feet — the posture of a disciple — clothed and in his right mind. The contrast with his previous condition could not be sharper: where there was nakedness, clothing; where there was madness, sanity; where there was isolation in the tombs, belonging at the feet of Jesus. This is restoration of full humanity, and it is visible to everyone who comes to see.

The community's response is fear, not joy — and they ask Jesus to leave. The loss of the pigs is one dimension; the deeper issue is that an encounter with this kind of power is unsettling in a way that ordinary healing is not. Jesus does not argue or insist; he gets back in the boat. The one who was healed is left behind as a living testimony to what happened. The community has chosen its pigs over its neighbour, and Jesus honours that choice by leaving.

verseByVerse.quote: The man from whom the demons had gone begged that he might be with him, but Jesus sent him away, saying, 'Return to your home, and declare how much God has done for you.' And he went away, proclaiming throughout the whole city how much Jesus had done for him.
verseByVerse.commentary: The restored man wants to follow Jesus — to be with him, as the Twelve are with him. Jesus sends him home instead. The man becomes the first evangelist to Gentile territory: he goes to the city and proclaims how much Jesus has done for him. Luke notes that what Jesus had said was how much God has done for you; what the man says is how much Jesus has done for him. Luke leaves the equation standing, without comment. The man who was once naked and raving in the tombs is now the gospel's first herald east of the lake. The one who was most dramatically saved is the one most immediately sent to declare it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 40–56 — Jesus Heals a Woman and Raises Jairus's Daughter
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The final section of the chapter is Luke's most carefully interlaced double narrative — the healing of the woman with the flow of blood woven inside the story of the raising of Jairus's daughter. Jairus is a ruler of the synagogue — a man of religious standing and social prominence. He falls at Jesus's feet and begs him to come to his house: his only daughter, twelve years old, is dying. Jesus begins to make his way there. The crowd presses around him. And a woman who has had a discharge of blood for twelve years reaches through the crowd and touches the fringe of his garment. Immediately her bleeding stops, and Jesus feels that power has gone from him.

The woman's story is the mirror image of Jairus's. She has suffered for twelve years — the same number as Jairus's daughter's age. She has spent everything she had on physicians; she is penniless, exhausted, ceremonially unclean, and has “no one” to advocate for her. Her approach is furtive — she touches from behind, hoping to remain anonymous in the crowd. When Jesus stops and asks who touched him, the disciples are incredulous (“Master, the crowd surrounds you and is pressing against you!”), but Jesus insists: he knows that power has gone from him. The woman, knowing she has been found out, falls before him trembling and declares before all the people why she touched him and how she was immediately healed. “Daughter, your faith has made you well; go in peace.” He does not rebuke her for the furtive touch; he names her — “daughter” — and sends her away healed and at peace.

While he is still speaking, word comes from Jairus's house: “Your daughter is dead; do not trouble the Teacher any more.” The delay caused by the hemorrhaging woman has cost Jairus his daughter. Or so it appears. Jesus says: “Do not fear; only believe, and she will be well.” He comes to the house, sends away the professional mourners who are already weeping and wailing, enters with only Peter, James, John, and the parents. He takes the girl by the hand and says: “Child, arise.” Her spirit returns; she gets up immediately. He tells them to give her something to eat — the practical, physician's detail — and charges them to tell no one. The chapter ends with a resurrection and a meal, and the parents “were amazed.”
verseByVerse.theology:
The interlacing of the two stories is a masterpiece of narrative theology. The woman who is healed on the way to Jairus's daughter teaches Jairus — and the reader — that the delay caused by the woman's healing did not diminish Jesus's power or exhaust his compassion. The one who felt power go out of him for the woman has more than enough power for the dead girl. Jairus is being taught, through the woman's healing, to “only believe” — to resist the word that says “it is too late” and to trust the one who is walking beside him. The “too late” of the messengers is not too late for the Lord of life.

The woman's healing through touching “the fringe of his garment” (tou kraspedou tou himatiou autou) may refer to the tassels (tzitzit) Jewish men wore on the corners of their outer garments (Numbers 15:38–40; Deuteronomy 22:12) as a reminder of the commandments. Malachi 4:2 promised that “the sun of righteousness shall rise with healing in its wings” — the word “wings” (kanaphim) is the same word used for the corners of a garment. The woman who touches the fringe of Jesus's garment may be, knowingly or not, reaching for the healing in the wings of the sun of righteousness. The detail is medically specific (Luke the physician) and theologically resonant.
verseByVerse.examples:
The woman's twelve years of suffering, her exhausted resources, her ritual uncleanness, her invisibility in the crowd — all of these are the conditions in which she finally comes to Jesus. She did not come while she had resources left; she comes when she has nothing. She does not come with a formal petition; she comes with a touch of desperate faith. Jesus's response — stopping in the middle of a crowd, insisting on finding her, naming her “daughter,” declaring her faith before everyone — is the public vindication of the person who came to him from the bottom of her resources. The crowd is not the obstacle to encountering Jesus; it is the context in which Jesus finds the one person who has come with nothing left to lose.

Jairus's journey — from the moment of his daughter's death-news to the moment of her raising — is the journey of faith pushed to its absolute limit. He has done everything he could: he found Jesus, he fell at his feet, he asked for his daughter's life. And then the delay, and then the word that it is too late. “Do not fear; only believe.” The faith Jesus calls for at the end of Jairus's rope is not the faith of a man who still has options; it is the faith of a man who has been stripped of every option except trusting the one who is walking with him. This is the faith that carries the weight of the resurrection — not the comfortable faith of the unchallenged, but the naked faith of the bereft.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when Jesus returned, the crowd welcomed him, for they were all waiting for him. And there came a man named Jairus, who was a ruler of the synagogue. And falling at Jesus's feet, he implored him to come to his house, for he had an only daughter, about twelve years of age, and she was dying. As Jesus went, the people pressed around him.
verseByVerse.commentary: The contrast between the Gerasene community (who asked Jesus to leave) and the Galilean crowd (who were all waiting for him) is immediate and stark. The crowd welcomes; Jairus falls at Jesus's feet. He is a synagogue ruler — a man of religious standing — and he prostrates himself in public. The need of his daughter has levelled every consideration of dignity. His daughter is his only daughter, about twelve years old, dying. The detail of twelve years is not accidental; it will connect to the other story nested inside this one. He begs Jesus to come. Jesus goes.

verseByVerse.quote: And there was a woman who had had a discharge of blood for twelve years, and though she had spent all her living on physicians, she could not be healed by anyone. She came up behind him and touched the fringe of his garment, and immediately her discharge of blood ceased.
verseByVerse.commentary: The woman's condition — twelve years of hemorrhage — has made her perpetually ritually unclean under Levitical law (Lev. 15:25–27). For twelve years she has been unable to participate in synagogue worship, touch another person without making them unclean, or live in normal community. She has spent everything she had on physicians and is no better. She approaches Jesus from behind — she does not announce herself or make a request. She simply reaches for the fringe of his garment, believing that contact with him is sufficient. The healing is immediate: the flow of blood stops the moment she touches him.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus said, 'Who was it that touched me?' When all denied it, Peter said, 'Master, the crowds surround you and are pressing in on you!' But Jesus said, 'Someone touched me, for I perceive that power has gone out from me.'
verseByVerse.commentary: Jesus's question is not a request for information — he knows who touched him. The question is an invitation: he wants the woman to identify herself, to come forward, to receive more than the healing she took in secret. Power has gone out from me — the same word, dynamis, used throughout Luke for the healing energy that flows from Jesus. The healing was real and the power was real, but it was not an impersonal transaction. Jesus wants a person, not just a recovered patient.

verseByVerse.quote: And when the woman saw that she was not hidden, she came trembling, and falling down before him declared in the presence of all the people why she had touched him, and how she had been immediately healed. And he said to her, 'Daughter, your faith has made you well; go in peace.'
verseByVerse.commentary: She comes trembling — afraid, perhaps, that taking the healing without asking was presumptuous, or that her uncleanness has somehow contaminated Jesus. She falls before him and declares everything publicly. Jesus addresses her as Daughter — a word of belonging and tenderness, the only time in the Gospels Jesus uses this term directly to a woman. Her faith has made her well: the reaching out toward Jesus was the faith; the healing flowed through it. Go in peace — the Hebrew concept of shalom, wholeness, right-orderedness — suggests that what she has received is more than the cessation of bleeding. She is restored to community, to worship, to the wholeness that her condition had taken from her for twelve years.

verseByVerse.quote: While he was still speaking, someone from the ruler's house came and said, 'Your daughter is dead; do not trouble the Teacher any more.' But Jesus on hearing this answered him, 'Do not be afraid; only believe, and she will be well.'
verseByVerse.commentary: The delay caused by the woman has, from a human perspective, cost Jairus his daughter. The messenger arrives with the word that ends hope: she is dead. The advice is pragmatic and reasonable: do not trouble the Teacher anymore. What could even a miracle-worker do against death? Jesus intercepts the message before it can take root in Jairus's heart: do not be afraid; only believe, and she will be well. The command has the same structure as his command to Simon in the boat — do not be afraid, but act on the word. What Jairus is being asked to believe is not that Jesus will try to help; it is that death is not the end of the story.

verseByVerse.quote: And when he came to the house, he allowed no one to enter with him, except Peter and John and James, and the father and mother of the child. And all were weeping and mourning for her, but he said, 'Do not weep, for she is not dead but sleeping.' And they laughed at him, for they knew that she was dead.
verseByVerse.commentary: Jesus takes only the inner three — Peter, John, and James — into the house. They will be the same three at the Transfiguration (9:28) and at Gethsemane (22:8). The mourners are already present, weeping and beating their breasts in the formal expressions of grief. Jesus's word — she is not dead but sleeping — is met with laughter and derision. They know she is dead; they do not understand that from the perspective of the one who can wake her, sleeping is the appropriate category. Jesus does not argue with them; he puts them outside. The miracle will be for the family and the disciples. The mockers will hear about it from others.

verseByVerse.quote: But taking her by the hand he called, saying, 'Child, arise.' And her spirit returned, and she got up at once. And he directed that something should be given her to eat. And her parents were amazed, but he charged them to tell no one what had happened.
verseByVerse.commentary: He takes her hand and calls. The spirit returns; she stands immediately. Then the most humanly attentive detail in the whole passage: Jesus tells them to give her something to eat. After the miracle of resurrection, he thinks of her hunger. The one who raised her from the dead is also concerned that she has a meal. This combination — the cosmic and the domestic, the miraculous and the ordinary — is characteristic of Jesus throughout Luke's Gospel, and it is one of the most compelling evidences of his genuine incarnation. He is not a supernatural figure visiting the world; he is the one who knows that a twelve-year-old girl who has just come back from death needs something to eat.

9.title: The Turning Point: Cross, Glory, and the Road to Jerusalem
9.overview:
Chapter 9 is the pivot of Luke's Gospel — the hinge on which the whole narrative turns. Everything before it is the Galilean ministry of proclamation, healing, and gathering; everything after it (from 9:51 onward) is the great journey to Jerusalem, the road that leads to the cross. Within this single chapter, the Galilean ministry reaches its theological summit and its geographical end. The chapter contains the feeding of the five thousand, Peter's confession, the first and second passion predictions, the transfiguration, the healing of the epileptic boy, and the setting of the face toward Jerusalem. It is the most theologically dense chapter in Luke's Gospel.

The pivot on which chapter 9 turns is v. 51: “When the days drew near for him to be taken up, he set his face to go to Jerusalem.” The phrase “set his face” is the language of prophetic determination — Isaiah uses it of the Servant who “set his face like a flint” (Isaiah 50:7) in the face of suffering and shame. From this moment, every step Jesus takes in Luke is a step toward the cross. The transfiguration (vv. 28–36), which precedes this turning point, is the divine confirmation of the way that is being chosen — Moses and Elijah appear and speak of “his departure, which he was about to accomplish at Jerusalem.” The Greek word translated “departure” is exodos. The cross is not a defeat; it is the Exodus, the supreme act of divine liberation toward which all of Israel's history has been moving.

The chapter's central theological contribution is the collision between two kinds of glory. The crowds see a miracle-worker; Herod is perplexed by a rumoured prophet; the disciples feed five thousand from five loaves; Peter confesses the Christ of God — and immediately Jesus reframes everything. The Son of Man must suffer. Anyone who wants to follow must take up their cross daily. Whoever tries to save their life will lose it. The glory of the transfiguration is flanked on both sides by the shadow of the cross — and that is exactly the point. The glory and the cross are not opposites; they belong together. The cross is the path to the glory; the glory is the validation of the cross.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–9 — The Twelve Sent Out; Herod's Perplexity
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Jesus calls the twelve together and gives them power and authority over all demons and to cure diseases, and sends them out to proclaim the kingdom of God and to heal. The instructions are deliberately spartan: take nothing for the journey — no staff, no bag, no bread, no money, no extra tunic. They are to depend entirely on the hospitality of those they visit, staying in whatever house receives them and not moving between houses for better accommodation. Where they are not received, they are to shake the dust from their feet as a testimony against that place — the Jewish practice of shaking off Gentile dust when returning to the Holy Land, here applied to Jewish cities that reject the kingdom's messengers.

The sending of the twelve is the commissioning of Israel's representative leaders to extend the ministry of the kingdom beyond the reach of the one teacher and healer. The authority they receive is a delegated authority — the same authority Jesus has exercised, now given to them to exercise in his name. This is the pattern that will extend through Acts: the Spirit-empowered community carrying the same authority of the same word into the same world. The twelve are the first instance of the apostolic mission; Pentecost is its full inauguration.

Herod the tetrarch's perplexity — “John I beheaded, but who is this about whom I hear such things?” — is the question of a man who has killed the greatest prophet and is now hearing that something even greater than that prophet is happening. The three popular theories about Jesus (John raised from the dead; Elijah appeared; one of the old prophets risen) are all inadequate — and Herod knows it. “He sought to see him” — curiosity, not faith. He will see Jesus eventually, in 23:8–12, at the trial. It will not satisfy him. The question he asks here is the right question, but asking it without the humility to receive the answer is the condition that closes the door of grace.
verseByVerse.theology: The instructions to take nothing for the journey are not a practical travel policy but a theological statement about the nature of kingdom mission. The missionaries are not to carry resources that would make them independent of those they are sent to; they are to be entirely dependent on the hospitality of their hosts. This creates a bond of mutual vulnerability: the messenger depends on the receiver; the receiver depends on the message. The mission is not a delivery service where the messenger is self-sufficient; it is a relationship of shared need. The church that carries the gospel in the posture of self-sufficiency has lost something essential to the way Jesus designed the mission.
verseByVerse.examples: The shaking of the dust from their feet (v. 5) is the act that takes the refusal of a community seriously enough to mark it. The messenger who walks away from rejection without marking it has treated the rejection as inconsequential. The shaking of the dust says: what you have turned away from has eternal significance, and your turning away has eternal consequences. This is the missionary posture that neither abandons the rejected nor pretends the rejection doesn't matter — it bears witness to the reality of both the offer and its refusal, and moves on.

verseByVerse.quote: And he called the twelve together and gave them power and authority over all demons and to cure diseases, and he sent them out to proclaim the kingdom of God and to heal.
verseByVerse.commentary: The Twelve have been watching Jesus heal, cast out demons, and preach since chapter 5.
