Now he gives them what they have been watching — power and authority — and sends them to do what he has been doing. The two words together are significant: power (dynamis) is the capacity; authority (exousia) is the right. Both are given, not earned. They do not graduate into this role; they are sent into it. This is the pattern of all Christian mission: the one who is sent does not go on their own resources or with their own authority. They go under a commission from someone else, bearing what that someone else has given them.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, 'Take nothing for your journey, no staff, nor bag, nor bread, nor money; and do not have two tunics. And whatever house you enter, stay there, and from there depart. And wherever they do not receive you, when you leave that town shake off the dust from your feet as a testimony against them.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The instructions about what not to take are instructions about dependence. The Twelve go empty-handed so that they must rely on the hospitality of those who receive them — and, behind that hospitality, on the provision of God. They are not to stockpile resources against uncertainty; they are to trust the one who sent them to provide what is needed through the people they serve. This is not asceticism for its own sake; it is a structural embodiment of the truth that the mission does not belong to the missionaries.

The shaking off of dust — a gesture Jews used when leaving Gentile territory — applied to an Israelite town that rejects the word is a solemn act of witness. It says: the opportunity has passed; what happens next is your responsibility. Rejection of the gospel is never a neutral act.

verseByVerse.quote: And they departed and went through the villages, preaching the gospel and healing everywhere.
verseByVerse.commentary: Luke reports the mission in a single compressed verse. They went; they preached; they healed; everywhere. The simplicity of the summary is its own point: they did what they were sent to do. The instructions of vv. 3–5 were not theories about mission; they were the actual conditions under which the actual mission happened. Obedience to the specifics of the commission produced the results the commission was for.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Herod the tetrarch heard about all that was happening, and he was perplexed, because it was said by some that John had been raised from the dead, by some that Elijah had appeared, and by others that one of the prophets of old had risen. Herod said, 'John I beheaded, but who is this about whom I hear such things?' And he sought to see him.
verseByVerse.commentary: The fame of Jesus's ministry has reached Herod's court, and Herod is perplexed — the same word Luke will use for the women at the empty tomb (24:4). He has already answered the John question with a sword; now he cannot account for what continues to happen. His question — who is this? — echoes the disciples in the storm (8:25) and will resound through the rest of the Gospel. The difference is that Herod's question is driven by political anxiety, not awe. He wants to see Jesus — which in Luke's vocabulary often carries a mixed or threatening quality (cf. 23:8). He will eventually get his wish, under circumstances neither of them would choose.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–17 — Jesus Feeds the Five Thousand
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The twelve return from their mission, and Jesus withdraws with them to the town of Bethsaida for rest and debrief. The crowds follow. Jesus receives them, speaks about the kingdom of God, and heals those who need healing. As the day declines, the disciples suggest sending the crowd away to find food and lodging — there are approximately five thousand men (plus women and children). Jesus's response turns the problem back to them: “You give them something to eat.” They have five loaves and two fish. Jesus takes them, looks up to heaven, blesses and breaks them, gives them to the disciples to distribute — and the crowd is fed, with twelve baskets of fragments left over.

The feeding of the five thousand is the only miracle, besides the resurrection, recorded in all four Gospels — which signals its significance. The action is dense with typology: the five loaves and two fish in the hands of the Son of God feed a multitude in a desolate place, as the manna fed Israel in the wilderness. Moses interceded for bread from heaven; the one greater than Moses gives bread from his own hands. The twelve baskets of fragments (one for each tribe of Israel? one for each of the twelve disciples?) signal superabundance — the kingdom of God does not give minimum rations; it gives more than enough. The eucharistic language — took, blessed, broke, gave — anticipates the Last Supper and every celebration of the Lord's Supper since, where the same Lord takes what is offered, blesses it, breaks it, and gives it to be distributed to his people.
verseByVerse.theology:
The feeding of the five thousand is the New Testament's great sign of the messianic banquet — the feast of the kingdom that Isaiah promised (Isaiah 25:6–9) and that the book of Revelation describes as the marriage supper of the Lamb (Revelation 19:9). Every time the church gathers at the Lord's table, it is participating in a foretaste of the final feast — the feast that the feeding in the wilderness points toward. The eucharistic action of Jesus (took, blessed, broke, gave) is the action that defines the church's life from its beginning: receiving grace, returning it in blessing, breaking it in service, giving it to the world.

“You give them something to eat” is one of the most demanding commands Jesus gives the disciples — not because the disciples can actually feed five thousand people from five loaves, but because the command is the invitation to bring what they have and trust him with the outcome. They bring the five loaves and two fish — everything they have, which is laughably inadequate — and Jesus multiplies it. The miracle happens not despite the disciples' involvement but through it. This is the New Testament pattern: bring what you have, however inadequate it feels; the one who multiplies is not you, but he works through your bringing.
verseByVerse.examples: The disciples' suggestion to “send the crowd away” is the reasonable, responsible, logistically sensible response to the situation. It is also the response that misses what Jesus is about to demonstrate. The disciples see a problem (hungry people, no food, late hour, remote location); Jesus sees an opportunity (the same hungry people, the same remote location, and the authority of the kingdom). Every pastoral and ministry crisis can be read through either lens: the lens that sees the limits of the available resources and suggests managed retreat, or the lens that sees the resources in the hands of the one who has already fed Israel in the wilderness. The disciples who suggest “send them away” are the same disciples who will distribute the bread. The command “You give them something to eat” transforms their perspective from the logistics of the problem to the resources of the kingdom.

verseByVerse.quote: On their return the apostles told him all that they had done. And he took them and withdrew apart to a town called Bethsaida. When the crowds learned it, they followed him, and he welcomed them and spoke to them of the kingdom of God and healed those who had need of healing.
verseByVerse.commentary: Jesus takes the returning apostles aside — they need rest and debriefing after the mission. But the crowd follows, and instead of sending them away, he welcomes them. He does not resent the interruption; he responds to the need in front of him. This is a pattern throughout Luke: Jesus tries to withdraw; the crowd comes; he serves them. The rest will come later. The person in front of him now is the priority now. That is worth sitting with before moving on.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the day began to wear away, and the twelve came and said to him, 'Send the crowd away to go into the surrounding villages and countryside to find lodging and get provisions, for we are here in a desolate place.' But he said to them, 'You give them something to eat.' They said, 'We have no more than five loaves and five fish — unless we are to go and buy food for all these people.'
verseByVerse.commentary: The disciples' solution is sensible and practical: send the people away to solve their own problem. Jesus refuses the solution and redirects the responsibility: you give them something to eat. The disciples' response is the response of people doing honest arithmetic — five loaves, five fish, five thousand people. The numbers do not work. They are correct. What they have not yet included in the calculation is the one standing in front of them. When Jesus is included in the equation, the arithmetic changes.

verseByVerse.quote: For there were about five thousand men. And he said to his disciples, 'Have them sit down in groups of about fifty each.' And they did so, and had them all sit down. And taking the five loaves and the two fish, he looked up to heaven and said a blessing over them. Then he broke the loaves and gave them to the disciples to set before the crowd.
verseByVerse.commentary: The organisation of the crowd into groups of fifty — an orderly, structured arrangement — is a pastoral detail: Jesus feeds them as a community, not as a mass. The action over the loaves is the action of a Jewish householder at a meal: take, look up to heaven, bless, break, give. These four verbs will appear again at the Last Supper (22:19) and at Emmaus (24:30). Luke is inviting his reader to see this meal as an anticipation of those later meals — a foretaste of the eucharistic feast of the new covenant, and beyond that of the great banquet of the kingdom.

verseByVerse.quote: And they all ate and were satisfied. And what was left over was picked up, twelve baskets of broken pieces.
verseByVerse.commentary: They all ate and were satisfied — not merely given enough to stop complaining, but satisfied. The word (echortasthēsan) is used in the Psalms for the satisfaction God provides (Ps. 132:15; 107:9). And twelve baskets remain — one for each apostle, or one for each tribe of Israel, depending on how you read the symbol. The abundance exceeds the supply. What was offered — five loaves and two fish — was not enough. What was received — after passing through the hands of Jesus — was more than enough. This is the gospel in a meal.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–27 — Peter's Confession and the Cost of Discipleship
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Jesus is praying alone, with the disciples nearby. He asks two questions. First: “Who do the crowds say that I am?” Answer: John the Baptist, Elijah, one of the old prophets risen. Second: “But who do you say that I am?” Peter answers: “The Christ of God.” And immediately, without celebration or expansion, Jesus charges them to tell no one — and begins to teach what “the Christ of God” actually means. “The Son of Man must suffer many things and be rejected by the elders and chief priests and scribes, and be killed, and on the third day be raised.” The Messiah must suffer. This is the interpretive revolution at the centre of the Gospel.

The passion prediction is followed immediately by the call to discipleship on the same terms: “If anyone would come after me, let him deny himself and take up his cross daily and follow me.” The cross is not merely an event in Jesus's biography; it is the shape of the discipleship it requires. To follow a crucified Messiah is to follow in the pattern of crucifixion — the daily denial of the self that wants to save its own life, the daily taking up of the cross that looks like loss but is the path to the life that cannot be lost. “For whoever would save his life will lose it, but whoever loses his life for my sake will save it.” The great paradox of the kingdom is stated as cleanly as it will ever be: the way to life passes through death; the path to glory passes through the cross.

The teaching concludes with a statement about the Son of Man's coming glory — “when he comes in his glory and the glory of the Father and of the holy angels” — and the enigmatic promise: “Truly, I say to you, there are some standing here who will not taste death until they see the kingdom of God.” The most natural reading identifies this as the transfiguration, which follows immediately: a foretaste of the coming glory given to the three disciples who are present. The glory that is coming is shown in advance, in a borrowed moment on a mountaintop, so that the disciples who will stand at the foot of the cross will know what the cross is purchasing.
verseByVerse.theology:
Peter's confession — “The Christ of God” (ton Christon tou theou) — is the correct answer to the question about Jesus's identity, and it receives no commendation from Jesus in Luke (Matthew's version adds the blessing of Peter). Instead, it receives an immediate reframing: the Christ of God is the suffering, dying, rising Son of Man. The Messiah that first-century Judaism expected was a conquering king, a military deliverer, a new David who would defeat Israel's enemies. The Messiah Jesus announces is the Servant of Isaiah — the one who suffers, is rejected, and dies. The confession is right; the understanding of what the confession means requires the rest of the Gospel to complete.

The word “must” (dei) in the passion prediction — “the Son of Man must suffer” — is the divine necessity word that Luke uses at every major turning point of the Gospel. The cross is not an accident, not a political miscalculation, not the defeat of the mission. It is the goal. The suffering, rejection, and death of the Messiah are what the Old Testament has been pointing toward; the resurrection on the third day is what the Old Testament promised. What looks like defeat is the precise fulfilment of the divine plan announced in advance in the Scriptures.
verseByVerse.examples:
“Take up his cross daily” — the word “daily” (kath' hēmeran) is Luke's distinctive addition to the saying (Matthew 16:24 and Mark 8:34 do not have “daily”). The cross is not the dramatic act of martyrdom reserved for the exceptional disciple; it is the daily practice of self-denial available to every disciple. The daily cross is the daily decision not to live for the self — not to arrange life around the comfort, the security, the reputation, and the pleasure of the self. It is the decision to follow, which means to go where Jesus goes, even when Jesus goes toward suffering. The daily cross is not suffering for its own sake; it is suffering as the consequence of following a Lord whose path leads through the cross to resurrection.

“What does it profit a man if he gains the whole world and loses or forfeits himself?” — the question is addressed to people who will never gain the whole world, but who are making daily calculations about smaller versions of the same trade: what do I sacrifice of my relationship with God in order to gain security, approval, pleasure, position? The exchange rate is always the same, and it is always catastrophic: the self gained at the cost of the soul is the self that has lost everything that makes the gain worthwhile. Jesus is not prohibiting success; he is revealing its price.

verseByVerse.quote: Now it happened that as he was praying alone, the disciples were with him. And he asked them, 'Who do the crowds say that I am?' And they answered, 'John the Baptist. But others say, Elijah, and others, that one of the prophets of old has risen.' Then he said to them, 'But who do you say that I am?' And Peter answered, 'The Christ of God.'
verseByVerse.commentary: The question comes out of prayer. Luke alone specifies that Jesus is praying when he asks it — the central identity question of the whole Gospel emerges from the context of communion with the Father. Who do the crowds say? — the popular options are all honourable (John, Elijah, a prophet) and all wrong in the same way: they place Jesus within the prophetic tradition rather than beyond it. The personal question — but who do you say? — drives past the census data to the apostles' own conviction. Peter's answer is the pivot of Luke's Gospel: the Christ of God. Not a prophet. The anointed one. The Messiah. Everything before this point has been preparing for the answer; everything after this point will be shaped by its implications.

verseByVerse.quote: And he strictly charged and commanded them to tell no one, saying, 'The Son of Man must suffer many things and be rejected by the elders and chief priests and scribes, and be killed, and on the third day be raised.'
verseByVerse.commentary: The command to silence is immediately followed by the first passion prediction. This is deliberate: the confession that Jesus is the Christ must be held alongside the content of what that means. The kind of Messiah Jesus is — a suffering, rejected, killed, and raised Messiah — is not the kind anyone expected. The silence is not false modesty; it is protection against the premature formation of the wrong idea of what the Messiahship of Jesus involves. Must (dei) — divine necessity drives the passion, not human failure or bad luck. The cross is not an accident that happens to the Messiah; it is the appointed means by which the Messiah accomplishes what he was sent to accomplish.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to all, 'If anyone would come after me, let him deny himself and take up his cross daily and bear it, and follow me. For whoever would save his life will lose it, but whoever loses his life for my sake will save it.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The passion prediction is followed immediately by the cost of discipleship — and the word daily is Luke's addition to the tradition (cf. Mark 8:34). This is not a crisis decision made once; it is a daily orientation of the whole self away from self-preservation and toward the way of the cross. Deny himself — not deny himself things, but deny the self itself: the instinct to protect, preserve, and promote the ego as the primary value. Taking up the cross is not bearing hardship in general; it is the willingness to follow the crucified one in the direction he went, which is the direction of apparent loss and actual life.

The paradox of v. 24 is the heart of the Christian understanding of human existence: the person who makes self-preservation the supreme value will ultimately lose the self they were trying to preserve. The person who surrenders the self for Jesus will find the self — and more — on the other side of the surrender.

verseByVerse.quote: 'For what does it profit a man if he gains the whole world and loses or forfeits himself? For whoever is ashamed of me and of my words, of him will the Son of Man be ashamed when he comes in his glory and the glory of the Father and of the holy angels. But I tell you truly, there are some standing here who will not taste death until they see the kingdom of God.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The gain-the-world question is one of the most searching Jesus ever asked. Put the full weight of the world's offer on one side of the scale — all the power, pleasure, wealth, status, and security that the world can give — and set against it the loss of the self, the loss of the only thing that makes any of the world's goods worth having. The exchange is catastrophic in the direction no one expects. A person can acquire everything and be left with nothing that matters.

The saying about shame cuts in both directions: to be ashamed of Jesus before men is to forfeit his acknowledgement before the Father. The final promise — that some standing there will see the kingdom of God — is fulfilled in the Transfiguration that follows within the week (v. 28) and ultimately in the resurrection and Pentecost.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Eight days after Peter's confession and the first passion prediction, Jesus takes Peter, James, and John up a mountain to pray. As he is praying, the appearance of his face is altered and his clothing becomes dazzling white. Moses and Elijah appear in glory and speak with him. And the three disciples, heavy with sleep, wake to see the glory and the two men standing with him — and Luke tells us what they were talking about: “his departure, which he was about to accomplish at Jerusalem.” The Greek word is exodos. They are talking about the cross.

The transfiguration is the theological mountaintop of the Galilean ministry — the moment when the veil between the present age and the age to come is momentarily lifted, and the disciples see what Jesus actually is behind the form of servant he has taken. The dazzling whiteness is the radiance of the divine glory — the same glory that filled the tabernacle and the temple, now emanating from the person of Jesus. Moses and Elijah, representing the Law and the Prophets, stand with him — testifying to their fulfilment in him. The voice from the cloud confirms what the Father declared at the baptism: “This is my Son, my Chosen One; listen to him.” But now, in the context of the passion predictions and the call to the cross, the command “listen to him” has a specific content: listen to him about the cross. Listen to him about the exodos.

Peter's instinct — “Master, it is good that we are here. Let us make three tents” — is the instinct of someone who wants to stay on the mountain, to prolong the glory, to build structures that will make it permanent. It is also the instinct of someone who has not yet understood that the glory and the cross belong together. You cannot keep the glory without the exodos; you cannot experience the transfiguration without following the transfigured one to Jerusalem. The cloud that comes over them while Peter is still speaking, and the voice from the cloud, is the divine interruption of the plan to make tents: the disciples are overshadowed by the presence of God, and when the cloud lifts, Moses and Elijah are gone and Jesus is alone. The Law and the Prophets have done their work; now listen to the Son.
verseByVerse.theology:
The transfiguration is simultaneously a christological event (revealing who Jesus is) and an eschatological event (revealing what the coming kingdom will look like). What the disciples see is not a separate divine form that Jesus can put on and take off; it is the radiance that belongs to who he always is, momentarily unrestrained. The humanity that veiled the glory at Bethlehem is, at the transfiguration, momentarily transparent to the glory it contains. This is what John means when he says “we have seen his glory, glory as of the only Son from the Father” (John 1:14) — the glory was always there; the transfiguration made it visible.

Moses and Elijah's conversation with Jesus about his exodos is the most extraordinary biblical conversation never recorded — two of the greatest figures of the Old Testament discussing with the Son of God the cross that will accomplish the ultimate Exodus. Moses led the first Exodus — from Egypt, through the sea, by the blood of the Passover lamb. Jesus will accomplish the last Exodus — from sin and death, through his own blood, by the power of his resurrection. The conversation on the mountain is the Old Testament endorsing the cross before it happens.
verseByVerse.examples:
Peter's desire to build three tabernacles is the perennial temptation to institutionalise the moment of glory — to capture the experience, preserve it, replicate it. Every significant encounter with the living God carries the same temptation: to build something that keeps the experience alive rather than following the Lord who gave it forward into the next thing he has planned. The disciples who want to stay on the mountain of transfiguration must come down the mountain to encounter the suffering boy (v. 37), the second passion prediction (v. 44), and eventually Jerusalem. The glory is always given for the journey, not as a substitute for it.

The command “listen to him” is the transfiguration's practical legacy for the church. The disciples have been given an extraordinary visual confirmation of who Jesus is; they are now told that the appropriate response is not to build tents but to listen. The Christian life is not primarily about spectacular experiences of divine glory — though God gives those in his mercy. It is primarily about listening to the voice of the Son: in Scripture, in prayer, in the community of faith. The mountain gives way to the road; the vision gives way to the word.

verseByVerse.quote: Now about eight days after these sayings he took with him Peter and John and James and went up on the mountain to pray. And as he was praying, the appearance of his face was altered, and his clothing became dazzling white.
verseByVerse.commentary: The connection to the preceding passage is the eight days — close enough to link the Transfiguration to the passion prediction and the call to cross-bearing. Jesus takes the inner three up the mountain to pray. The Transfiguration happens in the context of prayer — as with the baptism, as with the choosing of the Twelve, as with Gethsemane. The alteration of his face and the dazzling white of his clothing are the breaking through of his divine glory into the visible, physical world — not a new state but the revelation of what has always been true of him. This is not Jesus becoming something he was not; it is the veil drawn back briefly on what he always is.

verseByVerse.quote: And behold, two men were talking with him, Moses and Elijah, who appeared in glory and spoke of his departure, which he was about to accomplish at Jerusalem.
verseByVerse.commentary: Moses and Elijah — the Law and the Prophets — appear and speak with Jesus about his departure. The word in Greek is exodos: his exodus, his departure, his death-and-resurrection, which he is about to accomplish at Jerusalem. The choice of word is pregnant with meaning. As Moses led the first exodus out of Egypt through death and into life, Jesus is about to lead the ultimate exodus through his own death into resurrection, liberating his people from a slavery deeper than Pharaoh's. Moses and Elijah are not curiosities from the past; they are the witnesses to a fulfilment they both anticipated. They speak of it in glory because it is glorious.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Peter and those who were with him were heavy with sleep, but when they became fully awake they saw his glory and the two men who stood with him. And as the men were parting from him, Peter said to Jesus, 'Master, it is good that we are here. Let us make three tents, one for you and one for Moses and one for Elijah' — not knowing what he said.
verseByVerse.commentary: The disciples almost miss it — heavy with sleep, they struggle awake just in time to see the glory and the two figures departing. Peter's proposal to build three tents is the response of a man overwhelmed and grasping for something to do — something active, something that might prolong the moment. Luke's comment is candid: he did not know what he was saying. The suggestion betrays a misunderstanding: it places Moses and Elijah alongside Jesus rather than beneath him, and it tries to institutionalise a moment that was not given to be institutionalised but to be heard.

verseByVerse.quote: As he was saying these things, a cloud came and overshadowed them, and they were afraid as they entered the cloud. And a voice came out of the cloud, saying, 'This is my Son, my Chosen One; listen to him!' And when the voice had spoken, Jesus was found alone. And they kept silent and told no one in those days anything of what they had seen.
verseByVerse.commentary: The cloud is the shekinah — the cloud of God's presence that filled the tabernacle (Exod. 40:34–35) and led Israel through the wilderness. God is not making a new appearance; he is appearing in the form in which Israel always knew him. The voice repeats the baptism declaration — this is my Son, my Chosen One — with one addition: listen to him. This is the Father's answer to Peter's tent proposal: do not enshrine the moment; hear the word. Moses and Elijah are gone; Jesus is alone. The Law and the Prophets have pointed to him; now he is the one to hear.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 37–50 — Healing, Humility, and the Second Passion Prediction
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Coming down from the mountain, Jesus is immediately confronted with a father whose son is seized by a spirit that throws him into convulsions. The disciples who were not on the mountain were unable to cast it out — a failure that sharply juxtaposes the glory of the transfiguration with the impotence of a faithless generation. Jesus heals the boy, returns him to his father, and the crowd is astonished at the majesty of God. In the midst of this astonishment, Jesus speaks the second passion prediction — “Let these words sink into your ears: The Son of Man is about to be delivered into the hands of men.” The disciples do not understand; the saying is hidden from them; they are afraid to ask. The glory the crowd is celebrating and the suffering Jesus is announcing exist in two completely different registers — and the disciples cannot hold both at once.

The dispute about greatness (vv. 46–48) follows immediately — a bitter irony. The disciples, who cannot understand the passion prediction, are arguing about who among them is greatest. Jesus places a child beside him and says: “Whoever receives this child in my name receives me, and whoever receives me receives him who sent me. For he who is least among you all is the one who is great.” The child — in the ancient world, a person without legal standing, without the capacity to confer honour, without anything to offer in return — is the measure of greatness in the kingdom. Greatness is measured not by the capacity to receive honour from the powerful but by the willingness to receive the powerless in the name of Jesus.

The incident of the man casting out demons in Jesus's name (vv. 49–50) adds a further dimension: “Do not stop him, for the one who is not against you is for you.” The disciples have been concerned about institutional control — this man is not “with us,” not part of the recognised group. Jesus is unconcerned: the one doing good in his name is on the right side of the line. This is not an endorsement of doctrinal indifferentism — the context is a man doing something genuine (casting out demons) in the name of Jesus. It is a caution against the ecclesial parochialism that treats the boundaries of one's own group as the boundaries of the kingdom of God.
verseByVerse.theology: The disciples' inability to cast out the demon (v. 40) after their successful mission in vv. 1–6 raises the question of what has changed. Jesus's lament — “O faithless and twisted generation, how long am I to be with you and bear with you?” — identifies the problem as faith, but the faith in question seems to be a corporate or generational condition rather than the disciples' individual failure. Matthew's account (17:20) records Jesus telling them their failure was due to “little faith” — the faith that moved a mountain but was not present in this specific moment of confrontation. The lesson is the one that the whole chapter has been teaching: the authority delegated to the disciples is not their own; it flows from the one who gives it and is sustained by the relationship of trust with him. When that relationship is not cultivated — when the disciples have not prayed, when they have not stayed close to Jesus — the delegated authority does not function.
verseByVerse.examples: The child placed beside Jesus as the measure of greatness is a consistent and searching challenge to every form of Christian leadership that measures success by influence, platform, numbers, or reputation. The kingdom measure is entirely different: how do you treat the person who has nothing to offer you? How do you receive the child — the person without status, without resources, without the capacity to advance your interests? The answer reveals where you actually stand in the kingdom's ordering of things. Every pastor who gives the same quality of attention to the congregation's least influential member as to its most powerful is measuring greatness by the right measure.

verseByVerse.quote: On the next day, when they had come down from the mountain, a great crowd met him. And behold, a man from the crowd cried out, 'Teacher, I beg you to look at my son, for he is my only child. And behold, a spirit seizes him, and he suddenly cries out. It convulses him so that he foams at the mouth, and shatters him, and will hardly leave him. And I begged your disciples to cast it out, but they could not.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The descent from the Transfiguration into this scene is as stark as the descent from Sinai was for Moses. The glory of the mountain gives way immediately to the need of the valley: a father with an only child, possessed by a convulsing spirit, whom the disciples have tried and failed to heal. The father's description of his son's suffering is precise and painful — the spirit seizes, convulses, makes him foam, shatters him. And the disciples could not cast it out. The gap between the mountain and the valley is the gap between revelation and its application in a broken world, and it is the territory where most ministry happens.

But stop on the father's description, because a modern reader will recognise it and will want to ask about it. A spirit seizes the boy, he cries out, he is convulsed, he foams at the mouth, and it shatters him and will hardly leave him. Any doctor today would read that paragraph and name it: a tonic-clonic seizure, with the postictal exhaustion that follows. So was this boy ill, or was he possessed? And behind that question sits the sharper one people actually mean: were these pre-scientific people simply calling a disease of the brain a devil?

The answer comes from Luke himself, and it is worth having, because Luke is the last man in the New Testament who can be accused of not knowing the difference. He is a physician, and this Gospel is full of his clinical eye — the woman who had spent all she had on doctors (8:43), the sweat like drops of blood in the garden (22:44). And he consistently keeps the two categories apart. He writes that they brought Jesus those who were sick with various diseases, and that demons also came out of many (4:40-41). He describes a crowd who came to be healed of their diseases, and those troubled by unclean spirits who were cured (6:17-18) — two groups, named separately, in a single breath. Jesus himself speaks the same way: “I cast out demons and perform cures” (13:32). A man who thought every convulsion was a devil would not write like that. Luke reports the symptoms as symptoms, and then tells us that in this particular boy something else was behind them.

Two errors do harm here, and Luke's own care rules out both. The first makes every seizure, every darkness of the mind, a work of the enemy — a cruelty this Gospel forbids by the simple fact that its author lists sickness and spirits as different things. A Christian with epilepsy is not in the devil's grip; he needs good medicine and the love of his church, not an interrogation about hidden sin. The second error is the fashionable one, that “demon” was merely the old word for a disorder we can now diagnose properly. But notice what happens in the next verse: Jesus rebukes the thing, and it obeys and comes out. You do not reprimand a neurological condition and have it answer you. The father came with a boy no one could help; and whatever the diagnosis, he went home with his son.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus answered, 'O faithless and twisted generation, how long am I to be with you and bear with you? Bring your son here.' While he was coming, the demon threw him to the ground and convulsed him. But Jesus rebuked the unclean spirit and healed the boy, and gave him back to his father. And all were astonished at the majesty of God.
verseByVerse.commentary: The rebuke — O faithless and twisted generation — is addressed to the whole scene, not only the disciples. There is something in the collective failure of faith that Jesus finds genuinely painful. He does not analyse it; he acts. The demon makes one last violent display before it obeys — the convulsion on the ground is the power throwing its weight around at the moment of its defeat. Jesus rebukes it and heals the boy. Then: he gave him back to his father. The same phrase Luke used at Nain (7:15). The same tenderness. The miracle is framed as a gift, from Jesus to a father. The crowd's response — astonishment at the majesty of God — is the only appropriate response.

verseByVerse.quote: But while they were all marvelling at everything he was doing, Jesus said to his disciples, 'Let these words sink into your ears: The Son of Man is about to be delivered into the hands of men.' But they did not understand this saying, and it was concealed from them, so that they might not perceive it. And they were afraid to ask him about this saying.
verseByVerse.commentary: In the middle of the crowd's astonishment, Jesus takes his disciples aside for the second passion prediction. The contrast is pointed: the crowd marvels at the miracle; Jesus wants the disciples to hear something harder. Let these words sink into your ears — not a casual announcement but a solemn insistence that this must be heard and held. The disciples do not understand, and Luke says it was concealed from them — not because Jesus was obscure, but because the meaning of the cross was something that could only be fully grasped in the light of its fulfilment. They were afraid to ask. Fear often prevents the question that most needs to be asked.

verseByVerse.quote: An argument arose among them as to which of them was the greatest. But Jesus, knowing the reasoning of their hearts, took a child and put him by his side and said to them, 'Whoever receives this child in my name receives me, and whoever receives me receives him who sent me. For he who is least among you all is the one who is great.'
verseByVerse.commentary: The sequence is devastating in its honesty. Jesus has just told them he will be delivered into the hands of men — and they start arguing about which of them is the greatest. The argument is not an aberration from the disciples' character; it is a revelation of it. The second passion prediction has not yet touched the level where ambition lives. Jesus does not rebuke the argument; he redefines its terms. He places a child beside himself — someone with no social status, no power, nothing to offer — and says: to receive this one is to receive me. Greatness in the kingdom is measured by willingness to receive those who have nothing to give in return.

verseByVerse.quote: John answered, 'Master, we saw someone casting out demons in your name, and we tried to stop him, because he does not follow with us.' But Jesus said to him, 'Do not stop him, for the one who is not against you is for you.'
verseByVerse.commentary: The disciples have just been arguing about greatness, and now they report having tried to stop someone doing good because he was outside their group. The impulse is understandable — but Jesus corrects it without hesitation. The one who is not against you is for you. This is the generous principle, not the suspicious one: the criterion is whether someone is working against the kingdom, not whether they are credentialed by the right community. Jesus will later give the opposite formulation — whoever is not with me is against me (11:23) — but in that context he is speaking about his own mission; here he is speaking about the disciples' institutional boundary-keeping.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 51–62 — The Face Set Toward Jerusalem; The Cost of Following
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
“When the days drew near for him to be taken up, he set his face to go to Jerusalem.” With this single sentence, Luke's narrative pivots. The Galilean ministry is over. The great journey to Jerusalem — the “travel narrative” that will run from 9:51 to 19:44 — begins. Everything that follows in Luke until the triumphal entry is set in the context of this journey: the parables, the healings, the controversies, the teaching — all of it takes place on the road that leads to the cross. The phrase “set his face” is the language of Isaiah 50:7 — the Servant who “set his face like a flint” in the knowledge of what lay ahead. Jesus goes to Jerusalem knowing what awaits him, willing, determined, purposeful.

The immediate obstacle is a Samaritan village that refuses to receive him — precisely because his face is set toward Jerusalem (the Samaritans and Jews worshipped at rival sites: Gerizim and Jerusalem respectively). James and John want to call down fire from heaven, like Elijah (2 Kings 1:10, 12). Jesus rebukes them and moves to another village. The rebuke is instructive: the instinct to destroy those who reject Jesus is the instinct of the wrong spirit. The one who has “set his face” toward a cross does not call down fire on those who reject him; he presses on toward the greater sacrifice that will make it possible for even the Samaritans to receive him.

Three encounter stories about the cost of following close the chapter. A man offers to follow Jesus wherever he goes; Jesus warns that the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head — the itinerant, homeless, radically dependent life of the one who follows must be faced honestly. Another man is called to follow but wants to bury his father first; Jesus says “let the dead bury their own dead” — the hyperbolic shock of the saying signals that the kingdom call is categorically urgent, brooking no delay. A third man offers to follow but wants to say farewell to his household; Jesus says “no one who puts his hand to the plow and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God.” The three stories together define the cost of following: homelessness, urgency, and undivided attention to the road ahead.
verseByVerse.theology:
The travel narrative that begins at 9:51 is Luke's unique structural contribution to the Synoptic tradition. Matthew and Mark move much more quickly from Galilee to Jerusalem; Luke devotes ten chapters to the journey, filling it with teaching and encounter that Matthew includes in other contexts or that is unique to Luke. The journey structure is theological before it is geographical: Luke wants his reader to understand that following Jesus means being on the road to Jerusalem, which is to say on the road to the cross. The whole of the travel narrative is lived in the shadow of the “set face” of 9:51.

“Let the dead bury their own dead” is among the most shocking sayings of Jesus in the Gospels — an apparent violation of the Fifth Commandment (honouring parents) and the universal obligation of burial (an honour so important in the ancient world that the Old Testament names its absence as a mark of divine judgment: Jeremiah 22:18–19). The saying is not an abolition of family obligation; it is a hyperbolic statement of priority. The kingdom of God, inaugurated in the person of Jesus, is the most urgent fact in the universe — more urgent than any human obligation, including the most solemn ones. The one who is called to preach the kingdom must not delay even for the burial of a father. The urgency is not cruelty; it is eschatology.
verseByVerse.examples:
The “hand to the plow” saying is the chapter's closing image of undivided commitment. Plowing in the ancient world required keeping your eyes forward — looking back while plowing produced a crooked furrow, wasting the seed and the labour. The disciple who begins to follow Jesus while looking back at what has been left behind is the disciple whose furrow will be crooked — whose discipleship will be compromised by the competing pull of the life they have not fully surrendered. The call of 9:51–62 is the call to follow with the same undivided determination with which Jesus himself has set his face: eyes forward, hand to the plow, toward Jerusalem.

The three would-be disciples of vv. 57–62 represent three different failure modes of discipleship. The first fails by underestimating the cost (following wherever Jesus goes sounds easy until you realise it means homelessness and the cross). The second fails by delay (there is always a reasonable reason to defer the call). The third fails by divided attention (following while looking back). All three are self-generated obstacles rather than external barriers. The call is clear; the obstacle is always within. The one who actually follows, in each case, is the one who hears the call, counts the cost, and goes.

verseByVerse.quote: When the days drew near for him to be taken up, he set his face to go to Jerusalem. And he sent messengers ahead of him, who went and entered a village of the Samaritans, to make preparations for him. But the people did not receive him, because his face was set toward Jerusalem.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He set his face to go to Jerusalem — one of the great pivotal statements in Luke's Gospel. The Greek is stronger than the English suggests: he fixed his face, he determined his direction. The language echoes the Suffering Servant of Isaiah 50:7 — I have set my face like a flint. From this point on, everything in Luke is oriented toward Jerusalem, toward the cross, toward the exodus he will accomplish there. He is not drawn toward Jerusalem; he goes deliberately, knowing what awaits him.

The Samaritan village refuses to receive him — not because of anything he has done, but because his destination is Jerusalem. Jews and Samaritans had deep mutual hostility rooted in a centuries-long dispute about where God was truly to be worshipped. His face is set toward the wrong place, from their perspective. The rejection is ideological, not personal. Jesus does not force himself on those who will not have him.

verseByVerse.quote: And when his disciples James and John saw it, they said, 'Lord, do you want us to tell fire to come down from heaven and consume them?' But he turned and rebuked them. And they went on to another village.
verseByVerse.commentary:
James and John — the Sons of Thunder (Mark 3:17) — ask for permission to call down fire. Their reference point is Elijah, who called down fire on the soldiers of Ahaziah (2 Kings 1:10). They are not being malicious; they are being scriptural, in their way. But they have misread both the moment and the man. Jesus has just set his face toward a cross, not a throne; he is moving toward the place where he himself will be consumed by the fire of divine judgment on behalf of those who deserve it. There is no rebuke of the Samaritans; there is a rebuke of the disciples. The question of what to do with those who reject Jesus does not have the answer James and John proposed. They go on to another village.

If you are reading an older Bible you will find more here than the modern versions print. The King James adds to v. 55 that Jesus said, Ye know not what manner of spirit ye are of. For the Son of man is not come to destroy men's lives, but to save them. Those words are absent from the earliest and best manuscripts, and the modern translations drop them to a footnote — which is why your neighbour's Bible may be shorter than yours at this exact point. Two things are worth saying. The words are almost certainly not what Luke wrote; a scribe seems to have supplied the content of the rebuke that Luke leaves unstated, and once written in the margin it moved into the text. But the sentence that was added is entirely true, and it is true from Luke's own pages: the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost (19:10), and within a chapter the hero of his most famous story will be a Samaritan (10:33). The copyist guessed rightly what the rebuke contained. He simply had no business putting his guess into the Gospel.

verseByVerse.quote: As they were going along the road, someone said to him, 'I will follow you wherever you go.' And Jesus said to him, 'Foxes have holes, and birds of the air have nests, but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head.'
verseByVerse.commentary: The first would-be follower volunteers enthusiastically — wherever you go. Jesus responds not with a welcome but with a disclosure: following him means sharing his homelessness. The one through whom all things were made has no house. He does not own the road he walks on. This is not a discouragement of the call but a clarification of its cost. The enthusiasm that says wherever you go needs to know where he is going before it makes the promise.

verseByVerse.quote: To another he said, 'Follow me.' But he said, 'Lord, let me first go and bury my father.' And Jesus said to him, 'Leave the dead to bury their own dead. But as for you, go and proclaim the kingdom of God.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Burying one's father was among the most sacred obligations in Jewish law and culture — one of the few duties that could override even the Passover pilgrimage. Jesus's response is therefore not a callous dismissal of family duty; it is a radical statement about the urgency of the kingdom's claim. Leave the dead to bury their own dead — those who are spiritually dead can attend to the socially necessary; the living are needed for the proclamation of life. The kingdom does not wait for us to complete our existing obligations and then, if convenient, follow. It asks for the first claim on the life, not the remainder.

One thing is worth knowing before this hardens into a picture of Jesus refusing a grieving son a funeral. In that world burial happened the same day, or the next at the latest — a man whose father had died that morning would be at the tomb, not standing on a road listening to a travelling preacher. The request almost certainly means what it still means in parts of the Middle East today: let me stay until my father dies. It is not a plea for three days off for a funeral. It is a request for an indefinite postponement — a few years, perhaps many, until the family duty is discharged and the inheritance settled and the man is free to go with nothing left owing.

That is why the answer lands as it does. Jesus is not being cold about a coffin; he is refusing the word first. There will always be one more reasonable thing to finish before following becomes convenient, and the reasonable things are genuinely reasonable — that is exactly what makes them so effective at postponing everything. The kingdom does not accept a place in the queue behind the rest of a life. It asks for today.

verseByVerse.quote: Yet another said, 'I will follow you, Lord, but let me first say farewell to those at my home.' And Jesus said to him, 'No one who puts his hand to the plough and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God.'
verseByVerse.commentary: The third would-be follower also volunteers, and also asks to go back first — this time to say goodbye, a request that echoes Elisha's farewell when Elijah called him (1 Kings 19:20). Jesus's answer draws on the ploughing image: the person who looks back while ploughing drives a crooked furrow. The issue is not the farewell; it is the divided attention it reveals. Following Jesus requires an undivided orientation toward what is ahead. This does not mean family relationships are severed; it means the direction of the life is set, and that direction does not accommodate the kind of backward glance that means you have not yet fully left.

10.title: The Seventy-Two, the Samaritan, and the Better Part
10.overview:
Chapter 10 gives us three of Luke's most theologically rich scenes — each one, in its own way, a complete world. The sending of the seventy-two (vv. 1–24) expands the mission beyond the twelve, shows what kingdom authority looks like in practice, and culminates in the most intimate expression of Jesus's joy in the entire Gospel. The parable of the Good Samaritan (vv. 25–37) is the world's most famous story about neighbourly love — and simultaneously one of its most searching challenges to religious self-justification. And the scene at the home of Martha and Mary (vv. 38–42) is the New Testament's most precise statement about the one thing that is necessary in a life pulled in every direction by legitimate demands.

The chapter is the opening movement of the great travel narrative (9:51–19:44) — the long road to Jerusalem during which Jesus pours himself into his disciples and into the crowds that gather around him. The sending of the seventy-two models the missional multiplication that will characterise the church after Pentecost. The Samaritan parable models the ethics of the kingdom in the most concrete possible terms. The Mary-and-Martha scene models the devotional centre that makes the mission and the ethics sustainable. Together, the three scenes answer three questions: What does the kingdom produce in the world? What does the kingdom demand of its citizens? And what does the kingdom require of those who would receive it?

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–16 — Jesus Sends Out the Seventy-Two
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Jesus appoints seventy-two others — beyond the twelve — and sends them ahead of him in pairs to every town and place he is about to go. The number is significant: in Numbers 11:16–17, 24–25, Moses appointed seventy elders to help him carry the burden of Israel; here, the number is exceeded, suggesting a mission that goes beyond Israel. Alternatively, the table of nations in Genesis 10 lists seventy (or seventy-two, depending on whether one follows the Hebrew or the Greek text) nations — making the seventy-two a symbolic representation of the whole human race. Either way, the expansion from twelve to seventy-two signals that the mission of the kingdom is wider than the twelve tribes; it is moving toward the ends of the earth.

The instructions to the seventy-two largely echo those given to the twelve (9:1–6), with some expansions. The harvest is plentiful and the labourers few — the urgency of the mission is rooted in the size of the need, not in the enthusiasm of the workers. They are lambs among wolves — the mission is genuinely dangerous. They travel light and move purposefully: no greetings on the road (a Semitic idiom for avoiding the time-consuming social courtesies that could consume the day). They eat what is provided and do not move from house to house for better accommodation. They heal the sick and announce the kingdom. And where they are not received, they shake the dust from their feet and pronounce a solemn warning: the kingdom was near, and it was refused.

The woes on Chorazin, Bethsaida, and Capernaum (vv. 13–15) are the most severe judgment sayings in Luke's Gospel — directed not at Gentile cities but at the Jewish towns where Jesus himself performed his greatest miracles. They have seen more than Tyre and Sidon, more than Sodom — and have repented less. The principle is terrifying in its logic: greater light received without repentance produces greater accountability. The towns that had Jesus himself walking through their streets, healing their sick, teaching in their synagogues — and still did not repent — will fare worse on the day of judgment than the cities that never heard.
verseByVerse.theology:
The chain of representation in v. 16 — “The one who hears you hears me, and the one who rejects you rejects me, and the one who rejects me rejects him who sent me” — establishes the principle that governs all Christian mission. The missionary is not merely a messenger carrying information; they are a representative whose reception or rejection carries the weight of the reception or rejection of the one who sent them. This is a principle of enormous pastoral comfort (the one who receives the missionary's word receives Christ) and enormous seriousness (the one who rejects the missionary's word rejects Christ). The gospel is never merely a neutral offer; it is always a personal encounter with the Lord who sends and the Father who sent him.

The woes on the Galilean cities introduce the concept of graduated accountability — that judgment will be proportional to the light received. This is not a popular doctrine but it is a consistent one: Romans 2:12–16 develops the principle in Paul; Matthew 11:20–24 parallels the woes; Hebrews 10:26–31 applies it to those who have known the covenant. The implication for the church is challenging: the community that has heard the gospel most fully, received the most teaching, witnessed the most evidence of the Spirit's work — bears the greatest accountability for its response. The privileged place in the kingdom is also the most exposed position under judgment.
verseByVerse.examples:
The harvest metaphor — “The harvest is plentiful, but the labourers are few; therefore pray earnestly to the Lord of the harvest to send out labourers into his harvest” (v. 2) — is one of the most searching missionary texts in the Gospels. The problem is not the harvest; it is the workers. The response Jesus calls for is not immediate self-commissioning (“go!”) but prayer — asking the Lord of the harvest to solve the labour shortage by sending out workers. The prayer for missionaries precedes and sustains the sending of missionaries. The church that does not pray for labourers should not be surprised when the harvest goes ungathered.

The instruction to say “peace be to this house” when entering a home (v. 5) and the promise that “if a son of peace is there, your peace will rest upon it” is the New Testament's most explicit picture of the way the gospel moves through networks of pre-existing relationship. The “son of peace” (a Semitic idiom meaning a person who is ready for, and belongs to, the peace you bring) is the person of spiritual receptivity within a household — the person whose openness to the gospel becomes the channel through which the whole household receives it. Missional evangelism has always worked this way: finding the person of peace, staying with them, and letting the gospel radiate outward from that relationship.

verseByVerse.quote: After this the Lord appointed seventy-two others and sent them on ahead of him, two by two, into every town and place where he himself was about to go. And he said to them, 'The harvest is plentiful, but the labourers are few. Therefore pray earnestly to the Lord of the harvest to send out labourers into his harvest.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
If your Bible says seventy where this one says seventy-two, nothing is wrong and nothing much hangs on it. The manuscripts divide almost evenly between the two numbers here and again at v. 17, and translators go different ways; the older English versions read seventy, several modern ones seventy-two. Either figure carries the same symbolism, since the Old Testament itself supplies both — the elders Moses appointed number seventy in Numbers 11:16, but two more were left in the camp and prophesied anyway (Num. 11:26), and the table of nations in Genesis 10 comes to seventy in the Hebrew and seventy-two in the Greek. A copyist working from either tradition could tidy the other toward it. The mission is what matters, and the mission is the same size either way.

The mission of the Seventy-Two extends the pattern of the Twelve: the number likely echoes the seventy elders of Israel (Num. 11:16) and possibly the seventy nations of Genesis 10 — suggesting a mission with universal scope. They are sent two by two, which provides mutual accountability and fulfils the requirement of two witnesses. They go ahead of Jesus — they are not independent agents but advance heralds, preparing the towns he is about to visit.

The harvest image is striking. The problem is not a small harvest; it is a plentiful harvest with too few workers. The prescribed response is prayer — asking the Lord of the harvest to send out labourers. This is important: even those already sent as labourers are told to pray for more labourers. The mission is always larger than any one group's capacity, and the right response to the scale of the need is not despair but petition to the one who owns the harvest.

verseByVerse.quote: 'Go your way; behold, I am sending you out as lambs in the midst of wolves. Carry no moneybag, no knapsack, no sandals, and greet no one on the road.'
verseByVerse.commentary: The image of lambs among wolves is strikingly candid. Jesus does not promise safety; he promises danger, and sends them anyway. The mission is inherently vulnerable — not by accident but by design. The absence of provisions (money, bag, sandals) deepens the dependence noted in ch. 9: they go without safety nets. The instruction to greet no one on the road is not rudeness; it is urgency. Eastern greetings could be lengthy affairs. The mission is too pressing for the social rituals of a normal journey.

verseByVerse.quote: 'Whatever house you enter, first say, "Peace be to this house!" And if a son of peace is there, your peace will rest upon it. But if not, it will return to you. And remain in the same house... eating and drinking what they provide... Do not go from house to house. Whenever you enter a town and they receive you, eat what is set before you. Heal the sick in it and say to them, "The kingdom of God has come near to you."'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The greeting of peace (shalom) is not a courtesy; it is a prophetic act that either finds a receptive heart or returns unreceived. The son of peace is the person prepared by God to receive the message — the one whose heart is already opened. The instruction to stay in one house (not shopping for better hospitality) is practical wisdom about the nature of genuine welcome. Eating what is set before you without discrimination — important for a Jewish mission moving through Gentile or mixed territory — is a foretaste of the table fellowship that the gospel will ultimately produce across ethnic and culinary boundaries.

The sequence of healing and proclamation is deliberately ordered: the physical sign accompanies the verbal announcement. The kingdom of God has come near — not merely as a future hope but as a present reality touching bodies and lives in the healing that precedes the word.

verseByVerse.quote: 'But whenever you enter a town and they do not receive you, go into its streets and say, "Even the dust of your town that clings to our feet we wipe off against you. Nevertheless know this: the kingdom of God has come near." I tell you, it will be more bearable on that day for Sodom than for that town.'
verseByVerse.commentary: The rejection of the messengers is treated with great seriousness. The kingdom has come near — the opportunity is real, the offer is genuine, and the rejection of it is not a neutral act. Sodom's judgment (Gen. 19) was severe; to be judged more severely than Sodom is an almost incomprehensible warning. The difference is proximity to the gospel: Sodom sinned without the light; these towns have rejected the kingdom announced and demonstrated in their streets. Greater light received and refused incurs greater judgment. This is not a comfortable principle, but Jesus states it plainly.

verseByVerse.quote: 'Woe to you, Chorazin! Woe to you, Bethsaida! For if the mighty works done in you had been done in Tyre and Sidon, they would have repented long ago... But it will be more bearable in the judgment for Tyre and Sidon than for you. And you, Capernaum, will you be exalted to heaven? You shall be brought down to Hades... The one who hears you hears me, and the one who rejects you rejects me, and the one who rejects me rejects him who sent me.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The woes over Galilean towns that have witnessed Jesus's ministry and not repented carry the same logic as the Sodom comparison. Tyre and Sidon were proverbially wicked Gentile cities; yet Chorazin and Bethsaida — towns that have seen miracles — will be judged more harshly than they. Capernaum, which has received more ministry from Jesus than almost anywhere, faces the sharpest judgment. The principle is consistent: privilege received and refused is more culpable than ignorance.

The concluding statement — the one who hears you hears me — grounds the authority of the Seventy-Two in the authority of Jesus, and his authority in the authority of the Father. The chain of representation means that the rejection of the missionary is ultimately the rejection of God himself. This gives the mission its solemnity and its urgency.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 17–24 — The Return of the Seventy-Two
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The seventy-two return with joy: “Lord, even the demons are subject to us in your name!” Jesus's response is one of the most dramatic in the Gospels: “I saw Satan fall like lightning from heaven.” The return of the missionaries with their report of authority over demons is, for Jesus, not merely encouraging news about a successful preaching tour. It is a glimpse of the cosmic reality that the mission represents: the advance of the kingdom is the retreat of the adversary; every demon cast out is a moment in the larger defeat of Satan that the cross will accomplish definitively. The seventy-two have been fighting a battle whose outcome was decided before they began.

But Jesus immediately redirects their joy: “do not rejoice in this, that the spirits are subject to you, but rejoice that your names are written in heaven.” The authority they exercise over demons is a gift for the mission — remarkable, real, important. It is not the foundation of their security. The foundation of their security is not what they have done but what has been done for them — their names written in heaven, the book of life, the covenant record of those whom God knows and keeps. The missionary who finds their identity in the effectiveness of their ministry is vulnerable to exactly the temptation the disciples have just experienced: the exhilaration of power can displace the quiet security of grace.

Jesus then turns to the Father in what Luke calls an expression of joy in the Holy Spirit — the only time in the Synoptic Gospels where Jesus is described as experiencing joy. “I thank you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, that you have hidden these things from the wise and understanding and revealed them to little children.” The revelation of the kingdom to the unlikely — the seventy-two who have no credentials except the name of Jesus — is itself the expression of the Father's sovereign, gracious will. And Jesus speaks the beatitude of the disciples: “the eyes that see what you see” are blessed. Kings and prophets longed to see and did not; the disciples are living in the fulfilment of what they waited for. This moment of Jesus's expressed joy is one of the most tender in the whole Gospel.
verseByVerse.theology:
The vision of Satan falling like lightning from heaven (v. 18) is Jesus's own interpretation of the significance of the mission just completed. He is not describing a past event (the primordial fall of Satan — Isaiah 14, Revelation 12) but a present reality: in the advance of the kingdom, in the casting out of demons in his name, the power of the adversary is being broken. Every act of kingdom mission — proclamation, healing, the casting out of darkness — is a battle won in a war whose decisive engagement will be the cross. The seventy-two are not aware that they are fighting a cosmic battle; Jesus sees it clearly.

The joy of Jesus “in the Holy Spirit” is a Trinitarian moment: the Son's joy is expressed in the Spirit's gift of joy, directed to the Father in prayer. The Trinitarian life of God — the mutual delight of Father, Son, and Spirit in one another — overflows into the mission of the kingdom and into the lives of those who participate in it. The joy that Jesus experiences as the seventy-two return is the joy of the Father's will being accomplished through the Son's mission in the Spirit's power.
verseByVerse.examples:
“Rejoice that your names are written in heaven” is the reorientation of the missionary's identity from achievement to grace. The most fruitful missionary and the least productive missionary share the same ground of rejoicing: their names are written in heaven, not by their performance but by the grace of the one who wrote them there. This does not diminish the importance of fruitfulness; it liberates it. The missionary who rejoices in election rather than effectiveness is freed from the anxiety of measuring their worth by outcomes, and freed to give themselves to the mission without the distortion of ego that turns the mission into a performance.

The beatitude of the disciples — “blessed are the eyes that see what you see” — is the beatitude of the ordinary Christian in the age of the Spirit. We have the completed Scripture; we have the indwelling Spirit; we have the testimony of the resurrection; we live on the other side of the cross that the disciples saw approaching. The prophets and kings who longed to see and did not — they would give anything to stand where we stand. The boredom that sometimes afflicts long-standing Christians — the sense that the gospel is familiar and the faith is unremarkable — is the failure to perceive what we have actually been given. To see what we see is an extraordinary privilege.

verseByVerse.quote: The seventy-two returned with joy, saying, 'Lord, even the demons are subject to us in your name!' And he said to them, 'I saw Satan fall like lightning from heaven.'
verseByVerse.commentary: The return of the Seventy-Two is a moment of pure joy — they have discovered that what Jesus gave them actually worked. The demons submitted to them in his name. Jesus's response is both affirmation and perspective: I saw Satan fall like lightning from heaven. The exorcisms performed by the Seventy-Two are not isolated events; they are episodes in a cosmic battle that is being won. The fall of Satan is either a vision of the primordial fall, now being enacted in these missions, or a prophetic vision of his ultimate defeat (cf. Rev. 12:9) — or both. Every demon cast out in Jesus's name is a down-payment on the final victory.

verseByVerse.quote: 'Behold, I have given you authority to tread on serpents and scorpions, and over all the power of the enemy, and nothing shall hurt you. Nevertheless, do not rejoice in this, that the spirits are subject to you, but rejoice that your names are written in heaven.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The authority is comprehensive — all the power of the enemy — and the protection is real. But Jesus immediately redirects the source of joy: not the authority over spirits, impressive as it is, but the fact that their names are written in heaven. The authority is functional and situational; the inscription in heaven is permanent and personal. It is possible to have significant spiritual power and to use it well and still find one's identity in the wrong place. Jesus wants their joy rooted in who they are before God, not in what they can do for God.

Two things in that promise need guarding, because both have been badly misused. The first is the serpents. Set beside the longer ending of Mark — “they will pick up serpents with their hands” (Mark 16:18) — this verse has been made the charter of the snake-handling churches, where believers lift live rattlesnakes in worship to demonstrate their faith, and where people have died doing it. But look at what Jesus is actually saying. Serpents and scorpions are standard biblical shorthand for hostile and demonic power — the language comes from Psalm 91:13, “you will tread on the lion and the adder” — and the whole sentence explains itself in its next clause: and over all the power of the enemy. He is describing the authority the seventy-two have just been exercising over demons, not issuing an invitation to pick up vipers. And there is a sharper point still, from Luke's own pages. Psalm 91 is the very psalm the devil quoted in the wilderness, urging Jesus to throw himself from the temple because angels would catch him — and Jesus refused with a single line: “You shall not put the Lord your God to the test” (4:9-12). To engineer a danger in order to make God prove a promise is not faith; it is the precise thing Jesus called temptation. A man who deliberately handles a rattlesnake to demonstrate his trust is not obeying this verse. He is repeating the devil's use of Scripture.

The second is the phrase nothing shall hurt you, which, read as bodily immunity, is contradicted by almost everyone who first heard it. James was killed with the sword (Acts 12:2). Stephen was stoned. Paul was beaten, stoned, and shipwrecked, and at the last beheaded — though he was also, once, shaken off a viper into the fire without harm (Acts 28:3-6), which shows that God can preserve, not that he always will. So what does the promise mean? Luke answers it himself, and he does it by putting both halves in a single breath: “some of you they will put to death... but not a hair of your head will perish” (21:16-18). Both sentences are true at once, which settles the sense beyond argument. The protection is not a guarantee that the body will be untouched; it is a guarantee that the enemy cannot finally destroy them — that nothing done to a disciple's body can undo what has been secured for his soul. Which is exactly why Jesus moves in the very next breath from the power they wield to the names they bear. Authority over demons can be exercised today and be irrelevant tomorrow; a name written in heaven is the one thing that no serpent, no scorpion, and no executioner can reach.

verseByVerse.quote: In that same hour he rejoiced in the Holy Spirit and said, 'I thank you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, that you have hidden these things from the wise and understanding and revealed them to little children; yes, Father, for such was your gracious will. All things have been handed over to me by my Father, and no one knows who the Son is except the Father, or who the Father is except the Son and anyone to whom the Son chooses to reveal him.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Luke records that Jesus rejoiced in the Holy Spirit — one of the very few places in the Gospels where Jesus's emotion is specified as joy. The prayer is a doxology for the sovereignty of the Father in revelation: the hidden things are concealed from the sophisticated and disclosed to the nēpioi, the infants, the simple, those without pretension. This is not anti-intellectualism; it is a statement about the posture required to receive revelation — the posture of dependence and openness that the learned often find hardest to maintain.

The claim of vv. 21–22 is among the most explicitly high-Christological statements in the Synoptic Gospels: all things have been given to the Son; the mutual knowledge of Father and Son is unique and exclusive; the Son mediates all access to the Father. This is not the language of a prophet or a teacher; it is the language of one who stands in a category by himself.

verseByVerse.quote: Then turning to the disciples he said privately, 'Blessed are the eyes that see what you see! For I tell you that many prophets and kings desired to see what you see, and did not see it, and to hear what you hear, and did not hear it.'
verseByVerse.commentary: The beatitude for the disciples is a beatitude of historical privilege. The prophets and kings of the Old Testament — those who longed most intensely for the coming of the kingdom, who prayed over the promises and strained toward their fulfilment — did not live to see what the disciples are seeing every day. They are standing at the fulfilment of everything Israel's greatest men and women hoped for. The danger for the disciples — and for every Christian — is that familiarity with the extraordinary can dull the sense of its extraordinary character. The word blessed is a call to see clearly what is in front of them.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 25–37 — The Parable of the Good Samaritan
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
A lawyer stands up to test Jesus: “Teacher, what shall I do to inherit eternal life?” Jesus turns the question back to the expert in the law: “What is written in the Law? How do you read it?” The lawyer answers perfectly — love the Lord your God with all your heart, soul, strength, and mind, and love your neighbour as yourself. Jesus commends him: “You have answered correctly; do this, and you will live.” But the lawyer, “desiring to justify himself,” asks the follow-up question that will produce the world's most famous parable: “And who is my neighbour?” The question sounds reasonable; it is actually the question of someone who wants to know the minimum — who do I have to love, and who can I exclude from the obligation?

Jesus answers with a story. A man going down from Jerusalem to Jericho — a notoriously dangerous road, dropping seventeen miles through desert and limestone cliffs from 2,500 feet above sea level to 800 feet below — falls among robbers who strip him, beat him, and leave him half dead. A priest passes and goes by on the other side. A Levite passes and goes by on the other side. A Samaritan — the hated half-breed of the Jewish world, the man no Jewish teacher would use as a hero in a moral example — sees the man, has compassion, binds his wounds, pours oil and wine, puts him on his own animal, brings him to an inn, cares for him through the night, and the next day pays the innkeeper two denarii (two days' wages) and promises to repay whatever more is spent. Then Jesus reverses the question: “Which of these three do you think was a neighbour to the man who fell into the robbers' hands?” The lawyer cannot bring himself to say “the Samaritan” — he says “The one who showed him mercy.” Jesus says: “You go, and do likewise.”

The reversal of the question is the parable's most important move. The lawyer asked “who is my neighbour?” — a question designed to define the scope of obligation, to locate the boundary beyond which love is not required. Jesus answers with a question that makes the asking person the subject: “Which one proved to be a neighbour?” The question is no longer about who qualifies to be loved; it is about whether you are the kind of person who loves. The lawyer wanted to know who is inside the circle of obligation; Jesus shows that the question of the kingdom is not where the circle is drawn but whether you are the kind of person who acts like the Samaritan when you find someone half dead on the road.
verseByVerse.theology:
The priest and the Levite who pass by have been subject to various sympathetic interpretations: they may have feared defilement from a corpse (if the man was already dead), they may have feared an ambush (robbers sometimes used decoys), they may have been in a hurry to perform temple duties. Luke offers none of these mitigations. He simply says they “passed by on the other side.” Whatever their reasons, they made a choice — and the choice was to prioritise something else over the man in front of them. The Samaritan, by contrast, “when he saw him, had compassion.” The seeing leads to the compassion; the compassion leads to the action. There is no gap in the Samaritan's response between perception and action — which is the model of love that the parable commends.

The parable has been read allegorically from Origen onward: the traveller is Adam (or humanity), the robbers are the devil, the priest and Levite are the law and prophets which cannot save, the Samaritan is Christ, the inn is the church, the two denarii are the two sacraments or the two testaments, the innkeeper is Paul or the apostles. The allegorical reading is not without insight — it captures the christological dimension of the story, since Jesus himself is the one who binds wounds, pays the debt, and promises to return. But the primary thrust of the parable is ethical: “Go and do likewise.” Whatever the allegorical depth, the surface command is non-negotiable.
verseByVerse.examples:
