When one of the guests at the table hears Jesus's teaching about the resurrection of the just, he offers a pious exclamation: “Blessed is everyone who will eat bread in the kingdom of God!” Jesus responds with the parable of the great banquet — and the exclamation that prompted it turns out to be more ironic than the guest intended. A man gives a great banquet and invites many. When the time comes and everything is ready, he sends his servant to tell those who were invited: “Come, for everything is now ready.” And they all begin to make excuses. One has bought a field and must go see it. One has bought five yoke of oxen and must go test them. One has married a wife and cannot come. The master is angry and sends the servant out to bring in the poor, the crippled, the blind, and the lame from the streets and lanes — the same people Jesus had just told the host to invite. Then further: go out to the highways and hedges and compel people to come in, so that my house may be filled. “For I tell you, none of those who were invited shall taste my banquet.”

The parable is transparent in its application. The original guests are Israel — specifically the religious establishment that has received the invitation through the whole of the Old Testament and is now declining it with polite excuses. The poor, crippled, blind, and lame brought in from the city are the tax collectors and sinners, the marginalised of Israel who are responding to Jesus's ministry. The people from the highways and hedges are the Gentiles — those beyond the covenant who will be pressed into the feast when the original guests decline. The movement of the banquet follows the movement of Acts: from Jerusalem, to Judea and Samaria, to the ends of the earth.

The excuses of the original guests deserve close attention. None of them is implausible; all of them are legitimate activities (buying property, testing new equipment, enjoying a new marriage). The problem is not the activity but the priority — they have placed legitimate things above the most important thing, and in doing so have said, in effect, that the banquet is less important than the field, the oxen, and the wife. This is the form that rejection of the gospel most often takes: not hostility but prior commitments; not contempt but competing loves; not “I don't want to come” but “I've already got something else on.”
verseByVerse.theology: The master's anger and the final exclusion — “none of those who were invited shall taste my banquet” — is the definitive statement of judgment on the rejection of grace. The banquet is not cancelled because the original guests declined; it proceeds, filled with unexpected guests. But the original guests are excluded not merely from the event but from the fruit of the event — the kingdom feast, the resurrection of the just that the pious guest had just invoked. The polite decline of the gospel invitation carries eschatological consequences that no subsequent regret can reverse. The door that was open is now shut; the feast that was prepared is proceeding without those who said “I cannot come.”
verseByVerse.examples: The three excuses cover the three great competing loves: possessions (“I have bought a field”), work (“I have bought five yoke of oxen”), and family (“I have married a wife”). Jesus has already addressed all three as potential thorns that choke the word (8:14) and as the competing loyalties that discipleship must supersede (9:57–62; 14:26). The parable compresses the three into the form of polite regrets — which is the form most of the world's rejection of the gospel takes. Very few people say “I reject Christ.” Many people say “I'm very interested, but not right now — I have other things I need to deal with first.” The parable names this for what it is: a refusal.

verseByVerse.quote: When one of those who reclined at table with him heard these things, he said to him, 'Blessed is everyone who will eat bread in the kingdom of God!'
verseByVerse.commentary: The remark is pious and comfortable — a beatitude about the future kingdom that allows the speaker to nod approvingly without being personally implicated. It is the religious equivalent of saying what a wonderful idea in principle. Jesus's response — a parable — turns the comfortable future-tense beatitude into an urgent present-tense challenge. The question is not whether the kingdom feast will be blessed; it is whether you will be there.

verseByVerse.quote: But he said to him, 'A man once gave a great banquet and invited many. And at the time for the banquet he sent his servant to say to those who had been invited, "Come, for everything is now ready." But they all alike began to make excuses. The first said to him, "I have bought a field, and I must go out and see it. Please have me excused." And another said, "I have bought five yoke of oxen, and I go to examine them. Please have me excused." And another said, "I have married a wife, and therefore I cannot come."'
verseByVerse.commentary: The three excuses share a family resemblance: each is about something good — property, business, marriage — that has taken priority over the invitation. None of the excuses involves an emergency; all of them involve choosing something else over the banquet. The field buyer has already purchased the field; viewing it now is curiosity, not necessity. The oxen buyer is similarly at leisure. The newly married man has a genuine celebration — but it does not prevent him from attending; it simply means he would rather be elsewhere. The excuses are not lies; they are revelations. The things that seem most important have displaced the one thing necessary.

verseByVerse.quote: 'So the servant came and reported these things to his master. Then the master of the house became angry and said to his servant, "Go out quickly to the streets and lanes of the city, and bring in the poor and crippled and blind and lame." And the servant said, "Sir, what you commanded has been done, and still there is room." And the master said to the servant, "Go out to the highways and hedges and compel them to come in, that my house may be filled. For I tell you, none of those men who were invited shall taste my banquet."'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The anger of the master is not petulance; it is the anger of refused grace. The feast has been prepared at great cost; the invited guests have preferred their fields and oxen. The master's response is to fill the table with those who were not on the original list: the poor, crippled, blind, and lame — exactly the people Jesus told the host to invite in vv. 13–14. And when even they have come and there is still room, the invitation extends to the highways and hedges — the margins of society, the Gentiles, the outsiders. The feast will be full. But those who were first invited and refused will not taste it. Refusal is permanent only in this sense: the feast does not wait indefinitely, and the door does not stay open after the house is full.

One phrase here has done real damage and should be handled plainly: compel them to come in. Augustine, pressed by the Donatist controversy, used this line to justify the state coercing schismatics back to the church, and it was quoted for centuries afterwards in defence of forced baptisms, penal laws and worse. It will not carry that weight. The word means to urge strongly, to press, to insist — and the setting is the ordinary courtesy of that world, where a poor man summoned from a hedgerow to a nobleman's banquet would assume a mistake had been made and would need pressing hard before he would believe the invitation was meant for him. The compulsion in view is the servant taking a beggar by the arm and saying, no, truly, he means you.

Which is exactly the opposite of force. Everyone actually compelled in this parable is someone who thought themselves too far outside to be wanted; the only people who stay out are those who were invited politely and had other plans. Nobody is dragged to this table against their will — the whole grief of the story is a master who will not do that, and a set of first guests who walk away untouched. If the verse presses anything on the church, it is urgency in persuading the people who assume the gospel cannot possibly be for them.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Great crowds are travelling with Jesus, and he turns and addresses them directly with the most demanding discipleship saying in Luke's Gospel. “If anyone comes to me and does not hate his own father and mother and wife and children and brothers and sisters, yes, and even his own life, he cannot be my disciple.” The word “hate” (misein) is Semitic hyperbole for “love less than” — the same kind of comparative language used in Genesis 29:30–31 where Jacob “loved Rachel more than Leah,” and the text describes Leah as “hated.” Jesus is not commanding the feeling of hatred for family; he is commanding a priority so absolute that, in comparison to the priority of Jesus, every other love appears as hatred.

Two parables press the same point: the tower-builder who does not first count the cost, and the king who does not first calculate whether his army can defeat the larger force coming against him. Both parables say the same thing: unthinking commitment is worse than no commitment. The person who begins to build without counting the cost is the person who starts to follow Jesus without understanding what following costs — and becomes the laughingstock of those who watched the unfinished foundation. The decision to follow Jesus should be made with open eyes, clear calculation, and full understanding of what is being asked. What is being asked is everything: “Any one of you who does not renounce all that he has cannot be my disciple.”

The saying about salt (vv. 34–35) closes the section: salt that has lost its saltiness is worthless — it cannot season food or fertilise the land; it is thrown away. The disciple who has begun to follow but has not counted the cost — who follows without the absolute priority the discipleship demands — has become the unsalty salt. Presence without function; identification without transformation; the name without the reality.
verseByVerse.theology: The cost of discipleship teaching is the hardest word in the chapter — and it is addressed to those who are already following, already enthusiastic, already in the crowd around Jesus. They are not being warned before they commit; they are being warned that what they think they have committed to may not be what discipleship actually requires. The danger is not the uncommitted outsider but the enthusiastic follower who has not yet counted the cost of the absolute priority that Jesus demands. This is the word that separates the crowd from the disciples — not condemnation of the crowd, but the honest statement of what following the one who set his face toward Jerusalem actually involves.
verseByVerse.examples: The tower-builder and the king are the New Testament's invitation to deliberate, careful, calculating discipleship — the opposite of impulsive commitment. This does not mean that the decision to follow Jesus is primarily intellectual or that emotion has no place in conversion. It means that the commitment must be made by the whole person, including the mind that counts the cost. The person who “gave their life to Jesus” at a moment of emotional intensity, without ever thinking about what that commitment entails, is the person most vulnerable to the crisis that reveals whether the tower has a foundation. Count the cost — not to make the decision easier, but to make it real.

verseByVerse.quote: Now great crowds accompanied him, and he turned and said to them, 'If anyone comes to me and does not hate his own father and mother and wife and children and brothers and sisters, yes, and even his own life, he cannot be my disciple. Whoever does not bear his own cross and come after me cannot be my disciple.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The large crowds prompt the most demanding discipleship teaching in Luke. Hate in this Semitic idiom means to love less by comparison — to place the claims of Jesus above the claims of family when the two conflict (cf. Matt. 10:37's less stark formulation). This is not a call to hostility toward family; it is a statement about the hierarchy of ultimate allegiance. Jesus is not competing for second place. The cross-bearing that follows — the daily surrender of the self — is the concrete expression of what this priority looks like in practice.

The idiom explains the word, but a reader may still suspect the explanation of being convenient — a hard saying softened because we do not like it. So it is worth showing that the softer reading is not a rescue operation but the only one the rest of Scripture will allow. The same Lord who says this upheld the fifth commandment and enforced it with unusual severity. When the scribes had devised Corban — a way of declaring money dedicated to God so that it need not be spent supporting aged parents — Jesus called it making void the word of God by their tradition (Mark 7:9-13). That is precisely the manoeuvre a literal reading of this verse would license, and he condemned it in the strongest terms he ever used about religious practice. He also kept the commandment himself at the last possible moment: dying, with minutes left, he arranged for his mother's care and gave her to John (John 19:26-27). And Paul states the principle flatly: anyone who does not provide for his relatives, and especially for members of his household, “has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever” (1 Tim. 5:8). A man who neglects his family in order to serve Jesus more freely has not obeyed this verse. He has broken a commandment that Jesus defended.

What the saying does mean is a matter of collision, not of everyday temperature. Most of the time there is no conflict at all — loving Christ makes a man a better son, a better husband, a better father, not a worse one. The verse speaks to the moment when the two claims genuinely cannot both be honoured: when following Jesus will cost you your family's approval, or your inheritance, or your place at their table; when obeying him means being thought a fool, or a traitor, or lost. In that moment one loyalty has to give, and Jesus says plainly which one it must not be.

If you are living inside that collision, take two things from this verse. The first is that the cost is real and Jesus never pretends otherwise — he has already said he came to divide households (12:51-53), and he says it here to a crowd, not to specialists. The grief you feel is not a sign that you have done something wrong. The second is that the command does not license coldness. Nothing here permits you to write your family off, to argue with them at every meal, to make your faith a weapon, or to stop honouring them. You go on loving them, and in most cases loving them better than you did before; you simply stop letting their approval decide what you do with Christ. And note the last name on the list, which is the one that governs the rest: and even his own life. Family is not being singled out for sacrifice. The self is on the same list, and it is the harder renunciation of the two.

verseByVerse.quote: 'For which of you, desiring to build a tower, does not first sit down and count the cost, whether he has enough to complete it? Otherwise, when he has laid a foundation and is not able to finish, all who see it begin to mock him, saying, "This man began to build and was not able to finish."'
verseByVerse.commentary: The tower parable is an argument for honest self-assessment before committing. The point is not to discourage following Jesus but to discourage the kind of emotional, crowd-driven following that has not counted what it will cost. The half-built tower is the image of a discipleship that began in enthusiasm and collapsed under the weight of what it actually required. Jesus would rather have a smaller number of genuine disciples who have counted the cost than a larger crowd of enthusiasts who will scatter when the cost arrives. The counting of the cost is not a deterrent; it is an act of respect for the seriousness of what is being offered.

verseByVerse.quote: 'Or what king, going out to encounter another king in war, will not sit down first and deliberate whether he is able with ten thousand to meet him who comes against him with twenty thousand? And if not, while the other is yet a great way off, he sends a delegation and asks for terms of peace. So therefore, any one of you who does not renounce all that he has cannot be my disciple.'
verseByVerse.commentary: The military parable drives the same point from a different angle. A king facing twice his numbers needs to assess his position honestly and either fight with full commitment or negotiate. The middle option — half-committed engagement — is disastrous in war and in discipleship. The conclusion — any one of you who does not renounce all that he has cannot be my disciple — is the starkest statement of the cost in the whole passage. Renouncing all does not mean that every disciple immediately liquidates their possessions; it means that every disciple has settled the question of ownership: nothing is held back from the Lord's disposal.

verseByVerse.quote: 'Salt is good, but if salt has lost its taste, how shall its saltiness be restored? It is of no use either for the soil or for the manure pile. It is thrown away. He who has ears to hear, let him hear.'
verseByVerse.commentary: The salt saying closes the discipleship section with a warning about the loss of what made something useful. Salt without saltiness has no function — it cannot season food, cannot preserve meat, cannot fertilise soil. The disciple who has committed without the full surrender of vv. 26–33 is like unsalty salt: present but not effective, occupying space without contributing what disciples are for. The call to hear — he who has ears to hear, let him hear — is the same call issued after the parable of the sower. The teaching has landed; the question is what each person will do with it.

15.title: Lost and Found: The Three Parables of Grace
15.overview:
Chapter 15 is the theological heart of Luke's Gospel — the chapter that more than any other earns Luke the title “the Gospel of grace.” It contains three parables told in response to a single complaint: the Pharisees and scribes grumble that “this man receives sinners and eats with them.” The three parables are Jesus's answer to the grumbling — not an argument but a story, or rather three stories that together form a single, overwhelming answer to the question: why does the Son of God eat with sinners? Because this is what God is like. He is the shepherd who leaves the ninety-nine to find the one lost sheep. He is the woman who lights a lamp and sweeps the whole house until she finds the one lost coin. He is the father who runs to meet his returning son while he is still a long way off.

The three parables form a crescendo: from a sheep (something lost through its own wandering nature), to a coin (something lost through its owner's carelessness, possibly), to a son (someone lost through deliberate, calculated rebellion). The lostness becomes more personal, more chosen, more culpable at each step — and the joy at the finding becomes more extravagant, more communal, more absolutely centred on grace rather than on the condition of the lost. The sheep does nothing to return; it is carried home. The coin does nothing; it is found. The son turns around and prepares a speech about his unworthiness — and the father interrupts the speech with the best robe and the ring and the sandals and the fatted calf. The grace always exceeds the repentance.

The chapter's most searching moment is the elder son (vv. 25–32) — the one who has never left, who has served faithfully, who is furious at the welcome given to the prodigal. He is the Pharisees in the parable — the ones whose complaint prompted all three parables. And the father's final words to him are the most tender and most open-ended in the chapter: “Son, you are always with me, and all that is mine is yours. It was fitting to celebrate and be glad, for this your brother was dead, and is alive; he was lost, and is found.” The chapter ends without the elder son's response. Luke does not tell us whether the Pharisees came in to the feast. The question is left open — which is where Jesus leaves the invitation.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — The Parable of the Lost Sheep
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Tax collectors and sinners are drawing near to hear Jesus; the Pharisees and scribes grumble: “This man receives sinners and eats with them.” The grumble is the occasion for all three parables. Jesus begins with the most relatable image: “What man of you, having a hundred sheep, if he has lost one of them, does not leave the ninety-nine in the open country, and go after the one that is lost, until he finds it?” The question expects the answer “every one of us would do this” — and in doing so, it validates the behaviour Jesus has been accused of. The parable is not defending an unusual practice; it is identifying the objectors' own instinct and showing that God operates on the same instinct, only more completely.

The shepherd who finds the sheep does not drive it home; he lays it on his shoulders, rejoicing. He comes home and calls together his friends and neighbours: “Rejoice with me, for I have found my sheep that was lost.” And then the application: “Just so, I tell you, there will be more joy in heaven over one sinner who repents than over ninety-nine righteous persons who need no repentance.” The joy in heaven over one repentant sinner is the answer to the Pharisees' grumbling. They are grumbling at something that makes heaven rejoice. The gap between the Pharisees' response to the tax collectors and sinners and heaven's response to them is the gap between a theology of merit and a theology of grace.
verseByVerse.theology: The shepherd who leaves the ninety-nine to find the one is the most dramatic possible image of the divine initiative in salvation. The sheep does not seek the shepherd; the shepherd seeks the sheep. This is the consistent pattern of grace in the Scripture: “We love because he first loved us” (1 John 4:19); “No one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him” (John 6:44); “You did not choose me, but I chose you” (John 15:16). The lost sheep contributes nothing to its rescue; it is found, lifted, carried. The Reformed tradition has seen in this parable the perfect illustration of effectual calling: the shepherd does not call and then wait for the sheep to respond; he goes out and finds it and brings it home.
verseByVerse.examples: The ninety-nine left “in the open country” while the shepherd goes after the one is one of the most counter-intuitive images in the parables — it looks irresponsible. But it reveals something about the nature of the community that belongs to the shepherd: they are safe in his care even when he is searching for the lost one. The gathered community is not threatened by the shepherd's pursuit of the wanderer; it is the context from which the shepherd can go and to which he brings the found sheep. The church that begrudges the energy the shepherd expends on the lost has misunderstood its own situation: it was once the one that was lost and is now among the ninety-nine.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the tax collectors and sinners were all drawing near to hear him. And the Pharisees and the scribes grumbled, saying, 'This man receives sinners and eats with them.'
verseByVerse.commentary: The setting of the three parables of chapter 15 is the most important thing about them: tax collectors and sinners are drawing near to Jesus, and the Pharisees and scribes are grumbling about it. The three parables — the lost sheep, the lost coin, the lost son — are not general teachings about God's love; they are a defence of Jesus's behaviour, addressed to his critics. Why does Jesus eat with sinners? Because this is what God does when something lost is found. The question is not whether sinners should be welcomed; it is whether the Pharisees can understand the kind of God who does the welcoming.

verseByVerse.quote: So he told them this parable: 'What man of you, having a hundred sheep, if he has lost one of them, does not leave the ninety-nine in the open country, and go after the one that is lost, until he finds it? And when he has found it, he lays it on his shoulders, rejoicing. And when he comes home, he calls together his friends and his neighbours, saying to them, "Rejoice with me, for I have found my sheep that was lost." Just so, I tell you, there will be more joy in heaven over one sinner who repents than over ninety-nine righteous persons who need no repentance.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The shepherd's leaving of the ninety-nine to seek the one is not abandonment of the many; it is the expression of a love that cannot accept loss as the final state of what it owns. The sheep has not found its way back; it has been found. The initiative is entirely the shepherd's. The joy at the finding exceeds what the finding itself would seem to warrant: he calls friends and neighbours to celebrate, as if the return of one sheep were an occasion for a party. Jesus makes the arithmetic explicit: more joy in heaven over one sinner who repents than over ninety-nine who need no repentance. The ninety-nine are safe; they are not lost. But the one who was lost and is found again produces a joy disproportionate to the numbers involved — because what was at stake was not the sheep's value as livestock but its belonging to the shepherd.

The phrase ninety-nine righteous persons who need no repentance should be handled with care, because it can be taken two ways and both are held by serious readers. It may be straightforward: there really are people already safe in the fold, and no slight is intended toward them. But remember who Jesus is answering. Verses 1-2 tell us the audience: Pharisees and scribes, grumbling that this man receives sinners. On their lips, righteous, needing no repentance is exactly how they would have described themselves — and by the end of this same chapter Jesus will paint one of them as an elder brother standing outside his father's house, refusing to come in. Read against that ending, the phrase carries a dry edge: there is no joy in heaven over the ninety-nine, not because they are secure, but because nobody who believes he needs no repentance has yet given heaven anything to celebrate. If you find yourself untroubled by this parable, it is worth asking which number you have quietly assigned yourself.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–10 — The Parable of the Lost Coin
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The second parable shifts the seeking figure from a male shepherd to a woman — and the search from a hillside to a house. A woman has ten silver coins; she loses one. She lights a lamp, sweeps the house, searches carefully until she finds it. When she finds it, she calls together her friends and neighbours: “Rejoice with me, for I have found the coin that I had lost.” And again the application: “Just so, I tell you, there is joy before the angels of God over one sinner who repents.” The parable is the domestic counterpart to the pastoral — the kingdom of God is sought with the same tenacity in the house as on the hillside, with the same joy at the finding, and the same invitation to share the rejoicing.

The ten silver coins may represent a woman's dowry — worn as a headdress or necklace, the coins were both financial security and personal identity marker. The loss of even one would have been significant and distressing, not merely a minor inconvenience. The careful, thorough search — lamp, broom, every corner — is the search of someone who knows the value of what is lost and will not give up until it is found. The coin cannot seek itself; it can only be found. The divine initiative is even more pure in this parable than in the shepherd one.
verseByVerse.theology: The joy “before the angels of God” (v. 10) — slightly different from “in heaven” in the sheep parable — suggests that the angels are witnesses to and participants in the joy of God when a sinner repents. The book of Hebrews describes the angels as “ministering spirits sent out to serve for the sake of those who are to inherit salvation” (Hebrews 1:14); they are invested in the outcomes of the gospel. The rejoicing of the angels at one sinner's repentance is the heavenly community's participation in the same joy that the shepherd's friends and neighbours share on earth. The finding of the lost is a cosmic event — celebrated at every level of the created order that knows what was lost.
verseByVerse.examples: The woman's methodical search — lamp lit, house swept, careful looking — is the model of the kind of prayer and pastoral work that refuses to give up on those who are lost. She does not glance around casually and conclude “it's not here.” She lights the lamp (creating the conditions for seeing clearly), sweeps (removing what might be covering the coin), and searches carefully until she finds it. The work of intercession for the lost follows the same method: create the conditions for light (prayer, the word), remove the obstacles (confronting the things that obscure the gospel), and search persistently until the finding.

verseByVerse.quote: 'Or what woman, having ten silver coins, if she loses one coin, does not light a lamp and sweep the house and seek diligently until she finds it? And when she has found it, she calls together her friends and neighbours, saying, "Rejoice with me, for I have found the coin that I had lost." Just so, I tell you, there is joy before the angels of God over one sinner who repents.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The second parable gives the seeking a female face — unusual in the parable tradition and deliberate. The coin is not wandering like a sheep; it is simply lost in the house, passive, unable to seek or return. The woman lights a lamp, sweeps every corner, and seeks diligently until she finds it. The lost coin does not co-operate with its recovery; the recovery is entirely the woman's doing. This parable emphasises the completeness of the sinner's lostness even more than the first: the sheep could at least wander; the coin simply lies where it fell. The repentance that follows is entirely the result of being found by the one who sought.

The joy pattern repeats: she calls friends and neighbours; heaven rejoices. The community of heaven is drawn into celebration every time a sinner is found. The Pharisees, grumbling at the banqueting that surrounds Jesus's ministry, are grumbling against the very thing that produces joy in the presence of God.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–32 — The Parable of the Prodigal Son
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The third parable is the longest, the most complex, and the most theologically inexhaustible in the Gospels. A man has two sons. The younger asks for his share of the estate — a request that in the ancient world was roughly equivalent to wishing his father dead, since inheritance was distributed at death. The father divides the estate. The younger son takes his share, travels to a far country, squanders it in reckless living. A famine comes; he hires himself to a citizen of that country who sends him to feed pigs — the ultimate humiliation for a Jewish person; pigs were unclean animals, and tending them was unclean work. The son comes to himself: “My father's hired servants have more than enough bread, but I perish here with hunger! I will arise and go to my father, and I will say to him, 'Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you. I am no longer worthy to be called your son. Treat me as one of your hired servants.'”

He arises and goes. “But while he was still a long way off, his father saw him and felt compassion, and ran and embraced him and kissed him.” The father does not wait for the apology to be completed; he runs, he embraces, he kisses — before the son has finished his prepared speech. The best robe, the ring, the sandals, the fatted calf — each item is a specific restoration of status that the son has forfeited. The best robe replaces the far-country rags. The ring restores the family seal — the authority and identity of a son. The sandals distinguish the free person from the slave (slaves went barefoot). The fatted calf was the most prized animal, reserved for the most significant celebrations. Every element of the reception is an act of radical, extravagant, complete restoration.

The elder son returns from the fields to the sound of music and dancing. When he learns what has happened, he refuses to go in. The father comes out to him and pleads. The elder son's indictment is precise: “Look, these many years I have served you, and I never disobeyed your command, yet you never gave me a young goat, that I might celebrate with my friends. But when this son of yours came, who has devoured your property with prostitutes, you killed the fattened calf for him!” The father's response is the most important and the most open-ended statement in the chapter: “Son, you are always with me, and all that is mine is yours. It was fitting to celebrate and be glad, for this your brother was dead, and is alive; he was lost, and is found.” The parable ends there. We do not know if the elder son goes in.
verseByVerse.theology:
The father who runs to meet the returning son while he is “still a long way off” is the most dramatic image of prevenient grace in the Gospels. The father has been watching — his seeing the son “while he was still a long way off” implies he has been looking in the direction his son went. The running is undignified for a man of his social standing in the ancient world; a patriarch ran only in emergencies, or when moved by a passion that overwhelmed propriety. The father's run is the image of a love that cannot wait for the proper moment, cannot observe the social forms, cannot let the distance stand a moment longer than it must. This is the God who, in the words of Jonathan Edwards, “is not at all backward in pardoning the most heinous sinners.”

The elder son's complaint reveals the theology he has been operating under — the theology of merit and reward: “I have served you many years and never disobeyed.” His discipleship has been servitude — he has been in the house as a servant, not as a son. He has not understood that “all that is mine is yours” — that the inheritance he envied the prodigal receiving was already his. The elder son's crisis is the crisis of all religion that has not yet understood grace: it knows obedience but not sonship; it knows duty but not love; it knows the father's house but not the father's heart.
verseByVerse.examples:
The prodigal son's “he came to himself” (v. 17) is one of the most psychologically precise phrases in the Gospels — the description of repentance as a return to sanity, to reality, to the self that was being denied by the direction of the life. The far country, the pigs, the famine — these are the conditions that broke through the self-deception of the departure. Coming to himself is the first act of repentance: seeing clearly where he is, what he has done, and what he has lost. The prepared speech (“I am no longer worthy to be called your son”) is the right speech; it is just that the father interrupts it before the son can finish it, because the status the son is renouncing has already been restored before the renunciation is complete. Grace always exceeds repentance.

The elder son who has been “always with” the father but has never experienced the father's love — who has been in the house without being in the family — is the portrait of religious proximity without relational reality. He knows the father's rules; he does not know the father's heart. The father's “all that is mine is yours” is the revelation that the elder son has been living as a tenant in his own inheritance. The question the parable leaves open — does he go in? — is the question it leaves for every reader who recognises the elder son in themselves.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said, 'There was a man who had two sons. And the younger of them said to his father, "Father, give me the share of property that is coming to me." And he divided his assets between them. And not many days later, the younger son gathered all he had and took a journey into a far country, and there he squandered his property in reckless living.'
verseByVerse.commentary: The younger son's request is, in the social world of the first century, a demand that his father be dead to him: asking for the inheritance now was effectively wishing the father dead, a profound act of relational rupture. The father divides the assets without apparent protest — an act of extraordinary love that allows the son the freedom to destroy himself. The son liquidates everything — converts it to cash, which can be taken anywhere — and goes as far from home as possible. The far country is not only geographical; it is the distance a person can travel from God while still breathing. He squanders everything. The word (diaskorpizō) is the same word used for the scattering of the proud in Mary's Magnificat (1:51). What he possessed is gone.

verseByVerse.quote: 'And when he had spent everything, a severe famine arose in that country, and he began to be in need. So he went and hired himself out to one of the citizens of that country, who sent him into his fields to feed pigs. And he was longing to be fed with the pods that the pigs ate, and no one gave him anything.'
verseByVerse.commentary: The descent is calibrated in stages. First the money goes; then a famine removes his ability to recover through new employment; then he hires himself out to a Gentile — the ultimate social and religious abasement for a Jewish young man; then he is sent to tend pigs — unclean animals, the most degrading occupation imaginable; then he is hungry enough to envy the pigs their food. Each step down is worse than the previous one. No one gave him anything — the social world he entered with his father's money has nothing to give him now. The friends who received his squandering are absent from his need. He is alone, hungry, and utterly undone. He has arrived at the bottom of everything the far country can offer.

verseByVerse.quote: 'But when he came to himself, he said, "How many of my father's hired servants have more than enough bread, but I perish here with hunger! I will arise and go to my father, and I will say to him, 'Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you. I am no longer worthy to be called your son. Treat me as one of your hired servants."'
verseByVerse.commentary:
He came to himself — one of the most profound phrases in the parable. The far country was not where he truly was; returning to himself is also returning toward home. The calculation he runs is practical: his father's servants eat well; he is starving. But the speech he prepares is genuinely theological: I have sinned against heaven and before you. He knows what he did was not merely wasteful; it was sin against God and against his father. He does not expect restoration to sonship — his proposal is to return as a hired servant, outside the family, earning his keep. He is not calculating on his father's love; he is calculating on his father's generosity to employees. The actual reception will exceed everything he has imagined.

And this raises a question that troubles more honest Christians than almost any other, so let it be answered plainly. The boy did not come home because he missed his father. He came home because he was hungry. The text is entirely candid about it — the memory that turns him round is that his father's hired men have bread enough and to spare. So a reader looks at his own conversion and goes cold: I turned to God when my marriage collapsed. I prayed because the results came back. I came because I was frightened, or lonely, or had run out of options — was any of that real, or was I just desperate?

Watch what the father does with it. He does not interrogate the motive. He does not wait at the gate with folded arms to establish whether the boy has come for love or for supper. He sees him a long way off and runs. And Luke has been showing us this all through: the tax collector who could not lift his eyes came out of sheer misery and went home justified (18:13-14); the criminal on the cross came to Christ with a few hours left and nothing else on earth to try (23:42-43). God has never yet turned away a sinner for arriving by the wrong road.

The truth is that nobody's repentance is pure at the outset. Hunger is very often the first grace — the mercy that makes a man look up, because comfort never would have. What matters is not the elegance of the motive that got you onto the road, but whose house you are walking toward. The son's understanding of his father was far too small; he came expecting a job and got a robe. That is the ordinary experience of coming home. You start out hoping to be tolerated, and discover you have been watched for.

verseByVerse.quote: 'And he arose and came to his father. But while he was still a great way off, his father saw him and felt compassion, and ran and embraced him and kissed him. And the son said to him, "Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you. I am no longer worthy to be called your son."'
verseByVerse.commentary: The father sees him while he is still a great way off — which means the father has been watching the road. He does not wait for the son to arrive and present his case; he runs. In the first-century Middle East, a man of dignity did not run; running was undignified. The father runs anyway. He embraces him before the son can speak, kisses him before the confession is complete. The compassion (splanchnizomai again — the visceral, gut-level movement of love) produces the running before any reconciliation has been made. The son begins his prepared speech; the father has already made his decision.

verseByVerse.quote: 'But the father said to his servants, "Bring quickly the best robe, and put it on him, and put a ring on his hand, and shoes on his feet. And bring the fattened calf and kill it, and let us eat and celebrate. For this my son was dead, and is alive again; he was lost, and is found." And they began to celebrate.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The robe, ring, and shoes are not merely comfort; they are reinstatement. The best robe covers the rags; the ring restores the authority of a son (a signet ring was a token of authority); the shoes mark him as a free man, not a servant (servants went barefoot). The father does not take the son back as an employee; he restores him fully and immediately to his place in the family. The fattened calf — kept for a special occasion — is the feast. The father's explanation is the theological centre of the whole chapter: this my son was dead, and is alive again; he was lost, and is found. Death and resurrection. Lost and found. The language of miracle applied to a moral and relational catastrophe reversed by love.

And here an objection has to be met, because it is raised both by critics and by thoughtful believers, and it is raised about this parable more than any other. There is no atonement in it. No sacrifice is offered, no blood is shed, no mediator stands between the boy and his father; the father simply forgives. Some have built a great deal on that silence — arguing that the religion of Jesus had no cross in it, and that the doctrine of atonement was a later invention laid over a simpler gospel of divine good nature. And a believer can feel the force of it from the other side: if God pardons the way this father pardons, why was a crucifixion necessary at all?

Begin with what a parable is for. This one was told to answer a specific complaint — this man receives sinners and eats with them (vv. 1-2) — and it answers it completely. It was not told to explain how a sinner is justified, any more than the parable of the persistent widow was told to explain the character of God as judge. Require every story to contain the whole of theology and every parable in the Gospels becomes a heresy.

But the deeper answer is that this parable is not costless at all; we have simply been reading it from the son's side. Look at the estate. The younger son's portion was real property, liquidated and squandered in a far country, and it is not coming back — the father is permanently poorer, and stays poorer, for having let him go. Then look at the homecoming: the best robe, the signet ring, the sandals, the fattened calf. The elder brother's accountancy is petty in spirit but exact in fact — somebody pays for that party, and it is not the boy, who came up the road with nothing but the smell of pigs on him. Every single thing he receives is drawn from his father's own resources. The father does not forgive at no cost. He absorbs the entire cost himself, in silence, and never once mentions it. That is not a picture with the atonement left out. It is the atonement seen from the inside: the wronged party bearing the whole loss so that the guilty party can come home free.

And there is one more thing, which settles it. Ask who is telling this story and where he is going while he tells it. Luke has already recorded that he set his face to go to Jerusalem (9:51). The man saying bring quickly the best robe is a few months from being stripped of his own and having soldiers gamble for it (23:34). The parable does not describe the cross for the same reason a man does not describe his own face — the cross is standing in the room, telling the story. So when you come home expecting to be taken on as a hired hand and find yourself wearing the best robe in the house, do not conclude that it was free. It was free to you. Ask what the robe cost, and the answer is eight chapters further on.

verseByVerse.quote: 'Now his older son was in the field, and as he came and drew near to the house, he heard music and dancing. And he called one of the servants and asked what these things meant. And he said to him, "Your brother has come, and your father has killed the fattened calf, because he has received him back safe and sound." But he was angry and refused to go in. His father came out and entreated him.'
verseByVerse.commentary: The older son has been in the field — working, faithful, present. He hears the music before he knows the reason for it, and when he learns the reason, he refuses to enter. His anger is real and his grounds are not irrational: he has served faithfully while his brother squandered the family's resources, and the return of the spendthrift is being celebrated more lavishly than anything his faithfulness has ever received. The father comes out to him — as he ran out to the younger son. The same love that received the younger son now comes to the older one. The question is whether the older son will enter.

verseByVerse.quote: 'But he answered his father, "Look, these many years I have served you, and I never disobeyed your command, yet you never gave me a young goat, that I might celebrate with my friends. But when this son of yours came, who has devoured your property with prostitutes, you killed the fattened calf for him!"'
verseByVerse.commentary: The older son's speech is a full accounting of grievance: years of service, perfect obedience, no celebration; one prodigal's return, and a feast. He cannot bring himself to say my brother — he says this son of yours, placing the younger son in relation to the father but not to himself. He has already been distancing himself relationally before the younger son ever left. The details he adds — prostitutes — may be accurate or may be the embellishment of resentment; either way, they reveal the contempt behind the anger. He has been a servant in his father's house without understanding that he was a son. His faithfulness has been the faithfulness of an employee, not the joy of a child.

verseByVerse.quote: 'And he said to him, "Son, you are always with me, and all that is mine is yours. It was fitting to celebrate and be glad, for this your brother was dead, and is alive; he was lost, and is found."'
verseByVerse.commentary: The father's answer to the older son is the answer to the Pharisees who have been grumbling throughout the chapter. You are always with me, and all that is mine is yours — the older son has had everything all along; his resentment is based on a failure to understand what he already possessed. He has been living in the father's house as a stranger to the father's heart. And the celebration is not a reward for the younger son; it is the only appropriate response to what has happened. It was fitting — morally right, necessary, proportionate — to celebrate. Dead and alive. Lost and found. These are not small things. The parable ends without telling us whether the older son went in. The ending is open — and deliberately so. The Pharisees must decide for themselves whether they will enter the feast.

16.title: Money, the Law, and the Great Divide
16.overview:
Luke 16 is one of the most challenging chapters in all the Gospels. It contains two sustained teachings — the Parable of the Dishonest Manager and the story of the Rich Man and Lazarus — that bracket a cluster of sayings about the law, divorce, and divine valuation. What holds it together is money as a spiritual diagnostic: how a person handles wealth reveals the true condition of their heart before God.

The Parable of the Dishonest Manager shocks its hearers because Jesus appears to commend a fraudster. The commendation, however, is carefully qualified: the manager is praised not for his dishonesty but for his shrewdness — his ability to think clearly about the future and use present resources to secure it. Jesus turns the parable into an indictment of disciples who exercise less practical wisdom in spiritual things than worldly people do in material ones.

The story of the Rich Man and Lazarus is the only parable in which a character has a proper name, and it closes the chapter with one of Scripture's most sobering statements: if people will not be persuaded by Moses and the Prophets, they will not be persuaded even if someone rises from the dead. This is both a claim about the sufficiency of Scripture and a prophecy about the response to Jesus's own resurrection.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–13 — The Parable of the Dishonest Manager
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Jesus tells the parable to his disciples (v. 1) while the Pharisees are also listening (v. 14). A wealthy estate-owner discovers that his manager (oikonomos — steward, one entrusted with another's household) has been squandering his property. Facing dismissal, the manager quickly reduces the debts of two major creditors, apparently at his own expense — he was entitled to a commission on transactions, and he now forfeits it — to secure their friendship for the coming crisis. When the master hears of it, he commends the manager not for dishonesty but for shrewd forward-thinking.

The saying in v. 8 is one of Jesus's most pointed indictments: the sons of this world are more shrewd in dealing with their own generation than the sons of light. Worldly people think strategically about their financial futures; disciples often fail to think with equivalent clarity about their eternal ones. The Mammon saying (v. 9) applies the principle: use unrighteous wealth — Aramaic māmōnā, accumulated treasure — to make friends who will welcome you into eternal dwellings. By calling it “unrighteous Mammon” Jesus is not saying all money is sinful; he is saying that in a fallen world money is inevitably entangled with injustice, and disciples must hold it loosely.

The two-masters saying (v. 13) is absolute: you cannot serve God and Mammon with equal devotion. Douleuein (to serve as a slave) makes the point precisely — a slave cannot have two owners and give each full loyalty.
verseByVerse.theology:
The parable raises the doctrine of stewardship in its sharpest form. Every resource a believer holds is held in trust for the true Owner. God is the absolute owner of all things (Ps. 24:1; Deut. 8:17–18); human beings are appointed stewards whose accounting is inevitable and coming. The question is never whether we will give account but what that account will reveal.

“Unrighteous Mammon” is not a claim that money is inherently evil but that in a fallen world it corrupts — it becomes an idol, a rival lord, a false security. Jesus does not counsel poverty as such; he counsels detachment — the freedom to use money strategically for kingdom purposes rather than being used by it.
verseByVerse.examples:
A retired businessman reflects on his estate planning. For decades he assumed he was “building for the future,” but as he reads this passage he realises he has been thinking almost entirely about his children's material inheritance and almost nothing about how his accumulated resources might be deployed for eternal purposes in his remaining years. The parable invites him to become shrewd in the right direction.

A young professional earns a significant raise and immediately decides how much more she can give before lifestyle inflation absorbs it. She does not think of herself as especially virtuous — she simply applied forward-looking thinking to her new income. This is exactly the practical shrewdness Jesus commends.

verseByVerse.quote: He also said to the disciples, 'There was a rich man who had a manager, and charges were brought to him that this man was wasting his possessions. And he called him and said to him, "What is this that I hear about you? Turn in the account of your management, for you can no longer be manager." And the manager said to himself, "What shall I do, since my master is taking the management away from me? I am not strong enough to dig, and I am ashamed to beg."'
verseByVerse.commentary: The parable of the dishonest manager is one of the most puzzling in the Gospels — and the puzzle is deliberate. The manager has been squandering his master's wealth and faces dismissal and a reckoning. His situation is urgent: he has no future employment, no physical ability to labour, and too much pride to beg. He must act quickly, before the dismissal is formalised and his leverage is gone. The parable begins with a man who is about to face judgment and knows it, and who uses the time remaining to prepare for what comes next. The question Jesus will draw from this is whether his disciples have the same shrewdness about the far more important judgment they face.

verseByVerse.quote: '"I have decided what to do, so that when I am removed from management, people may receive me into their houses." So, summoning his master's debtors one by one, he said to the first, "How much do you owe my master?" He said, "A hundred measures of oil." He said to him, "Take your bill, and sit down quickly and write fifty." Then he said to another, "And how much do you owe?" He said, "A hundred measures of wheat." He said to him, "Write eighty."'
verseByVerse.commentary: The manager's solution is to use his remaining authority — while he still has it — to reduce the debts of his master's debtors, who will then be obligated to him. The reductions are significant: fifty per cent on oil, twenty per cent on wheat. Whether he is reducing his own commission (which would make the act self-sacrificial) or reducing the master's actual receivables (which would make it dishonest) has been much debated. In either reading, he is using present resources to secure future relationships. This is the financial shrewdness Jesus is about to commend — not its moral content, but its structure: using what is available now to prepare for what is coming.

verseByVerse.quote: 'The master commended the dishonest manager for his shrewdness. For the sons of this age are more shrewd in dealing with their own generation than the sons of light. And I tell you, make friends for yourselves by means of unrighteous wealth, so that when it fails they may receive you into the eternal dwellings.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The commendation is for shrewdness, not for dishonesty — the master recognises a well-executed strategy even while acknowledging its character. Jesus draws the application explicitly: the children of this age are more shrewd in securing their future than the children of light are in securing theirs. This is the sting of the parable. Worldly people use money shrewdly to build relationships and secure futures. Disciples should use money at least as shrewdly — using it now, in ways that build the kingdom, care for people, and lay up treasure in heaven, so that when the money is gone, what it purchased remains. Unrighteous wealth is not evil money but the wealth of this unrighteous age — morally neutral material that can be used for eternal purposes or wasted on temporary ones.

The second half of verse 9 is harder than the first and needs facing directly: make friends for yourselves by means of unrighteous wealth, so that when it fails they may receive you into the eternal dwellings. Read flatly, that appears to say a man can purchase his welcome into heaven by spending money on the right people — and it has been read that way, in defence of almsgiving as a work that accumulates merit. Two questions have to be answered: who are they, and is this salvation for sale?

On the first, three readings are held by careful Christians. Some take they as the friends themselves — those helped in this life standing at the door of the next, glad to see their benefactor arrive. Some take it of angels, who carried Lazarus in the story a few verses later. But the likeliest is simpler: this is the Semitic way of saying you will be received without naming God directly, a reverent third-person plural. Luke has already used the identical idiom in this same discourse — this night your soul is required of you (12:20), where the Greek literally reads they require your soul, and nobody supposes a committee. It is God who receives; the wording simply keeps his name off the sentence.

On the second question the verse answers itself, and it does so in three words that are easy to read past: when it fails. The money is explicitly described as the thing that runs out. Whatever else a currency guaranteed to become worthless may be, it is not the purchase price of eternity. And Luke will not let the merit reading stand for a moment longer: the tax collector who could offer nothing but his breast went home justified (18:13-14); the criminal a few hours from death bought nothing whatever and was told today you will be with me in Paradise (23:43); and in this very chapter, a rich man's fortune procures him not one drop of water. If money could buy an eternal dwelling, the man in torment was the best-funded soul in the story.

What the verse actually teaches is that generosity is evidence, not currency. The paragraph ends four verses later with you cannot serve God and money — that is the conclusion this saying is travelling toward. How a man treats his wealth shows which master owns him, and the friends made by open-handed giving are not creditors waiting to call in a favour at the gate; they are the visible fruit of a heart that has already changed hands. Which is exactly why the parable sits here. The manager's shrewdness was to take what was about to be removed from him and turn it into something that would outlast the removal. Everything currently in your hands stands on the same footing. It is all going to fail. The only question worth asking is whether it will have done any good before it does.

verseByVerse.quote: 'One who is faithful in a very little is also faithful in much, and one who is dishonest in a very little is also dishonest in much. If then you have not been faithful in the unrighteous wealth, who will entrust to you the true riches? And if you have not been faithful in that which is another's, who will give you that which is your own?'
verseByVerse.commentary: The principle of faithful stewardship in small things qualifying for greater things is a consistent theme in Luke (cf. 19:17). Money is described here as both very little and another's — it is not the most important thing, and it does not ultimately belong to you. How you handle it reveals your character in the things that matter most. The person who treats money carelessly is revealing something about how they will handle the true riches — the things of the kingdom that are genuinely important and genuinely yours. Faithfulness in the lesser thing is the evidence of capacity for the greater.

verseByVerse.quote: 'No servant can serve two masters, for either he will hate the one and love the other, or he will be devoted to the one and despise the other. You cannot serve God and money.'
verseByVerse.commentary: The conclusion is absolute. The word for money is mamōnas — Mammon, which in the Aramaic tradition had the character of a god, a competing claim on ultimate loyalty. Jesus does not say you should not serve both; he says you cannot. The divided service that appears possible in theory — giving God Sunday and money Monday through Saturday — is not actually available. The heart has one master; the question is only which one it is. This is not an argument against wealth as such but against the condition in which wealth becomes the functional centre of a life, displacing God.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–18 — The Law, the Kingdom, and Human Exaltation
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The Pharisees, described as philargyroi (silver-lovers), respond to Jesus's teaching by ridiculing him. Jesus's response cuts to the heart of the conflict: they justify themselves before men, but God knows their hearts. The very thing they take as evidence of divine favour — material prosperity and social honour — Jesus names as idolatry.

The sayings about the law and the kingdom (vv. 16–17) are among the most compressed in Luke. The law and the prophets were until John; since then the kingdom is being proclaimed — and yet not one stroke of the law will pass away. This is not a contradiction: the kingdom is the fulfilment, not the abolition, of everything the law and prophets anticipated. The divorce saying (v. 18) connects to this: the Pharisees were known for permissive divorce interpretations (Hillel's school allowed it for almost any reason). Jesus reaffirms God's original design — permanent, exclusive, one-flesh union — as the law's continuing moral claim, not as something the kingdom relaxes.
verseByVerse.theology: The contrast between divine and human valuation runs throughout Scripture (Isa. 55:8–9; 1 Sam. 16:7). Jesus gives it specific content: the metric of social honour linked to wealth is precisely inverted in God's economy. The law's permanence (v. 17) guards against antinomianism — the moral content of the law is not set aside by the kingdom; it is fulfilled in it and written on the hearts of those who enter it (Jer. 31:33; Rom. 8:4).
verseByVerse.examples: A church elder is regarded as a model of godliness partly because of his visible financial success — the implicit assumption being that God blesses faithfulness with prosperity. This passage does not say prosperity is sinful; it warns that prosperity can become a currency of spiritual reputation, convincing both the prosperous person and their community that outward honour equals inward reality. God sees the heart.

verseByVerse.quote: The Pharisees, who were lovers of money, heard all these things, and they ridiculed him. And he said to them, 'You are those who justify yourselves before men, but God knows your hearts. For what is exalted among men is an abomination before God.'
verseByVerse.commentary: The Pharisees' ridicule is the response of people who have been exposed. Their love of money — which they have probably rationalised as the blessing of God on their righteousness — is incompatible with the teaching just given. Their laughter is the defence mechanism of those who cannot afford to take the word seriously. Jesus's response goes to the root: they are justifying themselves before men, managing their reputation carefully, but God knows the hearts. The gap between public reputation and inner reality — which is the definition of hypocrisy — is where the Pharisees live. What the world exalts, God often finds abominable; the world's honour system is not God's.

verseByVerse.quote: 'The Law and the Prophets were until John; since then the good news of the kingdom of God is preached, and everyone forces his way into it. But it is easier for heaven and earth to pass away than for one dot of the Law to become void.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The apparent tension between these two verses is important. John marks the transition from one era to another: the Law and the Prophets were the shape of the covenant until John; since then the kingdom is being preached and entered with urgency. This is not an abolition of the Law but its fulfilment — a new phase in which what the Law always pointed toward is now arriving in person. The Law does not become void; not one dot of it will pass away. But its purpose — to lead to Christ — is now being achieved. The new covenant does not replace the moral framework of the old; it establishes it on the foundation of the one who kept it perfectly.

"Everyone forces his way into it" — a strange phrase, worth a pause. The verb can be read two ways: everyone is urgently pressing into the kingdom (crowds straining to enter — so most translations), or everyone enters it with violent determination. Either way the point stands: since John announced the King, entering the kingdom is no polite formality. It is not drifted into; it is entered like a man pressing through a closing door — with decision, urgency, everything (cf. Matt. 11:12).

verseByVerse.quote: 'Everyone who divorces his wife and marries another commits adultery, and he who marries a woman divorced from her husband commits adultery.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The saying on divorce appears here in the context of the Pharisees' love of money and the discussion of the Law. The connection may be that the Pharisees were using liberal interpretations of the divorce law (Deut. 24:1) to dismiss wives in favour of wealthier ones — a form of financial and sexual opportunism dressed in legal language. Jesus's statement restores the original intention of marriage (Gen. 2:24) against the permissive interpretations of his day. The law that cannot pass away includes its sexual ethics. This saying does not address all possible exceptions (cf. Matt. 5:32's exception clause); it addresses the casual, interest-motivated divorce that was being practised.

That parenthesis will not do for the person actually holding this verse, so let it be worked out. Luke gives the saying flat, with no exception attached, and a reader who has only Luke will conclude that every divorce and every remarriage without qualification is adultery. Set the whole New Testament out and the picture fills in. Matthew records the same teaching twice and both times includes an exception for sexual immorality (5:32; 19:9). Paul adds a second case: if an unbelieving spouse insists on leaving, the believer is not enslaved (1 Cor. 7:15). On that basis the Reformed churches have historically recognised two grounds on which a marriage may be dissolved without sin — adultery and desertion — and that is the position confessed in the Westminster standards.

Why then does Luke leave the exception out? Because he is giving the rule, not the case law, which is how anyone states a principle. A doctor who says never take this on an empty stomach is not contradicting the note in the leaflet. Luke's flat form is the shape of the thing: marriage is for life, and the exceptions are exceptions — narrow doors in a solid wall, not the wall itself.

But there is a further question, and it is the one that keeps people out of church. What about the man or woman already divorced and already remarried, on no ground the New Testament allows? Does this verse mean they are living in a state of ongoing adultery, that every day of the new marriage is a fresh sin, that the only repentance available is to break the second home apart? No. Notice how Jesus himself handles it: he tells the woman at the well that she has had five husbands and the man she has now is not her husband (John 4:18) — he names the truth exactly, and he does not instruct her to go back and unpick it. A second marriage, once made, is a real marriage; it is not an ongoing act of adultery but a covenant that now exists and carries real obligations to a real spouse and real children. Where there was sin, it is to be confessed and forgiven like every other sin — and then left at the cross, not dragged out and re-committed every morning. Paul lists adulterers among those who shall not inherit the kingdom, and then writes the sentence that has rescued more consciences than almost any other: and such were some of you. But you were washed (1 Cor. 6:9-11).

None of which is a loophole, and it must not be heard as one. The fence stands exactly where Jesus put it, and he put it there to protect something — chiefly the wife who in that world could be dismissed at her husband's convenience and left with nothing. But a fence is not a cage, and the gospel does not leave a man locked outside his own forgiveness. If that is your history, the word to you is not go back. It is be washed, and be faithful now.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 19–31 — The Rich Man and Lazarus
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
This is the most extended treatment of life after death in any of the Synoptics, told as the direct sequel to the teaching on money. The story — which Jesus tells without calling it a parable — depicts two men whose earthly circumstances are completely reversed in eternity. The rich man is unnamed; Lazarus (Hebrew Eleazar — “God helps”) is known to God though unknown to the world. Purple clothing was reserved for royalty and the very wealthy — the dye harvested from murex shellfish at enormous cost. The rich man lived at the very top of the ancient social pyramid. At his gate, placed there by others because he could not walk, lay Lazarus — covered with sores, hungry for crumbs, with dogs (unclean scavengers in Jewish culture) licking his wounds.

At death, Lazarus is carried by angels to “Abraham's bosom” (eis ton kolpon Abraam) — the place of honour at the messianic banquet, the position of the beloved guest reclining next to the host (cf. John 13:23). The rich man is in Hades in torment. There is no suggestion that wealth itself condemned him; Luke 16 has been building toward the point that what wealth reveals — where the heart is, which lord is truly served — is what matters.

The dialogue that follows is striking for its precision about the afterlife: conscious existence after death, reversal of earthly circumstance, a fixed and impassable gulf between the two destinations (v. 26), and no possibility of communication, rescue, or transfer. The rich man's two requests — first for relief, then for a warning to his brothers — are both refused, not out of cruelty but because of the sufficiency of what God has already given: Moses and the Prophets. The final line is devastating: if they do not hear Moses and the Prophets, neither will they be convinced if someone rises from the dead. Jesus is speaking of his own resurrection.
verseByVerse.theology:
The story teaches several interconnected theological truths. First, there is conscious existence after death, prior to the final resurrection — the rich man is aware, has desires, feels pain, and recognises Lazarus. This is consistent with the intermediate state described in Luke 23:43 and Paul (2 Cor. 5:8; Phil. 1:23). Second, the final state of the wicked involves torment — Jesus uses odynaomai (to be in anguish) and describes flame. Third, the final state is irreversible — the great gulf is fixed (v. 26). Post-mortem universalism and annihilationism are both excluded by the plain sense of the text.

The closing emphasis on Scripture is a major theological claim. The Bible is sufficient not because it is the only possible revelation but because it is the one God has chosen to give, adequate for its purpose. If Scripture does not persuade, no additional miracle will. This is why the resurrection of Jesus did not produce universal belief — those whose hearts were closed to the Scriptures that anticipated him remained closed even when the event they anticipated occurred.
verseByVerse.examples:
A hospital chaplain sits with a dying man who has lived comfortably and given little thought to eternity. The man is not wicked by the world's standards; he has simply never arranged his life around anything beyond the present. This story is not a threat — it is a map. It describes the landscape of eternity not to terrify but to instruct: the arrangements of eternity are already shaped by what the heart has loved in time.

A congregation debates whether to include a significant amount of their capital campaign for relief work among the urban poor. Someone objects that charity is “not the gospel.” This chapter suggests that how a congregation handles money is a spiritual diagnostic — that generosity toward the Lazaruses at the gate is not a supplement to the gospel but an expression of it.

verseByVerse.quote: 'There was a rich man who was clothed in purple and fine linen and who feasted sumptuously every day. And at his gate was laid a poor man named Lazarus, covered with sores, who desired to be fed with what fell from the rich man's table. Moreover, even the dogs came and licked his sores.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The contrast is drawn with precise strokes. The rich man is clothed in purple — the most expensive dye of the ancient world, reserved for royalty and the very wealthy — and feasts extravagantly every day, not occasionally. Lazarus is laid at his gate — passive, placed there, unable to move himself. He is covered with sores; the dogs lick them, which is not a kindness in this context but a further degradation. He desires the crumbs from the table — not a share of the feast, just what falls. The gate between them is not merely architectural; it is a moral boundary that the rich man has chosen not to cross. He is not described as actively cruel; his sin is the sin of comfortable blindness — Lazarus is at his gate every day, and he has learned not to see him.

One thing the parable never says needs saying out loud, because the story's shape invites the wrong conclusion. Lazarus is not told to have believed anything; the rich man is not accused of any crime. Read carelessly, this becomes a story in which poverty saves and wealth damns, and a poor man is safe on the strength of his sores. That cannot be right, and Luke has already guarded it: the beatitude at 6:20 blesses the poor because empty hands are where faith is usually found, not because an empty purse is a ticket. Abraham himself is in this parable, and Abraham was a wealthy man. Note also the one name in the story. The rich man, who had every name worth having in this life, is anonymous; the beggar is called Lazarus, which means God has helped — the single hint the parable gives about where his hope actually lay. What condemns the rich man is not his purple but the gate he walked past daily; what saves Lazarus is not his sores but the God whose help he was named for.

verseByVerse.quote: 'The poor man died and was carried by the angels to Abraham's side. The rich man also died and was buried, and in Hades, being in torment, he lifted up his eyes and saw Abraham far off and Lazarus at his side.'
verseByVerse.commentary: Both men die — the one certainty they shared in life. The reversals are total and immediate: Lazarus is carried by angels to Abraham's side — the place of honour at the messianic feast — while the rich man is buried (the elaborate burial of the wealthy) and finds himself in Hades, in torment. The first thing the rich man sees from his place of torment is Lazarus at Abraham's side — the man he would not see at his gate now visible at an uncrossable distance. The reversal is the reversal announced in Mary's Magnificat, in the Beatitudes and Woes of ch. 6, in the parable of the great banquet. It is the consistent logic of the kingdom applied to the final accounting.

verseByVerse.quote: 'And he called out, "Father Abraham, have mercy on me, and send Lazarus to dip the end of his finger in water and cool my tongue, for I am in anguish in this flame." But Abraham said, "Child, remember that you in your lifetime received your good things, and Lazarus in like manner bad things; but now he is comforted here, and you are in anguish. And besides all this, between us and you a great chasm has been fixed, in order that those who would pass from here to you may not be able, and none may cross from there to us."'
verseByVerse.commentary: The rich man's request — a drop of water — is denied not out of cruelty but because a chasm has been fixed that cannot be crossed. The finality of the after-death state is the point: what was determined in the life is now settled for ever. Abraham's summary is not an accusation; it is a description. The rich man received his good things in his lifetime; Lazarus received his bad things. The reversal is the completion of what began in life. The great chasm is not punishment imposed arbitrarily; it is the permanent establishment of the direction each life was already moving. One caution on reading this rightly: Jesus is not drawing a surveyor's map of the afterlife. He speaks in the vivid imagery his hearers already knew — 'Abraham's side,' a fixed gulf, a cry across the divide — to press home truths that stand however the scene is pictured: death settles our destiny beyond changing, the comforts and miseries of this life can be exactly reversed by God's justice, and no messenger from the dead will persuade those who will not hear Moses and the Prophets already in their hands (v. 31). The imagery serves the warning; it was never meant to be quarried for geography.

verseByVerse.quote: 'And he said, "Then I beg you, father, to send him to my father's house — for I have five brothers — so that he may warn them, lest they also come into this place of torment." But Abraham said, "They have Moses and the Prophets; let them hear them." And he said, "No, father Abraham, but if someone goes to them from the dead, they will repent." He said to him, "If they do not hear Moses and the Prophets, neither will they be convinced if someone rises from the dead."'
verseByVerse.commentary: The second request — warn my brothers — is refused with one of the most theologically loaded statements in the Gospel. They have Moses and the Prophets; let them hear them. The word of God already given is sufficient for repentance; the demand for additional miraculous confirmation is a symptom of the very problem that needs to be repented of. The final line is a foreshadowing that Luke's first-century reader would hear unmistakably: even a resurrection from the dead — which Jesus will accomplish — will not convince those who have already decided not to hear Moses and the Prophets. The evidence is not the issue; the heart is. And the heart is dealt with by the word, not by spectacle.

17.title: Forgiveness, Faith, Gratitude, and the Coming Son of Man
17.overview:
Luke 17 gathers teachings that might appear loosely connected but share a common thread: the shape of life in the kingdom as it moves toward its final consummation. Disciples are warned about causing others to stumble, commanded to forgive repeatedly, confronted about the nature of faith, and then — after the extraordinary healing of ten lepers — taught about gratitude.
