The chapter then pivots to sustained teaching about the coming of the Son of Man: apocalyptic instruction that would be at home in the Olivet Discourse.

The healing of the ten lepers is one of the most poignant episodes in Luke, precisely because of what does not happen: nine healed men simply walk away. The one who returns is a Samaritan — an outsider — and his return becomes the occasion for Jesus to say something remarkable: “your faith has saved you.” The Greek is sesōken se — the same word used for salvation throughout Luke. The nine received physical healing; the one received something more.

The eschatological teaching (vv. 20–37) is deliberately disorienting. The kingdom does not come with observable signs (v. 20); it is already in your midst (v. 21). Yet the day of the Son of Man will come with lightning-like sudden visibility (v. 24). The tension is not a contradiction: the kingdom is already present in the person of Jesus, but its final manifestation remains future — and when it comes, it will be unmistakable, inescapable, and final.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–10 — Stumbling Blocks, Forgiveness, Faith, and Duty
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Four short teachings are clustered here, each pressing the disciples on a different aspect of their calling. The stumbling-block saying (vv. 1–2) is severe: causing a little one to stumble is so serious that drowning in the sea would be preferable to facing its judgment. The word skandalon (stumbling block) is used elsewhere for animal traps; to place one in front of a vulnerable believer is an act of spiritual violence.

The forgiveness command (vv. 3–4) is radical: if a brother sins against you seven times in a day and turns seven times saying “I repent,” you must forgive him. The disciples' response — “Increase our faith!” — is telling: they understand intuitively that this level of forgiveness exceeds ordinary human capacity. Jesus's reply about the mustard seed is not a lesson in quantity but direction: the issue is not having more faith but having genuine, directed faith — even a tiny amount rightly placed moves what seemed immovable.

The servant parable (vv. 7–10) is one of the most stringent sayings in the Gospels. After a full day's work the servant continues serving without expectation of special reward: “We are unworthy servants; we have only done what was our duty.” This is not a counsel of despair but of proper proportion: everything we do for God is a response to grace already given, not a contribution that places God in our debt.
verseByVerse.theology:
The forgiveness teaching anticipates the Lord's Prayer: “forgive us our sins, as we ourselves forgive everyone who is indebted to us” (11:4). The connection between receiving forgiveness and extending it is foundational. This does not make forgiveness a condition of justification; it describes the transformative effect of genuine justification on the human heart. Those forgiven much love much (7:47) — and those who love much forgive much.

The servant parable is a protection against what Bonhoeffer called “the religious achievement” — presenting obedience as a claim upon God. The Calvinist tradition rightly emphasises that even our best works are possible only by grace, are mixed with sin, and are accepted only in Christ. There is no surplus merit; there is only faithfulness that is itself a gift.
verseByVerse.examples: A woman in a small group has been hurt repeatedly by the same family member, who apologises and then repeats the pattern. Well-meaning friends tell her that forgiveness means forgetting, and that any expectation of change is unforgiving. This passage distinguishes forgiveness (required, concerning her own heart before God) from reconciliation (which requires genuine repentance from the other party). She can forgive while maintaining appropriate boundaries — and trust God with the outcome.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to his disciples, 'Temptations to sin are sure to come, but woe to the one through whom they come! It would be better for him if a millstone were hung around his neck and he were cast into the sea than that he should cause one of these little ones to sin.'
verseByVerse.commentary: The inevitability of stumbling blocks is stated without illusion — they will come. But inevitability does not remove culpability from those who provide them. The little ones are the spiritually vulnerable, the newly converted, the weak in faith — those who can be led astray by the behaviour or teaching of those with influence over them. The millstone is a vivid measure of the severity Jesus attaches to causing another person's spiritual ruin. The person who destroys their own soul faces judgment; the person who destroys someone else's soul faces something worse. Leadership in the community of faith carries proportionate accountability.

verseByVerse.quote: 'Pay attention to yourselves! If your brother sins, rebuke him, and if he repents, forgive him, and if he sins against you seven times in the day, and turns to you seven times, saying, "I repent," you must forgive him.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Three obligations in sequence: watch yourself, rebuke the sinning brother, forgive the repentant one. The rebuke is not optional — it is an act of love toward the person in the wrong. But it depends on the prior self-examination: pay attention to yourselves first. The forgiveness that follows genuine repentance is not conditional on the convincingness of the repentance or the track record of the offender. Seven times in a single day — a number expressing completeness — tests whether forgiveness is a genuine orientation or a limited resource that gets used up. The exhaustion of forgiveness is not a Christian option.

But Luke tells us what to do when the brother repents and leaves the other case open. What if he never says I repent? The silence is worth pressing, because that is where most real wounds live. The answer begins with a distinction Luke's own wording invites: forgiveness and reconciliation are not the same act. Forgiveness is what you do before God with your own heart — releasing the debt, refusing to nurse the injury, declining to make yourself the creditor. Jesus does this from the cross for men who had not repented and never would (23:34). Reconciliation is the restored relationship, and that takes two: Jesus attaches it to if he repents. You can be commanded to forgive unilaterally. You cannot be commanded to reconcile unilaterally, because you do not hold both ends.

The rest of the procedure is recorded by Matthew: go alone, then with witnesses, then tell it to the church, and if he refuses even the church, “let him be to you as a Gentile and a tax collector” (cf. Matt. 18:15–17). On Luke's pages that sentence cannot possibly mean abandonment. Luke is the Gospel of the tax collector. Levi throws a feast and fills the room with his own kind (5:27–32). The grumble that sets up the three great parables of grace is “This man receives sinners and eats with them” (15:1–2). A tax collector goes home justified while a Pharisee does not (18:9–14). Jesus invites himself to a chief tax collector's house and calls him a son of Abraham (19:1–10). Outsider status in Luke is never a closed door — it is the address to which Jesus goes. The unrepentant brother changes category, not value: he is no longer a brother to be restored, but an outsider to be sought.

This protects both people. It frees the one who was wronged from the cruelty of having to pretend nothing happened, and from being bound to endless re-injury in the name of grace. And it keeps the one who did wrong from being quietly written off, because he remains someone Christ came for. Hold the two together and the opening command does its work: pay attention to yourselves. The gravest danger in a long unrepented offence is not that the other man stays hard. It is that you do.

verseByVerse.quote: The apostles said to the Lord, 'Increase our faith!' And the Lord said, 'If you had faith like a grain of mustard seed, you could say to this mulberry tree, "Be uprooted and planted in the sea," and it would obey you.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The apostles hear the demand to forgive seven times in a day and respond: we need more faith for this. The request is honest — they recognise the gap between what is asked and what they feel capable of. Jesus's answer is both encouraging and challenging: you do not need more faith; you need the faith you have to be genuinely faith. Mustard-seed faith — real, though tiny — can accomplish the apparently impossible. The problem with forgiveness is rarely a shortage of faith; it is the unwillingness to use the faith already given. The mulberry tree illustration is not a promise about horticulture; it is an illustration of faith's power when it is actually exercised.

But the verse needs a guard, because it has been lifted out of this paragraph and turned into something else: a promise that sufficient faith secures whatever is asked. On that reading, the tree stays rooted because you did not believe hard enough — and the corollary follows at once, that the tumour did not shrink, the marriage did not mend, and the child did not recover, for the same reason. That teaching has been preached to a great many people at the worst hour of their lives, and it is worth saying plainly that it cannot be got out of this text.

Start with where the saying sits. The apostles have not asked for power to work wonders. They have just been told to forgive a brother seven times in one day, and they have said increase our faith because that command feels beyond them. The mulberry tree is Jesus's answer about forgiveness. To pull it out of that setting and make it a lever for moving circumstances is to use a sentence about pardoning your brother as a technique for rearranging your life.

Then consider that Luke wrote the sequel. If this were a promise about relocating vegetation, Acts is where we would watch it being claimed — and in the whole of that book, men who heal the lame and raise the dead and shake off vipers never once move a tree or a hill. Luke shows us instead what faith the size of a mustard seed actually does: it takes frightened men out of a locked room and puts them in front of the Sanhedrin. And Luke has already shown us, in this same Gospel, the one prayer in history offered in perfect faith — Father, if you are willing, remove this cup from me — and the cup was not removed (22:42). Nobody will suggest that the faith in Gethsemane was too small. Paul asked three times for his thorn and was told no, and the answer he got was not believe harder but my grace is sufficient for you (2 Cor. 12:8-9).

So what is promised? Not that faith is a force whose output rises with its volume, but that its power lies in what it is attached to. A very small faith joined to God can do what a very large confidence in yourself never will — which is precisely the encouragement these men needed. They wanted a bigger supply before they attempted the impossible thing. Jesus tells them the supply is not the issue: what you already have, actually used, is enough for the seventh apology today. And if you have been told that your faith failed because the thing you begged for did not come, put that down. The measure of your faith is not the size of what it moved. It is whether, when it moved nothing you could see, you were still holding on to the same God.

verseByVerse.quote: 'Will any one of you who has a servant ploughing or keeping sheep say to him when he has come in from the field, "Come at once and recline at table"? Will he not rather say to him, "Prepare supper for me, and dress properly, and serve me while I eat and drink, and afterward you will eat and drink"? Does he thank the servant because he did what was commanded? So you also, when you have done all that you were commanded, say, "We are unworthy servants; we have only done what was our duty."'
verseByVerse.commentary: The parable of the unworthy servant checks the pride that might arise from obedience. After the demanding teaching of vv. 1–6, a disciple might feel that doing all this entitles them to special acknowledgement. Jesus corrects the assumption: a servant who does what is required has done nothing beyond the requirement. There is no credit beyond duty. This is not a statement about whether God appreciates his servants — elsewhere he promises generous reward (12:37; 19:17) — but about the posture in which the service should be rendered. The disciple who has done everything commanded is to say: we are unworthy servants; we have only done our duty. That posture — not contempt for one's service but honest assessment of its creaturely character — is the antidote to spiritual pride.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Jesus is travelling along the border region between Samaria and Galilee — a liminal zone where two peoples who despised each other met. Ten lepers stand at a distance (as the law required — Lev. 13:45–46 mandated that lepers warn others and keep apart) and cry out: “Jesus, Master, have mercy on us.” The title Epistata (Master) is Luke's distinctive term, used only by disciples and those approaching Jesus with urgent acknowledgment of his authority.

Jesus heals them with a word, directing them to go show themselves to the priests (the required verification of cleansing — Lev. 14). As they go, they are cleansed — the healing happens in the act of obedience-in-faith, not at the moment of the request. Nine continue to the priests. One, seeing that he was healed, turns back, glorifying God with a loud voice, falls at Jesus's feet, and gives thanks. And this one — this one — is a Samaritan.

Jesus's response carries three questions: Were not ten cleansed? Where are the nine? Was no one found to return and give glory to God except this foreigner? The nine received the healing they asked for. The Samaritan received healing and something more: sesōken se — your faith has saved you. Gratitude is not an optional supplement to healing; it is the mark of a heart that has understood what has happened and who has given it.
verseByVerse.theology:
The story illustrates precisely the difference between receiving a benefit from God and responding to God himself. All ten received cleansing. Only one responded to the Giver. This is a picture of the difference between religion that uses God for benefits and faith that worships God as an end in himself. The nine were not ingrates by worldly standards — they were doing exactly what Jesus told them (going to the priests). Their failure was not defiance but distraction: they moved from the gift to the system without pausing to return to the Giver.

The Samaritan's outsider status is theologically loaded in Luke. Samaritans appear three times in especially positive light (the Good Samaritan, 10:33; this leper; and Samaria as the first step of the Gentile mission, Acts 1:8). Luke consistently shows that the kingdom breaks ethnic and religious boundaries, and that those on the margins of Israel often receive the kingdom with greater clarity than those at its centre.
verseByVerse.examples: A family prays earnestly for a sick child. The child recovers. Within weeks the language of thankfulness has given way entirely to relief and resumed normal life — no particular increase in worship, no acknowledgment that anything received was a gift. The nine lepers are not villains; they are ordinary people. The story calls ordinary people to a richer life: to come back, to fall at Jesus's feet, to connect the gift to the Giver.

verseByVerse.quote: On the way to Jerusalem he was passing along between Samaria and Galilee. And as he entered a village, he was met by ten lepers, who stood at a distance and lifted up their voices, saying, 'Jesus, Master, have mercy on us.' When he saw them he said to them, 'Go and show yourselves to the priests.' And as they went, they were cleansed.
verseByVerse.commentary: The ten lepers observe the legally required distance (Lev. 13:46) while still crying out for mercy. Their address — Master — is respectful but not yet the full confession of Lordship. Jesus's instruction to go and show themselves to the priests is the instruction given to the cleansed leper in 5:14 — the showing to priests is the legal certification required before reintegration into community. He sends them before the healing is visible. They go in obedience and are cleansed as they go. Faith acts on the word before it sees the result.

verseByVerse.quote: Then one of them, when he saw that he was healed, turned back, praising God with a loud voice; and he fell on his face at Jesus's feet, giving him thanks. Now he was a Samaritan.
verseByVerse.commentary: One turns back. The detail that he is a Samaritan — the ethnic and religious outsider — prepares the sting of what follows. He falls on his face at Jesus's feet: the posture of worship. He praises God with a loud voice: the response that the healing of the bent woman produced in the synagogue. He gives thanks specifically to Jesus, thereby attributing to Jesus the action that only God can perform. The healing has become, for him, a revelation of who Jesus is. His gratitude is inseparable from his recognition.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Jesus answered, 'Were not ten cleansed? Where are the nine? Was no one found to return and give praise to God except this foreigner?' And he said to him, 'Rise and go your way; your faith has made you well.'
verseByVerse.commentary: The three questions — were not ten cleansed, where are the nine, was no one found to return? — are not angry but genuinely sorrowful. Nine people received healing and went on with their lives. One received healing and came back to give thanks. The nine are not condemned; they are simply absent from the moment of recognition and gratitude. The one who returned is commended with the same words given to the woman who anointed Jesus's feet (7:50) and the woman with the hemorrhage (8:48): your faith has made you well. The physical healing all ten received; the deeper wholeness — the encounter with Jesus that produces recognition and worship — came only to the one who turned back. Gratitude is the evidence of the deeper healing.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 20–37 — The Kingdom and the Coming of the Son of Man
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The Pharisees ask when the kingdom of God is coming — the question assumes an observable, datable, dramatic arrival. Jesus denies this framework: the kingdom does not come with signs to be observed, and you cannot say “Look, here it is!” Why? Because the kingdom of God is entos hymōn — in your midst. This phrase is contested: “within you” (internal, spiritual) or “in your midst” (present in the person of Jesus)? In context, addressing Pharisees who are not disciples, “within you” is unlikely. “In your midst” is the more natural reading: the King himself is standing among them, and they are asking when the kingdom will come.

Jesus then turns to his disciples (v. 22) and speaks of the days of the Son of Man — the period following his departure. He warns against false reports: when the Son of Man comes it will not require anyone to point it out. It will be like lightning flashing from one end of the sky to the other — unmistakable, universal, instantaneous. But first he must suffer many things and be rejected by this generation (v. 25). The cross precedes the crown.

The comparisons to Noah's days and Lot's days (vv. 26–29) are not warnings about moral decline but about sudden interruption: people were eating, drinking, marrying, buying, selling, planting, building — ordinary life — right up until the moment of catastrophic judgment. Life continued until it was suddenly and utterly over. The applications are sharp: don't turn back for possessions; remember Lot's wife; seek to save your life and lose it. The enigmatic closing image (v. 37) — wherever the body is, there the eagles will gather — communicates that judgment falls completely and inescapably where it falls.
verseByVerse.theology:
The tension between “the kingdom is already here” (v. 21) and “the days of the Son of Man are coming” (vv. 22–30) is the foundation of the New Testament's already-not-yet eschatology. The kingdom has come in the person and work of Jesus — his healings, exorcisms, and proclamation of forgiveness are all kingdom-presences. But the kingdom has not yet come in its fullness: judgment has not been executed, the resurrection of the dead has not occurred, the new creation has not been inaugurated. Believers live in the overlap of the ages.

The Lot's wife warning (v. 32) — the briefest verse in the narrative — is one of the NT's starkest cautions against nostalgia. She looked back at what was being destroyed, preferring it to what she was being delivered into (Gen. 19:26 LXX: apestrapthen). The disciple who in the moment of final crisis turns back to save what is already being consumed has traded the unlosable for the unsaveable.
verseByVerse.examples: The second coming is hard to hold rightly: talk of it easily tips into sensationalism, or else into an embarrassed silence that empties it of force. This passage gives the framework: the second coming is not a secret event requiring special knowledge to locate (v. 23) nor an event ordinary vigilance might miss (v. 24). It will be unmistakable. The call to readiness is not the call to calculate a date but to live in such a way that the arrival finds you facing the right direction.

verseByVerse.quote: Being asked by the Pharisees when the kingdom of God would come, he answered them, 'The kingdom of God is not coming in ways that can be observed, nor will they say, "Look, here it is!" or "There!" for behold, the kingdom of God is in the midst of you.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Pharisaic question about the timing of the kingdom assumes that it will arrive as an observable, dateable event — the kind of thing you can point to and say there it is. Jesus refuses the assumption: the kingdom does not come with spectacular external signs that can be tracked. And the reason is already in front of them: the kingdom of God is in the midst of you. The most natural reading is among you — the kingdom is present in the person of the king. The Pharisees are looking for signs of what is standing before them. They are asking the astronomer when the sun will rise while the sun is shining in their faces.

This verse deserves a note, because in its older wording it has probably been misquoted more than any other line in Luke. The King James renders it the kingdom of God is within you, and that sentence has been carried off to mean something Jesus never said — that the kingdom is an inner spiritual glow native to every human heart, that God's reign is simply the divinity we already carry, that religion is a journey inward and needs no king outside us at all. Tolstoy built a book on it; a great deal of gentle modern spirituality still runs on it.

The Greek word can indeed mean within, so the translation is not dishonest. What settles it is who Jesus is talking to. Look back at the first line: he is answering the Pharisees — the men who in a few chapters will hand him over to be killed. He is not telling them that the kingdom of God is glowing quietly inside their hearts. He is telling them it is standing in the room. In the midst of you is the reading the sentence demands, and it is a far sharper word than the one it is usually replaced with: the kingdom is not a feeling you locate by looking inward, it is a Person you have so far managed to look straight past.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to the disciples, 'The days are coming when you will desire to see one of the days of the Son of Man, and you will not see it. And they will say to you, "Look, there!" or "Look, here!" Do not go out or follow them. For as the lightning flashes and lights up the sky from one side to the other, so will the Son of Man be in his day.'
verseByVerse.commentary: Jesus now addresses the disciples about a different danger: in the days after his departure, when his presence is no longer physically visible, they will long for him and will be vulnerable to false claims about his return. Do not go out or follow them — the instruction against chasing signs is repeated emphatically. The actual coming of the Son of Man will not require announcement or tracking; it will be as unmistakable as lightning illuminating the entire sky. No one will need to be directed to it; everyone will see it simultaneously. The false prophets who say look here or look there are identifiable by the very fact that they need to point. The real event needs no pointer.

verseByVerse.quote: 'But first he must suffer many things and be rejected by this generation.'
verseByVerse.commentary: Before the glory of the Son of Man's coming, the cross. The must (dei) of divine necessity appears again. The disciples' longing for the day of the Son of Man must be held alongside the prior necessity of his suffering and rejection. The glory does not bypass the cross; it passes through it. Any vision of the second coming that skips past the first coming and its cost is a distorted vision. The disciples are being prepared to understand that the Son of Man who will come in lightning-flash glory is the same one who will be rejected and suffer at Jerusalem.

verseByVerse.quote: 'Just as it was in the days of Noah, so will it be in the days of the Son of Man. They were eating and drinking and marrying and being given in marriage, until the day when Noah entered the ark, and the flood came and destroyed them all. Likewise, just as it was in the days of Lot — they were eating and drinking, buying and selling, planting and building, but on the day when Lot went out from Sodom, fire and sulphur rained from heaven and destroyed them all...'
verseByVerse.commentary: The Noah and Lot examples share a common structure: ordinary life continues right up to the moment of judgment, with no warning that arrival is imminent. The people eating, drinking, marrying, buying, selling, planting, building are not engaged in exceptional wickedness — they are simply living as if judgment is not coming. The catastrophe overtakes normal life in mid-sentence. This is Jesus's warning about the character of the end: it will not be heralded by a general deterioration that gives everyone time to adjust. It will arrive while life is proceeding as usual.

verseByVerse.quote: 'So will it be on the day when the Son of Man is revealed. On that day, let the one who is on the housetop, with his goods in the house, not come down to take them away, and likewise let the one who is in the field not turn back. Remember Lot's wife. Whoever seeks to preserve his life will lose it, but whoever loses his life will keep it.'
verseByVerse.commentary: The urgency of the day of the Son of Man's revealing demands a response with no backward movement. Lot's wife looked back — not in disobedience exactly, but in attachment to what was being left behind — and was destroyed (Gen. 19:26). The attachment to possessions, home, and the life being left behind is the danger. The one who pauses to collect goods is the one who does not understand the magnitude of what is happening. The paradox of v. 33 — lose your life to keep it — is the same principle as 9:24 applied to the eschatological moment: the instinct of self-preservation, at the decisive moment, is the thing that destroys.

verseByVerse.quote: 'I tell you, in that night there will be two in one bed. One will be taken and the other left. There will be two women grinding together. One will be taken and the other left.' And they said to him, 'Where, Lord?' He said to them, 'Where the corpse is, there the vultures will gather.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The images of two in a bed, two grinding — side by side in identical circumstances — divided by the coming of the Son of Man. The identical outward circumstances conceal a difference that the day will reveal: one taken, one left. The disciples ask where. The proverbial answer about vultures and corpses is enigmatic but its direction is clear: the gathering happens where the event demands it. The disciples are asking the wrong question again — where, how, when — when the question that matters is whether they are among those who are ready when the moment arrives. Jesus has spent the whole discourse pointing away from speculation about signs and toward the readiness of the person asking.

A word on taken, because most readers arrive at this verse already certain which they would rather be. Popular retellings have fixed the picture: the taken are caught up to safety and the left are abandoned to disaster. That reading belongs to a particular scheme of the end times held sincerely by many Christians, and nothing here needs to be unkind about it. But notice what Jesus has just been talking about. Two paragraphs earlier the examples were Noah and Lot — and in both, it was the judgment that did the taking. The flood took them all away (Matt. 24:39); the fire fell on those who stayed in Sodom while Lot was left alive outside it. If the Lord's own illustrations set the sense of the word, then to be taken here is to be swept off, and to be left is to be spared.

Honest readers land on both sides of this, and the passage does not force the issue. What it does force is the thing the disciples immediately tried to avoid. They hear the saying and ask where? — a question about mechanics, exactly as we ask whether the taken go up or the left stay put. Jesus answers with a proverb that tells them nothing useful about geography, and the silence is the sermon. Two people in one bed; two women at one mill; the same house, the same work, the same day, and the difference between them invisible until the moment it is everything. That is the point being pressed, and it survives whichever way the word is finally construed. The question is not which group you would prefer. It is whether the day, arriving without warning in the middle of an ordinary night, would find you facing the right direction.

18.title: Prayer, Humility, Children, Wealth, and Sight
18.overview:
Luke 18 is constructed around a series of contrasts: persistent widow versus unjust judge; Pharisee versus tax collector; those who would keep children from Jesus versus Jesus who receives them; a rich young ruler who goes away sorrowful versus disciples who have left everything; blind Bartimaeus who cries out versus those who rebuke his cry. In each pair, the unexpected person receives what they need — and the principle is always the same: those who come to God with empty hands receive; those who come convinced they already have what is required leave empty.

Luke tells us explicitly why Jesus told the opening parables. The widow-and-judge parable is told to show that “they ought always to pray and not lose heart” (v. 1). The Pharisee-and-tax-collector parable addresses “those who trusted in themselves that they were righteous, and treated others with contempt” (v. 9). Together they define authentic prayer: persistent, humble, directed entirely toward a God who can do what we cannot.

The final section (vv. 31–43) contains the third passion prediction — which the disciples cannot understand — and closes with blind Bartimaeus, a man who cannot see physically but sees Jesus with perfect spiritual clarity: “Son of David, have mercy on me.”

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — The Persistent Widow and the Unjust Judge
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The parable works from the lesser to the greater. If even an unjust judge — explicitly described as one who neither feared God nor respected man — will eventually grant justice to a persistent widow simply to end her appeals, how much more will a just, loving, attentive God grant justice to his elect who cry to him day and night? The contrast is designed to overwhelm doubt: if the worst possible judge eventually gives justice, the best possible Judge certainly will.

The widow is a figure of absolute vulnerability in the ancient world. Without husband, father, or male relative, she had no social leverage, no economic resources, no advocate. Her only weapon was persistence — literally wearing out the judge (hypopiazē me, a word from boxing meaning to give someone a black eye or batter them relentlessly, v. 5). The judge does not become just; he simply becomes desperate to end the harassment.

The parable closes with an eschatological question: “When the Son of Man comes, will he find faith on earth?” (v. 8). Persistent prayer is placed in the context of the long wait for the final coming of the kingdom. Will disciples maintain their prayerful expectation — their posture of crying out to God — through the entire period of waiting? The parable is not about techniques for answered prayer but about the disposition of those who genuinely believe their Judge is just and their case is good.
verseByVerse.theology: Prayer is not a mechanism for overcoming divine reluctance. The unjust judge is the contrast, not the model — the point is a fortiori. The delay that the parable implicitly acknowledges (“crying to him day and night,” v. 7) is not God's reluctance but God's timing — the working out of his purposes in ways the widow cannot see from her vantage point. God knows what we need before we ask (Matt. 6:8); persistent prayer is not about informing God but about maintaining the posture of dependence and sustaining expectant faith across the long stretches when answers are not visible.
verseByVerse.examples: A church elder confesses that his prayer life has all but collapsed. He prays in a crisis, but sustained daily prayer feels pointless — God knows what he needs, so why ask repeatedly? This parable addresses him directly: the purpose of persistent prayer is not to overcome divine ignorance but to keep the heart oriented toward the right Source, and to sustain the posture of a person who genuinely believes help is coming from outside themselves.

verseByVerse.quote: And he told them a parable to the effect that they ought always to pray and not lose heart. He said, 'In a certain city there was a judge who neither feared God nor respected man. And there was a widow in that city who kept coming to him and saying, "Give me justice against my adversary." For a while he refused, but afterward he said to himself, "Though I neither fear God nor respect man, yet because this widow keeps bothering me, I will give her justice, so that she will not beat me down by her continual coming."'
verseByVerse.commentary: The parable follows immediately from the eschatological discourse: the disciples who are waiting for the coming of the Son of Man must wait in prayer, not in passive fatalism or active despair. The judge is defined by what he lacks — fear of God, respect for man — the two foundations of justice in the Old Testament. He is the worst possible judge. The widow is the most powerless person in first-century society. Yet she persists, and the very persistence that annoys the judge is what secures her justice. The word translated beat me down (hypōpiazō) was used for a boxer delivering a blow under the eye. Her relentless coming is wearing him out.

verseByVerse.quote: And the Lord said, 'Hear what the unrighteous judge says. And will not God give justice to his elect, who cry to him day and night? Will he delay long over them? I tell you, he will give justice to them speedily. Nevertheless, when the Son of Man comes, will he find faith on earth?'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The argument is from lesser to greater, reversed. If even an unjust, godless judge eventually gives justice because of persistence, how much more certainly will God — who is neither unjust nor indifferent — give justice to those who cry to him? The answer is given before the question is completed: I tell you, he will give justice to them speedily. The apparent delay is not reluctance; it is the appointed time working toward the appointed end. The closing question — will the Son of Man find faith on earth? — is the sting: the issue is not whether God will deliver, but whether his people will persist in prayer until he does. The parable was told to address the danger of losing heart. That danger is real.

Which brings us to the word that snags on real life. He will give justice to them speedily — and the person reading this has perhaps prayed for the same thing for eleven years. A marriage. A son who will not come home. A body that does not heal. Speedily? Luke tells us at the top of the chapter exactly who this parable is for: those in danger of losing heart. So it is worth being honest about what the promise does and does not say.

It does not promise a quick answer. It promises that when God moves he will not dawdle, and that the waiting is not indifference. The widow's problem was that her judge did not care; the parable exists to tell you that yours is not that judge. Your delay has a different cause from hers. Hers was neglect. Yours is timing — and the difference is everything, because a delay from a Father who has already given you his Son is not the silence of a man who cannot be bothered. Note also what the elect in the parable are actually crying for: justice, the setting right of all things, which arrives in full at the coming of the Son of Man mentioned in the very next line. Some prayers are answered in this life. Every prayer of God's people is answered at that day, and none of them a minute late.

And notice where Jesus leaves the question. He does not ask whether God will keep faith with us; that he settles flatly. He asks whether he will find faith in us — when the Son of Man comes, will he find faith on earth? The risk this parable is worried about is not an unanswering God. It is a widow who stops coming. If you are still praying after eleven years, that is not evidence that God has ignored you. It is the very thing he said he would be looking for.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–14 — The Pharisee and the Tax Collector
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Two men go up to the temple at the hour of prayer. The Pharisee prays pros heauton (v. 11) — a phrase meaning either “by himself” in isolation or, more pointedly, “to himself,” addressed not to God but to his own satisfaction. His prayer is formally addressed to God but its content is pure self-congratulation: he is not like other men — extortioners, unjust, adulterers — and specifically not like that tax collector. He fasts twice a week (beyond the single required fast of Yom Kippur) and tithes everything he receives. Everything he says is probably true; the problem is that it is entirely self-referential.

The tax collector stands far off (expressing unworthiness) and will not even lift his eyes to heaven — a gesture of shame in a culture where prayer was offered with eyes and hands raised. He beats his breast — a gesture of grief and contrition. And he prays a prayer of seven Greek words: ho theos, hilasthēti moi tō hamartōlō — God, be merciful to me, a sinner. Hilasthēti is the passive imperative of hilaskomai, the same root as hilastērion (propitiation/mercy seat) in Romans 3:25 and Hebrews 2:17. He is asking God to make propitiation — to cover his sin with atoning mercy. He is praying the theology of the mercy seat onto his own situation.

Jesus's verdict is the reversal that defines the entire chapter: this man, not that one, went home justified (dedikaiōmenos — declared righteous, passive voice, accomplished by Another). The Pharisee left exactly as he entered — self-satisfied. The tax collector left justified by God.
verseByVerse.theology:
The parable is a pre-Pauline statement of justification by faith alone. The tax collector contributes nothing to his justification except his need and his cry. He does not promise reformation, offer religious performance, or compare himself favourably to anyone. He offers only sin and appeal to divine mercy — and he goes home justified. This is the theological structure of the Reformation's sola fide: justification is God's declaration of righteousness received through faith, not earned through performance.

Hilasthēti is worth pausing on: it is not merely “be kind to me” or “overlook my sin.” It is a request for propitiation — for God to deal with sin through atoning mercy rather than through just punishment. The tax collector, consciously or not, is praying for the Cross.
verseByVerse.examples: A man in a small group shares prayer requests — always articulate, always theologically sophisticated, always focused on what he is doing for God and what God might do to support his plans. A woman in the group prays simply: “Lord, I don't know what to say. I'm a mess. Have mercy.” Observing the contrast, the group leader realises which prayer more closely resembles the tax collector's — and that authentic prayer is measured not by eloquence but by honesty about need.

verseByVerse.quote: He also told this parable to some who trusted in themselves that they were righteous, and treated others with contempt: 'Two men went up into the temple to pray, one a Pharisee and one a tax collector. The Pharisee, standing, prayed thus with himself: "God, I thank you that I am not like other men, extortioners, unjust, adulterers, or even like this tax collector. I fast twice a week; I give tithes of all that I get."'
verseByVerse.commentary: The target of the parable is identified before the story begins: those who trust in their own righteousness and despise others. The Pharisee's prayer begins correctly — thanksgiving to God — but immediately becomes a résumé of moral achievements and social comparisons. His gratitude is not for grace received but for virtue accumulated. The comparison with the tax collector beside him is the most revealing detail: he is aware of the tax collector, watches him, and his own sense of standing is partly defined by the contrast. His prayer is addressed to God but structured around himself. Luke notes: he prayed with himself — the phrase suggests the prayer went no further than his own ears.

verseByVerse.quote: 'But the tax collector, standing far off, would not even lift up his eyes to heaven, but beat his breast, saying, "God, be merciful to me, a sinner!" I tell you, this man went down to his house justified, rather than the other. For everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, but the one who humbles himself will be exalted.'
verseByVerse.commentary: The tax collector stands far off — at the edge of the court, at the outer limit of his own sense of entitlement to be there. He will not raise his eyes. He beats his breast — the gesture of grief and penitence. His prayer is seven words in the Greek: God, be propitiated toward me, the sinner. Not a sinner but the sinner — he is not making a general confession; he is naming himself specifically. The word for be merciful (hilaskomai) is the language of propitiation — the removal of God's righteous displeasure through an accepted sacrifice. He is not asking for sympathy; he is asking for atonement. And Jesus says he went home justified. The theological precision of the verdict is exact: this is the language of the law court — acquitted, declared righteous, the verdict in his favour.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Parents bring infants (ta brephē — a specific word for newborns and very young children, not older children) to Jesus so that he might touch them. The disciples rebuke them. Jesus calls the children to himself and says: “Let the children come to me, and do not hinder them, for to such belongs the kingdom of God.” The verb “hinder” (kōluein) is used elsewhere in Luke–Acts for preventing baptism (Acts 8:36; 10:47) — a connection early readers familiar with baptismal practice would have noted.

The theological statement has two layers: the kingdom belongs to such as these (infants are welcomed by the King); and whoever does not receive the kingdom like a child will not enter it. The child is not a moral model — children are not theologically innocent — but a model of receptivity. Children receive, accept, trust, and depend in ways that self-sufficient adults have often learned to suppress. The kingdom is received, not achieved; entered, not earned.
verseByVerse.theology: This passage has been central to the debate about infant baptism. The Reformed and Presbyterian tradition notes: (1) Jesus receives infants specifically into his presence and blesses them; (2) he says the kingdom belongs to them; (3) the disciples who sought to exclude them are explicitly rebuked. If infants can belong to the kingdom and receive blessing from its King, the parallel with covenant circumcision in the OT — the initiatory sign of belonging given to infant males — carries significant weight. This passage alone does not mandate infant baptism, but it contributes substantially to the covenantal case.
verseByVerse.examples: A family brings their newborn to be presented at church. The pastor wonders whether to spend time explaining the theological weight of what is happening. This passage gives content: this child is being presented to Jesus, exactly as the infants were brought in v. 15. Jesus's posture is not reluctance but welcome. Whatever else the service communicates, it communicates that Jesus receives them.

verseByVerse.quote: Now they were bringing even infants to him that he might touch them. And when the disciples saw it, they rebuked them. But Jesus called them to him, saying, 'Let the children come to me, and do not hinder them, for to such belongs the kingdom of God. Truly, I say to you, whoever does not receive the kingdom of God like a child shall not enter it.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The disciples' rebuke of those bringing infants reflects a reasonable assumption about the appropriate demands on Jesus's time: infants have nothing to offer and bring nothing to the encounter. They cannot ask a question, make a confession, or demonstrate faith. Jesus overrules the rebuke and uses the very helplessness of the children as the model of kingdom reception. To receive the kingdom like a child is to receive it as one who has nothing to contribute, no credentials to present, and no negotiating position. Children in the ancient world had no legal standing; they were entirely dependent. That dependence — not their innocence or simplicity — is what Jesus commends. The kingdom belongs to those who receive it as a pure gift from one who has all the power, to one who has none.

That is the passage's own point and it should not be crowded. But a Reformed reader will want the question asked, because this is one of the two texts most often brought to it: does let the children come to me support the baptism of infants? Honestly, it neither settles it nor is irrelevant to it. Those who baptise infants point out that Jesus takes up children who can offer nothing, declares the kingdom theirs, and blesses them — and that God has dealt with families as units since Abraham, putting the covenant sign on children long before they could profess anything (Gen. 17:7; cf. Acts 2:39, the promise is for you and for your children). Those who baptise only believers answer, fairly, that Jesus blesses these infants and does not baptise them, and that every baptism recorded in Acts follows a profession of faith.

The text will not carry the whole argument by itself, and Christians who love the same Lord have divided over it for centuries without either side being able to close the case from this verse alone. What the passage does say, and says with force, is the thing both sides should agree on: no one comes into this kingdom by contributing. If an infant can be blessed by Christ, then the door is not opened by understanding, or by maturity, or by anything a person brings — and every adult who enters comes in on precisely the same terms as the baby in his mother's arms.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
A ruler (archōn — a man of significant standing, possibly a synagogue official) kneels before Jesus and asks: “Good Teacher, what must I do to inherit eternal life?” Jesus first addresses the address: “Why do you call me good? No one is good except God alone.” This is not a denial of his deity but an invitation to think carefully about what the title implies: if Jesus is genuinely good in the absolute sense, the question of his identity is unavoidable.

The ruler claims to have kept all the commandments Jesus lists since his youth. Jesus looks at him and loves him — ēgapēsen auton (Mark 10:21; the affectionate regard is implicit in Luke) — and then gives him the one thing he lacks: sell everything, give to the poor, and come and follow. The man's face falls; he goes away sorrowful, for he is extremely wealthy. The disciples are stunned: “Then who can be saved?” Their surprise reveals that they shared the assumption Luke 16 has been combating — that wealth indicates divine favour, and therefore the wealthy would be first into the kingdom.

Jesus's response is both devastating and merciful: it is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle than for a rich person to enter the kingdom. And yet: what is impossible with man is possible with God. The disciples who have left everything are promised a hundredfold return — in this age, houses and family; in the age to come, eternal life. The passage does not close in despair; it closes in the promise that God can do what money cannot buy and human effort cannot achieve.
verseByVerse.theology:
Is Jesus prescribing poverty as a universal requirement? The Reformed tradition answers: no — the command was specific to this man, whose particular idol was wealth. The general principle (which does apply universally) is: whatever competes with full allegiance to Christ must be surrendered. For this man it was wealth; for another it might be reputation, family security, or professional ambition. The specificity is the point — Jesus reads this man's heart and addresses its particular attachment.

“What is impossible with man is possible with God” (v. 27) is the gospel in miniature. Salvation cannot be purchased, earned, or willed into existence. It is entirely God's act — which means it is available to the rich, the poor, the religious, and the scandalous, all on the same terms: divine grace received through faith.
verseByVerse.examples: A wealthy member of a congregation serves faithfully — on the board, in generous financial giving, in every visible way. But there is one area of his life he has never submitted to Christ's scrutiny: his business ethics. The rich young ruler was, by most measures, an exemplary man. The issue was not what he had done but what he would not surrender. The question Jesus poses to him is the same question the Spirit quietly poses to every disciple: is there a camel that will not fit through the needle?

verseByVerse.quote: And a ruler asked him, 'Good Teacher, what must I do to inherit eternal life?' And Jesus said to him, 'Why do you call me good? No one is good except God alone. You know the commandments: "Do not commit adultery, Do not murder, Do not steal, Do not bear false witness, Honour your father and mother."' And he said, 'All these I have kept from my youth.'
verseByVerse.commentary: The ruler is wealthy, religious, and sincere — Luke describes him as having kept the commandments from his youth, and there is no indication Jesus doubts him. The address — Good Teacher — prompts Jesus's question about goodness: not a denial of his own divinity but a probe of the ruler's categories. If he means good in the merely human sense, the title is inadequate; if he means it in the full sense, he is saying more than he realises. The ruler's claim to have kept the commandments is the claim of a man who has measured himself by what he can see and has not yet found his limit. The limit is about to be revealed.

verseByVerse.quote: When Jesus heard this, he said to him, 'One thing you still lack. Sell all that you have and distribute to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me.' But when he heard these things, he became very sad, for he was extremely rich.
verseByVerse.commentary: The one thing he lacks is the surrender of the one thing he has kept back. Jesus does not give this instruction to everyone he calls — he does not say it to Zacchaeus (19:1–10), for instance, who is also wealthy. He says it to this man because for this man, wealth is the functional lord of his life. The command to sell everything is not a universal law for disciples; it is a diagnostic instrument applied to the specific idol of a specific person. The ruler becomes very sad — the Greek suggests deep grief, not mere disappointment. He is genuinely torn. He wanted eternal life; he discovers it costs the very thing he cannot give up. His departure is one of the most tragic moments in the Gospels, and Luke records it without editorial comment.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus, seeing that he had become sad, said, 'How difficult it is for those who have wealth to enter the kingdom of God! For it is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle than for a rich person to enter the kingdom of God.' Those who heard it said, 'Then who can be saved?' But he said, 'What is impossible with man is possible with God.'
verseByVerse.commentary: The camel and the needle are not a metaphor that needs softening. Various attempts to explain the needle as a small gate in Jerusalem's wall, or the camel as a rope, all miss the point: Jesus intends the absurdity. A camel through a needle's eye is impossible. Wealth does not make salvation impossible in the sense that it disqualifies; it makes the surrender that salvation requires uniquely difficult, because wealth is the most effective substitute for dependence on God that the world offers. The disciples' question — who then can be saved? — is the right question, and Jesus's answer is the gospel in miniature: what is impossible with man — the self-sufficient, self-securing person — is possible with God. Salvation is God's work, not humanity's achievement.

verseByVerse.quote: And Peter said, 'See, we have left our homes and followed you.' And he said to them, 'Truly, I say to you, there is no one who has left house or wife or brothers or parents or children, for the sake of the kingdom of God, who will not receive many times more in this time, and in the age to come eternal life.'
verseByVerse.commentary: Peter's observation is not boasting; it is a question about whether the cost has been worth it. Jesus affirms that it has — and with interest. What is surrendered for the kingdom is returned multiplied, in this life and the next. This does not mean hardship is absent — the life of following Jesus has included and will include much loss. But the losses are absorbed into a larger economy in which nothing surrendered for the kingdom is ultimately lost. The community of disciples becomes the new family (8:21); the eternal life at the end is not a compensation for loss but the destination to which the whole journey was always moving.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 31–43 — Third Passion Prediction and Blind Bartimaeus
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Jesus takes the Twelve aside and delivers his third and most detailed passion prediction (vv. 31–33): everything written about the Son of Man by the prophets will be accomplished — he will be delivered to the Gentiles, mocked, shamefully treated, spat upon, flogged, and killed; on the third day he will rise. Luke adds a striking note: the disciples understood none of these things. The word was hidden from them; they did not grasp what was said. This is not a condemnation but an explanation: the full meaning of these words would only become clear retrospectively, in the light of resurrection (24:45–46).

The chapter closes with the healing of a blind man near Jericho (named Bartimaeus in Mark 10:46, unnamed in Luke). As Jesus approaches, the man hears the crowd, learns that Jesus of Nazareth is passing by, and immediately cries out: “Jesus, Son of David, have mercy on me!” Those in front rebuke him. He cries out all the more. Jesus stops, calls him, asks what he wants — “Lord, let me recover my sight” — and heals him with a word: “Recover your sight; your faith has saved you.” The man follows Jesus, glorifying God; all the people give praise.

The juxtaposition is deliberate and devastating: the disciples, who have eyes, cannot see what Jesus has just told them. The blind man, with no eyes, sees Jesus with perfect clarity — as Son of David, as Lord, as the one whose mercy is his only hope. The chapter ends exactly where it should: a man receiving sight and following Jesus, and a crowd glorifying God.
verseByVerse.theology:
The third passion prediction is the most explicit of the three (9:22; 9:44; 18:31–33) and the only one that explicitly grounds the events in prophetic Scripture: “everything written about the Son of Man by the prophets will be accomplished.” The suffering of the Messiah is not an accident but the fulfilment of a divine script written long before Calvary. This is a foundational claim for biblical theology: the OT does not merely foreshadow the cross; it writes it in advance under divine inspiration. The verb telesthēsetai (will be accomplished/completed) shares a root with tetelestai in John 19:30 — “It is finished.” The cross is the completion of what was written.

Bartimaeus's title “Son of David” is messianic — the Jewish expectation of a Davidic king who would restore Israel. By crying this out against the crowd's opposition, he makes a public messianic confession. Jesus receives it and heals. The entry into Jerusalem in chapter 19 is set against exactly this backdrop.
verseByVerse.examples: A natural question for anyone working through Luke: should he preach the passion prediction as a separate unit or in conjunction with Bartimaeus? The juxtaposition is the point — the disciples see and do not understand; the blind man does not see and understands perfectly. Any congregation contains both: those who have heard the gospel many times and still find it somehow vague, and those who hear it once and cry out with Bartimaeus's directness: “Lord, let me recover my sight.” Both need to hear what the other hears.

verseByVerse.quote: And taking the twelve, he said to them, 'See, we are going up to Jerusalem, and everything that is written about the Son of Man by the prophets will be accomplished. For he will be delivered over to the Gentiles and will be mocked and shamefully treated and spit upon. And after flogging him, they will kill him, and on the third day he will rise.' But they understood none of these things. This saying was hidden from them, and they did not grasp what was said.
verseByVerse.commentary: The third and most detailed passion prediction is given as they approach Jerusalem. The specificity increases: delivered to Gentiles, mocked, shamefully treated, spat upon, flogged, killed, raised on the third day. The whole sequence is drawn from the prophets — Isaiah's Suffering Servant, the Psalms of lament — and Jesus identifies himself as the one in whom all of it will be fulfilled. The disciples' complete failure to grasp any of it is stated three times in a single verse: they understood none of these things, this saying was hidden from them, they did not grasp what was said. Luke does not want the reader to miss how total the incomprehension was. The cross will not be recognised when it comes; it can only be understood after the resurrection illuminates what it meant.

verseByVerse.quote: As he drew near to Jericho, a blind man was sitting by the roadside begging. And hearing a crowd going by, he asked what this was happening. They told him, 'Jesus of Nazareth is passing by.' And he cried out, 'Jesus, Son of David, have mercy on me!' And those who were in front rebuked him, telling him to be silent. But he cried out all the more, 'Son of David, have mercy on me!'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The contrast with the blind disciples of vv. 31–34 is pointed: those who can see cannot understand the passion prediction; the man who cannot see recognises who Jesus is. Son of David — a Messianic title, not used of Jesus anywhere else in Luke's Gospel. The blind man, who has heard about Jesus (the reports of ch. 7 have spread), calls him by the title that identifies him as the fulfilment of God's covenant with David. The crowd tries to silence him; he cries out more. His persistence echoes the widow of 18:1–8: those who are most in need are most relentless in their appeal. He will not be quiet. The need is too great for social embarrassment to override.

A reader with the three Gospels open will stop at the first line of this paragraph, and the difficulty is worth facing squarely because sceptics have made a good deal of it. Luke says the healing happened as he drew near to Jericho, and then opens the next chapter with Jesus entering the town (19:1) — so on Luke's account the man was healed before Jesus ever got there. Matthew and Mark both say it happened as he was going out of Jericho (Matt. 20:29; Mark 10:46). On top of that, Matthew reports two blind men where Mark and Luke report one, and only Mark supplies a name — Bartimaeus.

The number and the name are the easy half. None of the three writers says only one, and one never denies two. Mark gives us not just a name but a father's name, Bartimaeus, son of Timaeus — which is how you identify a man his readers could go and ask; he had evidently become known in the church, and both he and Luke fix on the man who mattered to the tradition, while Matthew, careful of the whole scene, notes that there were in fact two.

The harder half is settled by the ground itself. There were two Jerichos in the first century, roughly a mile apart. The ancient city — Joshua's Jericho — stood as a ruin on its old mound; Herod the Great had built a splendid new town to the south, with his winter palace, and the road ran between them. A traveller on that stretch of road was leaving one Jericho and approaching the other in the same few minutes. Matthew and Mark date the event by the town at his back; Luke dates it by the town ahead. Both statements are exactly true of one man on one road on one afternoon. (Some have suggested instead that the man called out as Jesus went in and was healed as he came out; possible, but the geography makes it unnecessary.)

What looks at first like three writers contradicting each other turns out to be the ordinary signature of independent witnesses standing in different places and reporting the same event honestly. Three men copying one document do not produce discrepancies of this kind; three men who were there, or who talked to people who were, produce exactly these. And none of it touches the thing Luke is actually pressing: a man who could not see, sitting in the dust outside a town, who understood who was passing better than the twelve who had just been told plainly and grasped nothing.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus stopped and commanded him to be brought to him. And when he came near, he asked him, 'What do you want me to do for you?' He said, 'Lord, let me recover my sight.' And Jesus said to him, 'Recover your sight; your faith has made you well.' And immediately he recovered his sight and followed him, glorifying God. And all the people, when they saw it, gave praise to God.
verseByVerse.commentary: Jesus stops the entire procession to Jerusalem for one blind beggar. What do you want me to do for you? — the same question he will ask James and John in Mark's parallel account (Mark 10:36), where the answer reveals the disciples' self-seeking. Here the answer reveals simple, clear need: Lord, let me recover my sight. The healing is immediate; the commendation follows: your faith has made you well. He followed him — at once, the same immediacy as the first disciples — glorifying God. The whole crowd joins the praise. The journey to Jerusalem, heavy with the passion prediction of vv. 31–34, ends with a burst of sight and praise. What the disciples could not see, the formerly blind man now follows with open eyes.

19.title: Zacchaeus, the Minas, and the Triumphal Entry
19.overview:
Luke 19 is a chapter of arrivals. Jesus arrives at Jericho and finds Zacchaeus — a chief tax collector who has climbed a tree to see him and who will descend, transformed, to receive salvation in his house. Then Jesus tells the Parable of the Ten Minas — a kingdom parable about accountability and fruitfulness during the time of the absent king. Then Jesus arrives at Jerusalem itself, riding on a colt, welcomed by his disciples with Hosannas, weeping over the city as he approaches it, and then cleansing the temple. The chapter is a compressed journey from private transformation (Zacchaeus) to public confrontation (the temple), with the parable providing the theological framework for understanding the entire sequence.

Zacchaeus is one of Luke's most vivid portraits of salvation. He is a chief tax collector (architelōnēs — a word found nowhere else in Greek literature), wealthy, despised, short of stature, and apparently desperate to see Jesus. He runs ahead and climbs a tree — an undignified act for a man of his status. Jesus's response is overwhelming: “Zacchaeus, hurry and come down, for I must stay at your house today.” The word dei (must) is a divine necessity — the same word used for the Son of Man's suffering. Salvation has come to this house; the Son of Man has come to seek and to save the lost.

The Triumphal Entry (vv. 28–44) contains one of the most emotionally powerful moments in all of Luke: Jesus weeping over Jerusalem. The parade of praise, the disciples crying out about the king who comes in the name of the Lord — and then Jesus stopping on the descent and weeping, because she did not know “the things that make for peace.” This is not despair; it is the grief of the shepherd for the sheep who will not come.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Zacchaeus is described with three details that should make him unsympathetic: he is a chief tax collector, he is rich, and he is too short to see over the crowd. Tax collectors were despised as collaborators with Rome and as men who enriched themselves on the margin between what Rome required and what they actually collected. A chief tax collector (architelōnēs) was the district supervisor — the one who made the most from the system and who was therefore the most despised. Jericho was a major customs point on the road from Peraea; Zacchaeus would have been wealthy and hated.

Yet he wants to see who Jesus is — not merely to observe a curiosity but with a seeking quality that Luke presents as genuine. He runs ahead (running was undignified for a man of status in the ancient world) and climbs a sycamore tree. Jesus stops, looks up, calls him by name, and announces that he must stay at his house that day. The crowd mutters: he has gone to be the guest of a sinner.

Zacchaeus's response is extraordinary: standing before Jesus, he says he will give half his goods to the poor, and if he has defrauded anyone, he will restore it fourfold. The fourfold restitution goes beyond the Mosaic requirement (Ex. 22:1 required fourfold for a stolen ox; Lev. 6:5 required repayment plus 20%). Jesus's declaration is immediate: “Today salvation has come to this house.” And the theological climax: “For the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost.” This is the programmatic statement that summarises not just this episode but Luke's entire Gospel.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Zacchaeus episode is a case study in sovereign grace. Jesus does not wait for Zacchaeus to demonstrate worthiness; he announces the visit before any repentance has occurred. The repentance and restitution follow the encounter — they are the fruit of salvation received, not the ground of it. This is the exact pattern of Luke 15: the shepherd finds the lost sheep; the sheep does not find its way home. Zacchaeus did not earn a visit from Jesus by climbing the tree; he was found by the one who came to seek the lost.

The crowd's murmuring (“he has gone to be the guest of a sinner”) recapitulates the Pharisaic complaint of chapter 15. Jesus's response to both is the same: this is precisely what he came to do. The lost sheep, the lost coin, the lost son, and now Zacchaeus — each is a variation on the same theme: the seeking, finding, rejoicing God.
verseByVerse.examples: A man in a congregation has a reputation. Everyone knows what he was before he became a Christian — the financial impropriety, the broken relationships, the trail of damage. He is welcomed into membership but watched carefully; there is a persistent sense that his inclusion is provisional. The Zacchaeus story is addressed to the crowd as much as to Zacchaeus: those who murmur at Jesus's table fellowship with notorious sinners share the Pharisees' theology. Jesus does not share it.

verseByVerse.quote: He entered Jericho and was passing through. And behold, there was a man named Zacchaeus. He was a chief tax collector and was rich. And he was seeking to see who Jesus was, but on account of the crowd he could not, because he was small in stature. So he ran on ahead and climbed up into a sycamore tree to see him, for he was about to pass that way.
verseByVerse.commentary: Zacchaeus is a chief tax collector — not merely a collector but one who supervised other collectors, which means he extracted a percentage from each of his subordinates' takings in addition to his own. He is wealthy at others' expense. He is also seeking to see Jesus — not to make a confession or seek forgiveness, simply to see who this person is. The crowd blocks him; he is short. His solution is undignified for a man of his wealth and social position: he runs ahead and climbs a tree. Dignity and position have been quietly abandoned in the urgency of seeing Jesus. Something is already moving in him before Jesus has said a word.

verseByVerse.quote: And when Jesus came to the place, he looked up and said to him, 'Zacchaeus, hurry and come down, for I must stay at your house today.' So he hurried and came down and received him joyfully.
verseByVerse.commentary: Jesus stops beneath the tree, looks up, calls Zacchaeus by name — which implies prior knowledge — and announces that he must stay at his house. Must (dei) — divine necessity again. This is not an impromptu invitation; it is the arrival of the appointed moment in Zacchaeus's life. Jesus does not wait for Zacchaeus to come down and ask; he invites himself in. The initiative is entirely his. Zacchaeus comes down hurrying and receives him joyfully — not cautiously, not with the calculated reserve of a man deciding whether to let a controversial figure into his home, but with joy. Something has been released in him by the simple fact of being called by name by this man.

verseByVerse.quote: And when they saw it, they all grumbled, 'He has gone in to be the guest of a man who is a sinner.' And Zacchaeus stood and said to the Lord, 'Behold, Lord, half of my goods I give to the poor. And if I have defrauded anyone of anything, I restore it fourfold.'
verseByVerse.commentary: The crowd's grumble — he has gone in to be the guest of a man who is a sinner — echoes the Pharisees in 15:2. The gospel produces this reaction reliably. Zacchaeus's response is the evidence of the transformation that Jesus's presence has already produced. He does not wait to be commanded; he volunteers. Half of his goods to the poor — a level of generosity that exceeds the Mosaic requirement. Fourfold restoration for anything defrauded — the penalty prescribed for the most serious theft (Exod. 22:1). He is not earning his way back; he is demonstrating that the kingdom has already arrived in him. The fruit is the evidence of the root.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus said to him, 'Today salvation has come to this house, since he also is a son of Abraham. For the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost.'
verseByVerse.commentary: Today salvation has come to this house — the characteristic Lucan word (sēmeron) marking the realised presence of the kingdom (cf. 2:11; 4:21; 13:32; 23:43). The salvation is not Zacchaeus's generosity; the generosity is the evidence of the salvation. He also is a son of Abraham — the tax collector who was dismissed from the covenant community by his occupation is declared by Jesus to belong fully to the people of God. Not because he has now earned it, but because the Son of Man has found him. The mission statement of v. 10 — the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost — is the summary of Luke 15 applied to a single person. Zacchaeus was lost; he has been found; salvation has come to his house.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–27 — The Parable of the Ten Minas
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Jesus tells this parable because the disciples think the kingdom of God is about to appear immediately (v. 11) — they expect a triumphal political establishment in Jerusalem. The parable is designed to correct this: the king will go away, a long time will pass, servants will be entrusted with resources, and the king will return to hold an accounting. The primary message is not about compound interest but about faithfulness in the absence of the king.

A mina was approximately three months' wages — not an enormous sum, but significant. Ten servants each receive one. At the king's return, three are examined. The first has multiplied his mina tenfold and receives authority over ten cities; the second fivefold and receives five cities. The third has hidden his mina in a cloth, returning it untouched — explaining that he was afraid of the master, who takes what he did not deposit and reaps what he did not sow. The master rebukes him sharply: even banking the mina for interest would have been better than nothing. His mina is given to the one who has ten.

The subplot about citizens who hated the king and sent a delegation to prevent his coronation (vv. 14, 27) is often noted as a historical echo of the actual political situation: Herod Archelaus traveled to Rome in 4 BC to secure his kingship, and a Jewish delegation of 50 followed to oppose it (Josephus, Ant. 17.11.1). Luke's readers would have caught the allusion. The enemies of the king who refused his rule are brought before him and executed — a grim note about the judgment awaiting those who reject Jesus as king.
verseByVerse.theology:
The parable teaches two related truths. First, the kingdom has a “not yet” dimension: the king goes away and returns; faithful servants must live faithfully in the in-between time. Second, stewardship in the in-between is not optional maintenance — it requires active, risk-taking investment of what has been given. The servant who thought the safest response was preservation rather than growth was wrong: the king expected multiplication. This has direct application to the entrusted gospel, gifts, and opportunities of every disciple.

The saying “to everyone who has, more will be given” (v. 26) is not a celebration of the rich getting richer; it is a statement about the compounding nature of faithful stewardship. Those who use what they have been given grow in capacity; those who preserve without using discover that even what they have diminishes.
verseByVerse.examples: A congregation receives a significant bequest and immediately debates whether to save it, spend it on building maintenance, or invest it in mission. The parable does not prescribe the specific answer but it firmly excludes one option: burying it in a cloth and returning it untouched, on the grounds that it is safer to hold than to risk. The king expects investment, multiplication, and return. The question is not “how do we keep this safe?” but “how do we multiply this for the kingdom?”

verseByVerse.quote: As they heard these things, he proceeded to tell a parable, because he was near to Jerusalem, and because they supposed that the kingdom of God was to appear immediately. He said therefore, 'A nobleman went into a far country to receive for himself a kingdom and then return. Calling ten of his servants, he gave them ten minas, and said to them, "Engage in business until I come."'
verseByVerse.commentary: The parable is given because the crowd expects an immediate Messianic triumph in Jerusalem. Luke specifies the reason for the parable: they supposed the kingdom would appear immediately. Jesus corrects the misunderstanding by describing a period of absence and an accounting at the master's return. The nobleman goes to a far country — the kingdom will not arrive by immediate conquest. The servants are given minas (each worth about three months' wages) and told to do business until he returns. The task during the absence is not passive waiting but active engagement with what has been entrusted.

verseByVerse.quote: 'But his citizens hated him and sent a delegation after him, saying, "We do not want this man to reign over us." When he returned, having received the kingdom, he ordered these servants to whom he had given the money to be called to him, that he might know what they had gained by doing business.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The citizens' rejection of the nobleman — we do not want this man to reign over us — is the voice of Jerusalem in the parable, the people who will cry crucify him within days. The nobleman returns anyway, with his kingdom, and calls for the accounting. The master's return is the certain end point that gives the servants' interim activity its urgency. Everything done during the absence will be assessed at the return. The parable is not primarily about financial management; it is about the accountability of the disciple community during the period between the ascension and the return of the Son of Man.

The detail about the citizens is not invented for the story, and Jesus's hearers would have known it instantly. In 4 BC, on the death of Herod the Great, his son Archelaus travelled to Rome to have his kingship confirmed by Caesar — and a delegation of fifty Jews followed him there to argue that he should not be given it (Josephus, Antiquities 17.11.1). They failed. He came back with power, and he dealt with those who had opposed him. Jesus is telling this parable on the road up to Jerusalem, within living memory of the event, in a country that had watched it happen. A nobleman goes to a far country to receive a kingdom; his own citizens send word after him that they will not have this man reign over them. Everyone listening knew the story he was borrowing.

Which sharpens what he is doing with it. He is walking toward the city that is about to say exactly that about him — we will not have this man to reign over us — and he says it out loud, in a shape they cannot miss, days before they prove it true.

verseByVerse.quote: 'The first came before him, saying, "Lord, your mina has made ten minas more." And he said to him, "Well done, good servant! Because you have been faithful in a very little, you shall have authority over ten cities." And the second came, saying, "Lord, your mina has made five minas." And he said to him, "And you are to be over five cities."'
verseByVerse.commentary: The first servant has multiplied tenfold; the second fivefold. Both receive the master's approval, though the rewards are proportionate rather than identical. Because you have been faithful in a very little, you shall have authority over ten cities — the principle of 16:10 applied eschatologically. The mina entrusted is very little in comparison to what faithful stewardship of it produces. Faithfulness with small things is the qualification for larger responsibilities in the kingdom. The servants who traded were not merely following orders; they were demonstrating the character that makes them suitable for the greater responsibility to come.
